signals.title: Apply `SORT + LIMIT` before `ARRAY JOIN`
signals.text: ## Use case ```sql SELECT payload FROM t ARRAY JOIN arr ORDER BY ts LIMIT 10; ``` With an average array size `k`, the `ORDER BY` currently sorts `rows(t) * k` rows, although the sort key does not depend on the array at all. The same holds for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`: the truncation happens above the expansion, so the expansion is performed for rows that are immediately discarded. The plan is: ``` Limit(10) Sorting(ts, limit=10) Expression ArrayJoin(arr) ReadFromMergeTree ``` The `ARRAY JOIN` is already *below* the sort, so the fix is a reorder, not a push-down of a new step. Note that this is not about avoiding column replication — that is largely solved already. `enable_lazy_columns_replication` defaults to `true` (`src/Core/Settings.cpp:6641`), the joined element column *is* the array's nested column (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:280`, `getDataPtr`), all other columns are only index-wrapped (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:288-292`), and `transformColumnsWithSharedIndex` (`ColumnReplicated.cpp:784`) transforms the shared index once per block. What remains is that the sort itself processes `k` times more rows than it has to. ## Why the reorder is sound `ArrayJoinResultIterator::next` walks input rows in order and takes elements from the nested column in order. So every input row expands into a **contiguous run** of output rows, and the runs preserve input order. Therefore, if every input row produces at least one output row, the first `n` output rows come from the first `k <= n` input rows, and a plain row-count limit of `n` may be evaluated below the `ARRAY JOIN`. The only counterexample is an input row that produces zero output rows: an empty array under an inner `ARRAY JOIN`. `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` is immune, because `emptyArrayToSingle` in the iterator constructor already guarantees at least one element. This means **no weighted limit is needed for correctness** — an emptiness guard is enough. The same reasoning is already written down for the `arrayJoin`-in-expression form in `liftUpFunctions.cpp:96-103`, where the reorder is currently refused only when a `LIMIT` is present. ## Proposed implementation ### 1. Emptiness guard below an inner `ArrayJoinStep` Insert `Filter(length(c) > 0)`. This removes exactly the rows the `ARRAY JOIN` removes itself, so it is a valid rewrite on its own, independent of any limit — a small first commit with a trivial correctness argument. - `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` — no guard needed. - inner, aligned — `length(c1) > 0` for any one joined column; `hasEqualOffsets` (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:277`) enforces equal sizes anyway. - inner, unaligned — `greatest(length(c1), ..., length(cn)) > 0`, because `arrayResize` pads every array to the maximum size. - `Map` columns — `length(m)` is defined and is the right function here. - Constant arrays — the guard const-folds away. - Several chained `ARRAY JOIN`s — one guard per step (the multiplicities multiply). - Use `length(arr) > 0`, not `arr.size0 > 0`: `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` is a query-tree pass and cannot rewrite a filter created by the plan optimizer. The subcolumn form is only needed by the follow-up issue below. ### 2. Teach `ArrayJoinStep` that it preserves order `getTraits` sets `preserves_sorting = false` (`ArrayJoinStep.cpp:26`), so `applyOrder` drops all sortedness across the step. Contiguous runs mean order *is* preserved for every sort prefix that does not touch the joined columns, so the flat bool should become a prefix rule in `applyOrder.cpp`: keep the prefix up to the first joined column. Trap: a joined column keeps its **name** across the step — `ArrayJoinAction::prepare` replaces the column in place and only the type changes. So the rule must exclude joined columns by name; checking that a sort key is present in the input header is not sufficient. `buildSortingDAG` already performs exactly this removal (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:313-318`). ### 3. Move `Sorting` below `ArrayJoin` Swap the two steps and keep `limit = n` unchanged. This is the change that matters: an `n * k`-row top-N becomes an `n`-row top-N. - Precondition: no sort key is a joined column (by name, see above), and all sort keys are present in the step's input header. - First version: `SortingStep::Type::Full`, `!hasPartitions()`, no `limit_by` hint. - Only cross the `ArrayJoinStep` itself and `ExpressionStep`s that preserve order and cardinality (no `arrayJoin` inside). A `FilterStep` between the sort and the `ARRAY JOIN` blocks the move, since the guard cannot account for it. - Pass ordering: `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` normally lifts the intervening `Expression` above the sort first, so run after it and match a direct child. ### 4. Move `Limit` below `ArrayJoin` `ArrayJoinStep` fails the `preserves_number_of_rows` check in `tryPushDownLimit` (`limitPushDown.cpp:136`), so the case without `ORDER BY` needs an explicit branch that inserts the guard and swaps the steps. Expected payoff on its own is modest — roughly one block of expansion, because `LimitTransform` already finishes the pipeline and `ArrayJoinResultIterator` is `max_block_size`-windowed (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:222-233`). Its real value is that it makes the follow-up issue (deferring the array read) possible. There is no offset work to do: `LimitStep::getLimitForSorting` already returns `limit + offset` (`LimitStep.h:29`), and the planner sets `partial_sorting_limit = limit_length + limit_offset` (`Planner.cpp:525`). ### 5. Optional follow-up: exact weighted limit Instead of the guard, the sort could keep rows until the prefix sum of `length(arr)` reaches `n`, which prunes harder (`n / avg_size` rows instead of `n`) and needs no filter. The cost is that `limit` is a scalar threaded through `PartialSortingTransform` (the `limit - 1`-th row threshold, `PartialSortingTransform.cpp:152-160`), `MergeSorter`, the remerge heuristic `limit * 2 < sum_rows_in_blocks` (`MergeSortingTransform.cpp:210-214`), `MergedData`, and `TopKThresholdTracker`. This is a sharpening, not a prerequisite; it should be driven by performance tests. ## Read-in-order interaction `buildSortingDAG` zeroes the limit when it sees a `FilterStep` (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:297-298`), so the guard blocks the read-in-order limit hint. This is not a regression: the hint is *already* zero for inner `ARRAY JOIN` (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:309-310`), and `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` keeps it because it needs no guard. Recovering it for the inner case is what the weighted limit above would buy. `optimizePrimaryKeyConditionAndLimit` walks through `FilterStep`, so that path is unaffected. ## Scope limits This issue covers only the `ARRAY JOIN` clause form, that is, a real `ArrayJoinStep`. The `arrayJoin` function form lives inside `ActionsDAG` and is invisible to plan passes; extracting it into an `ArrayJoinStep` is tracked separately and would unblock roughly twenty `hasArrayJoin` bail-outs at once. ## Test plan - Correctness matrix: inner / `LEFT`, aligned / unaligned, several joined arrays, `Map`, empty arrays, all arrays empty, `Nullable`, constant arrays, `LIMIT` with `OFFSET`, `LIMIT WITH TIES` (must be refused), `LIMIT BY` between the steps, `ORDER BY` mentioning a joined column (must be refused), chained `ARRAY JOIN`s. - `EXPLAIN` plan shape tests, plus plan-serialization tests for the new step shape. - Check that `rows_before_limit_at_least` and `exact_rows_before_limit` are unchanged. - `tests/performance/` case with a large average array size and a small `LIMIT`. - Each stage behind its own setting, default off, flipped in a later commit.

signals.title: Expression in SELECT evaluated on rows filtered out by WHERE when JOIN runtime filter fuses with Prewhere Actions (regression 26.1 → 26.2)
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong Since 26.2, a SELECT expression that is only valid for rows matching a WHERE predicate can throw because the SELECT expression and its WHERE guard are fused into sibling nodes in a single Prewhere Actions step. The SELECT expression is evaluated on rows that the WHERE clause should have already eliminated. This is a regression introduced by #95838, which postpones PREWHERE optimization until after JOIN runtime filter construction, causing the runtime filter, WHERE predicates, and SELECT expressions to all be folded into the same ActionsDAG step. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Reproducer: https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/bfadcea1-3c93-4960-9d16-71db35056613 ``` CREATE TABLE t (a UInt8, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'x'); SELECT toUInt64(s) AS k FROM t INNER JOIN (SELECT toUInt64(1) AS wh) AS r2 ON toUInt64(s) = r2.wh WHERE a = 1 AND s LIKE '1%'; ``` Does not reproduce on 26.1. Reproducer on 26.2 can be mitigated by disabling the optimization: `SETTINGS enable_join_runtime_filters = 0` ### Expected behavior Queries should always follow the "filter before project" concept in the SQL standard ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Received exception from server (version 26.2.1): Code: 6. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:9000. DB::Exception: Cannot parse string 'x' as UInt64: syntax error at begin of string. Note: there are toUInt64OrZero and toUInt64OrNull functions, which returns zero/NULL instead of throwing exception: while executing 'FUNCTION toUInt64(s : 0) -> toUInt64(__table1.s) UInt64 : 4': While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CANNOT_PARSE_TEXT) (query: SELECT toUInt64(s) AS k FROM t INNER JOIN (SELECT toUInt64(1) AS wh) AS r2 ON toUInt64(s) = r2.wh WHERE a = 1 AND s LIKE '1%';) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/95838 ### Additional context #95838 (26.2) postponed PREWHERE optimisation to run after JOIN runtime filter construction so that runtime filters can also be pushed to PREWHERE. The side effect is that the runtime filter, the WHERE conditions, and the SELECT expressions are fused into a single Actions step as siblings at the table scan level: ``` FUNCTION like(s, '1%') -- WHERE guard FUNCTION toUInt64(s) -- SELECT expression — should only run on rows surviving the guard ``` Because they are siblings, toUInt64(s) runs on every row before the LIKE filter eliminates them.

signals.title: mergeTreeIndex table function ignores the source table's row policy
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **A user restricted by a SELECT row policy can read the primary-key (and minmax-index) column values of the rows the policy hides, by calling `mergeTreeIndex(db, table)` instead of selecting from the table.** - **Root cause:** [`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp:413`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp#L413) - the access check is grant-only; there is no row-policy lookup for `source_table->getStorageID()` before the primary-key values are exposed. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `StorageMergeTreeIndex::readImpl` ([`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp:413`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp#L413)) checks only `AccessType::SELECT` on the source table and then streams primary-key granule values straight out of the parts. It never calls `Context::getRowPolicyFilter`, unlike its two siblings: `StorageMergeTreeTextIndex::readImpl` ([`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp:446`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp#L446)) and, as of this PR, `StorageFromMergeTreeProjection::read` ([`src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp:51`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp#L51)). **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp:413`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp#L413) — readImpl: grant-only access check, no row-policy lookup before streaming primary-key values - [`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp:446`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp#L446) — sibling that DOES enforce the row policy - the shape the fix should follow - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp:51`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp#L51) — the sibling this PR fixes **Impact:** Row-policy bypass. Any user holding plain SELECT on a table (the normal case for a row-policy-restricted user) can enumerate primary-key column values for every row, including rows the policy hides. With `index_granularity = 1` every row's key is exposed; at the default granularity every 8192nd row's key is. `with_minmax = true` additionally exposes per-part min/max of the key columns across hidden rows. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `9c7ecedbfc68c`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test: a row policy on the source table must not be bypassed by the mergeTreeIndex table function. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_mt_index_rp; DROP ROW POLICY IF EXISTS rp_mt_index ON t_mt_index_rp; CREATE TABLE t_mt_index_rp (id UInt64, department String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (department, id) SETTINGS index_granularity = 1; INSERT INTO t_mt_index_rp VALUES (1, 'engineering'), (2, 'finance'), (3, 'engineering'), (4, 'hr'); CREATE ROW POLICY rp_mt_index ON t_mt_index_rp FOR SELECT USING department = 'engineering' TO ALL; SELECT '-- base table honours the policy'; SELECT id, department FROM t_mt_index_rp ORDER BY id; SELECT '-- mergeTreeIndex must not expose primary key values of policy-hidden rows'; SELECT DISTINCT department FROM mergeTreeIndex(currentDatabase(), 't_mt_index_rp') ORDER BY department; -- { serverError ACCESS_DENIED } DROP ROW POLICY rp_mt_index ON t_mt_index_rp; DROP TABLE t_mt_index_rp; ``` ### Expected behavior ``` -- base table honours the policy 1 engineering 3 engineering -- mergeTreeIndex must not expose primary key values of policy-hidden rows ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` -- base table honours the policy 1 engineering 3 engineering -- mergeTreeIndex must not expose primary key values of policy-hidden rows engineering finance hr ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Mirror `StorageMergeTreeTextIndex::readImpl`: in `StorageMergeTreeIndex::readImpl`, after the `checkAccess`, fetch `context->getRowPolicyFilter(source_storage_id.getDatabaseName(), source_storage_id.getTableName(), RowPolicyFilterType::SELECT_FILTER)` and throw `ACCESS_DENIED` when it is set and not always-true (the index dump is per-granule, so the policy cannot be applied per row). </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `mergeTreeAnalyzeIndexes` and `mergeTreeCodecBlockCounts` were audited and expose no column values (part names, granule ranges, byte/codec counts only), so they are out of scope - but the granule ranges they report do reveal row counts of a policy-restricted table. Found during automated review of [PR #112329](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112329). Severity P1 · Finding `h_pr112329_001` </details> cc @yariks5s @KochetovNicolai (from #112329) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115304 - Backported to: `26.7.6.5`, `26.6.4.10` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: `timeZoneOffset` and `parseDateTime` are wrong by 24 hours for timezones that crossed the international date line
signals.text: 🕵️ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour For the seven timezones that permanently shifted their UTC offset by a whole day when they moved across the international date line, `timeZoneOffset` returns the zone's **pre-jump** offset, and `parseDateTime` (which uses it) produces an instant exactly 86400 s off. ```sql SELECT timeZoneOffset(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')); -- -36000 (-10h) WRONG -- Pacific/Kiritimati has been UTC+14 since 1995, so +50400 SELECT toUnixTimestamp(parseDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', '%Y-%m-%d %H:%i:%S', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')); -- 1750024800 WRONG -- exactly +86400; correct is 1749938400 -- (toDateTime / parseDateTimeBestEffort on the same string give 1749938400) ``` Affected zones, checked across all 597 rows of `system.time_zones` at 2010‑01‑01, 2025‑01‑01 and 2025‑07‑01 — no other zone is wrong: | zone | true offset | `timeZoneOffset` | error | jumped | |---|---|---|---|---| | `Pacific/Kiritimati` | +50400 (+14h) | −36000 (−10h) | −86400 | 1994‑12‑31 | | `Pacific/Apia` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 2011‑12‑30 | | `Pacific/Fakaofo` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 2011‑12‑30 | | `Pacific/Enderbury` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 1994‑12‑31 | | `Pacific/Kanton` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 1994‑12‑31 | | `Pacific/Kwajalein` | +43200 (+12h) | −43200 (−12h) | −86400 | 1993‑08‑20 | | `Kwajalein` | +43200 (+12h) | −43200 (−12h) | −86400 | 1993‑08‑20 | Before its jump each zone is reported correctly (e.g. `Pacific/Apia` is right at 2010‑01‑01), which is consistent with the offset being frozen at the pre-jump value. `Pacific/Chatham` (+13:45) is **correct**, so this is not a "offset larger than +12h" problem — it is specifically the whole-day component that is lost. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Reproduced on 26.8.1.1 and 26.8.1.1599 (four local builds). Not a recent regression — the implementation below has carried this assumption for a long time. ### How to reproduce Any server or `clickhouse local`, default settings: ```sql SELECT timeZoneOffset(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')) AS reported, toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'UTC')) - toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')) AS actual; -- reported = -36000, actual = 50400 ``` Cross-checked against Python's `zoneinfo` (system tzdata), which agrees with `actual`: ```python datetime(2025,6,15,12,0,0,tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Pacific/Kiritimati")).utcoffset() # 14:00:00 ``` Sweep for all zones: ```sql -- per zone (the timezone argument must be a constant), compare SELECT toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime(D,'UTC')) - toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime(D,TZ)) = timeZoneOffset(toDateTime(D,TZ)); ``` ### Expected behavior `timeZoneOffset(t)` should return the zone's actual UTC offset at instant `t` (+50400 for Kiritimati in 2025), and `parseDateTime` should map a wall-clock string to the same instant that `toDateTime` and `parseDateTimeBestEffort` already produce. ### Additional context Root cause is in `src/Common/DateLUTImpl.h`, `DateLUTImpl::timezoneOffset`: ```cpp Time res = (lut[index].date - lut[daynum_offset_epoch].date) % 86400; /// As so far to know, the maximal DST offset couldn't be more than 2 hours, so after the /// modulo operation the remainder will sits between [-offset --> 0 --> offset] ... res = res > 43200 ? (86400 - res) : (0 - res); ... return res + offset_at_start_of_epoch; ``` It reconstructs only the *DST delta relative to the start of the epoch* and adds the zone's 1970 offset. A date-line jump changes the base offset by exactly one day, so that component is an exact multiple of 86400 and `% 86400` discards it — leaving the result anchored to `offset_at_start_of_epoch`, i.e. the pre-jump offset. Chatham is unaffected because its +13:45 has no whole-day part. `parseDateTime` inherits the error at `src/Functions/parseDateTime.cpp:581`: ```cpp if (!has_time_zone_offset) time_zone_offset = time_zone.timezoneOffset(seconds_since_epoch); seconds_since_epoch -= time_zone_offset; ``` Subtracting an offset that is 86400 too small moves the instant 86400 forward, matching the observed error. **Affected functions:** `timeZoneOffset`, `timezoneOffset`, `parseDateTime`, `parseDateTimeOrNull`, `parseDateTime64`, `parseDateTimeInJodaSyntax`. **Verified unaffected** (all agree with `zoneinfo`): `toDateTime`, `toDateTime64`, `toString`, `formatDateTime`, `toTimeZone`, `toStartOfDay`, `toHour`, `makeDateTime`, `makeDateTime64`, `YYYYMMDDhhmmssToDateTime`, `parseDateTimeBestEffort`, `parseDateTimeBestEffortUS`, `parseDateTime64BestEffort`. There is already a regression test for exactly these zones — `tests/queries/0_stateless/01252_weird_time_zone.sql` covers Kiritimati, Kwajalein, Apia, Enderbury and Fakaofo — but only via `toDateTime`, `toStartOfDay` and `toHour`, which are all correct. Extending it with `timeZoneOffset` and `parseDateTime` would cover this. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115332 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1888` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: typeIsSigned omits Time/Time64: JIT zero-extends negative Time to Time64
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **`if`/`multiIf`/`CASE` that mixes a `Time` and a `Time64` operand returns a garbage, max-clamped value for negative `Time` inputs once the expression is JIT compiled. `SELECT if(number % 2 = 0, toTime('-100:00:00'), toTime64('50:00:00', 3)) FROM numbers(2)` yields `999:59:59.000` instead of `-100:00:00.000`. With `compile_expressions=0` the same query is correct. Both settings are on by default (`compile_expressions=true`, `min_count_to_compile_expression=3`), so a repeated query flips to the wrong answer on its 4th execution.** - **Root cause:** `typeIsSigned` (`[`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:32-34`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L32-L34)`) enumerates `isInt() || isFloat() || isEnum() || isDate32() || isDecimal() || isDateTime64()` and never adds `isTime()` / `isTime64()`. `WhichDataType::isDecimal()` (`[`src/DataTypes/IDataType.h:407`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/IDataType.h#L407)`) covers only `Decimal32/64/128/256`, which is exactly why `isDateTime64()` had to be spelled out — the two time types were missed. `canBeNativeType` (`[`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:53-59`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L53-L59)`) does accept `isTime()` and `isTime64()`, so both reach the JIT and are widened with a zero-extend: `Time` -360000 (`Int32`) becomes 4294607296 before the x1000 scale multiply. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `FunctionIf::compileImpl` -> `nativeCast(b, {Time value, DataTypeTime}, DataTypeTime64)` -> `[`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:180`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L180)` (scale differs) or `:205` (scale equal) -> `b.CreateIntCast(value, i64, typeIsSigned(*from_type))` -> `typeIsSigned` at `[`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:30`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L30)`. **Affected locations:** - [`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:32`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L32) — typeIsSigned type list — missing isTime()/isTime64() - [`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:180`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L180) — scale-conversion widening cast for DateTime/Time family uses typeIsSigned - [`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:205`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L205) — generic integer-to-integer nativeCast uses typeIsSigned - [`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:55`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L55) — canBeNativeType admits isTime()/isTime64() **Impact:** Silent wrong results for any query that JIT-compiles a `Time`-to-`Time64` widening and can see a negative `Time` (a clock reading before midnight — `Time` is a signed second count). Reachable with stock settings via `if`, `multiIf` and `CASE` over mixed `Time`/`Time64` operands. The value is not merely off — it lands past the type maximum and prints clamped at `999:59:59`. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `8b9c617362bf7`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/f323b20a-7a5f-4c00-96ce-23bef7bed244) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- no-fasttest: JIT compilation is not available in fasttest -- Regression test for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/96619 -- When JIT-compiling expressions that convert DateTime to DateTime64, -- the scale multiplier was not applied, causing the value to be -- reinterpreted instead of converted (e.g., seconds treated as milliseconds). DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t; SET compile_expressions = 1, min_count_to_compile_expression = 0; SELECT '--- DateTime to DateTime64 via multiIf ---'; SELECT multiIf( number = 0, toNullable(toDateTime('2001-02-03 04:05:06')), number = 1, toNullable(toDateTime('2001-02-03 04:05:06')), '1970-01-01 00:00:00'::Nullable(DateTime64(3)) ) FROM numbers(2); SELECT '--- DateTime to DateTime64 via if ---'; SELECT if( number % 2 = 0, toNullable(toDateTime('2001-02-03 04:05:06')), '1970-01-01 00:00:00'::Nullable(DateTime64(3)) ) FROM numbers(2); SELECT '--- CASE expression ---'; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t; CREATE TABLE t (date1 Nullable(DateTime), date2 Nullable(DateTime)) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO t(date1, date2) VALUES ('2001-02-03 04:05:06', NULL); SELECT CASE WHEN date2 IS NOT NULL THEN date2 WHEN date1 IS NOT NULL THEN date1 ELSE '1970-01-01 00:00:00'::Nullable(DateTime64(3)) END FROM t; DROP TABLE t; SELECT '--- Time to Time64 via if ---'; SELECT if(number % 2 = 0, toTime('-100:00:00'), toTime64('50:00:00', 3)) FROM numbers(2) ORDER BY number; SELECT '--- Time to Time64 via multiIf ---'; SELECT multiIf(number % 2 = 0, toTime('-100:00:00'), toTime64('50:00:00', 3)) FROM numbers(2) ORDER BY number; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` --- Time to Time64 via if --- -100:00:00.000 50:00:00.000 --- Time to Time64 via multiIf --- -100:00:00.000 50:00:00.000 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` --- Time to Time64 via if --- 999:59:59.000 50:00:00.000 --- Time to Time64 via multiIf --- 999:59:59.000 50:00:00.000 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Add `|| data_type.isTime() || data_type.isTime64()` to `typeIsSigned` at `[`src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:32-34`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/8b9c617362bf7/src/DataTypes/Native.cpp#L32-L34)`. Both are signed (`Int32` / `Decimal64`-derived) and both are already accepted by `canBeNativeType`. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `src/DataTypes/Native.cpp:201` (`typeIsSigned ? CreateSIToFP : CreateUIToFP`) reads the same oracle, so a compiled `Time64`-to-float cast would be wrong the same way. I could not construct a JIT-compiled float conversion from `Time64` in SQL, so this arm is unproven — the `typeIsSigned` fix covers it regardless. Found during automated review of [PR #114168](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114168). Severity P1 · Finding `h_pr114168_001` </details> cc @groeneai @Manerone @alexey-milovidov (from #114168) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115146 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1864` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Malformed ORC/Avro files reach `LOGICAL_ERROR` through the exception formatter (aborts on debug builds, silently, from schema inference)
signals.text: 🕵️ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour A truncated ORC file makes `clickhouse local` / `clickhouse-server` abort with **no output at all** — no error, no stack trace, nothing on stdout or stderr. The same signature is reachable from Avro. The cause is not in the ORC reader itself but in the error-handling path: schema inference catches the reader's failure and calls `getCurrentExceptionMessage()` to format it, and that function deliberately aborts when the in-flight exception derives from `std::logic_error`. The bundled parsing libraries throw `std::logic_error` subclasses for malformed input, so untrusted data reaches an assertion that is meant to catch internal bugs only. The process dies *while composing the error message*, which is why nothing is ever printed. ### How to reproduce The input is a plain truncation of a file already in the repo — no bit-level fuzzing needed: ```bash head -c 289 tests/queries/0_stateless/data_orc/orc_nested_union_type.orc > t289.orc clickhouse local --query "SELECT * FROM file('t289.orc', ORC) FORMAT Null" ``` ``` Aborted (core dumped) ``` Reproducible 3/3. Total output produced: 0 bytes. Sending the same file to a server via `SELECT * FROM file('t289.orc', ORC)` takes the server down. Note the neighbouring truncation lengths behave correctly — `head -c 100`, `-c 200`, `-c 400`, `-c 600` all return a clean `Code: 636 CANNOT_EXTRACT_TABLE_STRUCTURE`, as does the untruncated fixture. Only this length reaches the bad path. A second input with the same signature, from a different format: `SELECT count() FROM file('x.avro', Avro)` on an Iceberg manifest `.avro` fixture with four bit flips (attached, 4245 bytes) also aborts and also takes the server down. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Reproduced on 26.8.1.1599 and 26.8.1.1. **Important caveat:** both builds I have are `BUILD_TYPE = Debug`. The abort is gated on `debug_or_sanitizer_build || abort_on_logical_error`, so on a release build these inputs presumably raise a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception instead of crashing. I had no release build to confirm that. Either way a `LOGICAL_ERROR` should not be reachable from an input file. ### Expected behavior A malformed input file should produce an ordinary parse error (`CANNOT_EXTRACT_TABLE_STRUCTURE`, `INCORRECT_DATA`, …). It should never reach `abortOnFailedAssertion`, and error formatting should never be able to kill the process — least of all silently. ### Error message and/or stacktrace There is no error message; that is part of the problem. `gdb` backtrace: ``` #4 __GI_abort () #5 DB::abortOnFailedAssertion (description=..., format_string=..., trace=...) at src/Common/Exception.cpp:66 #6 DB::abortOnFailedAssertion (description=...) src/Common/Exception.cpp:72 #7 DB::getCurrentExceptionMessageAndPattern (with_stacktrace=false, ...) at src/Common/Exception.cpp:548 #8 DB::getCurrentExceptionMessage (...) src/Common/Exception.cpp:477 #9 DB::readSchemaFromFormatImpl (format_name=..., ...) src/Formats/ReadSchemaUtils.cpp:278 #10 DB::readSchemaFromFormat (...) src/Formats/ReadSchemaUtils.cpp:569 #11 DB::StorageFile::getTableStructureAndFormatFromFileImpl (...) src/Storages/StorageFile.cpp:1209 #13 DB::StorageFile::setStorageMetadata (...) src/Storages/StorageFile.cpp:1371 #21 DB::TableFunctionFile::getStorage (...) src/TableFunctions/TableFunctionFile.cpp:168 ``` The relevant code, `src/Common/Exception.cpp` (~L537-550): ```cpp if (debug_or_sanitizer_build || abort_on_logical_error.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) { try { throw; } catch (const std::logic_error &) { if (!with_stacktrace) stream << ", Stack trace:\n\n" << getExceptionStackTraceString(e); abortOnFailedAssertion(stream.str()); } catch (...) {} } ``` and its caller, `src/Formats/ReadSchemaUtils.cpp:278`: ```cpp catch (...) { auto exception_message = getCurrentExceptionMessage(false); ``` ### Root cause: which exception escapes Caught in the debugger at `abortOnFailedAssertion`, the message being formatted when the process dies is: * **ORC** — `std::exception. Code: 1001, type: orc::NotImplementedYet, e.what() = Unknown compression codec 6` * **Avro** — `std::exception. Code: 1001, type: std::domain_error, e.what() = Object end` Both are `std::logic_error` subclasses (`orc::NotImplementedYet` derives from it, and `std::domain_error` *is* one), which is precisely the branch that aborts: ```cpp // src/Common/Exception.cpp, getCurrentExceptionMessageAndPattern (~L537) if (debug_or_sanitizer_build || abort_on_logical_error.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) { try { throw; } catch (const std::logic_error &) { ... abortOnFailedAssertion(stream.str()); } catch (...) {} } ``` The truncated ORC file simply has a garbage byte where the compression codec goes; liborc reports that as `NotImplementedYet` rather than a parse error, so it sails past the guards that already exist. ### Possible fix **1. Widen the library-boundary catches (the fix that matches existing precedent).** `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/NativeORCBlockInputFormat.cpp` already wraps liborc at two points, but only for `orc::ParseError` (L1376, L1462). Per `contrib/orc/c++/include/orc/Exceptions.hh` the hierarchy splits: ```cpp class NotImplementedYet : public std::logic_error {...}; // L29 -> aborts class SchemaEvolutionError: public std::logic_error {...}; // L62 -> aborts class ParseError : public std::runtime_error {...}; // L40 -> already caught class InvalidArgument : public std::runtime_error {...}; // L51 -> not caught, but harmless ``` so the two `logic_error` branches — plus any `std::out_of_range` from bounds checks — sail past the existing guards. The comments on those catches say the intent was "instead of letting it propagate as a generic std::exception", so widening them is in keeping with the original design. Widening those catches, and adding the equivalent at the Avro boundary, follows exactly the shape used to fix #106259: ```cpp catch (const DB::Exception &) { throw; } catch (const std::exception & e) { /// liborc throws orc::NotImplementedYet / orc::SchemaEvolutionError (std::logic_error /// subclasses) on malformed input. Untranslated they reach the top level as /// LOGICAL_ERROR (code 1001) and abort via abortOnFailedAssertion. throw Exception(ErrorCodes::CORRUPTED_DATA, "Cannot read ORC data: {}", e.what()); } ``` That is the same boundary-translation used in `ThetaSketchData::read` for `datasketches` (#106260 / commit `899dd77`), and the same rationale applies. **2. Map the third-party namespaces to real error codes (complementary, not sufficient).** `getCodeForSTDException` (`src/Common/Exception.cpp` ~L189) already special-cases one library: ```cpp std::string name = demangle(typeid(exc).name()); if (name.starts_with("avro::")) return ErrorCodes::AVRO_EXCEPTION; return ErrorCodes::STD_EXCEPTION; ``` Adding `orc::`, `parquet::` and `arrow::` would at least give a meaningful code instead of `STD_EXCEPTION`. **On its own this does not stop the abort** — the abort keys off the C++ type being a `std::logic_error`, not off the error code — so it only helps alongside (1). **3. Reconsider the blanket `std::logic_error` ⇒ internal-bug assumption (broader, optional).** The assumption behind the abort is that a `std::logic_error` can only be a ClickHouse bug. Bundled parsers violate that routinely: they use `domain_error`, `out_of_range`, `invalid_argument` and `NotImplementedYet` to report *bad input*. As long as that holds, fix (1) has to be applied at every third-party parse boundary, and each new one is a fresh instance of this issue — the fuzz run reached the same abort through ORC, Avro, Parquet and ArrowStream. Narrowing the abort to exceptions that genuinely originate in ClickHouse code would fix the class rather than the instances, at the cost of losing an assertion that is presumably valuable in CI. Whichever route, a regression test in the shape of `tests/queries/0_stateless/04307_uniqTheta_corrupted_state_106259` (added by the #106260 fix) would fit — the 289-byte ORC input is deterministic and needs no fuzzing to regenerate. ### Additional context Found by a fuzzer that mutates valid Parquet/ORC/Avro/Arrow files and complete Iceberg and DeltaLake tables, then checks that reading them fails with an ordinary exception. Over the run the server went down 27 times; `ReadSchemaUtils.cpp` was by far the most frequent frame in the fatal records, and the crashing queries were Avro (28), Parquet (12) and ORC (4) — consistent with this one shared path rather than three separate parser bugs. Prior art: **#106259** / **#106260** fixed the identical pattern for `datasketches` (`std::out_of_range` from a malformed `AggregateFunction(uniqTheta)` state). The instances here are the same class in liborc / avro / arrow, which that fix did not cover. Worth noting a maintainer's comment on #106259 — *"a LOGICAL_ERROR is not a crash. It's an exception."* — which is consistent with the debug-build caveat above; on release these are bad error codes rather than aborts. One related observation from the same run, filed here for context rather than as a separate issue: * **Allocation driven by corrupted length fields.** 9 inputs pushed the reader past a 3 GB per-query memory limit; with no `max_memory_usage` set, a few corrupted bytes are a memory-exhaustion vector. Everything else behaved correctly: 55 545 corrupted inputs were rejected with ordinary errors (636 `CANNOT_EXTRACT_TABLE_STRUCTURE`, 117 `INCORRECT_DATA`, 742 `DELTA_KERNEL_ERROR`, …), and the DeltaLake and Iceberg metadata layers in particular rejected every corruption cleanly.
signals.author: PedroTadim

signals.title: Text index written by 26.6 is unreadable by older replicas in the same cluster — breaks rolling upgrades
signals.text: ### Company or project name Nebius ### Describe what's wrong Since 26.6, ClickHouse writes the `text` skip index with sparse index version 1, which no earlier version can read. An older replica that receives such a part through normal replication fails every query that uses the index: ``` Code: 246. DB::Exception: Unsupported version of sparse index (1): While reading part all_0_0_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CORRUPTED_DATA) ``` **This is not a downgrade problem.** It breaks the upgrade itself. During a rolling restart of a replicated cluster, an already-upgraded replica writes parts with a v1 text index, replication delivers them to replicas that have not been restarted yet, and those replicas start failing reads — while both versions are running normally and no data directory has been touched. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Three files and six commands. This runs **one ReplicatedMergeTree cluster with both versions live at the same time** — the state a rolling upgrade passes through. Nothing is downgraded and no data directory is moved. ```bash mkdir ch-textindex && cd ch-textindex cat > keeper.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <listen_host>0.0.0.0</listen_host> <keeper_server> <tcp_port>9181</tcp_port> <server_id>1</server_id> <log_storage_path>/var/lib/clickhouse-keeper/log</log_storage_path> <snapshot_storage_path>/var/lib/clickhouse-keeper/snapshots</snapshot_storage_path> <raft_configuration> <server><id>1</id><hostname>keeper</hostname><port>9234</port></server> </raft_configuration> </keeper_server> </clickhouse> EOF cat > repl.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <zookeeper><node><host>keeper</host><port>9181</port></node></zookeeper> <macros> <shard>1</shard> <replica from_env="REPLICA"/> </macros> </clickhouse> EOF cat > docker-compose.yml <<'EOF' services: keeper: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper:26.6.2.160 volumes: [./keeper.xml:/etc/clickhouse-keeper/keeper_config.xml:ro] old: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-server:26.3.10.60 environment: {REPLICA: old} volumes: [./repl.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/repl.xml:ro] new: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-server:26.6.2.160 environment: {REPLICA: new} volumes: [./repl.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/repl.xml:ro] EOF docker compose up -d for r in old new; do until docker compose exec -T $r clickhouse-client -q "SELECT 1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done; done # 1. the same replicated table on both replicas for r in old new; do docker compose exec -T $r clickhouse-client -q " CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, s String, INDEX idx s TYPE text(tokenizer = array)) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/1/t', '{replica}') ORDER BY id"; done # 2. write on the already-upgraded replica, let replication carry the part over docker compose exec -T new clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number, hex(number) FROM numbers(20000)" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SYSTEM SYNC REPLICA t" # 3. the old replica only fetched that part, it never wrote one docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SYSTEM FLUSH LOGS" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SELECT DISTINCT event_type FROM system.part_log WHERE table = 't'" # 4. the same query on each replica docker compose exec -T new clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t WHERE s = '3039'" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t WHERE s = '3039'" docker compose down -v ``` Output of the last three steps: ``` DownloadPart <- step 3: fetched, not written locally 1 <- step 4 on the new replica Code: 246. DB::Exception: Unsupported version of sparse index (1): While reading part all_0_0_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CORRUPTED_DATA) <- step 4 on the old replica ``` No special settings are needed — the optimizer chooses the index on its own, which is how we hit it in production. `hasToken(s, '3039')` fails identically. `SELECT count() FROM t` still works, so only queries that touch the index break. [ch-textindex-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31214857/ch-textindex-repro.zip) ### Expected behavior Either of: 1. A reader that meets a sparse index version it does not understand skips the index and reads the granules, instead of failing the query. Skip indexes are an optimisation; an unreadable one should not be fatal. 2. Failing that, the format bump is called out as backward-incompatible in the changelog with a "drop the text index before upgrading" note, as was done for the 25.12 v3 change in #91518. Currently it is neither: the query fails, and the 26.6 changelog does not mention it. Related: #91518 introduced the sparse-index version header in 25.12 and *was* flagged backward-incompatible. #111550 (open) received review feedback describing this same hazard for a later layout change — *"older binaries misparse new ones, so rolling upgrades/downgrades ... have no safe migration path"* — recommending a versioned reader that migrates or throws an explicit rebuild-required error. The 26.6 bump shipped without either. ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests A search for the error text (`"Unsupported version of sparse index"`, `"version of sparse index"`) returns no existing report. - **#91518** — *Inverted Text Index v3* (merged, 25.12). Introduced the version header for the text index sparse index. It was explicitly flagged backward-incompatible, with a changelog note telling users to drop the index before upgrading and rebuild it. The 26.6 bump changes the same field with no equivalent note. - **#111550** — *Text index: introduce new storage layout for positions* (open). Review feedback on it describes this exact hazard for a later layout change: *"older binaries misparse new ones, so rolling upgrades/downgrades on tables that already use `support_phrase_search` have no safe migration path"*, and recommends giving the layout a new persisted version while keeping a reader that either migrates or throws an explicit rebuild-required error. That is the same remedy this issue asks for. - **#103398** — *Upgrade from 25.x to 26.x ends with CORRUPTED_DATA* (closed). The same failure shape in a different subsystem: rolling upgrade of a replicated cluster, error 246, `Unknown version of serialization infos (1). Should be less or equal than 0`. It was resolved by manual intervention (`SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA`) rather than by making the reader tolerant, so the pattern of a version field that older binaries reject outright is recurring. - **#94494** — *Fix text index mrk file incompatibility* (merged 26.1, backported 25.12.4.32). A different text index format problem (`.mrk` with non-adaptive `index_granularity`, triggered by merges). Listed to distinguish it: it is not this bug. - **#84606** — *Text index: remove multi format versions handling* (merged, July 2025, not-for-changelog). Consolidated `Format::v2` into `v1` and removed multi-version handling. Predates the version header, so it is not the cause, but it is context for how format-version tolerance in this index has been treated. ### Additional context **Workaround** On the not-yet-upgraded replicas, `SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0` makes the query succeed; `ALTER TABLE ... DROP INDEX` also works. Both give up the index for the duration. - Reproduced on `clickhouse/clickhouse-server` and `clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper` docker images, linux/aarch64. - Single shard, two replicas, one keeper. Nothing else required.

signals.title: `SELECT count()` never terminates on corrupted Avro / MsgPack / ProtobufList files — the `optimize_count_from_files` fast path counts rows without requiring forward progress
signals.text: 🕵️ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour `SELECT count()` over a corrupted file can run forever, emitting billions of phantom rows from a tiny input. Reading the same file normally rejects it immediately, so only the count fast path is affected. The smallest reproducer is **two bytes**: ```bash printf '\x00\x00' > bad.pb clickhouse local --query " SELECT count() FROM file('bad.pb', ProtobufList, 'a UInt64, b Int32, c Float64, d String')" # never returns ``` Measured on a server with `max_execution_time = 0`: ``` elapsed 6 s -> 958.50 million rows read, 5.37 MiB elapsed 12 s -> 1.92 billion rows read, 4.36 MiB elapsed 18 s -> 2.89 billion rows read, 362.43 KiB ``` Memory does not grow — it falls — so this is pure unbounded counting, not an allocation problem. **The decisive observation:** it is only the count fast path. For the same file, | query | result | |---|---| | `SELECT count() FROM file(...)` | **never returns** | | `SELECT count() FROM file(...) SETTINGS optimize_count_from_files = 0` | clean error in ~0 s | | `SELECT * FROM file(...) FORMAT Null` | clean error in ~0 s | | `SELECT a FROM file(...) LIMIT 5` | clean error in ~0 s | The real reading path validates the data and rejects it. `countRows()` does not. ### Affected formats Confirmed identical behaviour in three formats — in every case `count()` hangs while `SELECT *` and `optimize_count_from_files = 0` return a clean error in under a second: | format | reproducer | behaviour with default settings | |---|---|---| | ProtobufList | 2 bytes (`00 00`) | 2.89 billion rows in 18 s | | Avro | 57 KB (valid file + 1000 appended bytes) | 4.89 billion rows in 25 s | | MsgPack | 3.8–210 KB, five independent inputs | 66–145 million rows/s | Neighbouring inputs behave correctly, which narrows the ProtobufList case usefully: | input | result | |---|---| | empty file (0 bytes) | returns `0` | | `00` (1 byte) | returns cleanly | | `00 00` (2 bytes) | **never returns** | ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Reproduced on 26.8.1.1599. Not build-dependent — nothing here relies on debug assertions. ### Expected behavior `countRows()` must not report more rows than the input can contain, and must terminate. A loop that produces a row without consuming any input should stop and raise `INCORRECT_DATA`, matching what the normal read path already does for these same files. ### Root cause The three `countRows()` implementations share one shape: the loop condition never requires the input position to advance. **`ProtobufListInputFormat::countRows`** — the return value of `readFieldNumber` is discarded, and a zero-length nested message consumes nothing, so `eof()` never becomes true: ```cpp size_t num_rows = 0; while (!reader->eof() && num_rows < max_block_size) { int tag = 0; reader->readFieldNumber(tag); // return value ignored reader->startNestedMessage(); reader->endNestedMessage(); // zero-length message consumes no input ++num_rows; } ``` **`AvroRowInputFormat::countRows`** — `hasMore()` is true while the block's `objectCount_` is non-zero, and `decr()` only decrements that counter. A corrupted object count in the block header is therefore a licence to count that many rows: ```cpp while (file_reader_ptr->hasMore() && num_rows < max_block_size) { file_reader_ptr->decr(); file_reader_ptr->decoder().drain(); ++num_rows; } ``` `contrib/avro`'s `DataFileReaderBase::readDataBlock()` decodes `objectCount_` and `byteCount` straight from the file and validates neither, so the count comes directly from the corrupted bytes. **`MsgPackRowInputFormat::countRows`** — `readObject` with a null visitor can consume nothing on malformed input, so `buf->eof()` never becomes true: ```cpp while (!buf->eof() && num_rows < max_block_size) { for (size_t i = 0; i < columns; ++i) readObject(null_parser); ++num_rows; } ``` ### Possible fix Roughly **13 lines in total**, and the bulk of it is one shared change. #### 1. A shared forward-progress guard — 3 lines, fixes all three formats There is a single call site for `countRows()`, in `IRowInputFormat::generate()` (`src/Processors/Formats/IRowInputFormat.cpp`, ~L90-102), and it **already captures the input offset before the call and computes the delta after it** for `approx_bytes_read_for_chunk`. So the check needs no new plumbing: ```cpp size_t chunk_start_offset = getDataOffsetMaybeCompressed(getReadBuffer()); ... num_rows = countRows(params.max_block_size_rows); + if (num_rows > 0 && getDataOffsetMaybeCompressed(getReadBuffer()) == chunk_start_offset) + throw Exception(ErrorCodes::INCORRECT_DATA, + "Counted {} rows while consuming no input; the file is malformed", num_rows); if (num_rows == 0) { readSuffix(); return {}; } ``` This covers every format implementing `countRows()`, not just the three found here. *Caveat worth checking before relying on it alone:* a format that counts a whole block out of an already-filled buffer would trip the guard on a valid file. It looks safe — valid 200 000-row Avro and MsgPack files still count correctly, because the first `countRows()` call fills the buffer and therefore advances the offset, and later calls that return 0 rows never reach the check — but that is a two-format spot check, not a proof across all thirteen. Running the format test suite would settle it. #### 2. Per-format hardening — about 10 lines, and each is unambiguous * **ProtobufList** (~2 lines) — honour `readFieldNumber`'s return value and stop when it is `false`, instead of discarding it. * **MsgPack** (~4 lines) — the same forward-progress check locally, using `buf->count()`; the null-visitor parse can silently consume nothing. * **Avro** (~4 lines + a submodule bump) — bound the block header in `readDataBlock()` (`lang/c++/impl/DataFile.cc`): reject `objectCount_ < 0`, `byteCount < 0`, and `objectCount_ > byteCount`. An object occupies at least one byte, so a block cannot hold more objects than it has bytes; that single comparison kills the Avro case and cannot reject a well-formed file. This one is the only part needing two repositories. `contrib/avro` is a submodule of ClickHouse's own fork, **https://github.com/ClickHouse/avro** (currently pinned at `7b7f6a5bc42e56b6f74de9fc8f52a2a629c53145`, tracking `master`), so it is a PR there followed by a ClickHouse PR bumping the pointer. There is direct precedent for exactly this kind of hardening in that fork — the pinned commit itself is *"Bound Avro string/bytes decode allocation to actual input"*, and ClickHouse carries *"Avro: bound string/bytes decode allocation (bump avro submodule)"* and *"Add hard limit (256) to the max depth in avro internal parser"*. If only one change is taken, take #1: it is the smallest, needs no submodule work, and is the only one that also protects the formats this corpus never reached. ### Workaround `SET optimize_count_from_files = 0` — verified to make all three cases fail cleanly and fast. ### Additional context The `Protobuf` / `ProtobufList` split is informative: the two share the message decoder and differ in the length-delimited list framing and its `countRows()`, which is exactly where the defect is.
signals.author: PedroTadim

signals.title: RESTORE DATABASE ... AS ... corrupts/crashes views using FROM table AS alias FINAL,  other_table
signals.text: ### Company or project name Critical Manufacturing S.A. ### Describe what's wrong Restoring a database backup under a different name (`RESTORE DATABASE src AS dst FROM ...`) mishandles views whose `SELECT` uses a table alias immediately followed by `FINAL` in a multi-table (comma-joined) `FROM t1 AS a FINAL, t2 AS b`. This is valid, documented syntax (["When a table has an alias, FINAL must come after the alias, not before it"](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/select/from#final-modifier)), and views are created and queried correctly before any rename-restore. Depending on the query's complexity, this produces one of two failures only when the database is renamed during restore: 1. Silent alias drop (minimal repro below): the restored view's stored definition loses the alias(es) entirely, silently corrupting the view — it then fails when queried. 2. Hard crash (seen on a more complex, real production view with CTEs/multiple joins — full trace below): the restore itself fails with a `SYNTAX_ERROR` while ClickHouse tries to re-resolve the qualified table name for the rename. No issue occurs if the database is restored under its original name (no `AS `) or if the `CREATE VIEW` is executed directly (not via backup/restore) — pointing at the backup-restore-time table-name rewrite (`DB::BackupMetadataFinder::findTableInBackupImpl`) as the common cause, not the general SQL parser. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Tested and reproducible in these versions: - 25.3.6.56 - 26.3.9.8 - **26.3.19.3** ``` CREATE DATABASE testdb; USE testdb; CREATE TABLE t1 (id UInt32, val String) ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE t2 (id UInt32, label String) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (1, 'a'); INSERT INTO t2 VALUES (1, 'x'); CREATE VIEW v1 AS SELECT a.id, b.label FROM t1 AS a FINAL, t2 AS b WHERE a.id = b.id; -- Works fine so far: SELECT * FROM v1; BACKUP DATABASE testdb TO Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); --Restoring under a DIFFERENT name silently drops both aliases from the view definition: RESTORE DATABASE testdb AS restoredtestdb FROM Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); USE restoredtestdb; SHOW CREATE VIEW v1; -- Actual: -- FROM restoredtestdb.t1 -- FINAL, -- restoredtestdb.t2 -- WHERE a.id = b.id -- (aliases `a` and `b` are gone, but the WHERE clause still references them) SELECT * FROM v1; -- Code: 47. DB::Exception: Unknown expression identifier `a.id` in scope -- SELECT a.id, b.label FROM restoredtestdb.t1 FINAL, restoredtestdb.t2 WHERE a.id = b.id. -- Maybe you meant: ['t1.id']. (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- Restoring under the ORIGINAL name works correctly (no alias loss): DROP DATABASE testdb; RESTORE DATABASE testdb FROM Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); USE testdb; SHOW CREATE VIEW v1; -- Actual: -- FROM testdb.t1 AS a -- FINAL, -- restoredtestdb.t2 AS b -- WHERE a.id = b.id -- (aliases `a` and `b` are present) SELECT * FROM v1; ``` ### Expected behavior Aliases are kept when restoring with a rename. Fix expected for 26.3 LTS. ### Error message and/or stacktrace Complete statements and error messages present as comments in the reproduction example. ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ ### Version info - Resolved by: #115645 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1859` (included in `26.8` and later)
signals.author: bernardolopes8

signals.title: ReplicatedMergeTree replica becomes permanently readonly (Code 122) when power loss reverts an applied ALTER's local metadata commit; force_restore_data / RESTART REPLICA / RESTORE REPLICA all fail to recover
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong When a `ReplicatedMergeTree` replica applies an `ALTER` (its `/replicas/<r>/metadata_version` znode is durably advanced in [Zoo]Keeper) but the local side of that commit — the rename that replaces `metadata/<db>/<table>.sql` — is reverted by a power loss, the replica can never start again: `ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread` fails initialization with `Code: 122` `Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure` and logs `Initialization failed, table will remain readonly`. The state is permanent across restarts, and none of the documented recovery paths repair it: | Recovery attempt | Result | |---|---| | restart the server | same `Code: 122`, still readonly | | `SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA t` | still readonly | | `flags/force_restore_data` + restart | still readonly (the flag only skips part sanity checks) | | `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t` | refuses: `Replica path is present at ... - nothing to restore` | The only way out is `SYSTEM DROP REPLICA` plus re-creating the replica (or hand-editing the `.sql` file to match ZooKeeper). The window is real on default settings: the `ALTER`'s local metadata commit is `writeMetadataFile` of an fsynced `.sql.tmp` (`fsync_metadata = 1` covers only the file content) followed by `DatabaseAtomic::commitAlterTable` doing `renameExchange`/`replaceFile` with no fsync of the file or parent directory — the same never-made-durable commit rename described in #111348, and the code itself carries `/// NOTE: replica will be lost if server crashes before the following rename` right at that spot. On ext4 the rename becomes durable only when the journal happens to commit, so a power cut within that interval rolls the local file back to the pre-`ALTER` structure while the replica's own `metadata_version` znode (updated durably in Keeper as part of applying the `ALTER_METADATA` entry) stays advanced. On the next start the replica's recorded metadata version claims the new structure while the local file carries the old one, and the attach thread refuses. A normal lagging replica (killed before applying the `ALTER`) recovers fine — its local structure and its `metadata_version` znode are consistently old, so the queued `ALTER_METADATA` entry replays. The brick needs exactly the torn state this unfsynced rename produces: znode ahead, local file behind. Since initialization refuses before the queue is even loaded, the `ALTER_METADATA` replay that would repair the structure never gets a chance to run. Secondary effects observed while the replica sits in this state: its `/replicas/<r>/parts` set keeps hundreds of stale entries for parts that no longer exist locally (the startup fetch-or-remove reconciliation also never runs), and the broken local parts accumulate in `detached/`. Observed organically first: a 3-replica cluster under a concurrent INSERT/mutation/DDL workload where one replica's data directory sat on a dm-flakey device that lost power (drop_writes + remount) while the other replicas and Keeper stayed durable — 2 of 5 such runs on 26.8 ended with the recovered replica permanently readonly with `Code: 122`. The deterministic reproduction below simulates only the rename rollback, which is what the device power loss does by itself. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — 26.8.1.1708 (official master build), deterministic with the reproduction below; also observed under real device power loss. ### How to reproduce Two `ReplicatedMergeTree` replicas (`r0`, `r1`) of one table over one Keeper, each server with its own data directory: ```sql -- on both replicas: CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt8) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/t', '{replica}') PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id; -- on r0: INSERT INTO t SELECT number, number, 0 FROM numbers(100); ``` 1. Save a copy of r1's `metadata/default/t.sql`. 2. `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c UInt32` (on either replica); wait until r1's `t.sql` contains the new column (the `ALTER_METADATA` entry applied; r1's `/replicas/r1/metadata_version` znode advanced). 3. Kill r1's server (`kill -9` — any crash). 4. Write the saved pre-`ALTER` content back into r1's `metadata/default/t.sql`. This simulates the power-loss rollback of the never-fsynced commit rename (#111348's mechanism); under a real device power cut inside the filesystem journal window this step happens by itself. 5. Start r1. r1 logs `ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread: Initialization failed, table will remain readonly. Error: Code: 122. DB::Exception: Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure` and `system.replicas.is_readonly` stays `1` forever. `SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA t`, the `flags/force_restore_data` flag and `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t` all fail as in the table above. A control run without step 4 recovers to `is_readonly = 0` immediately. ### Expected behavior An applied `ALTER` whose local metadata commit was lost to power loss leaves the replica in a state its own queue already knows how to repair — the replica's structure is simply behind ZooKeeper's. The replica should reconcile the local metadata from ZooKeeper (or reapply the `ALTER_METADATA` diff) instead of refusing initialization forever, or at minimum `force_restore_data` / `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA` should cover this state. Alternatively, making the metadata commit rename durable (fsync the parent directory when `fsync_metadata` is enabled) closes the window at its source. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` <Error> default.t (ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread): Initialization failed, table will remain readonly. Error: Code: 122. DB::Exception: Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure. Local columns: ... ``` `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t`: ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Replica path is present at /clickhouse/tables/t/replicas/r1 - nothing to restore. If you are sure that metadata is lost and that replica path contains some garbage, then use SYSTEM DROP REPLICA query first.. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct open reports of the same unfsynced-commit-rename mechanism with different consequences: #111348 (table-level `DROP`/`RENAME`/`EXCHANGE` on an Atomic database silently revert) and #111802 (`ON CLUSTER` DDL marked finished in Keeper while one host's local effect is lost, never retried). This report is the `ReplicatedMergeTree` column-`ALTER` flavor, where the outcome is not a silent revert but a replica that permanently refuses to initialize, with no working documented recovery short of dropping and re-creating the replica.

signals.title: Role settings profiles are not enforced on SET ROLE only at session-start
signals.text: ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the unexpected behaviour `SETTINGS PROFILE ... TO <role>` silently has no effect if the role activated with `SET ROLE` (or HTTP `?role=`) mid-session. It fails to change settings imposed by the profile and fails to enforce `CONST`ness of settings that the settings profile locks. The settings profile is only applied if the role is active when the session is initiated. This is surprising and undocumented. <details> <summary>Detailed explanation</summary> Attaching a settings profile to a role via `CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ... TO <role>` causes the profile's settings and constraints to be applied **only when the role is enabled at connect time** (typically via `DEFAULT ROLE`). When the same role is activated in an existing session with `SET ROLE <role>` (or in an HTTP request with the `?role=<role>` query parameter) the role's privileges and row policies engage, but the profile does not: neither its settings values, nor its `CONST` / `READONLY` / `MIN` / `MAX` constraints, nor its `readonly = N` enforcement take effect. This is not documented on the [`CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE`](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/create/settings-profile), [`SET ROLE`](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/set-role), or [Settings profiles](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/settings-profiles) pages. It has security implications for anyone building a trusted-gateway pattern where a single service user connects, activates a per-request role, and expects the role's profile (e.g. `readonly = 1 CONST`) to confine the session. </details> ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested on 26.8.1.1731 & 26.3.17.1 ### How to reproduce On Clickhouse 26.3.17.1 or 26.8.1.1731 (tested), such as the default clickhouse container image. Configuration should have `custom_settings_prefixes: SQL_,custom_` (only required for the `CONST` demo): ```sh mkdir -p ~/ch-config.d cat > ~/ch-config.d/custom-prefixes.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <custom_settings_prefixes>SQL_,custom_</custom_settings_prefixes> </clickhouse> EOF docker run -d --name ch \ -p 8123:8123 -p 9000:9000 \ -v ~/ch-config.d:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d:ro \ clickhouse/clickhouse-server:latest ``` ### `readonly = 1 CONST` profile is not applied on `SET ROLE` ``` -- Setup CREATE ROLE ro_role; GRANT SELECT ON system.one TO ro_role; CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ro_profile SETTINGS readonly = 1 TO ro_role; CREATE USER probe IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; GRANT ro_role TO probe; ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE NONE; -- role is granted but not default ``` Reconnect as `probe` and observe: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --query " SET ROLE ro_role; SELECT value FROM system.settings WHERE name = 'readonly'; SET some_random_setting = 1; " 0 -- readonly is still 0 (profile not applied) -- SET succeeded (would fail with READONLY if readonly = 1 were engaged) ``` Compare with the connect-time variant: ```sql ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE ro_role; ``` ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --query " SELECT value FROM system.settings WHERE name = 'readonly'; SET some_random_setting = 1; " 1 -- readonly is now 1 (profile applied) Code: 164. DB::Exception: ... : Cannot modify 'some_random_setting' setting in readonly mode. ``` ### HTTP `?role=` has the same behaviour <details> <summary>Show repro steps for http connections</summary> Same setup as Reproducer 1, with `probe` reverted to `DEFAULT ROLE NONE`. Send an HTTP request activating the role via query param: ``` $ curl -sS -G 'http://localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "user=probe" --data-urlencode "password=x" \ --data-urlencode "role=ro_role" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT value FROM system.settings WHERE name = 'readonly'" 2 ``` Note: the HTTP interface reports `readonly = 2` by default for URL-supplied queries (its own convention), not `1`. The role's profile pinning `readonly = 1` should would override this but the profile actually had no effect. Confirm this with a `SET`: ``` $ curl -sS -G 'http://localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "user=probe" --data-urlencode "password=x" \ --data-urlencode "role=ro_role" \ --data-urlencode "query=SET max_threads=3" # (empty body, exit 0 - the SET succeeded) ``` Under a real `readonly = 1` the `SET` would fail with code 164 `READONLY`. Compare with the connect-time variant (`ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE ro_role`): ``` $ curl -sS -G 'http://localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "user=probe" --data-urlencode "password=x" \ --data-urlencode "query=SET max_threads=3" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_threads' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` The role's grants let the query run. Only the former engages the profile. Dropping `?role=ro_role` on the first URL still returns `SELECT count() FROM system.one` correctly via HTTP-interface defaults, so the test uses `SET` rather than `SELECT` to distinguish "role activated" from "profile applied". </details> ### `CONST` binding on a custom setting is not enforced under `SET ROLE` When connecting directly as a role with a settings profile that enforces a setting as `CONST` and trying to `SET` the a setting, clickhouse reports an error like ``` Code: 452. DB::Exception: Setting custom_pinned_value should not be changed. ``` When switching to the role with `SET ROLE` instead, the setting change is permitted. <details> <summary>Show reproducer</summary> > [!NOTE] > Requires `custom_settings_prefixes` to include `custom_` server-side. Setup: ```sql CREATE ROLE ro_role_custom; GRANT SELECT ON system.one TO ro_role_custom; CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ro_custom_profile SETTINGS custom_pinned_value = 'pinned' CONST TO ro_role_custom; CREATE USER probe2 IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; GRANT ro_role_custom TO probe2; ALTER USER probe2 DEFAULT ROLE NONE; ``` As `probe2`: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe2 --password x --query " SET ROLE ro_role_custom; SET custom_pinned_value = 'overridden'; SELECT getSetting('custom_pinned_value'); " overridden ``` The profile pins the setting `CONST 'pinned'` on the role, but the user is free to rewrite it after `SET ROLE`. Compare with connect time: ```sql ALTER USER probe2 DEFAULT ROLE ro_role_custom; ``` ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe2 --password x --query " SET custom_pinned_value = 'overridden'; " Code: 452. DB::Exception: Setting custom_pinned_value should not be changed. ``` Cleanup: ```sql DROP USER probe2; DROP SETTINGS PROFILE ro_custom_profile; DROP ROLE ro_role_custom; ``` </details> ### Related: `readonly = 1` does not restrict role membership changes Moved to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115691 ### Expected behavior | Path | Expected (from current docs) | Actual (26.3.17.1 and 26.8.1.1731) | |---|---|---| | `DEFAULT ROLE role_with_profile` at connect | Profile applies | Profile applies ✓ | | `SET ROLE role_with_profile` mid-session | Profile applies (unstated) | Profile does NOT apply ✗ | | HTTP `?role=role_with_profile` | Profile applies (unstated) | Profile does NOT apply ✗ | | `SET ROLE NONE` under `readonly = 1` | Refused (unstated) | Succeeds ✗ | ### Error message and/or stacktrace As shown in repro steps above ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context A "trusted gateway" pattern is to: 1. Connect once as a service user. 2. Stamp a per-request setting (`SET somecustomsetting_confining_access = 'some_confining_scope'`). 3. Activate a role that carries a row policy reading that setting (`SET ROLE <reader_role>`). 4. Trust the role's attached profile to have engaged `readonly = 1 CONST` and to enforce the custom setting `CONST`, so user-supplied SQL forwarded on the same session cannot rewrite either to escape the safeguard 5. Use `somecustomsetting_confining_access` in row-security policies. The undocumented behaviour above makes step 4 silently a no-op. I worked around it. The gateway forces `readonly = 1` itself and relies on grants to confine roles. But the workaround isn't obvious and the failure mode is silent. An incorrectly-designed gateway looks correct, passes casual functional tests, and only fails against a knowledgeable attacker or deeper exploration.

signals.title: `count()`/`sum()` without `GROUP BY` returns zero rows instead of one when a single-shard `Distributed`/`Remote` table's only shard is skipped via `skip_unavailable_shards`
signals.text: **Describe the unexpected behaviour** An aggregate query with no `GROUP BY` is supposed to always return exactly one row, even over zero input rows (e.g. `SELECT count() FROM emptyTable` returns a single row containing `0`). This invariant breaks when the query reads directly from a `Distributed`/`Remote` table that has exactly one configured shard, and that shard gets skipped at runtime via `skip_unavailable_shards = 1` (e.g. because its target table doesn't exist). The query returns **zero rows** instead of one row with the aggregate's default value. Wrapping the exact same access in a derived subquery does *not* trigger the bug — it correctly returns one row. **Which ClickHouse versions are affected?** Confirmed on `26.8.1.1733` (master-built). The relevant code (`StorageDistributed::getQueryProcessingStage`'s `nodes == 1` shortcut) predates 26.8 and is unrelated to #100134's fix, so earlier versions are very likely affected too. **How to reproduce** ```sql CREATE TABLE t0 (c0 Int) ENGINE = MergeTree() PRIMARY KEY tuple(); CREATE TABLE t1 ENGINE = Remote('localhost:9000', default, t0) SETTINGS skip_unavailable_shards = 1; DROP TABLE t0; SET prefer_localhost_replica = 0; -- force the query through the remote/TCP path, not the local-execution shortcut SELECT count() AS s0 FROM t1; -- returns zero rows SELECT count() AS s0 FROM (SELECT c0 FROM t1) AS sub; -- returns one row: 0 ``` Not specific to `count()` — reproduces the same way with `sum(c0)`, and with `count(DISTINCT ...)` (which is how this was originally found, via BuzzHouse's `ifNull(count(DISTINCT expr), 0)` vs. `count()` over a `SELECT DISTINCT ... WHERE expr IS NOT NULL` consistency oracle — the two forms disagree on row count, and the oracle correctly flags it as a wrong-result bug). **Expected behavior** Throws an error, the same way it does with `skip_unavailable_shards = 0`: ``` Code: 279. DB::Exception: All connection tries failed. Log: There is no table `default`.`t0` on server: localhost:9000 : While executing Remote. (ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED) ``` **Error message and/or stacktrace** None — that's the problem. The query completes "successfully" with the wrong row count and no diagnostic. **Related issues and pull requests** Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/100134 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100141 **Additional context** Root cause: `StorageDistributed::getQueryProcessingStage` decides purely from the *static* configured shard count (`getClusterQueriedNodes`, from `cluster->getLocalShardCount() + getRemoteShardCount()`), with no knowledge of `skip_unavailable_shards`: ```cpp // src/Storages/StorageDistributed.cpp if (nodes == 1) return std::max(to_stage, QueryProcessingStage::Complete); // "the shard will finish this aggregation itself" if (nodes == 0) return QueryProcessingStage::FetchColumns; // "nobody to delegate to — aggregate on the initiator" ``` A single-shard `Remote`/`Distributed` table always takes the `nodes == 1` branch and gets `Complete`, so no local `Aggregating` step is ever built (confirmed via `EXPLAIN PIPELINE`: the plan is just `(ReadFromRemote)`, vs. `(Aggregating) → (ReadFromRemote)` for the subquery-wrapped form). When that one shard is skipped at runtime, there's nothing left to enforce the "≥1 row" invariant, and — unlike the case #100141 fixed — `query_plan.isInitialized()` is still `true` (a `ReadFromRemote` step *was* added), so the `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED` guard #100141 added in `StorageDistributed::read()` never fires either. The gap isn't in the plan-build-time guard from #100141; it's at execution time, where the "all connections gone, skip silently" shortcut doesn't know whether the pipeline had a local finalization step to fall back on: ```cpp // src/QueryPipeline/RemoteQueryExecutor.cpp, read() (~line 627) and needToSkipUnavailableShard() (~line 1221) if (context->getSettingsRef()[Setting::skip_unavailable_shards] && (0 == connections->size())) return ReadResult(Block()); // silent "no data", regardless of what stage was requested ``` `RemoteQueryExecutor` already tracks its own `stage` member. Proposed fix — reject silently when the requested stage was `Complete` (meaning the shard was trusted to fully compute the result, with no rescue path), reusing the same exception #100141 introduced for the sibling case: ```cpp if (context->getSettingsRef()[Setting::skip_unavailable_shards] && (0 == connections->size())) { if (stage == QueryProcessingStage::Complete) throw Exception(ErrorCodes::ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED, "No available shards to query"); return ReadResult(Block()); } ``` at both call sites. This only changes behavior in the actual failure case — normal single-shard queries where the shard stays reachable are untouched, so it shouldn't cost the "push the whole aggregate to the shard" optimization in the healthy path. cc @alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Quadratic complexity of applying MergeOnKey patch parts with long equal-key runs
signals.text: Applying `MergeOnKey` patch parts has quadratic complexity when the effective sorting key contains long equal-key runs: `applyPatchesMergeOnKey` is called for every result block (8192 rows during merges) and rebuilds the cursors and the per-run hash map (`EqualRunScratch::run_map` in `processEqualKeyCursors`) over **all** patch rows of the equal-key run every time. When the key is constant for the whole table — for example after `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY ORDER BY` shrinks the sorting key, as in the third scenario of `04509_lwu_sorting_key_common_prefix` — every result block re-inserts the entire patch into the hash map, so the total work is `O(result_blocks × patch_rows)`. Observed in a master stress test run (MSan): a background merge of `test_7.t_lwu_key_prefix` (854090 rows in 5 parts, 3 `MergeOnKey` patch parts of comparable size, effective key `k` equal to `0` for all rows) spent **~37 seconds per 8192-row block**, all inside patch application. The whole merge would have needed well over an hour. `gdb` caught the merge thread here: ``` #14 DB::(anonymous namespace)::processEqualKeyCursors (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:468 #15 DB::(anonymous namespace)::applyCursorsHeap (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:670 #16 DB::(anonymous namespace)::applyPatchesMergeOnKey (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:769 #17 DB::applyPatchesToBlock (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:818 #18 DB::MergeTreeReadersChain::applyPatches (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeReadersChain.cpp:861 #22 DB::MergeTreeSequentialSource::generate (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp:228 #33 DB::MergeTask::execute (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTask.cpp:2631 ``` Because server shutdown waited for this merge, the stress check reported `Possible deadlock on shutdown (see gdb.log)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=a013c79d6ac80373b820381527ea85823ab03834&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_msan%29&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_msan%29 (the shutdown side is addressed separately by cancelling in-flight merges on shutdown; this issue is about the complexity itself). The same pattern affects `SELECT` with `apply_patch_parts = 1`, not only merges: patch application runs per read block through `MergeTreeReadersChain`, with the same per-block rebuild of the run map. A possible fix: reuse the built run map across consecutive result blocks of the same equal-key run. The patch side of a run does not change between result blocks (the incremental patch readers keep all overlapping patch chunks resident), so the map built by `processEqualKeyCursors` could be cached in a small state object owned by `MergeTreeReadersChain` (per stream, single-threaded) and invalidated when the run key or the set of patch blocks changes. That makes the total work linear: build the map once per run, probe it with the result rows of each block. Reproducer (the merge is minutes-long in a release build already; scale `numbers(...)` up for more): ```sql SET enable_lightweight_update = 1, apply_patch_parts = 1; CREATE TABLE t_lwu_quadratic (k UInt64, u UInt64, v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree PRIMARY KEY k ORDER BY (k, u) SETTINGS enable_block_number_column = 1, enable_block_offset_column = 1, patch_parts_version = 'v2'; INSERT INTO t_lwu_quadratic SELECT 0, number, number FROM numbers(2000000); UPDATE t_lwu_quadratic SET v = v + 1 WHERE 1; ALTER TABLE t_lwu_quadratic MODIFY ORDER BY k; -- the effective key is now constant for the whole table OPTIMIZE TABLE t_lwu_quadratic FINAL; -- quadratic patch application ```
