signals.title: Automatic LowCardinality serialization based on uniq statistics
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/85145 --> This PR adds automatic `LowCardinality` serialization for `MergeTree`, analogous to the existing automatic `Sparse` serialization. A `String` or `FixedString` column whose declared type is **not** `LowCardinality` can now be stored on disk in dictionary-encoded form when it has a `uniq` statistic with a low cardinality estimate. The encoding is transparent: the column keeps its declared data type, flows through the query pipeline as a (non-native) `ColumnLowCardinality`, and is materialized to a full column at the boundaries that require it. **Motivation:** save disk space and read I/O for low-cardinality string columns without requiring users to declare the column type as `LowCardinality(...)`. **How it works** - A new per-part serialization kind `LOW_CARDINALITY` (shown as `LowCardinality` in `system.parts_columns.serialization_kind`). - The decision is made at write time from the **existing** `uniq` statistic — there are **no changes to statistics serialization**. In `MergeTreeDataWriter`, a `String`/`FixedString` column whose `uniq` estimate does not exceed the new `MergeTree` setting `max_uniq_number_for_low_cardinality` (default `0` = disabled), and which was not already chosen for `Sparse`, is stored with `SerializationLowCardinality`. The column must therefore declare `STATISTICS(uniq)` and have `materialize_statistics_on_insert` enabled. - A new `is_native` flag on `ColumnLowCardinality` makes `getDataType` report the nested type, so the "column class matches data type" invariant holds while such a column flows through the pipeline. It is materialized to a full column in `removeSpecialRepresentations` (aggregation, joins, squashing, blocks), in the merge-input step of `IMergingAlgorithm`, in the sorting and sparse-removing transforms, and in `IFunction`. The `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` pass skips columns stored as non-native `LowCardinality`, since the dictionary encoding does not expose the data type's regular subcolumns. - The kind is independent of sparse serialization: `SerializationInfo` entries for eligible columns are created in the writer, in merges, in mutations and in the per-table serialization hints even when `ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization = 1` disables `Sparse` entirely. **Notes** - Opt-in: disabled by default and requires an explicit `uniq` statistic, so existing tables are unaffected. Requires `allow_experimental_statistics`. - Reading a subcolumn of an encoded column (for example `s.size`) is not supported and reports `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`: the subcolumn's streams do not exist in a dictionary-encoded part. Making it read the full column and extract the subcolumn in memory needs a dedicated serialization and is left for a separate change. - Extracts and reimplements the automatic `LowCardinality` part of the draft #85145 against current `master`, without the statistics-serialization refactoring. That refactoring is still unmerged (#85145 and #109128 are open drafts). Validated locally with a server built from this branch: kind selection for `Wide` and `Compact` parts, `String` and `FixedString`, query correctness, functions, `GROUP BY`/`ORDER BY`/`DISTINCT`/`LIMIT BY`/window functions, joins, `IN` subqueries, `INSERT SELECT`, `UNION ALL`, `OPTIMIZE FINAL` (LowCardinality preserved through merges), mutations, `ALTER RENAME`/`MODIFY COLUMN`, `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, `PREWHERE`, input/output formats with and without `allow_special_serialization_kinds_in_output_formats`, and tables with mixed `Default` and `LowCardinality` active parts. The three tests also pass with `ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization` forced to `0.0` and `1.0`, with `enable_block_offset_column`/`enable_block_number_column`, with compact parts, and over repeated fully randomized runs. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added automatic `LowCardinality` serialization: a `String`/`FixedString` column that has a `uniq` statistic and low cardinality can be stored in dictionary-encoded form on disk while keeping its declared data type. signals.title: Add per-user filesystem cache disk usage metrics
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105020 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added opt-in Prometheus gauges for current filesystem cache usage (`filesystem_cache_size_bytes` and `filesystem_cache_elements`), labeled by `cache_name` and `user_id`. The gauges are exposed through `system.dimensional_metrics` and the Prometheus endpoint and controlled by the `expose_prometheus_cache_usage_metrics_per_user` cache setting, which is disabled by default. --- ### Description Adds two gauges exposed through `system.dimensional_metrics` and the Prometheus endpoint: | Name | Labels | |---|---| | `filesystem_cache_size_bytes` | `cache_name`, `user_id` | | `filesystem_cache_elements` | `cache_name`, `user_id` | **Motivation.** Operators can identify which users currently occupy filesystem cache space, measured both in bytes and in file segments, for each cache. **Mechanism.** Each enabled cache owns a `FileCacheUsageTracker` containing shared per-user atomic counters. Main cache-priority entries retain the corresponding counters and update them together with the existing cache size and element accounting. `ServerAsynchronousMetrics` periodically obtains a per-user snapshot through `getUsageStatPerClient` and updates the dimensional gauges. This keeps `DimensionalMetrics` updates out of cache mutation paths. Composite LRU, SLRU, and split-cache priorities share the same tracker, including during SLRU queue transitions. Counters use shared ownership so inactive users can be reclaimed safely. When a user no longer has cache entries and its counters are zero, the next snapshot removes it from the tracker. Stale dimensional metric label combinations are also removed. **Sampling.** The metrics reflect the most recent asynchronous metrics update. **Cardinality.** In-process cardinality is bounded by users currently retained by each cache, plus labels awaiting the next asynchronous metrics update. Stale `(cache_name, user_id)` label combinations are removed. The feature remains disabled by default because enabling per-user metrics can still create significant Prometheus time-series cardinality. ### Documentation entry: - [x] Documentation is updated.

signals.title: TTL CLEAR INDEX for MergeTree parts
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107804 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78714 TTL CLEAR INDEX lets a MergeTree table keep secondary indexes for recent parts while dropping the physical index files from old parts. I recommend reviewing commit-by-commit. The motivating case is Observability log storage. For log tables, the raw data is not always the dominant cost. Text indexes can be very large, and most queries only touch recent data. We want to keep the index where it helps and stop paying for it on old parts that are rarely searched. Example syntax: ```sql TTL timestamp + INTERVAL 7 DAY CLEAR INDEX message_text ``` This follows the existing meaning of `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR INDEX`: remove the per-part index files, but keep the index definition in table metadata. Queries remain correct. Parts without the index just fall back to scanning. ## What this changes The patch adds a new table TTL action, `CLEAR INDEX`, and stores its per-part min/max TTL info in `ttl.txt` as `index_clear_ttl`. When a part is fully past the TTL for a target index, future maintenance may remove that index’s files from the part. If the table later reads that part, the secondary index reader already handles missing index files and simply does not use that index for that part. The patch also adds system table visibility: ```text system.parts.index_clear_ttl_info.{index_name,expression,min,max} ``` ## Merge behavior There are two cases. First, normal merges apply the TTL policy to their output. If a merge output is fully past the `CLEAR INDEX` TTL, the merge should not retain the target index files. This is important for late-arriving data: a tiny old insert should not cause a merge that rebuilds a huge old text index. Second, there is a dedicated TTL maintenance merge type: `MergeType::TTLClearIndex`. This is used for the case where a single old part has expired index files and does not otherwise need a merge. The first implementation is intentionally conservative: it selects one source part and produces one replacement part. Dedicated `TTLClearIndex` selection obeys the normal full-part merge byte and row limits. This keeps cleanup conservative when preserving the part would require copying unchanged files rather than hardlinking them. For eligible full-storage parts, the implementation uses a fast path: hardlink or copy unchanged files, omit the expired index files, rewrite checksums and metadata, and publish the replacement part. Projection directories are copied wholesale because the row set is unchanged. This avoids reading and rewriting the raw data. If the fast path is not safe, the code falls back to the normal rewrite path. The fallback may rewrite the part, but it still must not retain expired index files in the final output. Parts with incomplete TTL metadata are not selected for dedicated cleanup; `MATERIALIZE TTL` or an ordinary merge must first recalculate the current TTL rules. The fast path currently opts out for cases like packed part storage, UUID parts, legacy parts without metadata-version files, metadata version mismatches, patch parts, part-format changes, and projection subdirectories it cannot copy as-is. On remote or zero-copy storage, it copies unchanged files instead of hardlinking them. It handles packed skip-index archives by excluding dirty `skp_idx.packed` files from the hardlink/copy set and rewriting the archive for surviving packed entries. ## Rollout safety `TTLClearIndex` is a new merge type, and merge types are serialized in replicated MergeTree log entries. Older replicas would not understand a new merge type. For that reason, generation is gated by a setting: ```sql enable_ttl_clear_index_merge_type_generation ``` The default is off. The binary can parse and execute `TTLClearIndex`, but a server will not write that merge type to the replicated log unless the setting is enabled. The intended rollout is: 1. deploy code everywhere; 2. once every replica that can read the log understands `TTLClearIndex`, enable generation; 3. later we can consider changing the default. With the gate off, replicas will not schedule dedicated `TTLClearIndex` maintenance work. Regular merges can still apply the clear-index TTL to their outputs, which is safe because missing per-part index files are already supported. ## Interaction with `SYSTEM STOP TTL MERGES` `CLEAR INDEX` is a TTL effect, so it respects the TTL merge blocker. If TTL merges are already stopped before a regular merge starts, the merge continues without applying clear-index TTL effects. If TTL merges are stopped after a merge has already decided to apply clear-index TTL effects, the merge is cancelled, matching existing TTL-delete behavior. ## Validation and edge cases covered The tests cover: - invalid target index names - per-part `index_clear_ttl_info` in `system.parts`, including the target index name - minmax index clearing - text index clearing - the late tiny insert case, where an old cleared part later merges with a small old part - adding `CLEAR INDEX` TTL to a table that already has old indexed data - TTL dependency recalculation after mutating a column used by the TTL expression - replicated execution with embedded Keeper - generation off vs generation on ## Things deliberately left conservative The fast path is narrow on purpose. Physically unsupported parts use the regular fallback, while parts with incomplete TTL metadata wait for recalculation. We can broaden the fast path later once we are comfortable with storage-specific details. The generation gate is also conservative. It is there to make rolling upgrades safe, not to disable all `CLEAR INDEX` TTL behavior. Possible follow-ups: - share more code with the existing `ALTER ... CLEAR INDEX` mutation path - add more schema-evolution tests around dropping or changing target indexes - add more direct instrumentation around which files were hardlinked vs copied in the fast path ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): MergeTree tables now support `TTL ... CLEAR INDEX index_name`, which clears secondary index files from parts once all rows in the part are past the TTL. This can help to manage the lifecycle of large indexes on older data, to conserve disk space. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108069&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108069](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108069+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Re-land: make Ctrl+C terminate the output of a result set in the client promptly
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/22426 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106430 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107845 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107828 ### Description This re-lands #106430 ("Make Ctrl+C terminate the output of a result set in the client promptly"), which was reverted by #107845, and folds in the data-race fix from the (now closed) #107828 so the feature can land safely this time. Why it was reverted: `BuzzHouse (amd_tsan)` reported a ThreadSanitizer data race on master (STID 5296-4b74) on the client's persistent stdout buffer (`std_out`, an `AutoCanceledWriteBuffer<WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor>`). The interruptible-output feature installed a cancellation hook on `std_out` at the start of `processOrdinaryQuery` and cleared it via `SCOPE_EXIT({ std_out->setCancellationHook({}); })` at the end of the same scope. When the result set is written with parallel formatting, `ParallelFormattingOutputFormat` runs a background collector thread that writes through `std_out` and reads its `cancellation_hook` in `WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor::nextImpl`. On the normal end-of-stream path the collector is joined by `output_format->finalize` before the scope guard runs, so the clear is safe; but on paths that leave `processOrdinaryQuery` by an exception without first finalizing the output (a `NetException`, or a `LocalFormatError` rethrown from `receiveResult`), the scope guard cleared the hook while the collector thread was still alive and reading it — a data race on the `std::function`. The fix (from #107828): the hook is cleared in `resetOutput` right after `output_format.reset()`, which destroys the parallel formatter and joins its collector thread, so the mutation is single-threaded with respect to `std_out`'s hook. The hook is also re-pointed for the teardown flushes that follow: on normal completion the interrupt handler is still armed and is honored, so a fresh Ctrl+C keeps interrupting a flush to a slow or stuck stdout; on exception paths the handler is already stopped (its `cancelled` is then unconditionally true), so the genuine cancellation flag is used instead to avoid discarding already-produced output. `resetOutput` runs on every exit path and at the start of the next query, so `std_out` (which outlives a single query) never carries a stale hook into the next query. The pager and `INTO OUTFILE ... AND STDOUT` buffers are per-query and destroyed in `resetOutput` after the collector join, so they were never affected. The change is split into two commits: the first reapplies #106430 verbatim (a revert of the revert #107845); the second folds in the #107828 fix, confined to `src/Client/ClientBase.cpp`. The low-level `WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor` (used server-wide on a hot single-threaded write path) is unchanged by the fix. Revert that motivated this: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107845 TSAN report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=73e97deb9abbc3258e75d297aabfc3fbe7c3ca5e&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_tsan%29&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_tsan%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Pressing Ctrl+C in `clickhouse-client`/`clickhouse-local` now promptly stops printing a large result set, even when the output is being written to a slow or stuck destination such as a slow terminal. Previously the first Ctrl+C could appear to have no effect. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108078&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108078](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108078+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support DEFAULT expressions inside Tuple data types
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/2797 `DEFAULT` expressions are now supported for named elements of `Tuple` data types, e.g.: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt8, c Tuple(a UInt8, s String DEFAULT 'Hello')) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; ``` Such defaults exist only at the syntax level: they are pulled up to the column level (for `CREATE TABLE` as well as `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` / `MODIFY COLUMN`), so the stored schema is normalized without any `DEFAULT` inside the data type. The column above is stored as type `Tuple(a UInt8, s String)` with a column-level `DEFAULT tuple(defaultValueOfTypeName('UInt8'), 'Hello')`. A default expression may reference other columns, but not other elements of the same tuple/nested; a reference that collides with an element name is rejected as ambiguous. Building an actual data type while a default is set throws. `DEFAULT` inside `Nested` (which is `Array(Tuple(...))`) or `Array` is not supported yet and is rejected with a clear `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` error, because a scalar element default cannot be represented as a static array column default. Note this is why issue #2797 (which asks specifically for `DEFAULT` on `Nested` elements) is linked as `Related` rather than `Closes`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `DEFAULT` expressions inside `Tuple` data types, e.g. `Tuple(a UInt8, s String DEFAULT 'Hello')`. The default is normalized away from the type and pulled up to the column level. Works for `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER TABLE ... ADD`/`MODIFY COLUMN`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108090&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108090](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108090+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108090&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108090](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108090+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Avoid copying data for the NONE compression codec when writing
signals.text: Avoid copying data for the `NONE` compression codec when writing. For `CODEC(NONE)` the compressed block on disk is byte-identical to the input, so the payload does not need to be copied between the compressor's working buffer and the output buffer. When a `CompressedWriteBuffer` exclusively owns its output buffer, the working buffer is now pointed directly into the output buffer (reserving room for the checksum and header in front of the data), so the caller writes the uncompressed data straight to where it will be flushed; `nextImpl` only fills in the header and checksum in place, with no payload copy. The header is written by a new `ICompressionCodec::writeHeader` helper factored out of `compress`. When the output buffer is too small, the writer falls back to the previous owned-buffer copy path. This is the same zero-copy buffer-aliasing technique that `HashingWriteBuffer` already uses. The zero-copy path (`out_buffer_is_exclusive`) is enabled only where the compressor is the sole, sequential writer of its output buffer: the wide-part column data streams, the primary-index stream, and the temporary-data buffer. It is intentionally left off where the output buffer is shared and written interleaved — the per-column streams of compact parts (which share one `plain_hashing`) and the network protocol buffer (interleaved with raw packet framing) — because there the reserved window could be overwritten by another writer. It is also left off for the marks streams of wide and compact parts: their `marks_file` has a small fixed-size buffer (4096 bytes), so the direct path would clamp `NONE`-coded mark blocks to it instead of the configured `marks_compress_block_size`; the regression test `04539_marks_compression_codec_none_block_size` covers this. Note: for `NONE`, compressed block sizes become bounded by the output buffer size, so the on-disk byte layout can differ slightly from before (an occasional shorter block at buffer boundaries). This is deterministic and does not affect reads. The read side already decompresses `NONE` data directly into the destination column via `readBig`, so no change is needed there. ### Performance evidence Measured with two `clickhouse` binaries built from the same base commit, differing only by this PR (cherry-picked onto the same parent), so the comparison isolates exactly this change. Isolated write-path microbenchmark — 4 GiB through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with the `NONE` codec into a discarding sink (no disk), 1 MiB blocks and output buffer, toggling only `out_buffer_is_exclusive`: | `out_buffer_is_exclusive` | throughput | |---|---| | `false` (old copy path) | ~8.5–9.2 GB/s | | `true` (zero-copy path) | ~13.6–14.0 GB/s | | **speedup** | **~1.5–1.6x** | End-to-end `INSERT` of 8 wide `String CODEC(NONE)` columns (3M rows, single insert thread, no dedup/squashing/sparse, merges stopped; baseline = exact parent commit; median of interleaved reps): **2.96s → 2.62s (~1.13x, ~13% faster)**. The end-to-end gain is below the disk-free microbenchmark because disk I/O and data generation (equal in both binaries) dominate the rest of the insert. A focused performance test, `tests/performance/codec_none_read.xml`, is added. It scans `CODEC(NONE)` columns, so in the PR-vs-master comparison the table is filled by each side's own write path (old vs new block layout) and then read by the identical read code. This guards against a read regression from the slightly changed `NONE` block layout, and tracks `NONE` read throughput in general (relevant for incompressible data such as vector embeddings). Measured read time is unchanged before/after (~0.62s vs ~0.61s for 100M rows, single thread), confirming the write-path change is read-neutral. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid an extra data copy when writing columns and temporary data compressed with the `NONE` codec by writing the data directly into the output buffer. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108096&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108096](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108096+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Exact-size parallel_hash build to avoid rehashing on cold builds
signals.text: Resolves https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111268 Builds `parallel_hash` hash tables exactly sized to the number of *distinct keys* so that cold builds (when no hash-table statistics are cached) avoid rehashing as the hash maps grow. Sizing now uses the distinct key count rather than the total number of buffered rows. This is the portion of #107189 focused on exact-size table builds, split out as requested by maintainers. The PR for compact index-based row references is a sibling update and not dependent on this one. ### Motivation Previously, when executing a cold build (no cached hash-table size statistics—e.g. first query run or stats collection off), `parallel_hash` would fill two-level maps incrementally, causing repeated rehashes as they expanded. However, by the end of the build phase, the count of distinct right keys per slot is essentially available, so we can size the maps exactly once and fill them in a single pass, skipping intermediary rehashing steps. ### What changed **Exact-size `parallel_hash` build (avoids rehashes on cold build).** In the absence of statistics hints, each `ConcurrentHashJoin` slot buffers its corresponding right-hand blocks during build. After build completion (`onBuildPhaseFinish`), the two-level buckets are pre-sized and populated in one go. This path is skipped if a reliable hint exists, for `any_take_last_row`, or for simple single-level `FixedHashMap` maps. These changes are tracked under `HashJoinDeferredPreallocatedElementsInHashTables` to keep the statistics-driven `HashJoinPreallocatedElementsInHashTables` event limited to that code path. **Table pre-sizing by distinct keys (using HLL), not buffered row count.** While buffering rows, each slot uses a HyperLogLog (precision 12, the `uniqHLL12` estimator) on the scatter hashes of its rows (with `intHash64`, since the scatter hash is a 32-bit CRC). Since slots are keyed by hash, the total distinct-key estimate is the sum of all per-slot HLL estimates. Both preallocation and spill projections are computed from this total, so builds with many duplicate rows no longer over-allocate memory by the redundancy factor. This eliminates the peak memory regression observed during initial test runs (see below for resolution details). **Deferred two-phase spill check.** During `SpillingHashJoin::addBlockToJoin`, live byte usage is checked per block (since no map exists during buffering), and a single projection-based check occurs during `onBuildPhaseFinish` just prior to replay and allocation. The projection (`getProjectedTotalByteCount`) covers post-replay table buffer sizes (based on the distinct key count), arena key copies, and a nearly exact bound for the `RowRefList::Batch` arena, allowing the final spill decision to compare directly to the cap. The allocation uses the full distinct-key count after this check passes, ensuring the replay will not trigger a rehash. **Skip deferred HLL-based sizing when a trusted statistics NDV is available.** If the query planner provides a reliable, uniq-backed NDV (number of distinct values) for the right join key (from `JoinStepLogical::result_column_stats`), there is no need to buffer and estimate; `deferred_build` is disabled and the streaming build preallocates hash maps to that count as with warm `ht_size` builds. A trust flag ensures that only real, `uniq`-backed values are used (never estimates like `0.1 × rows`). For composite/expression keys or non-MergeTree/non-subquery data sources, the deferred path remains active and uses HLL sizing. Correctness with `SpillingHashJoin`/`GraceHashJoin` and limits: - **Spill → grace transition based on projected byte usage.** During buffering the maps are empty; spill checks use `getProjectedTotalByteCount` (which includes buffered blocks, maps to be built, and the arena). If a spill is needed, it occurs before any replay that would overstep `max_bytes_before_external_join`, and buffered blocks are sent to `GraceHashJoin` instead of being built in-memory. - **Enforcement of size limits after replay.** Under `throw`, deferred building remains enabled and post-replay the real maps are validated against `max_rows_in_join` / `max_bytes_in_join` (row count is distinct key cells, bytes include arena), along with an early byte-cap check during buffering for fast failure. When `join_overflow_mode = 'break'` the deferred path is disabled since a truncated build can’t be replayed; the streaming build path enforces limits instead. - **Kill/cancellation during replay.** During map replay, `onBuildPhaseFinish` checks query status between buffered block replays, so `KILL QUERY` and `max_execution_time` will interrupt a large cold build. ### Limits and user-visible behavior Query results remain unchanged. Peak cold-build memory consumption is no longer artificially high for keys with many duplicates, since reserve sizing is based on the estimated distinct key count. The estimator (HLL) may undercount by many-sigma in rare cases, but such misses only result in bounded, correctness-safe rehashing. ### Known follow-ups (not part of this PR) - **Gate deferred path for tiny cold builds.** With the duplicate-aware (distinct-key) preallocation, prior issues in TPC-H Q16 are resolved. If performance regressions remain for small builds, consider directly gating the deferred buffer-then-replay path using an estimated build size threshold so very small cases stick to the streaming path. ### Changelog category - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry Improved the performance of `parallel_hash` `JOIN`s on cold builds: when no cached hash-table size statistics are available (the first execution of a query shape, or when statistics collection is off), `parallel_hash` now allocates hash tables up front to the number of distinct keys estimated while building—eliminating the repeated rehashing that previously occurred as tables grew. Best-case performance results showed a 2× speedup (first run of a large `INNER` join on mostly-unique `UInt64` keys), without increased peak memory on duplicate-heavy keys. ### Documentation entry - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Avoid per-row heap allocations in blocked Myers edit distance
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improved the performance of `levenshteinDistance` (and `editDistance`) for medium-length strings on ARM by avoiding per-row heap allocations in the blocked Myers code path. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 Fixes the ARM regression reported in #106595: `string_similarity` query `0` (`SELECT avg(levenshteinDistance(randomString(300), randomString(300))) FROM numbers(10000)`) was about +12.6% slower on Neoverse-V2. Root cause: the blocked Myers path (`BlockMyersEditDistance`, used for byte needles of 257..8192 bytes) allocated its per-row scratch buffers on the heap once per row through `VectorWithMemoryTracking`: the pattern-mask table `tbl` and the `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` bit vectors. Each allocation pairs a `malloc`/`free` with a `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomic update. On ARM those atomic updates are comparatively expensive, so this per-row churn showed up as the regression. Only this path was affected: the single-word Myers widths (`ByteEditDistanceMyersImpl`, needles up to 256 bytes) already use fixed stack scratch, which is why the other `string_similarity` queries did not regress. Fix: hold the per-row buffers in `PODArrayWithStackMemory`. It keeps an allocation up to its inline capacity in an inline buffer (no heap allocation, no `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomics) and transparently spills to a tracked allocation above it. The per-row allocation is therefore eliminated across each buffer's inline range, and the buffer management is a single idiomatic type instead of a hand-rolled stack-array + tracked-vector + raw-pointer split (suggested by @ nikitamikhaylov). The inline range differs per buffer because their shapes differ: - `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` hold one `Word` per block (1 KB each), so a 128-block inline buffer covers the full 8192-byte blocked-Myers range. - `tbl` is the ASCII pattern table, `256 * num_blocks` words (one row per byte value), so it is 256x larger per block. Its inline buffer covers needles up to 8 blocks (512 bytes, 16 KB); a full-range inline table would be about 256 KB, so longer needles transparently spill `tbl` to a tracked allocation while the bit vectors stay inline. The reported regression (300-byte needles, 5 blocks) is fully on the inline path for every buffer. Correctness: distances are unchanged. `02884_string_distance_function`, `03369_function_arrayLevenshtein` and `04125_array_levenshtein_types` pass, and a differential check of `editDistance` and `editDistanceUTF8` against a brute-force DP reference (1392 random pairs) matches exactly, including the block and inline/spill boundary lengths (64/128/192/256/512/8192). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108185&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108185](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108185+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1883` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix sort order violation for TTL GROUP BY with SET on a sorting key column
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108514 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108514 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110098 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results and a `Sort order of blocks violated` logical error for `MergeTree` tables that use `TTL ... GROUP BY ... SET`. Assigning a column the sorting key depends on no longer writes a part whose primary index disagrees with the data; every `MATERIALIZED` column that reads an assigned column is now recomputed instead of keeping its pre-`SET` value (so skip indices and projections over it are no longer built from stale data); and a table with several `GROUP BY` TTLs no longer loses or fragments groups when an earlier `SET` rewrites a later TTL's `GROUP BY` key or expiry input. Both new paths are bounded by new `MergeTree` settings, each spilling to disk past its threshold instead of holding the whole part in memory: `ttl_resort_max_bytes_before_external_sort` (default 256 MiB) for the repair sort, and `ttl_group_by_unsorted_max_bytes_before_external_group_by` (default 256 MiB) for the hash aggregation a later `GROUP BY` TTL performs when an earlier `SET` rewrote its grouping key. ### Description Found via the AST fuzzer / stress tests (`Stress test (arm_debug)`, `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted, old_compatibility)`), recurring under STID `3413-350b`. Example CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100173&sha=5cfd0f5aeabe1f357125fd015ebbaaf90717b30e&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_debug%29 **Reproducer** (master, any build with assertions aborts; release writes a corrupt part): ```sql CREATE TABLE t (k Float64, ts DateTime, v Float64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (k, toStartOfDay(ts)) TTL ts + toIntervalDay(1) GROUP BY k, toStartOfDay(ts) SET ts = max(ts) + interval 100 years, k = max(v) SETTINGS min_bytes_for_full_part_storage = 128; SYSTEM STOP MERGES t; INSERT INTO t VALUES (1.0, '2000-06-09 10:00', 96827); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1.0, '2000-06-10 10:00', 41302); SYSTEM START MERGES t; OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL; -- Logical error: 'Sort order of blocks violated for column number 0, left: Float64_96827, right: Float64_41302...' ``` **Root cause.** `TTLAggregationAlgorithm::finalizeAggregates` emits aggregated groups in the input (already-sorted) order. The merge writer trusts the stream order: it reads the primary-key columns by name (including the materialized sort-key expression column such as `toStartOfDay(ts)`, which still holds its pre-`SET` value) and writes them without re-sorting. When the `SET` clause rewrites a sort-key column, the produced part is therefore no longer ordered by the sorting key. A debug build catches this with the merge's `CheckSortedTransform` and aborts; a release build silently writes a part whose primary index does not match the data, which can return wrong results for primary-key-filtered queries. **Fix.** After the TTL step, when a `GROUP BY` TTL assigns a column the sorting key depends on, recompute the sort-key expression columns from the post-`SET` values (overwriting the now-stale materialized ones) and re-sort by the sorting key. This is done in both the merge pipeline (`MergeTask`) and the mutation pipeline (`MutateTask`, e.g. `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL`), where the rebuilt primary index and the skip-index expressions must see the same order. Every repair is gated on the `SET` targets of the `GROUP BY` TTLs that can actually fire in the part (`getFiringGroupByTTLSetTargets`), so it is a no-op for every other merge, and a not-yet-expired `GROUP BY ... SET` on the sorting key does not cost a whole-part re-sort. The re-sort of a whole part must not be unbounded in a background merge, so it is bounded by the new `MergeTree` setting `ttl_resort_max_bytes_before_external_sort` (default 256 MiB, `0` disables spilling). Background contexts inherit `max_bytes_before_external_sort = 0`, which would disable spilling entirely; `buildTTLResortSortingSettings` applies the table-level threshold and zeroes the query-memory gate derived from `max_bytes_ratio_before_external_sort`, so the threshold is the real bound. The temporary-data scope comes from the global context (`getSharedTempDataOnDisk`), which background merges and mutations have. Two further correctness gaps of `TTL ... GROUP BY ... SET`, both pre-existing on master, are fixed here as well, because the first shares the `MATERIALIZED` dependency analysis this change introduces and the second would otherwise be *worsened* by the repair sort — the shape stops failing with the loud `Sort order of blocks violated` and starts silently producing wrong aggregates instead: * **Stale `MATERIALIZED` columns.** `TTLAggregationAlgorithm` carries every column that is not a `GROUP BY` key or a `SET` target forward as `any(...)`, so a `MATERIALIZED` column keeps its pre-`SET` value even though its source was rewritten (`d Date MATERIALIZED toDate(ts)` with `... SET ts = ...`). The stored value, and any skip index or projection rebuilt from it, was written stale — a `minmax` index over `d` then pruned away rows that a brute-force scan returns. Every `MATERIALIZED` column that transitively reads a firing `SET` target is now recomputed from its default expression on both the merge and the mutation path, matching what `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE` already does through `column_to_affected_materialized`. A `MATERIALIZED` column that mixes an `EPHEMERAL` input with a `SET` target cannot be recomputed during a merge (ephemeral columns are never stored), so each one is reported with a warning instead of silently written stale, mirroring `MutationsInterpreter::prepare`. * **Several `GROUP BY` TTLs in one table.** `TTLTransform` runs each `TTLAggregationAlgorithm` sequentially on the same block, and each assumes its input is contiguous in its own `GROUP BY` keys. An earlier `SET` that rewrites a later TTL's key (`TTL ts1 + 1d GROUP BY k SET k = max(v), ts2 + 1d GROUP BY k SET payload = sum(payload)`) split one logical group into several partial aggregates, and a derived key or expiry input (a computed key, a subcolumn, or a `MATERIALIZED` column) was even read at its pre-`SET` value. Such a TTL is now detected by mapping its keys and expiry inputs back to their physical storage columns (`groupByKeysAffectedByEarlierSet`, `groupByTTLExpiryAffectedByEarlierSet`), told to aggregate the whole stream instead of taking the streaming flush-on-key-change path, and its stale derived columns are refreshed before it runs (`buildRefreshGroupByKeysDAG`). The lost-order state cascades, since finalizing an unsorted aggregation emits groups in hash-table order. That unsorted path holds every expired key of the part at once, so it is bounded by the new `ttl_group_by_unsorted_max_bytes_before_external_group_by`. Making the bound effective exposed a second defect in the same code: `Aggregator` can only spill a two-level hash table, so with both two-level thresholds at 0 the bound was dead letter, and had it ever fired, `finalizeAggregates` used `convertToChunks` on the in-memory state alone and would have silently dropped the spilled groups from the written part. `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes` is now tied to the bound so the spill sites are reachable, and `finalizeAggregates` flushes the in-memory remainder and merges the spilled generations back bucket by bucket via `Aggregator::mergeBlocks`, keeping the merge-back high-water mark at one bucket. Both halves are new in this pull request, so no release ever had a live spill here. **Tests.** `03545_number_of_rows_in_ttltransform`, which intentionally exercises `SET` on sort-key columns while the output stays ordered, passes unchanged. New: * `04327_ttl_group_by_set_sort_key_resort` — `Float64`, `String` and `LowCardinality(String)` sort keys with a non-monotonic `SET`, subcolumn and wrapped-subcolumn sorting keys, the `MATERIALIZE TTL` mutation path with skip-index rebuild, `MATERIALIZED` sort keys (direct, chained and over a subcolumn), the mixed-`EPHEMERAL` shape, and a control case that only sets a non-sort-key column. Each asserts the part is physically ordered by the sorting key. * `04511_ttl_multi_group_by_set_rewrites_key` — several `GROUP BY` TTLs whose keys and expiry inputs are rewritten by an earlier `SET`, including derived keys, the cascade, the not-yet-expired case that must keep the fast path, and stale non-sort-key `MATERIALIZED` columns with a `minmax` index over them. * `04661_ttl_group_by_set_resort_external_sort_spill` — forces `ttl_resort_max_bytes_before_external_sort = 1` and asserts via `ExternalSortWritePart` in `system.part_log` that both the merge and the `MATERIALIZE TTL` path really spill and still produce a correct, physically sorted part. * `04327_ttl_group_by_set_sort_key_resort` also forces `ttl_group_by_unsorted_max_bytes_before_external_group_by = 1` and asserts via `ExternalAggregationWritePart` that the unsorted aggregation really spills while the group count is preserved. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108550&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108550](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108550+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Switch the default compression to ZSTD(3) for table data and network
signals.text: Switch the default compression in ClickHouse from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`, for both on-disk table data and network communication. ### Motivation `LZ4` has been the default for a long time and optimizes for speed, but `ZSTD(3)` gives substantially better compression ratios at a still-modest CPU cost, reducing both storage footprint and network traffic out of the box. ClickHouse Cloud already uses a stronger default; this aligns the self-managed defaults. ### What changes - **On-disk table data.** `CompressionCodecFactory::getDefaultCodec` now returns `ZSTD(3)` instead of `LZ4`. For `MergeTree` column data the built-in default is *size-aware*: when a column specifies no codec and no `<compression>` server-config case matches, `CompressionCodecSelector::choose` uses the faster `LZ4` below 100 MB and `ZSTD(3)` at or above it, so freshly inserted data starts as `LZ4` and the bigger parts produced by background merges switch to `ZSTD(3)`. The threshold is applied to the part size known when the codec has to be chosen, before the data is written - `0` for a freshly inserted part and the source parts' size for a merge or a mutation - which is the same estimate the `<compression>` `min_part_size` conditions have always been matched against, not the size of the resulting part. A rewrite that shrinks its input, such as a `TTL DELETE` or a collapsing merge, is therefore classified by the input size and can emit a part below the threshold that is still `ZSTD(3)`. The direct `getDefaultCodec` users — the `Log` family, part checksums, the HTTP `compress=1` output, the `StripeLog` data stream, and the persistent `Set`/`Join` files — are not size-aware and switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. External temporary (spill) files are unaffected: they keep their own `temporary_files_codec` default (`LZ4`). - **Network.** The defaults of `network_compression_method` (`LZ4` → `ZSTD`) and `network_zstd_compression_level` (`1` → `3`) are changed, so the native client/server and Distributed (server/server) protocol uses `ZSTD(3)` by default. The changes are recorded in `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` so the `compatibility` setting restores the previous behavior for these paths. The distributed-query streaming exchange (`StreamingExchangeSink`) does not read `network_compression_method` and always uses the server default codec; this is safe because each frame is self-describing (the receiver auto-detects the codec) and the exchange is a transient, same-version channel — `StreamingExchangeProtocol` rejects peers on a different protocol version, so a stream is never read back by a node expecting a different codec. - **Upgrade safety.** The append-only `Log`/`TinyLog`/`StripeLog` engines resolve the default codec at write time, so a table written before the upgrade (`LZ4`) and appended to after it (`ZSTD(3)`) ends up with mixed-codec blocks in one file. Their readers now pass `allow_different_codecs = true` (as the `MergeTree` reader already does) so such files still read back correctly. The legacy custom-frame Keeper snapshot format (`compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format = false`) is pinned to `LZ4` so it stays the documented format. Columns, tables, and connections that specify a codec or method explicitly are unaffected — with one exception: streams written through the built-in default codec directly, which ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config. The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files (written by `SetOrJoinSink` and `StorageJoin::mutate` through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with no codec), and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`, via `MergeTreeDataPartChecksums::write`) always follow the new default; see the changelog entry below for the per-path rollback. ### Validation Built locally and verified against the new binary: - A `MergeTree` table created with no explicit codec follows the size-aware default: small parts report `LZ4` and parts whose write-time size estimate reaches 100 MB report `ZSTD(3)` as their `default_compression_codec` in `system.parts`. Direct `getDefaultCodec` streams (e.g. `StripeLog`) report `ZSTD(3)` regardless of size. - `system.settings` shows `network_compression_method = ZSTD` and `network_zstd_compression_level = 3`. - End-to-end `SELECT`/`INSERT` over the native protocol with default (now `ZSTD`) network compression work; all of `LZ4`/`lz4hc`/`zstd`/`none` still work and an invalid method still errors with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. - The `02995_new_settings_history` consistency check passes (both setting changes are recorded). - The on-disk byte-dump tests (`02047_log_family_*_data_file_dumps`) were regenerated for the new default: `Log`/`TinyLog` keep `LZ4`-pinned columns, while `StripeLog`'s shared `data.bin`/`index.mrk` reflect the `ZSTD(3)` default (it uses `getDefaultCodec` and ignores the per-column codec). Size-sensitive stateless and integration tests that assert compressed byte sizes were pinned back to `LZ4` (cache segment sizes, distributed-batch corruption offsets, full-disk thresholds, frozen-part checksums). The CI performance comparison does **not** measure this tradeoff: the harness pins the built-in default codec to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/config.d/compression.xml`) and `network_compression_method` to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/users.d/perf-comparison-tweaks-users.xml`) on *both* the reference and the tested server, deliberately, so the report measures query logic rather than drowning in expected codec regressions. It therefore serves only as a regression filter for the non-codec parts of this change; the storage/network-vs-CPU tradeoff of `LZ4` → `ZSTD(3)` itself is a well-known property of the two codecs and is not measured by this pull request's CI. Documentation updated accordingly, including the `Native` format and protocol specifications and the `<compression>` config examples. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The default compression method is changed from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. For client/server and server/server network communication it switches uniformly to `ZSTD(3)`. For on-disk table data, `MergeTree` column data now uses a size-aware built-in default — `LZ4` below 100 MB and `ZSTD(3)` at or above it, applied to the part size known at write time (the source parts' size for a merge or a mutation) rather than to the size of the resulting part — while the direct built-in-default streams (the `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and part checksums) switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. This improves compression ratios and reduces storage and network usage out of the box, at a modest increase in CPU usage. None of the on-disk or HTTP paths are controlled by `compatibility`; the previous behavior can be restored per path as follows. For client/server and Distributed network compression, use the `compatibility` setting (or set `network_compression_method = 'LZ4'`). For `MergeTree` column data, set a column/table `CODEC(LZ4)` or configure the server `<compression>` default to `LZ4`. For the `Log`/`TinyLog` engines, set a column `CODEC(LZ4)` (their default does not consult the `<compression>` config). The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`) use the built-in default codec directly — they ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config — so they always use the new `ZSTD(3)` default and have no runtime rollback; reading stays correct because every compressed frame is self-describing. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108786&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108786](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108786+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Allow Distributed and Remote tables in Replicated databases
signals.text: `database_replicated_allow_only_replicated_engine` rejects table engines that keep their own unreplicated data on disk in a `Replicated` database. Before this change, `Distributed` was also rejected because its optional background `INSERT` queue makes `storesDataOnDisk` return true, even though the queue is a transient send buffer and the table's actual data belongs to its destination shards. This change distinguishes table-owned on-disk data from auxiliary delivery state. The restriction applies to non-`ATTACH` `CREATE` queries when `database_replicated_allow_only_replicated_engine = 1`. | Engine or group | Result | Reason | |---|---|---| | `ReplicatedMergeTree` family and `SharedMergeTree` | Allow | The engine provides a replication or shared-storage contract. | | Writable non-replicated `MergeTree` with a local or remote storage policy | Reject | It owns unreplicated on-disk table data; a remote disk alone does not establish replication. | | Static read-only non-replicated `MergeTree` | Allow | It cannot create new table-owned data. | | `Log`, `TinyLog`, `StripeLog`, `Set`, `Join`, `EmbeddedRocksDB`, and database `File` | Reject | They own unreplicated on-disk table data. | | `MaterializedPostgreSQL` | Reject | It owns a local nested table. | | `Distributed`, `Remote`, and `RemoteSecure` | Allow | Their optional local queue is auxiliary delivery state rather than data of the table itself. | | `Memory`, `Buffer`, and `Null` | Allow | They do not own on-disk table data. | | `Merge`, `Alias`, and `View` | Allow | They are metadata-only. | | Views with inner tables | Depends | Each generated inner table is created and checked separately. | | External-storage engines, data lakes, external databases, and external queues | Allow | Their data is managed outside ClickHouse-owned table storage. | | Lazy `StorageTableProxy` | Reject conservatively | The nested storage is unknown without loading it. | `ATTACH` remains outside the existing gate. The `Distributed` background `INSERT` queue is local to the node accepting an insert and is not replicated. Users requiring acknowledgement only after data reaches the destination shards should set `distributed_foreground_insert = 1`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow `Distributed`, `Remote`, and `RemoteSecure` tables in `Replicated` databases when `database_replicated_allow_only_replicated_engine` is enabled, while continuing to reject writable non-replicated `MergeTree` tables using local or remote storage policies. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108820&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108820](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108820+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix LOGICAL_ERROR on premature S3 connection close through the filesystem cache
signals.text: ## Description When an S3 connection closes mid-read while the object still reports its full size, the read used to surface as a cache-layer `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Having zero bytes, but range is not finished`) for what is really a transient I/O failure. `ReadBufferFromS3` now heals a premature stream close by reconnecting and resuming from the current offset instead of reporting a truncated EOF. The expected end of the read is taken from `read_until_position` when set and from the known object `file_size` otherwise, so both the filesystem-cache range-reader path and full-object reads (`S3ObjectStorage::readObject`, `BackupWriterS3::readFile`, which read with `read_until_position == 0`) are covered. It falls back to a regular retryable `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` only when no progress can be made (an empty response for a non-finished range) and reports `S3_OBJECT_CHANGED_DURING_READ` if the object was overwritten during the read. Includes failpoints and stateless tests (`04417`, `04506`, `04507`, `04509`) that reproduce the premature-close, empty-response, changed-object, and full-object recovery paths. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108948 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Having zero bytes, but range is not finished`) that could occur when an S3 connection was closed prematurely while reading (both through the filesystem cache and for full-object reads). ClickHouse now reconnects and resumes the read from the current offset, and reports a regular retryable read error only when no progress can be made or the object changed during the read. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108950&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108950](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108950+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Assign merges for all partitions at once for OPTIMIZE FINAL
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/46770 For a non-replicated `MergeTree` table, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` without an explicit partition used to process partitions one by one: it selected and ran the merge for one partition, waited for it to finish, and only then moved on to the next one. On a table with many partitions this serialized all the work and only ever showed a single merge in `system.merges`. Now the per-partition merges are assigned and executed in parallel, so all partitions are merged at once. The degree of parallelism is bounded by the configured `background_pool_size` and reserves only currently available merge-executor capacity. This mirrors how `StorageReplicatedMergeTree::optimize` already assigns a merge per partition and then waits for all of them. Notes: - Tables inside an explicit transaction keep the sequential path, because parallel merges would otherwise share a single transaction object that is not made for concurrent use. - The wait for already-running merges inside `selectPartsToMerge` (the `OPTIMIZE FINAL` path) is now scoped to the current partition: merges in other partitions cannot prevent selecting all the parts of this one, and waiting for them would needlessly serialize the parallel assignment. Verified on a local build: on a table with 8 partitions, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` now runs 8 merges concurrently (observed via `system.merges`) instead of one at a time, and every partition is still correctly merged into a single part (checked for `MergeTree`, `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL DEDUPLICATE`, and `ReplacingMergeTree`, plus the `optimize_skip_merged_partitions` / `optimize_throw_if_noop` no-op paths and two concurrent `OPTIMIZE FINAL` queries). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on a non-replicated `MergeTree` table now assigns and runs the merges for all partitions at once instead of processing them one partition at a time. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109004&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109004](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109004+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Delete Iceberg table files on DROP with iceberg_delete_data_on_drop
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108524 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `DROP TABLE` on an Iceberg table with `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop = 1` not deleting the table's files, which made re-creating a table at the same path fail with `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS`. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108524 Long-standing (reproduces at least down to v25.9), not a recent regression. Two independent bugs, both in the self-managed Iceberg drop path: 1. `IcebergMetadata::drop` passed the table path as both the listing base and the prefix. `listFiles` keys on `path / prefix`, so it looked under `table_path/table_path` and matched nothing. Fixed with an empty prefix, matching the existing `create` and `Hudi` callers. 2. `StorageObjectStorage::drop` runs in a background pool and read `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop` from the global context, always the default `false`, so deletion never ran even with bug 1 fixed. The value is now captured from the query context in `checkTableCanBeDropped` and applied to the context passed to the background drop, the same `mutable`-flag pattern `StorageNATS`/`StorageRabbitMQ` use for drop-time state. The `DataLakeCatalog` path needed separate work: `DatabaseDataLake::dropTable` re-resolves a fresh storage instance, so it never saw the `checkTableCanBeDropped` snapshot and its uninitialized metadata made `configuration->drop()` a no-op. It now replays `checkTableCanBeDropped` with the query context, and `drop()` initializes metadata only when deleting data. With the setting off (default) files are left in place, as before. Failure handling is per owning database (`DropCleanupPolicy`): reattaching databases never get a partially deleted table back, async-retry databases keep their retry metadata, and the catalog path keeps its row and metadata anchor so a failed DROP stays retryable. Known residual, catalog-backed path only: a DROP failing midway is retryable but not atomic. If a later data delete throws, or the catalog removal does, the table stays visible with part of its data deleted. Atomicity needs the reverse ordering (trading this for orphaned files with no SQL retry path) or a persisted drop intent, both outside this fix. Regression tests `04365_iceberg_delete_data_on_drop_108524` and `04366_iceberg_drop_best_effort_cleanup_109071` fail without the fix and pass with it, plus catalog-path coverage in `test_database_iceberg`. Default-off behavior is checked unchanged. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109071&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109071](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109071+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix INNER JOIN cardinality underestimation in join reorder optimizer
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry Fixed the join reorder optimizer placing a large fact table on the hash-join build side in star-schema queries when column statistics are unavailable. A narrow guard now suppresses the build/probe swap when a statistics-less composite subtree that contains a base table larger than the other side is joined with a single smaller dimension table. ### Analysis The join reorder optimizer uses `1/max(NDV_left, NDV_right)` as join selectivity. Without per-column NDV statistics, `estimated_rows` of the table is used as a proxy for NDV. For a star schema query like `fact JOIN dim_a ON dim_a.key = fact.key_a JOIN dim_b ON dim_b.key = fact.key_b`, the selectivity of `fact JOIN dim_a` becomes `1/max(100000, 100) = 1/100000`, producing a cardinality estimate of `100000 * 100 / 100000 = 100` rows — far below the actual ~100000 rows. This makes the optimizer believe the intermediate result is tiny (100 rows) compared to `dim_b` (200 rows), so it swaps the join sides and puts the large fact table on the build side — exactly the wrong decision for a star-schema workload. ### Fix A narrow swap guard in `chooseJoinOrder` (`optimizeJoin.cpp`): do not swap build/probe sides when all of the following hold: - the left side is a composite (multi-table) subtree whose cardinality estimate is proxy-based. The join order optimizer records this in `DPJoinEntry::estimate_is_stats_based` (`markStatsBasedEstimates` in `joinOrder.cpp`), filled for the chosen plan before `cleanupJoinPredicates` rewrites the predicates. It mirrors every NDV lookup `computeSelectivity` makes: both sides of every equi-predicate attached to a step (including predicates routed to `residual_filter`) and every member of every column-equivalence class spanning the two sides — so a proxy-based lookup on the transitive-predicate path is caught even when predicate cleanup removes it from the step's expression. Since the step selectivity is the minimum over contributions of `1/max(ndv...)`, a proxy fallback only affects the estimate when its value actually wins that competition, so a step is marked proxy-based only when the largest proxy-backed NDV strictly exceeds every stats-backed one — a stats-less small dimension joined on a fact key with a real `uniq` statistic does not poison the flag. The flag is recursive over the whole subtree because the underestimation of an earlier proxy-based join propagates upward, - the right side is a single table (a dimension), - the composite contains a base table larger than the right side's estimate. The guard only gates the physical build/probe-side choice and never changes cardinality estimates, so the enumerated join order is unaffected. When column statistics are available, the standard formula already produces reasonable estimates and the guard does not fire. Regression tests: `04498_join_reorder_star_schema_cardinality` (no statistics at all), `04609_join_reorder_star_schema_mixed_stats` (an unrelated dimension statistic must not disable the guard), `04611_join_reorder_star_schema_partial_key_stats` (a statistic on a later join key must not mask an earlier proxy-based join inside the composite), `04621_join_reorder_star_schema_transitive_stats` (with `enable_join_transitive_predicates`, a stats-less fact key reachable only through the equivalence class must not be masked by a stats-covered retained predicate), `04622_join_reorder_star_schema_dominant_stats` (a proxy lookup that loses the NDV competition to a real fact-key statistic must not fire the guard, so the beneficial swap of the correctly-estimated composite is kept). (An earlier revision of this PR implemented this as an unconditional `INNER JOIN` cardinality floor, and an intermediate revision as an NDV cap in `estimateJoinCardinality`; both changed cardinality estimates globally and were replaced by this narrower guard.) Per review, the `03960_join_order_dphyp_basic`/`_cycle`/`_transitive_predicates` tests now pin `materialize_statistics_on_insert = 1` — they declared `uniq` statistics and set `use_statistics = 1` but never materialized the statistics, so their pinned plans were driven by the `estimated_rows` NDV proxy. Their references are regenerated for plans driven by real NDV estimates (the swap guard does not fire on them anymore); result-check hashes and row counts are unchanged. Example of a star-schema query whose performance was poor because `lineorder` (the fact table) was moved to the build side: ```sql SELECT l.*, c.C_NAME, s.S_NAME, p.P_NAME, d.D_YEAR FROM lineorder AS l INNER JOIN customer AS c ON c.C_CUSTKEY = l.LO_CUSTKEY INNER JOIN supplier AS s ON s.S_SUPPKEY = l.LO_SUPPKEY INNER JOIN part AS p ON p.P_PARTKEY = l.LO_PARTKEY INNER JOIN date AS d ON d.D_DATEKEY = l.LO_ORDERDATE; ```

signals.title: Require a join subquery alias only when it removes a real ambiguity
signals.text: `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 1` (the default) rejected every unaliased subquery, table function or union used in a multi-table join, even when the missing alias could not cause any ambiguity. That is stricter than necessary: an alias only serves to qualify a column, so it is only needed when the unaliased table expression exposes a column whose name also occurs in another table expression of the same join. `validateJoinTableExpressionWithoutAlias` now throws `ALIAS_REQUIRED` only on such a name collision (computed with the existing `getColumnsFromTableExpression` helper over the sibling table expressions), and otherwise allows the missing alias. Genuine ambiguities involving non-sibling table expressions are still caught later by the normal `AMBIGUOUS_IDENTIFIER` resolution, exactly as they are for ordinary tables. This lets standard queries such as TPC-DS q14 (whose `cross_items` derived table has no correlation name) run without setting `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 0`: ```sql SELECT i_item_sk FROM item, (SELECT iss.i_brand_id AS brand_id FROM store_sales, item AS iss ...) WHERE i_brand_id = brand_id; -- no shared column name -> no alias needed ``` Notes: - Validation in `resolveJoin`/`resolveCrossJoin` is moved to run after all table expressions of the join are resolved, so sibling columns are known when the collision is checked. - The change is purely permissive: it never turns a previously-succeeding query into an error. When the columns of any side cannot be determined it falls back to the old strict behavior. - Only the analyzer is affected; the deprecated non-analyzer path keeps the stricter behavior. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): With `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 1` (the default), the analyzer now rejects an unaliased subquery or table function in a join only when the missing alias would make one of its columns unreachable, for example because the name collides with another joined table expression or is shadowed by an in-scope alias; otherwise the query is allowed. If the analyzer cannot determine the exposed names up front, it keeps the old strict behavior. Unambiguous queries, such as some standard TPC-DS queries, no longer require adding an alias. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109368&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109368](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109368+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
