signals.title: Fix `bloom_filter` over-pruning for a wide string constant
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106924 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107076 --> Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112206 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a `bloom_filter` skip index dropping granules that contain matching rows when a `String` or `FixedString` column is compared for equality against a constant that is wider than the indexed type, so that queries such as `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE s = toFixedString('abc', 5)` no longer silently return too few rows. ### Description `String` and `FixedString` equality compares zero-padded, so a constant of `M` bytes matches an unbounded family of stored values: the value itself and every trailing-`\0` extension of it (`'abc'`, `'abc\0'`, `'abc\0\0'`, ...). The read path built a single hash from the converted constant while the index stores one hash per exact stored value, so at most one member of that family could match and granules holding any other member were pruned away. Because the family is unbounded, no finite set of hashes can represent it, so this declines index analysis for exactly those cases and falls back to a full scan. The rule is about byte length, not the constant's declared type. `convertFieldToType` pads a `String` constant into a `FixedString(N)` target only when it is shorter than `N` and never truncates, so a plain `String` constant wider than the index is also hashed over more bytes than the index stored, while zero-padded comparison still matches at runtime. The index is therefore used only when the indexed type is a `FixedString(N)` with `N` at least the constant's byte length. A `Variant` or `Dynamic` constant is declined for a related reason: it keeps its declared wrapper type while handing out the nested, already-padded value, so its active alternative cannot be recognised here. The guard is asymmetric and keeps pruning wherever the conversion is faithful, which the tests assert in both directions against an `ENGINE = Log` oracle. Two sound cases lose pruning: a constant wider than the index whose extra bytes are not all `\0`, which can never match any row, and a `Variant` or `Dynamic` constant whose active alternative is a plain `String`. Neither changes a result. Keeping the condition identical to the already-merged primary key rule in `KeyCondition` (commit 67f9c2c8a65067) was preferred over refining it. <details> <summary>Validation matrix (index type x constant, before and after)</summary> Each cell compares the indexed table against an `ENGINE = Log` oracle holding the same rows, with `use_skip_indexes = 0` as a third control. `FS(k)` is a `toFixedString(..., k)` constant; `str(k)` is a plain `String` literal of `k` bytes. | index type | `FS(2)` | `FS(3)` | `FS(4)` | `FS(5)` | `str(2)` | `str(4)` | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `String` | WRONG | WRONG | WRONG | WRONG | ok | ok | | `FixedString(2)` | ok | WRONG | WRONG | WRONG | ok | WRONG | | `FixedString(3)` | ok | ok | WRONG | WRONG | ok | WRONG | | `FixedString(4)` | ok | ok | ok | WRONG | ok | ok | The boundary is exactly `N >= M`, with a `String` index behaving as `N = 0`; a `String` constant against a `String` index is always sound because that comparison is byte-exact. After the fix every cell agrees with the oracle. Enumerating the predicate over (index type x constant declared type x byte length) shows the widened condition changes only cells that pair a `FixedString(N)` index with a `String` constant of more than `N` bytes, and no others. The wrapper carriers `LowCardinality(String)`, `Nullable(String)`, `LowCardinality(FixedString(3))` and `Nullable(FixedString(3))` were wrong before and are fixed, as are `LowCardinality(FixedString)` and `LowCardinality(Nullable(FixedString))` constants. A `bloom_filter` index on a `Variant` column is rejected at DDL validation, so that type cannot be indexed. Pruning is unchanged for the sound cells, verified through the granule reduction reported by `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`. `IN`, `NOT IN`, `has` on `Array(String)` and the `mapContains` family were measured byte-identical before and after. `notEquals` shares the branch and is covered, but that path never prunes, so nothing observable changes there. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112639&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112639](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112639+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Improve canceling queries in nested expression functions in FilterTransform
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103705 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve canceling queries by `KILL QUERY` and Ctrl+C in `clickhouse-client` while a long-running function is evaluated in a filter expression: `FilterTransform` (`WHERE`, including the `FilterSortedStreamByRange` path) and `TotalsHavingTransform` (`HAVING` with `WITH TOTALS`) now forward cancellation into nested expression functions. This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103705 by @rvasin (Roman Vasin), whose commits are preserved here — all credit for the feature goes to them. The original branch is in a fork with maintainer edits disabled, so the merge conflicts with `master` and the remaining review feedback could not be pushed there. On top of the original PR, this PR: - Merges `master` and resolves the conflicts (`FailPoint.cpp` failpoint list, `FilterTransform.cpp` includes). - Addresses the two unresolved review threads (the AI review "Request changes" verdict): - `FilterSortedStreamByRange` holds a private `FilterTransform` and calls its `transform` directly, but the pipeline cancels only the outer processor. Now `FilterSortedStreamByRange::onCancel` forwards the cancellation into the inner transform, so `cancelExecution` reaches functions of range-filter predicates from `PartsSplitter`. - `TotalsHavingTransform` evaluated the `HAVING` expression without a cancellation callback, so a long-running function in `HAVING` remained uninterruptible. It now mirrors `FilterTransform`: `onCancel` cancels function execution, `expression->execute` gets a `check_cancelled` callback, and the transform returns before the totals/filter bookkeeping when cancelled. - Adds a test `04658_kill_query_having_totals_pause` with a new `totals_having_transform_pause` failpoint, mirroring `04612_kill_query_filter_pause`. - Adds immediate pre-evaluation cancellation guards in `FilterTransform` and `TotalsHavingTransform`, with `04905_kill_query_cancelled_before_expression` covering the already-dispatched-task race. - Addresses the latest review thread: `ConvertingTransform::onCancel` now forwards cancellation into functions executing target-side conversion/default expressions, with `04909_kill_query_converting_transform_wasm` covering a cancelled `INSERT` through a `DEFAULT` WASM expression. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112705&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112705](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112705+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Use text and token skip indexes for IN with `transform_null_in = 1`
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111311 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111329 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111311 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111329 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Makes the `text`, `tokenbf_v1`, `ngrambf_v1` and `sparse_grams` skip indexes apply to `IN` when `transform_null_in = 1` and the set contains no NULL, so a query no longer loses index pruning just because that setting is enabled. Previously such a query read every granule, and one using `force_data_skipping_indices` failed with `INDEX_NOT_USED`. A set that does contain NULL keeps the original predicate, since `nullIn` also matches the column's NULL rows. ### Description Follow-up to #111329, which fixed `bloom_filter` only. With `transform_null_in = 1` the analyzer rewrites `x IN (...)` to `nullIn(x, ...)` and `globalIn` to `globalNullIn`. Two skip-index condition classes decide on the function name. `MergeTreeIndexConditionText` accepted only `in`/`globalIn`, so the atom stayed unknown and the index was dropped entirely. `MergeTreeConditionBloomFilterText` (shared by `tokenbf_v1`, `ngrambf_v1` and `sparse_grams`) did admit the new names, prepared the bloom filters and then discarded them, because its body assigned an RPN function only for `notIn` and `in`. Adding the names alone would give wrong results. Set elements are materialized from the left-hand key type, and `Set::getElementTypes` strips `Nullable` only when `transform_null_in` is off, so a `Nullable` key keeps the wrapper even for a NULL-free set. Measured on a `text` index over `Nullable(String)`, `x IN ('word5', NULL)` returns 1 row at `transform_null_in = 0` and 11 at `1`; pruning the second case would drop granules holding real results. So each site now tolerates a `Nullable` wrapper in its existing type rule and refuses per row via `isNullAt` at the tokenized position only, which keeps NULL in an unindexed tuple component prunable. Two further changes are disclosed rather than advertised. `globalIn` never pruned on the token bloom filter family even at `transform_null_in = 0`; the same one-line branch fixes that, so `transform_null_in = 0` is not untouched. And a predicate that now prunes every granule no longer reaches an execution-time error it previously reached. That is a pre-existing property of pruning, observable on the primary key alone, and it already applied to `in` on these indexes; the effect here is that `nullIn` now behaves like the `in` it mirrors, where master has the two spellings disagree. The added bound check mirrors the `text` sibling and is not reachable today. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Both directions, from one worktree with only the two source files reverted: | carrier | before, `transform_null_in = 1` | after | |---|---|---| | `text` `String` / `LowCardinality(String)` / `FixedString(12)` | index dropped | `Granules: 2/250` | | `text` `Nullable(String)` / `LowCardinality(Nullable(String))`, NULL-free | index dropped | prunes | | `text` tuple set, incl. indexed component at position 1 and a `Nullable` indexed component | index dropped | prunes | | `text` map element value, JSON subcolumn via `::String` | index dropped | prunes | | `tokenbf_v1` `String` / `LowCardinality(String)` / tuple set | `250/250` | `2/250` | | `ngrambf_v1` `String` / `LowCardinality(String)`, `sparse_grams` `String` | `250/250` | `29/250` | | `force_data_skipping_indices`, all four | `INDEX_NOT_USED` | returns rows | Row counts match between the two `transform_null_in` arms in every cell, so the test asserts correctness as well as pruning. Unchanged and verified: a NULL-containing set still does not prune and still returns 11 rows, `NOT IN` still never prunes, the empty-string and tokenizes-to-nothing bail-outs still bail out, and mixed-type tuples still prune on `text` and still do not on the token bloom filter family. Six mutation arms, each reddening a specific cell set: removing the `isNullAt` refusal makes the NULL-set query fail with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`; removing only the `Nullable` tolerance reddens exactly the five `Nullable` cells while the plain `String` cells pass; reverting either site reddens exactly that site's cells; making the bound check too eager reddens every token bloom filter cell. 50 tag-free randomized runs at `--jobs 8`: 50 OK. Regression sweep over 255 tests, identical selection in both arms with the ran-test sets asserted equal: 0 new failures, 1 improvement (the new test). </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112785&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112785](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112785+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Implement PromQL range functions present_over_time, absent_over_time, quantile_over_time and predict_linear
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 > [!IMPORTANT] > **Depends on #115073.** `04551_promql_phase3_range_functions` runs > `absent_over_time({__name__=~"up|up2",instance="host1"}[3m])` through `--dialect promql`, and the SQL > lexer rejects `=~` before the PromQL parser sees the text: > `Code: 62 ... Unrecognized token: Syntax error: failed at position 28 (~)`. > #115073 is what lets a raw-text dialect keep tokens the SQL lexer rejects. It is the only failing > test here, and it accounts for every red check on this PR; the rest of the suite is green. Existing > PromQL tests do not hit this because they pass the expression as a string literal to > `prometheusQuery(...)`, where the lexer never sees it. > > Merge #115073 first, then a master merge here turns this green. The test is deliberately left as-is > rather than rewritten to dodge the lexer bug. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented range functions `present_over_time()`, `absent_over_time()`, `quantile_over_time()` and `predict_linear()`. ### Description Implements four PromQL functions over range vectors that were previously rejected with a not-implemented error: - `present_over_time(v range-vector)` — for each grid point, `1` if its staleness window contains at least one sample, otherwise the series is dropped. - `absent_over_time(v range-vector)` — an empty vector if the range vector has any samples, otherwise a 1-element synthetic series with value `1` and the labels inferred from the selector's equality matchers (matching Prometheus `absent_over_time` / `absent` semantics). - `quantile_over_time(phi scalar, v range-vector)` — the φ-quantile of the sample values in each grid point's window, computed with the R-7 (inclusive) method (`quantileExactInclusive`). φ outside `[0, 1]` yields ±Inf and NaN φ yields NaN, as in Prometheus. - `predict_linear(v range-vector, t scalar)` — simple linear regression over the in-window samples, extrapolated `t` seconds past the evaluation time. **Implementation** - Two new grid aggregate functions: - `timeSeriesPresentToGrid` — `1` if a window has any sample, else `NULL`. - `timeSeriesQuantileToGrid` — R-7 inclusive quantile over a window (non-invertible summary that collects window values and sorts them in `getResult`). Both are registered inline in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp`. `predict_linear` reuses the existing `timeSeriesPredictLinearToGrid` aggregate (the `is_predict` variant of the linear-regression aggregate). - `present_over_time` is wired through `applyFunctionOverRange`'s `impl_map`. `quantile_over_time` and `predict_linear` have dedicated translators because they take an extra scalar argument. - `absent_over_time` builds a per-series presence grid via `present_over_time`, then at runtime counts present series per grid point (`countForEach`) and inverts the result, so it works whether or not the metric exists (a selector on a missing metric is a runtime subquery, not a compile-time-empty one). Output labels are derived from the selector's matchers, like `absent()`. No parser changes were needed — the grammar already accepts these function names and `getFunctionResultType` already returns the correct result types. **Testing**: new parser cases in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp` for `present_over_time` and `absent_over_time` (`quantile_over_time` / `predict_linear` were already covered); new stateless test `04551_promql_phase3_range_functions.sh` exercising all four functions (present/absent, quantile at φ = 0 / 0.5 / 1, predict_linear at offsets 0 and 60) against a multi-series TimeSeries table, with values verified against Prometheus semantics. **Update: time-varying `predict_offset` / `phi`** `predict_linear`'s `t` and `quantile_over_time`'s `phi` now also accept a per-grid-point-varying PromQL scalar (e.g. `time()` in a range query), not just a constant or single-row scalar. This is handled by two new, self-contained aggregate functions, `timeSeriesPredictLinearVaryingToGrid` / `timeSeriesQuantileVaryingToGrid`, which take the varying value as a 3rd `Array(Float64)` argument instead of a fixed aggregate parameter (ClickHouse aggregate parameters are bound once per instance and can't vary per row). They're isolated from `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase` (shared by ~10 other `timeSeries*ToGrid` functions) to avoid regression risk to those. Since these are public SQL aggregate functions, not just an internal translator detail, they validate that the 3rd-argument array is identical across every row/merged state and throw `BAD_ARGUMENTS` otherwise, rather than silently using whichever array was seen first. **Scope note**: the varying value is normalized to `Array(Float64)` in the translator so it works for `Float32`-valued `TimeSeries` tables too, not just `Float64`. However, the PromQL scalar's *own* grid representation (`fromFunctionTime.cpp`'s `SCALAR_GRID` output for `time()`) is cast to `Array(scalar_data_type)`, which is the *table's value type* — for a `Float32`-valued table, that means `time()`'s own raw values (Unix timestamps, ~1.7e9) already lose precision (~128-unit rounding at that magnitude) before my code ever sees them. This is a pre-existing property of `scalar_data_type` being shared between value-precision and timestamp-scalar-precision, not something this change introduces, but this change is what makes it reachable for `predict_offset`/`phi`. It only matters when the varying value is derived from `time()` on a non-`Float64` table. A bare `time()` (also inside `scalar()`/`vector()`) is rebuilt at native timestamp precision and works; any arithmetic around it (e.g. `predict_linear(m[5m], time() - 60)` or a `phi` normalized from `time()`) would see the already-rounded evaluation time, so `makeVaryingScalarPrecisionSafe` rejects it with `CANNOT_EXECUTE_PROMQL_QUERY` instead of returning silently wrong results — this is documented in the supported-functions tables. Fixing the root cause would mean changing `fromFunctionTime.cpp`'s shared `SCALAR_GRID` representation, which has ~15 other callers — out of scope here. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112842&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112842](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112842+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Make SQL SECURITY views an optimization barrier
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A view with `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` or `SQL SECURITY NONE` is now an optimization barrier, so an expression in the query reading the view is never evaluated on rows that the view itself filters out. Previously such an expression could observe the hidden rows through an exception, and a view used to restrict which rows a user may see did not actually restrict them. --- ## The problem `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` is widely used to build a view that restricts which rows a user may see: ```sql CREATE VIEW user_query_log DEFINER = default SQL SECURITY DEFINER AS SELECT * FROM system.query_log WHERE user = currentUser(); GRANT SELECT ON user_query_log TO alice; ``` `alice` has no grant on the source table, only on the view. But the outer `WHERE` and the view's own `WHERE` are merged into a single filter over the source table, and nothing guarantees which of the two decides first. Any function that can signal through a side channel therefore observes the rows the view is supposed to hide: ```sql -- as alice, whose only grant is SELECT ON user_query_log SELECT event_time FROM user_query_log WHERE throwIf(query LIKE '%some probe%', 'DISCLOSED'); -- DB::Exception: DISCLOSED ... While executing MergeTreeSelect ``` That is a one-bit oracle per query. Exception messages carry the offending value, which turns it into a plain read of the hidden rows: ```sql SELECT * FROM v_secrets WHERE if(owner = 'alice', 1, toUInt8(secret)) = 1; -- DB::Exception: Cannot parse string 'TOP-SECRET-BOB-42' as UInt8 ``` Both work on `SQL SECURITY NONE` as well, and both work with `enable_analyzer = 0`. Row policies are *not* affected: a row policy is a separate `row_level_filter` that the reading step always applies before PREWHERE and before any pushed-down filter. This PR gives a view's own filtering the same standing. ## The fix `IQueryPlanStep` gets a `security_barrier` flag. After `StorageView::readImpl` builds the view's subplan, every step that can drop rows is marked, and optimizations that move a step down the plan refuse to cross a marked step: - `tryMergeExpressions`, `tryMergeFilters`, `tryPushDownFilter` and `tryMergeFilterIntoJoinCondition` refuse when the child is a barrier; - `optimizePrewhere` refuses to pull an outer filter into a barrier source — conditions are combined into the prewhere DAG with `and`, which gives no ordering guarantee — and transfers the barrier onto the source when it absorbs the view's own filter; - `trySplitFilter` moves the flag onto the new lower `FilterStep`, which is the one that still drops rows. - `tryPushDownLimit` refuses to move the invoker's `LimitStep` below a barrier step: once across the seal it would seed `DistinctStep::limit_hint` or a sorting limit inside the view's subplan, and `optimizeLimitForAggregationInOrder` walked through the seal to seed `AggregatingStep::limit_hint` the same way — hints that stop reading the source once enough visible rows are produced, so `read_rows`, progress and timing depended on the rows the view drops or collapses. Both walks, and `pushLimitByIntoSort`, fail closed on a barrier step. Blocking the steps that evaluate expressions is not enough on its own, because index analysis reaches the source by a different route and skips granules by the values of the rows the view hides — `read_rows` then tells the invoker whether such a row exists, with no exception needed. Ten walks are fenced as well: - `optimizePrimaryKeyConditionAndLimit` walks up from the reading step and hands every `FilterStep` it meets to the source's key condition; it now stops once it has consumed a barrier. The barrier's own condition still reaches the source — it is the definer's, and it is what decides which rows exist for the view — but nothing above it does. - `StorageView::readImpl` forwarded `query_info.filter_actions_dag` into the view's inner analyzer, where `Planner::collectFiltersForAnalysis` injects it into the inner plan and the filters it collects reach the inner tables' index analysis. It is no longer forwarded for a barrier view, which costs such a view over `Distributed` its shard skipping on the outer predicate. - `buildSortingDAG` in the read-in-order analysis descended through the view subplan and pulled outer `FilterStep` predicates into the fixed columns and the merged DAG, so an outer `ORDER BY` / `GROUP BY` / `DISTINCT` / `LIMIT BY` could still shape how the source below the barrier reads. It now reports a barrier in the chain and every consumer (sorting, aggregation, `DISTINCT`, `LIMIT BY`, the normal-projection choice, top-K, and the `Merge` child-plan walk) skips the analysis for that chain. Unlike the primary-key walk, the barrier step cannot be consumed here: the sort description belongs to the top of the chain, and a DAG missing the steps above the barrier could resolve a renamed column by name to the wrong source column and change the result order — so the analysis is skipped entirely, which is fail-closed and keeps correctness because the sorting step stays in the plan. - `tryOptimizeTopK` rewrites an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` into a dynamic `__topKFilter` PREWHERE and minmax-skip-index granule pruning on the source, walking `LimitStep` → `SortingStep` → `ExpressionStep` → `FilterStep` → `ReadFromMergeTree` — and both rewrites are on by default. The walk now fails closed on the first barrier step it meets, including a reading step that carries the barrier after `optimizePrewhere` absorbed the view's own filter. - `tryTopKThroughJoin` peels the expression chain between the invoker's `Sorting` and a `Join` and grafts the invoker's `Sort + Limit` onto the join's preserved input, re-running the optimization passes on that subtree. For a barrier view whose inner query is a join, the graft landed below the seal — verified live pre-fix on both analyzers. The pass now fails closed on a marked `Limit`/`Sorting` (the pattern lies inside a view), a marked peeled expression (the seal), and a marked join (a join of a barrier view is always marked, not being row-preserving). Grafting above the seal of the invoker's own join input stays allowed: the inserted `Sort` consumes its whole input and the re-run passes are individually fenced. - `registerLeftSideIndexAnalysisSecondPass` of the join runtime filters walked from the `__applyFilter` step (which the fenced filter pushdown correctly keeps above the seal) down through every single-child expression or filter step — sealed or not — to the `ReadFromMergeTree` inside the view, and registered the invoker's build-side keys for granule pruning there. The walk now fails closed on the first barrier step. A live disclosure could not be constructed — the descriptor's key name has to match the read's namespace and the consumption path declined in every configuration tried — so this fence makes the contract structural rather than incidental. - The vector search rewrites — the vector-similarity-index pass and the quantized-codes shortlist — walk the same chain and prune the source to the top-N candidates of the invoker's `ORDER BY`. Both now fail closed on a barrier step the same way. - Projection planning: `QueryDAG::build` in `projectionsCommon.cpp` collects every filter of the chain below the aggregation — the invoker's predicates together with the view's own filtering — and both `optimizeUseAggregateProjections` (including `minmax_count_projection`) and `optimizeUseNormalProjections` prune parts and marks with it, so a projection-enabled table under a filtering barrier view still let the invoker's predicate shape the read. The DAG build now fails closed on the first barrier step, which makes the projection optimizations decline the read entirely. - Join reordering: `addChildQueryGraph` in `optimizeJoin.cpp` peeled the sealing step — as a trivial pass-through step, or by merging it into the child join, which `query_plan_merge_expression_into_join` enables by default — and then flattened the join inside the view into the join graph of the invoker, where the relations are reordered by their estimated sizes. A sealed subplan is now one opaque relation of the graph: the seal is neither peeled nor merged, a barrier child join is neither flattened nor pre-optimized for statistics, and the two walks that mirror this one (the overlapping-column-name pre-check and the exposed-column check) are fenced identically so that they keep agreeing with it. - `optimizeJoinByShards` (setting `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges`) merged the expression and filter DAGs of the chain through the seal and could then make the reading inside the view emit one output port per primary-key range of the invoker's join keys. The walk now produces no result for a barrier step, so nothing propagates above the seal; the sharding of the joins the view itself contains, which the invoker does not control, is still applied. One more family reaches the source without going through its index analysis at all. `optimizeDistinctPerPartition`, `optimizeLimitByPerPartition` and `optimizeAggregationPerPartition` walk down through the sealing step and ask the reading to output each partition through a separate port, and `applyStreamDisjointness` carries the resulting partition disjointness back up across the seal, so the invoker's `DISTINCT` / `LIMIT BY` / `GROUP BY` skips its stream merging as well. Read scheduling, progress and resource consumption below the view then depend on how the rows the view drops are spread over the partitions, and all three `allow_*_partitions_independently` settings default to `1`. Both directions now fail closed on a barrier step. Four passes endanger the barrier by rebuilding steps rather than by walking past them, and each now fails closed on a barrier step: - lazy materialization splits every `Expression` / `Filter` step of the chain into a main and a lazy half, and the rebuilt steps do not carry the barrier flag, so the post-lazy `tryMergeExpressions` / `tryMergeFilters` passes saw an unmarked chain and could merge an invoker predicate into the view's own filtering — reopening the exception oracle itself, not just the read-shaping one; - `tryLiftUpUnion` rebuilds the `UnionStep` and clones the parent step into the branches as fresh unmarked steps, so a barrier view over `UNION ALL` lost its seal and `tryPushDownFilter` could then duplicate an invoker predicate into the branches; - `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` replaces the expression under a `SortingStep` with two new unmarked steps, which would strip the seal of a wrapper view and let the read-in-order and top-K walks descend through it again. - `tryLiftUpArrayJoin` splits the expression or filter above an `ArrayJoinStep`, moves one half below the `ARRAY JOIN`, and rebuilds both halves as fresh unmarked steps. When the parent is the seal of a view whose plan contains `ARRAY JOIN` (the seal is non-trivial whenever the view declares explicit column names or types), the invoker's predicate descended below the `ArrayJoinStep` and was evaluated on rows hidden by empty arrays — a live disclosure through the exception oracle, on both analyzers. Measured on a `DEFINER` view that exposes no row, over 100000 rows sorted by `key`, reading `WHERE key = <a key only a hidden row has>` against `WHERE key = <a key nothing has>`: 576 rows read against 0 without this, and 1000000 against 1000000 with it, on both `enable_analyzer = 1` and `enable_analyzer = 0`. `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` is left alone. It builds `InterpreterSelectQuery` with `only_analyze`, whose plan reads from `ReadNothingStep`, so no expression of the outer query is ever evaluated on a row and the view is still inlined for the diagnostic. Two paths substitute the view into the outer query before a plan exists, so a plan-level barrier cannot see them, and both are closed the same way — such a view is not inlined and is read through `StorageView::read`, which keeps the outer predicate in a step above it: - with `enable_analyzer = 0`, `InterpreterSelectQuery` replaces the view with a subquery and `TreeRewriter` merges the predicates; - with `analyzer_inline_views = 1`, `QueryAnalyzer::inlineViewSubqueryIfNeeded` does the same in the query tree. Without this, `SET enable_analyzer = 0` or `SET analyzer_inline_views = 1` would bypass the fix entirely. The flag also travels with a serialized query plan. A distributed worker deserializes a fragment and optimizes it again, so a barrier it does not know about is a barrier it will optimize across. `QueryPlan::serialize` writes the flag per step and fails closed when the negotiated query plan serialization version predates it (the version is bumped to 7), rather than sending a plan that silently loses its protection. ## Views that hide nothing are left alone Only a view that can actually drop rows becomes a barrier. A step is row-preserving if it is an `ExpressionStep`, a `SortingStep` without a limit, or a source step without PREWHERE; if none of the view's steps is anything else, nothing is marked and the plan is what it is today. The pre-plan paths make the same distinction. `StorageView::canHideRows` proves over the view's definition that the inner query preserves every row of a plainly readable source, and only a view for which that proof fails loses inlining and the forwarded outer filter. The proof fails closed: filters, limits, aggregation, `DISTINCT`, joins, `ARRAY JOIN`, `SAMPLE`/`FINAL`, multi-select unions, table functions, and a `FROM` that is itself a view or a view-wrapping engine (`Merge`, `Buffer`, anything remote) all count as able to hide rows. The proof classifies the storage that actually serves the read, not the object the name resolves to: proxy layers (a lazily loaded table of a database with `lazy_load_tables = 1`, or a table created from a table function) and `Alias` tables are unwrapped first, failing closed on a chain that cannot be resolved, and a storage that rewrites its own reads with `FINAL` and a `_sign` filter (`MaterializedPostgreSQL`) counts as able to hide rows even without another wrapper. So a projection-only `DEFINER` view produces exactly the plan of the same view declared `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` on every path, which the test pins byte-for-byte. Measured on 20M rows with `SELECT sum(length(payload)) FROM v WHERE tag = 'RARE'`, from `system.query_log`: | view | barrier | read_rows | read_bytes | ms | |---|---|---|---|---| | `DEFINER`, filters rows | on | 20 000 000 | 1.43 GiB | 35 | | `DEFINER`, filters rows | off | 1 638 400 | 82.84 MiB | 14 | | `DEFINER`, projection only | on | 1 638 400 | 82.84 MiB | 9 | | `DEFINER`, projection only | off | 1 638 400 | 82.84 MiB | 11 | A projection-only view is unaffected. A filtering view does pay: PREWHERE then holds only the view's own condition, so it no longer skips granules on the outer predicate. That is the inherent price of the guarantee — PostgreSQL's `security_barrier` views behave the same way — and it applies only to views that restrict rows, which are exactly the ones where it matters. The new server setting `sql_security_views_are_optimization_barriers` (default `1`) turns it off. It is deliberately a **server** setting and not a user setting: a user setting would be turned off by the very query that is trying to read the hidden rows. ## Testing `04758_sql_security_view_barrier_read_rows` covers the `read_rows` oracle through index analysis, on both analyzers, and prints `DISCLOSED` on both with the setting off. `04670_sql_security_view_barrier` covers the leak on `DEFINER` and on `NONE`, with `enable_analyzer = 1`, with `enable_analyzer = 0` and with `analyzer_inline_views = 1`, the value leak through a cast error message, the same oracle through a shard with `serialize_query_plan = 1`, that a projection-only `DEFINER` view and an `INVOKER` view still have the outer predicate merged into the view's own filter, and that a projection-only view keeps PREWHERE. `04813_sql_security_view_barrier_read_in_order` pins the read-in-order fence: the `INVOKER` twin and a projection-only `DEFINER` view read `InOrder`, a filtering `DEFINER` view does not, under both analyzers, with unchanged results. `04817_sql_security_view_barrier_top_k` pins the top-K fence: the `INVOKER` twin gets the `__topKFilter`, the filtering `DEFINER` view does not, and `read_rows` of an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` over twin views is identical whether or not the hidden row holds the extreme minimum of the sort column that minmax pruning would rank first. `04818_sql_security_view_barrier_lazy_materialization` pins the lazy-materialization fence the same way and checks that an invoker predicate over the view is never evaluated on the hidden row. `04821_sql_security_view_barrier_projections` pins the projection fence: the `INVOKER` twin uses both a normal and an aggregate projection, the filtering `DEFINER` view uses neither, and `read_rows` of a predicate probe over twin views is identical whether or not the hidden row matches it. `04825_sql_security_view_barrier_union` pins that an outer predicate over a filtering `DEFINER` view on `UNION ALL` stays in a single filter above the union — before the `tryLiftUpUnion` fix it was duplicated into the branches — while the `INVOKER` twin keeps the pushdown. `04826_sql_security_view_barrier_functions_after_sorting` pins that an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` over a wrapper `DEFINER` view (a `Merge` table over a nested filtering view) produces no in-order reading and no `__topKFilter` with `query_plan_execute_functions_after_sorting` on, while the `INVOKER` twin exploits the source order. `04827_sql_security_view_barrier_masked_wrappers` pins that the classification survives engine masking: a `DEFINER` view over a `Merge` wrapper behind a lazy `TableProxy` (re-masked before every round, since planning materializes the proxy) or behind an `Alias` table plans differently from its `INVOKER` twin on both analyzers and with `analyzer_inline_views = 1`. `04832_sql_security_view_barrier_limit_pushdown` pins the LIMIT fence: over a `DISTINCT` `DEFINER` view the invoker's `LimitStep` stays above the sealing step on both analyzers — before the fix it crossed the seal and sat directly on the `DistinctStep`, where it seeds the hint — and `read_rows` of an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` over twin in-order `GROUP BY` views is identical whether the first group holds one raw row or almost all of them. `04837_sql_security_view_barrier_per_partition` pins the per-partition fence, with the `allow_*_partitions_independently` settings left at their defaults: an outer `DISTINCT` / `LIMIT BY` over a filtering `DEFINER` view produces none of the `Skip stream merging` / `Read each partition through separate port` markers its `INVOKER` twin gets, and the disjointness of a view whose own inner `DISTINCT` legitimately requests per-partition reading does not propagate across the seal into the invoker's `GROUP BY` / `LIMIT BY` — before the fix every `DEFINER` case was identical to its twin. `04840_sql_security_view_barrier_array_join` pins the `ARRAY JOIN` lift-up fence with an exception oracle on both analyzers: the `INVOKER` twin's predicate legitimately descends below the `ARRAY JOIN` and throws on the row an empty array hides, while the `DEFINER` view counts without throwing and its plan keeps every `throwIf` line above the `ArrayJoin` step — before the fix the `DEFINER` view threw as well. `04891_sql_security_view_barrier_top_k_through_join` pins the top-K-through-join fence: the `INVOKER` twin of a view over a `LEFT JOIN` gets the preserved-side `Sort + Limit` graft below the join, the `DEFINER` twin keeps its join input untouched — before the fix the `DEFINER` plan got the graft below the seal. `04892_sql_security_view_barrier_join_runtime_filter` pins the join-runtime-filter contract: with `enable_join_runtime_filters_index_analysis = 1`, twin filtering `DEFINER` views over tables identical except for the hidden row's primary-key value read exactly the same number of rows, while the `INVOKER` control is pruned by the build-side key. Every setting the plan shape depends on is pinned, because the test also runs with randomized settings. `04893_sql_security_view_barrier_join_reorder` pins the join-reordering fence: with `query_plan_merge_expression_into_join = 1` and no overlapping column names between the relations, the `INVOKER` twin of a view over an `INNER JOIN` with a `WHERE` is flattened and reordered into a three-relation graph with no step left converting the view subquery result, while the `DEFINER` twin keeps that step and stays one relation, with equal results. `04894_sql_security_view_barrier_join_shard_by_pk` pins the join-sharding fence: with `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges = 1` and `join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge'`, plain tables, a `DEFINER` view that hides nothing and the `INVOKER` twin of the filtering view all get a `Sharding` line, while the filtering `DEFINER` view gets none, with equal row counts. Those two fences are contract-made-real rather than live leaks: with the fence removed the `DEFINER` twin behaves the same, because a neighbouring fence of this PR happens to block the pass first — which is exactly why the barrier is checked explicitly. With `sql_security_views_are_optimization_barriers = 0` every one of those lines changes, so none of them passes vacuously. Ran 542 existing tests matching `view`, `prewhere`, `push_down`, `pushdown`, `row_policy`, `sql_security` and `definer`. 60 fail in my local environment, and the identical 60 fail with the barrier disabled on the same binary, so this introduces no regressions among them. ## Not covered here - The serialized-plan fence is defensive. With the serialization change reverted I could not make the barrier loss observable — neither the `throwIf` nor the failing-cast oracle leaks through `serialize_query_plan = 1`, `make_distributed_plan = 1`, or a `Distributed` table, because the initiator optimizes the fragment before shipping it. The flag is serialized so that the guarantee does not depend on that. - A separate hole remains: `additional_table_filters` and `additional_result_filter` from the invoker are copied verbatim into the definer's context by `StorageInMemoryMetadata::getSQLSecurityOverriddenContext`. Keyed on the view's *inner* table, the filter lands inside the view and its expression — which may contain scalar subqueries and table functions — is evaluated with the definer's privileges. That is a privilege escalation rather than a row disclosure, it is unaffected by this PR, and it needs its own fix. Until then it can be mitigated with a constraint on the definer's profile (`CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE p SETTINGS additional_table_filters = '' CONST TO <definer>`), which does not help for `SQL SECURITY NONE`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112847&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112847](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112847+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix startup hang when `max_thread_pool_size` is too small
signals.text: Setting `max_thread_pool_size` to a value that is too small made `clickhouse-server` hang forever at startup instead of reporting the problem. A `ThreadFromGlobalPool` created while all the threads of the global thread pool are already taken by other such jobs was silently put into the pool's queue instead of getting a thread. The queue is much larger than the number of threads by default (`thread_pool_queue_size` is 10000 against `max_thread_pool_size`), so scheduling succeeded, but nothing ever picked the job up, because the threads are held by jobs that never return. Its creator got a seemingly running thread whose function was never called, and any code that then waited for that thread to make progress hung forever. An idle server permanently occupies about 200 threads of the pool for the workers of the background pools and of the background schedule pools, and for the flush threads of the system logs, so a `max_thread_pool_size` below that ran out of threads while starting up: * With `max_thread_pool_size` of 128 the starved job was the loader worker of the `system` database, and startup hung forever right after `Wait load job 'startup Atomic database system'`. * With 100 it hung in the constructor of the merge/mutate background executor instead. * Values between roughly 130 and 200 appeared to start, but silently left some background threads unstarted - for example the flush threads of the system logs, so those tables never received any data. Jobs that occupy their worker for the whole lifetime of that worker are now scheduled through `ThreadPoolImpl::scheduleThreadOrThrow`, which hands them one of the `max_threads` slots at scheduling time and throws `CANNOT_SCHEDULE_TASK` naming `max_thread_pool_size` when there is none left, rather than queueing a thread that can never start. Two components started threads in their constructor and stopped them only in their destructor, so the resulting exception left those threads running while the destructor of the member thread pool blocked forever joining them. Both now stop their workers before letting the exception out, following the pattern `CacheDictionaryUpdateQueue` already uses: * `MergeTreeBackgroundExecutor` - this was the second hang above. Its `increaseThreadsAndMaxTasksCount` now starts the additional workers on a best-effort basis, so a configuration reload does not fail when the pool is saturated, and it reports the number of workers that actually started. * `BackgroundSchedulePool` - its handler used to `LOG_FATAL` and `abort`, turning a misconfiguration into signal 6 and a crash report. It now logs the same hint and rethrows, so the server exits cleanly. Note that the hint in that handler ("Please make sure max_thread_pool_size is considerably bigger than background_schedule_pool_size") was previously unreachable, because saturating the global pool never produced `CANNOT_SCHEDULE_TASK`. **Behaviour change.** Values of `max_thread_pool_size` that cannot hold the permanent threads of the server now make it refuse to start with a clear error naming the setting, where some of them used to start in a silently degraded state. This looks like the intended contract: `max_thread_pool_size` is documented as the maximum number of threads in the pool, and the documentation of `thread_pool_queue_size` already recommends keeping it equal to `max_thread_pool_size`, which makes saturation an error today. The requirement is now documented on the setting itself. No test configuration is affected: `tests/casa_del_dolor/properties.py` randomises `max_thread_pool_size` only down to 700. Tested by starting a server with values of 16, 32, 64, 100, 128 and 160 (all fail with the error, no `abort`, no crash report) and 192, 256 and the default (all start normally), plus a check for slot accounting leaks under concurrent load with `max_thread_pool_size` of 400. The full `unit_tests_dbms` suite passes, including `FunctionsStress`. The pre-existing `ThreadPool.GlobalFull1` and `ThreadPool.GlobalFull2` tests did not catch this because they give the global pool a queue as small as its thread count, which makes saturation fail on queue fullness instead. The new `ThreadPool.GlobalFullLargeQueue` covers the shape of the real pool, and the `test_thread_pool_size_too_small` integration test asserts that the server terminates with the error rather than hanging. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a hang at server startup when `max_thread_pool_size` was set too small to hold the threads that the server occupies permanently. Such a configuration is now reported with an error naming the setting, instead of hanging forever or starting with some background threads missing. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112928&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112928](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112928+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Rewrite WHERE filters on arrayJoin columns into arrayFilter before ex…
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112241 Add an analyzer pass that pushes top-level WHERE conjuncts constraining an `arrayJoin` / single-expression `ARRAY JOIN` column into `arrayFilter` on the source array, and drops those conjuncts when the expansion still remains elsewhere (typically the projection). This avoids materializing the full cartesian product of multiple independent `arrayJoin` calls when only a few elements match. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Queries that filter `arrayJoin` / `ARRAY JOIN` results in `WHERE` can now rewrite the predicates into `arrayFilter` before array expansion, reducing intermediate rows and memory for selective filters. Controlled by `optimize_rewrite_array_join_filter_to_array_filter` (enabled by default).

signals.title: Do not use a non-deterministic expression as a join key when rewriting a comma or `CROSS` join
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112965 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results for a comma or `CROSS` join whose `WHERE` compares columns of two tables through a non-deterministic expression such as `rand`. Such a query could return rows that contradict its own `WHERE` clause, because rewriting the join into an `INNER` join moved the expression into the join key, where it is evaluated again per row of each side. ### Description At default settings this query returns rows where `r.a` is not `3`: ```sql CREATE TABLE l (a UInt64) ENGINE = Memory; CREATE TABLE r (a UInt64) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO l SELECT number % 16 FROM numbers(500); INSERT INTO r SELECT number % 16 FROM numbers(500); SELECT uniqExact(r.a), countIf(r.a != 3) FROM l, r WHERE rand(l.a) % 16 = r.a AND rand(l.a) % 16 = 3; ``` Expected `1 0`. Master returns `10 29`: the second conjunct pins the key to `3`, yet 29 of the returned rows hold a different `r.a`. Only the new analyzer is affected, with `enable_analyzer = 0` the same query returns `1 0`. `CrossToInnerJoinPass` moves an `equals` conjunct out of the `WHERE` into the join `ON` and rebuilds the `WHERE` from the conjuncts it did not take. In the key position the expression is evaluated per row of each joined side instead of once per cross-product row, so the key a row was hashed under is unrelated to the value the surviving conjunct checked. The fix refuses a condition as a join key when its subtree holds a window function, a stateful function, one that is not deterministic in the scope of the query, or one fixed per executing node. A refused condition stays in the `WHERE`, exactly as `cross_to_inner_join_rewrite = 0` leaves it. The predicate is `isDeterministicInScopeOfQuery`, so `now`, `currentUser` and `randConstant` keep their rewrite. Several functions of that class did not declare the property and now do, so the pass compares no function names. `query_plan_merge_filter_into_join_condition` moves the same class of predicate into a join key and is fixed separately in #112965. No issue is linked because there is no existing report: I found this while auditing the pass. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112938&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112938](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112938+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support the Vortex file format
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87327 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/74 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added support for reading and writing the [Vortex](https://github.com/vortex-data/vortex) columnar file format (the `Vortex` input and output format). This closes [#87327](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87327). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The implementation uses the Rust `vortex` crate (v0.84.0) through a new C FFI crate `rust/workspace/vortex` (`_ch_rust_vortex`), following the same pattern as `prql` and `polyglot`. Data crosses the FFI boundary through the Arrow C Data Interface and is converted with the same `ArrowColumnToCHColumn`/`CHColumnToArrowColumn` code as the `Arrow` format. IO is delegated back to ClickHouse through callbacks: reads go through ClickHouse's own read buffers (range reads for seekable inputs, whole-file buffering otherwise), and the produced file is streamed into the output buffer. The library spawns no threads of its own: a scan is split into tasks that ClickHouse runs on its own thread pools (`max_parsing_threads` for decoding, `max_download_threads` for reads), writing is driven on the calling thread, and Rust panics are caught at the FFI boundary and turned into exceptions. Features: - Reading with projection pushdown: only the columns used by the query are read from the file. - Parallel reading (merged from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 by @m7kss1): the file is split into row ranges that are read, filtered, and decoded concurrently; nearby segment reads are coalesced into one request. Chunks are returned as soon as they are decoded, so the row order is not guaranteed unless `input_format_vortex_preserve_order` is set. - Schema inference and `count()`-only queries answered from file metadata without reading data. - Writing with the library's default adaptive compression (BtrBlocks-style cascading encodings + zstd), including a valid empty file for empty results. - Graceful errors on malformed and truncated files (fuzzer-friendly: no aborts, Rust panics become exceptions). Limitations (documented in `docs/reference/formats/Vortex.mdx`): - `Map`, `Int128`/`UInt128`/`Int256`/`UInt256`, `IPv6`, and `Interval` columns cannot be written (no corresponding Vortex type). - `String` and `FixedString` are written as Vortex `Binary` (ClickHouse strings are arbitrary bytes, while Vortex requires `Utf8` to be valid UTF-8). - The format is disabled in MSan builds: the MSan-instrumented library (with origin tracking) is so large that linking `unit_tests_dbms` overflows the 2 GiB `R_X86_64_PC32` relocation range (same approach as `wasmtime` and `delta-kernel-rs`). - Writing is single-threaded in this first version: the adaptive compressor samples many encodings per column, so writes are slower than `Parquet` — parallelism can be added later. Reading is parallel since https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 was merged into this PR: on ClickBench, reads went from geomean ~26.8x slower than `Parquet` to ~1.2x, winning 9 of 43 queries (see the [benchmark results](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112950#issuecomment-5337908877)). Filter pushdown (added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114373, `input_format_vortex_filter_push_down`, on by default) lets the scan skip the statistics zones the predicate rules out and decode only the matching rows of the rest: on a file of 1 000 000 sorted values, `WHERE n = 500000` reads 66 KiB with the pushdown against 7.5 MiB without it. The most selective ClickBench queries are nevertheless still 1.5-5.5x slower than `Parquet`. The 127 new vendored Rust crates are added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/74, and https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/79 moves them to 0.84.0 (the `contrib/rust_vendor` submodule points at the latter). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112950&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112950](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112950+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Convert the JOIN keys to the type of the values that they have in common
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/21794 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/21794 There is no type that is able to hold all the values of both `UInt64` and `Int64`, so a JOIN on such keys was rejected: ``` SELECT * FROM (SELECT number FROM numbers(10)) AS a INNER JOIN (SELECT number FROM numbers(10)) AS b ON a.number = b.number - 1 Code: 386. DB::Exception: There is no supertype for types UInt64, Int64 ... ``` But a JOIN does not need the least supertype. It is enough to convert both keys to the type of the values that they have in common - the most subtype, which is `UInt64` for this pair, holding the values from `0` to `9223372036854775807`. A value outside of this range is not equal to any value from the other side, so `accurateCastOrNull` converts it to NULL, and it does not match anything. This is applied to the equality conditions in the `ON` section, and to the `USING` section of an `INNER JOIN` or a `SEMI JOIN`, where the result contains only the matched values. It is not applied to: - the kinds of JOIN with `USING` that can emit unmatched rows (`LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL`, `ANTI`), where the key is also a column of the result and can hold the unmatched values; - null-safe comparisons (`IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`), where NULL matches NULL, so the values converted to NULL would match each other; - the ASOF inequality (the last column in the `USING` list), which needs the order of the values, not only their equality; - a `Join` table engine whose stored key is not itself the common type, because its hash table is prebuilt over the original key values and cannot be converted - the opposite direction, where only the probe key has to be converted, is supported. A runtime filter is not built for such a JOIN, because a `NOT IN` filter over a set with NULLs would drop the rows that have to be preserved. Only the queries that were failing before are affected - the type inference is unchanged whenever the least supertype exists. It is implemented in the analyzer, which is enabled by default; with `enable_analyzer = 0` the old `TableJoin::inferJoinKeyCommonType` path still rejects such a JOIN, exactly as before. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow a JOIN on keys that have no common supertype, such as `UInt64` and `Int64`. Previously such a query was rejected with `There is no supertype for types UInt64, Int64`. Now the keys are converted to the type of the values that they have in common, and a value outside of this range does not match anything. This requires the analyzer (`enable_analyzer = 1`, the default). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112951&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112951](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112951+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not report "Server died" for a signal-killed run with no failure
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106183 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description A functional-test job synthesizes a `Server died` failure whenever the test command dies from a signal, so an externally killed run reads as a crash nobody observed. On PR #108676 / `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, parallel)` the report read `Failed: 0, Passed: 10564, Skipped: 171` with `Server died` as the only failure, while the artifacts show the server answering `system flush logs` after the kill and stopping cleanly under `--do-not-kill`. As of 2026-08-21, 74 jobs across 41 PRs plus 3 master jobs carry this leaf alone in the preceding 30 days. Root cause: `ABORTED_RUN_EXIT_CODES` mixes `STOP_TESTING_EXIT_CODE`, where the parent observed a reason to stop, with the kill-by-signal codes, which establish only that the run was killed, never by whom, and labels both `Server died`. So when the exit code is a kill-by-signal one and no failure was parsed, emit a `Test command killed by signal` leaf instead. `STOP_TESTING_EXIT_CODE` stays excluded; a parsed failure is unchanged. The leaf is `ERROR`, the job result stays `FAIL`. `ERROR` on the leaf because `invert_bugfix_validation_status` flips any `FAIL` row to `OK` without reading its name, turning an exit code into a claimed reproduction; its guard is per-row, and `reconcile_bugfix_crash_repro` still downgrades that row on a `BLOCKER` fatal, so a real crash keeps validating (#105789). `FAIL` on the job result because `is_error` disables coverage collection for the whole job. Validated by 8 new unit tests (11 cases, one parameterized over all four exit code encodings), each load-bearing under mutation, taking the suite from 13 to 24 cases with the existing ones unchanged. The three job shapes carrying this signature were also driven against the pre-fix parser: job result, coverage gate and `pipeline_status` all match. Note `check_ci.can_process` skips `ERROR` rows, so a CIDB sweep needs `test_status IN ('FAIL','ERROR')`.

signals.title: Make array membership functions compare a constant `FixedString` needle zero-padded
signals.text:
Make array membership functions compare a constant `FixedString` needle zero-padded ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`, `indexOf`, `indexOfAssumeSorted`, `countEqual`, `mapContainsKey` and `mapContainsValue` returning a wrong result for a constant `FixedString` argument. String comparison ignores a `FixedString`'s trailing NUL padding, so `toFixedString('V0', 3)` equals both `'V0'` and `'V0\0'`, but these functions matched only one of them, and which one depended on whether the element type was wrapped in `LowCardinality`. `countEqual` under-counted and `indexOf` could return the wrong position. For a `LowCardinality` element, also fixes a constant of a different type matching a value it does not equal (`1.5` matched `1`, `-1` matched `255`, a non-midnight `DateTime` matched a `Date`), and a constant `NULL` matching the dictionary's default value. ### Description String equality is zero-padded, so `toFixedString('V0', 3)` equals both `'V0'` and `'V0\0'`. These functions reduced the needle to one exact value and matched only the member equal to it, differently in `executeString`, `executeConst` and the `LowCardinality` shortcut. A wider needle such as `toFixedString('V0', 5)` dropped every row. Rows `['V0']`, `['V0\0']`, `['X']`: | | `Array(String)` | `Array(LowCardinality(String))` | `=` | |---|---|---|---| | `has` | `[1]` | `[0]` | `[0,1]` | | `countEqual`, both members in one row | 1 | 1 | 2 | | `indexOf`, both members in one row | 2 | 1 | 1 | The comparison is now zero-padded in `executeString` and `executeConst`, using the primitive from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104858, which settled these semantics for `equals`. The `LowCardinality` shortcut resolves the needle to one dictionary index and compares indices, so it now runs only when the needle provably denotes a single element value: the width relation for the string family, otherwise a cast round trip back to the needle's own type, separating a `DateTime` at midnight (matches a `Date`) from one that is not (matches nothing). A `Float` element is refused outright: the lookup is by byte identity while `+0.0 = -0.0` and `NaN != NaN`. Declining costs the index-comparison speedup when the needle type differs from the element type, so `array_index_low_cardinality_numbers` may move. Most new assertions carry an inline `arrayExists(x -> x = needle, v)` oracle with `optimize_rewrite_array_exists_to_has = 0`, so the expected value comes from `=`. Left for their own PRs: a non-constant `FixedString` argument, `hasAny`/`hasAll`, a `bloom_filter` or text index hashing only the padded needle, and `has(map, key)`, which strips `LowCardinality` before the shortcut and so follows the plain path.
Reference change in 01414_low_cardinality_nullable Four lines move from `1` to `0`: `has(u8, -1)`, `has(u16, -1)`, `has(u32, -1)` and `has(u64, -1)` on `Array(LowCardinality(Nullable(UInt8/UInt16/UInt32/UInt64)))`. Each column stores the wrapped value (`255`, `65535`, `4294967295`, `18446744073709551615`), for which `x = -1` is false, so `has` must not match. Four independent oracles agree on `0` at every width (`arrayExists` with `=`, `arrayFilter`, `indexOf`, `countEqual`), as does scalar `=`. The reference recorded the defect. The positive control `has(u8, 255)` still returns `1`, and the `UInt8` cell is now pinned against both its `=` oracle and its plain-array control in the new test. A negative needle still matches an unsigned element in the plain `Array(UInt32/UInt64)` spelling, which has no dictionary and so reaches the integral comparison directly; that comparison suppresses `-Wsign-compare`, so `-1` equals its unsigned twin at widths 32 and 64. That is a separate pre-existing defect, measured identical before and after this change, and left for its own PR.

signals.title: Bound the integration-test job's post-run archiving so it cannot starve the result upload
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 An integration-test shard can publish a job-level `ERROR` with `results: []` even though every test produced a result. **What breaks.** On `6cdf4dfaea6e071cddeea4daeb74ea26e0d96e19`, `Integration tests (amd_asan_ubsan, db disk, old analyzer, 5/6)` reported `ERROR` with no children and is absent from the CI database, while its five siblings uploaded 600-1300 test rows each. Its job log holds 502 per-test outcome lines: the results existed and were discarded. Correcting the report: the harness survived both timeouts, then hung ~80 min in archiving. **Root cause.** `main` collects every result but dumps it only after unbounded post-processing. `Utils.compress_files_gz` sits in between with no timeout, archiving whole `tests/integration/<suite>` trees, so an archive that never returns costs a report already in memory. `Runner._get_result_object` runs the `on_error_hook` the same way, even earlier (comment: `# Add hook timeout once it's needed`). **The change.** Both paths are bounded at 30 minutes and fail non-fatally, so an overrun costs the tarball, not the report. `compress_files_gz` returns failure instead of raising, publishes by rename from a per-writer temporary, uses a direct `tar -czf` instead of `tar -cf - | gzip`, and judges the archive by reading it back, not by `tar`'s exit code; all four load-bearing, see below. Bounding needs a working watchdog, so `Shell._check_timeout` waits on an event set when the attempt's child is reaped, not sleeping the timeout out. `main` also checkpoints the results first. **Scope limits.** The checkpoint does not recover the job above, where the runner died, nor an externally cancelled job. 30 minutes comes from healthy shards' 4491-5747s of 18000s. **Validation.** 37 tests, each shown to fail against a mutation of what it pins: a 37-case matrix reddening exactly its predicted arms, plus a probe for the four it did not reach. Empty failure-set diff over `ci/tests/`, as host user and as root. <details> <summary>Why each detail of the change matters</summary> Four measured properties beyond the bound. * **Must not raise.** `Shell.check(..., strict=True, timeout=N)` raises `RuntimeError`, so merely adding `timeout=` turns the hang into an exception that still skips the dump. Nor an absent declared input (`Result.from_pytest_run` registers its log and report before running pytest) or a failed publish. * **Must not publish a partial archive.** A timed-out `tar` leaves a large truncated archive and the upload only checks the file exists. The temporary is per writer: both target one `ci/tmp/logs.tar.gz`, so sharing it lets the loser write into the published file. * **Must not reject a usable archive over `tar`'s exit code.** Two reachable cases exit non-zero with a complete, listable archive: 1 for a member appended to while read, which every archive here holds (`job.log`, the dockerd log, live `_instances` trees), and 2 for an unstattable input, which the hook hits whenever its `_instances*` glob is unexpanded because no cluster started. Rejecting on the code discards both, timeout unfired. So 0 and 1 are accepted and any other code is settled by `tar -tzf`: 0 on those, non-zero on every truncated archive (~1.6s for 367MB). * **Must see `tar`'s status at all.** `Shell.run` uses bash without `pipefail`, so the old `tar -cf - | gzip > out` reported only gzip's status: a `tar` failing part-way exited 0. The watchdog event is per attempt (a shared one is already set when attempt 2 starts waiting), and all three of its liveness tests - before SIGTERM, in the grace loop, at the SIGKILL gate - ask about the process GROUP. A descendant holding the inherited pipes keeps the readers blocked, so the event is unset while the leader is already reaped, and a leader-only `poll()` signals nothing or skips the SIGKILL. Only the first was a regression; a SIGTERM-ignoring descendant was unbounded on master too, so that part is a hardening. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112972&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112972](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112972+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Back off exponentially on transient GitHub API failures, in praktika
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Retry GitHub API reads with a capped exponential backoff instead of a fixed delay, so the `Upgrade check` rides out a longer transient `5xx` or `429` from `api.github.com` during setup instead of failing on a routine blip. The policy now lives in `praktika` as `GH.api_get`. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112205 `Upgrade check (*)` fails in setup (`Download script failed`) on a transient `5xx` from the GitHub releases API. `get_previous_release_tag.py` resolves it through `get_gh_api`, which retried 5 times with a **fixed** 3 s sleep, so `retries` bounded the attempt count but not the time window: a 12 s budget, which a routine blip outlasts. On PR #112205 a read timeout at 10:06:15 was followed by four `504` retries 3 s apart, exhausted at 10:06:27. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112205&sha=66f93bffd6aa9d3b6f038bf7a6b59ac02a5b3f10&name_0=PR&name_1=Upgrade%20check%20%28amd_release%29 The delay now grows as `sleep * 2 ** (attempt - 1)`, capped at 60 s, for the classes transient by definition: every `5xx`, `429`, and transport errors, giving a 45 s default window. Terminal statuses keep the flat sleep, and the growth base is the caller's own `sleep`, so the `pr_info.py` sites passing `RETRY_SLEEP = 0` still get none. An outage that outlasts the whole budget still raises, as the tests pin. Per review the policy lives in `ci/praktika/gh.py` as `GH.api_get`, reusable by any praktika job, with `get_gh_api` a thin shim over it. The failover has to stay in `tests/ci` because `get_robot_token` imports `boto3` and PyGithub at module level, so the shim keeps its signature, its `APIException` and the failover, driving the latter through an `on_http_error` callback that restarts the budget exactly once. signals.title: Compare array membership values the way the equals operator does
signals.text:
Compare array membership values the way the equals operator does Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112953 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104858 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`, `notHas`, `indexOf`, `countEqual`, `indexOfAssumeSorted`, `mapContainsKey` and `mapContainsValue` returning a wrong result when the element and needle types differ. A negative signed value equated with its unsigned bit-pattern twin at 32 and 64 bits, so `has([1, -1]::Array(Int32), 4294967295::UInt32)` returned 1 while `=` returns 0, and a wide integer equated with an imprecise `Float`. Over `Array(LowCardinality(T))` a needle that narrowed onto a different dictionary entry also matched it, including a `DateTime` needle against a `Date` element. `indexOfAssumeSorted` could also miss a value that is present. ### Description `executeIntegral` compared every pair of native number types with a raw C++ `==` under a suppressed `-Wsign-compare`, plus hand-rolled `static_cast` branches for a mixed integer/float pair. The usual arithmetic conversions turn the signed operand unsigned, so `int32_t(-1) == uint32_t(4294967295)` is true. `Int8` and `Int16` were correct against a same-width unsigned type, since both promote to `int` first, which is why this stayed hidden; against a wider needle they wrapped too. The float casts are lossy the same way. The helpers now call `accurate::equalsOp` and `accurate::greaterOrEqualsOp`, which is what `EqualsOp`, and therefore the scalar operator, already calls, so the two cannot disagree. Both suppressions and all six casts are deleted. `lowerBound`'s ordering moves with the equality it feeds, or the binary search descends the wrong half. Same-type pairs, which dominate, keep the identical comparison through that helper's fast path. `Array(LowCardinality(T))` with a constant needle is a second locus, since `executeArrayLowCardinality` returns before `executeImpl` strips `LowCardinality`. It resolved the needle to a dictionary index through `castColumn`, which wraps, so `UInt32(4294967295)` became `Int32(-1)` and matched that element. `dictionaryIndexForConstant` now asks `targetTypeRepresentsValue`, added by #114624 for the default slot, whether the constant survived that cast, and treats one that did not as absent. Any narrowing needle can land on a wrong entry, so it is asked at every index, including a temporal or `IPv4` element truncating a wider needle. The string family is the exception, since equality pads a shorter needle to the element width, so there it stays at the default slot. Most rows of the new test print an oracle beside the result, `arrayExists(x -> x = needle, v)`; 31 rows differ without the fix.
Reference change in 01414_low_cardinality_nullable Four lines move from `1` to `0`: `has(u8, -1)`, `has(u16, -1)`, `has(u32, -1)` and `has(u64, -1)` over `Array(LowCardinality(Nullable(UInt8/UInt16/UInt32/UInt64)))`. The second `INSERT` writes `negate(number)`, so each column stores the wrapped value (`255`, `65535`, `4294967295`, `18446744073709551615`), for which `x = -1` is false and `has` must not match. `arrayExists` with `=`, `arrayFilter` and scalar `=` all agree on `0`, and `accurateCastOrNull(-1, 'UInt32')` is `NULL`. The reference recorded the defect. The `Int8` control in the same block still returns `1`. This is the same four-line change as #112953, which fixes the `LowCardinality` half from the other side; whichever merges second resolves by taking either side of that one file.
