signals.title: Fix target access checks for the Alias engine
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> `Alias` table now requires `SHOW COLUMNS` on its target when a new definition is submitted. This prevents users from using `Alias` to reveal a target table's schema. The trivial `count` optimization is disabled when the user has no `SELECT` privilege on the target, allowing the normal read path to enforce access checks. `rows` and `bytes` statistics are also hidden unless the user has `SHOW TABLES` on the target. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114511 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an RBAC bypass in the `Alias` table engine that allowed users without privileges on the target table to reveal its schema, row count, size, and existence. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114596&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114596](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114596+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix a renamed and dropped column being read from the wrong file while the mutation is pending
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114562 ## Problem A column that is renamed, dropped and added again in one `ALTER` silently returns the **dropped** column's data instead of its own default, while the mutation is still pending: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, h UInt8 DEFAULT 0) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() SETTINGS min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, min_rows_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO t SELECT number + 100, 0 FROM numbers(1000); SET alter_sync = 0; -- mutation left pending ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN a TO b, DROP COLUMN b, ADD COLUMN b UInt64 DEFAULT 7; SELECT count(), min(b), max(b) FROM t; -- 1000 100 1099 <- the old `a` values -- expected: 1000 7 7 ``` No error and nothing in the log; it affects `Wide` and `Compact` parts alike. The added `b` is a different column from the one that was dropped, so its rows have to come from its `DEFAULT`. **Scope.** This fixes the answer while the mutation is pending. Once the mutation has materialised a `Wide` part still returns the dropped column's data — a separate, pre-existing defect that lives in `MutateTask`, see the follow-ups at the end. ## Root cause `AlterConversions` records a pending drop under the name the command used: ```cpp else if (command.type == DROP_COLUMN) { dropped_columns.emplace(command.column_name); } ``` while every consumer of `isColumnDropped` asks about a column under the name it has **in the part**: - `IMergeTreeReader::isColumnDroppedByPendingMutation` takes the name out of `columns_to_read`, which is built from `getColumnInPart` and therefore already has the rename mapping applied (`IMergeTreeReader.cpp:81`); - `injectRequiredColumnsRecursively` passes `column_name_in_part` (`MergeTreeBlockReadUtils.cpp:119`). Without a rename the two names are identical, so the hazard those checks exist for — a column dropped and re-added under the same name, whose data in the part is stale — behaves correctly. That is why this was never noticed. With a rename they diverge: the part holds `a`, the drop is recorded for `b`, the check asks about `a`, finds nothing, and the reader streams the `a` file into the new `b`. ## Solution Consume the ordering in `DROP_COLUMN`, where both halves of it are needed anyway. Commands arrive as issued, so the renames recorded so far are exactly those preceding the drop; the entry that gives the drop its part-side name is also the entry the drop makes obsolete, so one lookup does both: ```cpp auto name_in_part = command.column_name; auto it = std::ranges::find(rename_map, command.column_name, &RenamePair::rename_to); if (it != rename_map.end()) { name_in_part = it->rename_from; rename_map.erase(it); } dropped_columns.emplace(std::move(name_in_part)); ``` Every existing caller of `isColumnDropped` already passes a part-side name, so all of them become correct at once and none of them changes. Retiring the mapping matters on its own. `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b` used to leave **two** entries pointing at `b` — from the dropped `a` and from the live `c` — and the lookup returns whichever comes first, so `b` read the wrong column. Writing a `RenamePair` as `to <- from`, where `to` is the name in the metadata and `from` the name in the part, and remembering that `dropped_columns` now holds part-side names: | # | command | what happens | `rename_map` | `dropped_columns` | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | `RENAME a TO b` | not chained, insert | `[b <- a]` | `{}` | | 2 | `DROP b` | `b <- a` gives the part's `a` and is erased in the same step | `[]` | `{a}` | | 3 | `RENAME c TO b` | `b` is free, insert | `[b <- c]` | `{a}` | `getColumnOldName("b")` then answers `c`, and `a` stays dropped so nothing reads it. Both halves are needed to get this right: | variant | `min(b), max(b)`, want `5000 5999` | |---|---| | `master` | `100 1099` — the **dropped** column's data | | part-side drop only | `0 0` — the default | | both | `5000 5999` ✔ | ### Why in the drop and not when the name is taken over Retiring the entry in `RENAME_COLUMN` instead — erase whatever maps onto the new target and is already dropped — reads as the more targeted fix, and it is where the first two commits of this PR put it. It has to cover two paths, though, because a rename can reach the freed name through a chain: `RENAME c TO d, RENAME d TO b` updates the existing `d <- c` entry in place rather than appending, so an erase placed on the appending path alone leaves `[b <- a, b <- c]` again. That variant does not misread — it fails outright, because `b` resolves to the dropped `a` and the part-side name reaches the storage snapshot: ``` Code: 16. DB::Exception: There is no column a in table. (NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE) ``` Reaching it takes `ReplicatedMergeTree`: a single `ALTER` rejects transitive renames (`Transitive renames in a single ALTER query are not allowed`), and `StorageMergeTree::alter` always waits for the previous mutation before a metadata change (`StorageMergeTree.cpp:548`, *"alters should be executed in sequential order"*), so two of them can never both be pending there. Doing it in the drop is the same thing one step earlier and needs no case analysis: a mapping onto a dropped name simply never exists, so `RENAME_COLUMN` has nothing to clean up and the chained path needs no special handling. The two were measured equivalent on both the read path (all of `04872`) and the materialisation path (the mutation run to completion with `alter_sync = 2` for `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, ADD b`, `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b`, `RENAME a TO b, DROP b` and the chained Replicated case — byte-identical results). ### Why not fix it in the reader Checking the renamed-to name in the reader as well looks equivalent and is wrong. The opposite command order produces exactly the same `AlterConversions` state, and `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames` already pins the required behaviour for it: ```sql ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN value2_old, RENAME COLUMN value2 TO value2_old; ``` Here the drop hit a *different* column that merely carried that name, and `value2`'s data is live and must be readable as `value2_old`. The only thing separating the two situations is where the drop sits among the renames, which the readers cannot see. Measured with the reader-side variant applied, live data is replaced by defaults: ``` dropped, then the name reused by a rename -1000 100 1099 +1000 0 0 ``` Hence the ordering has to be consumed at construction time. ### Tests `tests/queries/0_stateless/04872_read_renamed_then_dropped_and_readded_column.sh` — seven cases: the defect on `Wide` and on `Compact`, the `RENAME/DROP/RENAME` case above and its chained variant, plus three controls that must not move — drop-and-re-add without a rename (what the check was written for), a pending rename with no drop, and the mirror case. The chained case runs the `ALTER`s with the partition detached and then attaches the part carrying the old column names to a table whose merges are stopped, so the mutations stay unapplied while it is read — the same shape as `03905_chained_rename_column_mutation`. Verified on a local server that it is load-bearing: with the retirement placed on the appending path of `RENAME_COLUMN` it fails with `NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE`, while the non-chained control passes either way. Because the two possible wrong answers fail in opposite directions, the result is checked three ways: | variant | the defect | the mirror case | |---|---|---| | `master` | `1000 100 1099` ✗ | `1000 100 1099` ✔ | | reader-side variant | `1000 7 7` ✔ | `1000 0 0` ✗ | | this change | `1000 7 7` ✔ | `1000 100 1099` ✔ | `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames`, `01278_alter_rename_combination`, `03905_chained_rename_column_mutation`, `04053_alter_add_rename_column_in_single_query` and `04011_detach_rename_attach_column` all pass. ### Notes for reviewers - **The retirement relies on the command sequence reaching `AlterConversions` without gaps, and it does.** Metadata mutations are exempt from every `params` switch — `needIncludeMutationToSnapshot` (`MergeTreeData.cpp:653`, *"Metadata mutations must be included into the snapshot regardless of the parameters"*) and `addSupportedCommands` (`MergeTreeData.cpp:704`) both admit `RENAME_COLUMN` and `DROP_COLUMN` unconditionally, so no caller can ask for a snapshot holding the renames but not the drops. Per-part filtering then takes a contiguous suffix, never a middle slice: both `getOnFlyMutationCommandsForPart` implementations walk in reverse and *stop* at the first mutation at or below the part's version (`StorageMergeTree.cpp:3549`, `ReplicatedMergeTreeQueue.cpp:2355`). A gap would need `RENAME a TO b` in the window with `DROP b` cut out, but the drop is the newer of the two, so cutting it necessarily cuts the rename that created the entry as well. Order is a documented contract: *"@return list of mutation commands in order: oldest to newest"* (`MergeTreeData.h:617`). The chained-rename collapsing that predates this PR rests on the same property. The replicated loop iterates by `mutation_version` while testing `alter_version`, so the suffix is contiguous only if the two are co-monotonic, and they are: the single site that creates a mutation entry with `alter_version != -1` (`StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:7092`) does so in one `tryMulti` that also carries `set /metadata` with a CAS on the current metadata version (`StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:7001`, and `alter_version` is that version plus one) and `set /mutations` with a CAS on its own version. Either CAS makes two of them serialise, and the sequential number is assigned inside that atomic commit, so the k-th alter mutation to commit gets both the larger sequence number and the higher metadata version. `mutate` — the other creator — leaves `alter_version` at `-1` and is handled by the loop's other branch. Confirmed by reading the raw znodes through `system.zookeeper`: with `ALTER UPDATE`s interleaved between the renames the metadata subsequence is `1, 2, 3, 4` in znode order, and ten concurrent renames from separate clients land as `alter_version` `1..9` matching the znode sequence exactly. - `isColumnDropped` now consistently answers about part-side names. That matches all four existing call sites, so it is a fix rather than a contract change for them, but a future caller holding a metadata name would have to resolve it first. - **Overlaps with #114562, in a way that is safe in either merge order.** That PR adds a second lookup in the empty-candidate accounting loop of `injectRequiredColumns`, mapping a part name forward to its renamed-to name and testing the drop under that, so that a single-statement `RENAME a TO b, DROP b` is recognised as accounted for. This change makes the *first* lookup answer that correctly, because the drop is then already recorded as `a`, so the second lookup becomes dead code once both are in. It is deliberately left in place here rather than removed pre-emptively: while only #114562 is merged the second lookup is what makes that case work. A small cleanup to delete it belongs after this merges. Checked on a scratch branch carrying both changes with that lookup deleted — `04870`, `04871`, `04872`, `03830`, `04011` and `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames` all still pass, so the cleanup is safe. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a column that was renamed, dropped and added again in one `ALTER` returning the dropped column's values instead of its own default while the mutation was still pending. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114601&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114601](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114601+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> ### Follow-ups found while testing, not fixed here Both are pre-existing, live in `MutateTask` rather than `AlterConversions`, and were measured identical on the pre-PR base and on this branch, so they are out of scope. Filed for follow-up: - `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, ADD b UInt64 DEFAULT 7` still returns `1000 100 1099` after the mutation has materialised. This PR fixes the answer only while the mutation is pending. Measured: `Wide` parts only (a `Compact` part gives the correct `7 7`), plain `MergeTree` **and** `ReplicatedMergeTree`, with default `alter_sync` and no fault injection at all; `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` and `DETACH`/`ATTACH` do not repair it. The same statement without the `ADD` leaves `b.bin` orphaned in the part while neither the table nor the part lists the column any more. - `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b` with `alter_sync = 2` makes the mutation fail permanently with `Code: 424 ... b.bin already exists and has a different inode ... (CANNOT_LINK)`, because the retired `a -> b` rename and the live `c -> b` collide on one destination file.

signals.title: Fix DPsub join reordering silently dropping single-table ON-clause filters
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111898 The `dpsub` join-order algorithm silently dropped single-table filter and constant predicates that live in a `JOIN ... ON` clause (e.g. `t1.value = 'x'`), returning extra rows. `greedy` uses a different placement path and was unaffected. The predicates are placed in `collectJoinEdgesMask`. Two placement conditions there each silently dropped such a predicate: - `two_relations` required the whole join step to be exactly two relations, so the predicate was dropped whenever its relation was introduced against an already-multi-relation subplan (e.g. `t1` at the top of `t1 JOIN (t2 JOIN t3)`). - `fromLeft() || fromRight() || fromNone()` dropped the predicate for any single-table filter on a relation whose id is >= 2, because `fromLeft`/`fromRight` test relation ids 0 and 1 specifically (they describe the two inputs of a binary join step, not "references a single relation"). The predicate is now attached at the join that introduces its relation (the split whose one side is exactly that relation), and pure constants at the earliest two-relation join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `dpsub` join-order optimization (`query_plan_optimize_join_order_algorithm = 'dpsub'`) silently dropping single-table filter conditions from a `JOIN ... ON` clause, which could return extra rows. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114629&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114629](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114629+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Re-land aggregate function `gini` in the `sum` family
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113868 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112280 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New aggregate function `gini`, which calculates the [Gini coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient) of a column of finite, non-negative numeric values. The result ranges from `0` (all values equal) towards `1` as inequality grows; for a sample of `n` values the maximum is `(n - 1) / n`. `NaN` values are skipped, while infinite and negative values are rejected. The function returns `Float64` and consumes `O(n)` memory. ### Description Re-lands the `gini` function that #113868 reverted, following the option-2 spec @ Manerone gave in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763#issuecomment-5217284116. `gini` now registers and folds exactly like `sum`. Relative to #112280 it drops the `getArgumentsThatCanBeOnlyNull` override, `.returns_default_when_only_null = true`, and the `argument_type->onlyNull()` branch in the creator, and touches no file under `src/AggregateFunctions/Combinators/`. The property was doing the work: it made `AggregateFunctionFactory::getImpl` skip its only-null guard and build a real `gini` over `Nullable(Nothing)`, so `gini(NULL)` returned `Float64` `nan` where every `sum`-family function folds to `Nullable(Nothing)`. Without it the fold happens in the `Null` combinator first, which is why `createAggregateFunctionSum` has no equivalent. It also drops `getOwnNullAdapter`, at @ Manerone's request in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114643#issuecomment-5354588069. Keeping it left `gini` the only function in the family whose plain and wrapped forms disagreed on nullability: the `Null` combinator consults that hook only on the object it wraps directly, and for `giniIf` / `giniDistinct` that is `AggregateFunctionIf` / `AggregateFunctionDistinct`, whose own adapters win. So `gini(x)` stayed `Float64` while `giniIf(x, c)` became `Nullable(Float64)`. Dropping it gives parity on the runtime axis too: over a `Nullable` column every form returns `Nullable(Float64)`, `NULL` when no non-`NULL` value qualifies and `nan` when fewer than two do. Non-nullable input is unchanged. Validated against `sum` on the same binary: every literal-`NULL` and `Nullable`-column cell matches its `sum` counterpart, and non-nullable results are unchanged from #112280. Docs: `gini.mdx` plus its slug-map, navigation and redirect entries are restored from their merged state in #114314, which #113868's revert had removed as collateral; the generated region is regenerated from the `FunctionDocumentation` block by `ci/jobs/scripts/docs/autogenerate/autogenerate_docs.py` (`--check` clean) and the page keeps its hand-written header. The slug-map row is needed, not cosmetic: without it the nightly generator resolves no Mintlify destination and fails for this page. The `pr-autogenerated-docs` label is what lets a page carrying the markers pass the generated-region guard, as the guard's own message asks for. cc @Manerone <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114643&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114643](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114643+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Speed up `IN (subquery)` set building by pre-deduplicating each `MergeTree` partition independently
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108326 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105126 The set for `IN (subquery)` is built by a single `CreatingSetsTransform`: all streams of the subquery are merged into one and every row is hashed serially, no matter how many threads read the data. If the partition expression of the subquery's table is a function of the subquery's output columns (the set is keyed on all of them), the reading will now emit each partition through a single port and each stream is deduplicated independently before the filling transform. Because a key then lives in exactly one stream, per-stream deduplication is complete, and the single filling transform only hashes unique rows — the serial part of the build shrinks from all rows to distinct rows, and the deduplication itself runs in parallel. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() PARTITION BY a % 8; INSERT INTO t SELECT number % 1000000 FROM numbers(100000000); OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL; EXPLAIN PIPELINE SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t) SETTINGS allow_creating_set_partitions_independently = 1, max_threads = 8; ``` ```response (CreatingSets) DelayedPorts 9 → 8 (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (Aggregating) Resize 1 → 8 AggregatingTransform (Expression) ExpressionTransform (Filter) FilterTransform (ReadFromSystemNumbers) NumbersRange 0 → 1 (CreatingSet) CreatingSetsTransform <- the single filling transform now hashes ~1M unique rows instead of 100M Resize 8 → 1 DistinctTransform × 8 <- new: parallel pre-deduplication on partition-disjoint streams (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (ReadFromMergeTree) MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder) × 8 0 → 1 <- per-partition reading (8 partitions → 8 streams) ``` On the table above (100M rows, 1M distinct keys, 8 balanced partitions; 64-core machine, average of 3 runs after 2 warm-ups): | query | off | on | speedup | |------------------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|---------| | `SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t)` | 0.643s | 0.113s | 5.7× | ### Adaptive abandonment of the preliminary deduplication The per-stream `DistinctTransform` in front of the set fill pays off only when it removes rows: the set deduplicates anyway, so on mostly-unique input the transform removes almost nothing while its hash tables hold roughly a second copy of the unique keys next to the set being built. To keep the optimization strictly non-regressing, the pre-deduplication observes its own effectiveness and gives up when it is not helping (`DeduplicationAbandonController`): * It accumulates, over all chunks seen so far, how many rows survived deduplication. The rate is first checked after 5 chunks — or earlier, once the observation itself retains 16 MiB of hash table, so wide keys (e.g. long strings) cannot hold multiples of that just to finish the window. From then on it is checked after every chunk, so duplicates concentrated at the head of a stream do not keep a useless hash table alive through a unique tail. * When at least 90% of the observed rows survive, the transform abandons: it frees its hash table and passes the remaining chunks through untouched. This is correct only because the consumer deduplicates anyway, so abandoning is allowed by an explicit constructor flag that only the set-fill call site enables. * The 0.9 threshold is calibrated on per-partition set builds over uniform data: keeping the deduplication is ~8–11x at ~1% uniqueness and ~1.2x at 10%, turns time-neutral but memory-negative once only about a quarter of the rows are duplicates — which the observation sees as a unique rate of about 0.9, because a stream's duplicates concentrate in its partition and repeat within the window. The transform also mirrors the set fill's `NULL` handling: with the default `transform_null_in = 0` the fill drops every row with a `NULL` in any key component, so the pre-deduplication drops them too (using the same `extractNestedColumnsAndNullMap` helper, plus the dictionary `NULL` entry for `LowCardinality(Nullable)` keys) instead of hashing them and letting them distort the abandon decision. Chunks fully resolved by the `LowCardinality` dictionary mask are likewise counted as duplicate rows. Together this keeps the abandon decision based on exactly the row population the fill would hash. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up set building for `IN (subquery)` on partitioned `MergeTree` tables by keeping each partition's rows within a single stream and deduplicating each stream independently, so the single set-filling transform — previously hashing every row serially — only sees unique rows. This applies when the partition expression is a deterministic function of the subquery's output columns. The optimization is not applied when the largest partition holds more than twice the rows of the average partition; the new setting `force_creating_set_partitions_independently` (disabled by default) bypasses this check. Controlled by the new setting `allow_creating_set_partitions_independently` (enabled by default). --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114645&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114645](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114645+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]

signals.title: Fix File row policy / PREWHERE breaking DEFAULT columns missing from the data file
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114616 When a file-backed table (`File`, and the same path for object storage) has a `DEFAULT` column that is not present in the data file, a row policy or `PREWHERE` could prune the inputs of that default expression before `AddingDefaultsTransform` ran. That led to `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` on current master, and on 26.7 to silently wrong row-policy results (type defaults instead of real values). This keeps columns required by `DEFAULT` expressions in the read set through prewhere pruning, and applies filters that reference defaulted columns after defaults are computed. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix queries over file-backed tables where a row policy or `PREWHERE` interacted with `DEFAULT` columns missing from the data file: they no longer fail with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`, and row policies are evaluated on real default values instead of type defaults.

signals.title: Fix ANY/SEMI RIGHT JOIN with OR conditions emitting rows twice or losing matches
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112640 `ANY RIGHT JOIN` and `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` emit every row of their right table at most once, and exactly once when the row has a match. With several OR-ed conditions in `ON` the claim for that was taken with a single CAS on the head row of the matched key's `RowRefList`, while `addFoundRowAll` then emitted every row of that list and discarded the result of the per-row `setUsedOnce` it called afterwards. With `OR` a right row is reachable through several keys in several hash maps, so a per-key claim does not partition the right rows: a list whose head row was claimed through another condition was skipped whole, orphaning its other rows, and a list whose head row was still free re-emitted rows another left row had already taken. Some right rows then appeared twice and others lost their match — padded with defaults for `ANY RIGHT JOIN`, dropped entirely for `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` — varying from run to run with the probe order under `max_threads > 1`. The claim is now taken per emitted row: `addFoundRowAll` claims a row before appending it and skips the rows whose CAS it loses, and returns whether it appended anything so the left row is filtered in only then. A single disjunct keeps the per-key claim, which is exact there, since one key owns all of its rows. The residual-condition path (`joinRightColumnsWithAdditionalFilter`) already claimed per row and is unchanged. Besides writing `ANY RIGHT JOIN` / `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` directly, this is reached by a plain `ANY LEFT JOIN` whenever the planner swaps the tables (`query_plan_join_swap_table`, `auto` by default), which is how the issue was reported. Measured on the reported query before and after, at `max_threads = 8`: 20 of 60 runs returned 5 or 6 rows for a 4-row left table, now 60/60 return 4. On a 1000-row shape, `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` returned 200 rows instead of 1000; `ANY LEFT JOIN` padded 416–736 rows with defaults although they had a match, and with `max_joined_block_size_rows = 7` also returned 1008 rows for 1000 left rows. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ANY RIGHT JOIN` and `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` with several `OR`-ed conditions in the `ON` section returning some rows of the right table twice and losing the matches of others. A written `ANY LEFT JOIN` was affected too, because the planner may swap the tables and execute it as `ANY RIGHT JOIN`.

signals.title: Precompute hashes and prefetch for fixed-size-keys aggregation methods
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104475 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): For the `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256` family of aggregation methods (several fixed-size keys packed into one integer), precompute the per-row canonical hashes in one pass over the batch-packed keys and reuse them to software-prefetch the target bucket and to skip rehashing the key in `emplace`. Previously the look-ahead prefetch computed every key and its hash twice per row. --- This extends the precomputed-hash + prefetch mechanism that #104475 introduced for the `prealloc_serialized` family to `HashMethodKeysFixed` (multi-key `GROUP BY` over numeric columns, e.g. ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q32). When the whole block of keys is batch-packed upfront (`prepared_keys`), the per-row canonical hashes are computed in one pass on the first `emplace`/`find` call and reused both for the look-ahead prefetch and for the insert itself, replacing the generic look-ahead in `Aggregator::executeImplBatch` that builds every key holder and hashes it a second time per row. Details: - The runtime gates mirror `prealloc_serialized`: batch-packed keys available, `enable_software_prefetch_in_aggregation`, and the `min_bytes_for_prefetch` hash-table size threshold (checked lazily on the first call, when `Data` is known). Nullable and low-cardinality variants never use `prepared_keys` and are excluded at compile time. - A new concept `HasPrefetchByHashMemberFunc` compiles the path out for tables without hash-addressed buckets (`FixedHashTable` behind `keys16`). Set, JOIN and `arrayUniq`-style callers of `HashMethodKeysFixed` pass no settings context, so nothing changes for them. - `HashMethodSerializedContext` carried only the settings and is now the shared `HashMethodSettingsContext`, also used by `HashMethodKeysFixed::createContext`. - `HashTable::isEmptyCell` (the `findKey` short-circuit for precomputed hashes, used in the `no_more_keys` mode) is made zero-key-aware: the zero key is stored outside the buffer, so an empty cell at the key's place proves nothing when the zero key is present. The existing user (`prealloc_serialized`) never produces empty keys, so this was latent; an all-zeros fixed key is common (the ClickBench `hits` table has a `SearchEngineID = 0, ClientIP = 0` group). Correctness was verified against an unpatched build of the same commit on the full ClickBench `hits` dataset (identical single part, 99,997,497 rows): full-result checksums for `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256`, nullable keys and `prealloc_serialized`; the all-zero key group; the `no_more_keys` path (`max_rows_to_group_by` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`); and external aggregation (spill + merge). All results are identical. An honest note on measured impact, from the investigation written up in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638#issuecomment-5285053418: in a local interleaved A/B on a (noisy, shared) 96-core aarch64 box, this change measures neutral on ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q35 — the generic look-ahead prefetch already covered these methods, so the remaining saving is one packed-key load plus one CRC per row. The issue's local reproduction numbers for these queries turned out to be dominated by an unrelated effect (the memory-based `max_threads` cap from #100383, which the pre-#100383 baseline build does not have — details in the issue). The perf tests that exercise these exact shapes (`tests/performance/clickbench.xml` Q30/Q31/Q32, `group_by_fixed_keys.xml`, `hash_table_sizes_stats.xml`) should be the arbiter on dedicated hardware. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114679&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114679](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114679+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support aggregate functions in the trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114637 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true`) now also fires for projections **with aggregate functions**, e.g. ClickBench Q17 (`SELECT UserID, SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) FROM hits GROUP BY UserID, SearchPhrase LIMIT 10`), while keeping the aggregate values of the returned keys **exact**. **Why it was restricted.** The settings-based rewrite (`max_rows_to_group_by = n + offset` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`) enforces the cutoff per aggregation stream: a key kept by one stream and rejected by another loses the other stream's rows and comes out of the merge with an undercounted value. Returning an unspecified subset of the groups is fine for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`; returning wrong values is not. **How it works now (shared kept keys, zero hot-path cost).** The streams aggregate completely normally until the first one exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys (the pre-existing per-block `checkLimits`). That stream publishes a frozen seed of exactly `n + offset` kept keys with empty aggregate states (`ManyAggregatedData::SharedKeptKeys`); every stream then rebuilds its hash table to exactly that key set — keeping the states it accumulated for the kept keys, dropping the rest — and continues on the pre-existing `no_more_keys` path against a table of `n + offset` keys. Streams that finished consuming before the freeze are rebuilt by the last stream before the merge. Every row before the freeze is aggregated normally and every later row of a kept key finds its key in the rebuilt table, so the merged values are exact; the dropped keys are absent from every rebuilt table and never reach the result. The rebuild reuses the existing two-stage machinery (`convertToChunks(final = false)` + `mergeOnBlock`), so the hot aggregation loops in `Aggregator.cpp` are untouched. **Where it fires.** The cutoff is detected in the planner and enabled only when the node performs the complete aggregation itself (first and second stage): partial states sent to a remote initiator would be merged with other nodes' states, whose kept keys differ, and the values would be undercounted again — across nodes instead of across threads. On the shards of distributed queries and on the replicas of parallel-replicas reading it stays off. The settings-based rewrite of `OptimizeTrivialGroupByLimitPass` remains for aggregate-free projections (it is sound cross-shard). For the 8/16-bit key methods (fixed hash maps bounded by the key space) the cutoff stays inert and the aggregation is complete and exact. External aggregation is disabled when the cutoff is armed (spilled buckets would bypass the restriction); memory stays bounded by roughly `n + offset` keys plus one block of keys per stream. **Guards for wrong results of the existing optimization.** The shape check (shared between the pass and the planner, `getTrivialGroupByLimit`) now also rejects `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions and `arrayJoin` in the projection. These consume or filter the groups after the aggregation, and all four cases were verified to return wrong results on master with the default settings (e.g. `SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 3` returned 1 row instead of 3; `SELECT count() OVER () FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 5` returned ~100 instead of 100000). Test `04837` pins all four in both the top-level (pass) and subquery (planner) forms. The guards are also submitted separately as the minimal backportable bug fix https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 (issue https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114693); whichever merges second needs a trivial conflict resolution. **Measured** on a 96-core aarch64 box, `SELECT number % 100000000 AS k, count() FROM numbers_mt(200000000) GROUP BY k LIMIT 10`: 0.06–0.13 s with the optimization vs 0.37–0.94 s without (interleaved hot runs on a shared machine). The values of the returned keys match the full aggregation exactly (verified by the `04836` join-against-truth tests for `UInt64`/`String`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable`/two-key shapes, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`max`/`uniqExact`, with `OFFSET`, under single-stream and 16-stream execution, from aggregate projections, and over `remote()`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (setting `optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`) now also applies to queries with aggregate functions in the projection, such as ClickBench Q17: once any aggregation thread exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys, all threads are restricted to a single shared set of kept keys, so the hash tables stay small while the aggregate values of the returned keys remain exact (about 2x on ClickBench Q17). Additionally, the optimization no longer fires for queries with `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions, or `arrayJoin` in the projection, where it could return wrong results. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114690&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114690](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114690+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Remove `WINDOW VIEW`
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61069 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75191 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/88706 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `WINDOW VIEW` feature is removed, together with the `WATCH` statement and the `windowID` function. It has been non-functional since version 24.12 (inserts into the source table were silently not delivered to window views) and was never supported by the analyzer, which is enabled by default since 24.3. The settings `allow_experimental_window_view`, `window_view_clean_interval`, `window_view_heartbeat_interval`, and `wait_for_window_view_fire_signal_timeout` are kept as obsolete no-ops. The time-window functions `tumble`, `tumbleStart`, `tumbleEnd`, `hop`, `hopStart`, and `hopEnd` are kept. If you still have window views defined, drop them before upgrading: a server that finds a window view in its metadata fails to start (`Cannot parse definition from metadata file ... (SYNTAX_ERROR)`), the same way the removal of the `Lazy` database engine behaves. Similar functionality will be reimplemented on top of streaming queries (issue [#114738](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738)). The removal, in detail: - `src/Storages/WindowView/` (`StorageWindowView`, `WindowViewSource`, `StorageBlocks`), `WatermarkTransform`, the `ParserCreateWindowViewQuery` parser, and the whole `WATCH` statement stack (`ParserWatchQuery`, `ASTWatchQuery`, `InterpreterWatchQuery`, the `IStorage::watch` virtual) — window views were the last implementor of `watch`, and the `WATCH` statement was already documented as deprecated. - The `ASTCreateQuery` watermark/lateness fields and their AST JSON serialization and validation. The `clickhouse_json` boundary fails closed rather than silently reinterpreting legacy payloads: `ASTCreateQuery::readJSON` rejects a set `is_window_view`, watermark strategy or `allowed_lateness` flag and the `watermark_function` / `lateness_function` children (otherwise such a payload deserialized as an ordinary `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` and was executed as an immediate-population table create), while `ASTViewTargets::readJSON` rejects the `Inner` target kind, which nothing produces any more and which formatted back to parser-impossible `INNER ENGINE ...` SQL. Both are covered by `04892_ast_json_removed_window_view_state`; the `PushingToWindowViewSink` and `ViewType::WINDOW` branches in `InsertDependenciesBuilder`; window-view special cases in `InterpreterCreateQuery`, `InterpreterInsertQuery`, `StorageFactory`, `DatabaseOrdinary`, `DatabaseReplicated`, `DDLDependencyVisitor`, `QueryFuzzer`, BuzzHouse, and the ArrowFlight table-type mapping. - The `windowID` function and the `UInt32` single-argument forms of `tumbleStart`/`tumbleEnd`/`hopStart`/`hopEnd` (they only accepted `windowID` output). The rest of the time-window function family stays, since these are ordinary functions usable in a regular `GROUP BY` and are exactly the vocabulary for the streaming-queries replacement. - The keywords `WATCH`, `EVENTS`, `ALLOWED_LATENESS`, and `STRICTLY_ASCENDING` (the `WATERMARK` keyword stays: the streaming-queries `WATERMARK FOR` clause uses it), the error code `QUERY_IS_NOT_SUPPORTED_IN_WINDOW_VIEW`, and the corresponding fuzzer dictionary and ANTLR grammar entries. - Kept for compatibility: `QueryViewsLogElement::ViewType::WINDOW` (so existing `system.query_views_log` tables keep their schema) and `ViewTarget::Inner` (so old DDL log entries still parse), following the same pattern as the `LIVE VIEW` removal. - No replay compatibility is provided for `Replicated` databases, again following the `LIVE VIEW` precedent: a lagging replica that upgrades and then replays a retained `CREATE WINDOW VIEW` DDL queue entry stalls on a plain `SYNTAX_ERROR` — the same long-standing behavior as for any queue entry with unknown syntax (for example, one written by a newer server) — and the replica should be recreated. An earlier revision of this PR carried a token-level rewriting layer in `DatabaseReplicatedWorker` that tried to skip such entries and their follow-ups; it was removed as an unmaintainable fallback path (review kept finding shapes of retained `RENAME`/`EXCHANGE`/`ATTACH` history that it silently mishandled), in favor of failing closed. - The `allow_experimental_window_view` constraint in `tests/docker_scripts/stress_tests.lib` is kept (only the constraint, not the profile value, which would mark an obsolete setting as changed and add a `system.warnings` entry): the upgrade check runs the previous release's suite under the previous release's binary, whose window-view tests are not dropped afterwards because `--upgrade-check` implies `--fake-drop`, and the leftover metadata would then stop the new server from starting. - Tests: the four remaining window-view tests are removed. The pure time-window-function coverage of `01049_window_view_window_functions` moved to a new `04891_time_window_functions` test, which also pins the new `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` behavior of `tumbleStart(UInt32)`. - Docs: the `Window View` section of `CREATE VIEW`, the `WATCH` page (with its navigation entries and locale twins) are removed and the old-slug redirects retargeted; the window-view entries are removed from the generated settings/functions reference pages (second commit, hence the `pr-autogenerated-docs` label): the `window-view.mdx` settings page, the four settings' entries in the pages/manifest/navigation/settings explorer, and the `windowID` section of `time-window-functions.mdx`. The unrelated drift accumulated on master since the last nightly regeneration is deliberately not included; the nightly docs-autogen job will pick it up. Why now: the feature has been non-functional since Dec 2024 — commit `ceae84c87a2` removed the explicit view-dependency registration and `DDLDependencyVisitor` never extracted the source table of a `CREATE WINDOW VIEW`, so inserts into the source table were silently not pushed to window views, and direct inserts failed with `std::out_of_range` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493). Nobody noticed for ~1.5 years. It was never ported to the analyzer (with `enable_analyzer = 1`, the default, existing window views load permanently inert), its tests were removed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/73822 because they were inherently flaky, and it kept costing triage time (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 is a recent server SIGSEGV through `getSourceTableSelectQuery`). The full assessment, including the plan for reimplementing this functionality on top of streaming queries (`SELECT ... FROM t STREAM`, `WATERMARK FOR`, emit-on-watermark windowed aggregation), is in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114747&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114747](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114747+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add byte-weighted bytes_to_do and progress to system.mutations
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114678 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `system.mutations` now exposes byte-weighted mutation progress: `bytes_to_do` (the on-disk size of the data parts that still need to be mutated) and `progress` (an estimated finished fraction from 0 to 1, including the live fraction of the parts currently being rewritten). Part counts are a poor work proxy — parts are unequal in size and a regular merge can retire many pending parts at once — so the byte view is the honest one; the docs gain an "Estimating mutation progress" section with an equivalent parameterized-view recipe for older releases. Implements the conclusion of the research on the issue in two layers: **Columns** (`bytes_to_do` UInt64, `progress` Float64 in `system.mutations`): derived on read like `parts_to_do` — no persisted state, no replication protocol or znode format change. For plain `MergeTree` the sizes ride along the existing per-part scan in `getMutationsStatus`; for replicated tables the queue keeps returning name-only statuses under its state lock and the storage resolves sizes afterwards, so no parts lock is ever taken under the queue mutex (parts gone by then were retired and contribute nothing). The in-flight fraction comes from the merge list (`system.merges` rows with `is_mutation = 1`). Values are estimates by nature: a merge can retire pending parts at any moment, making `progress` jump forward. **Docs**: an "Estimating mutation progress" section on the `system.mutations` page explains why part-count percentages mislead and ships a parameterized-view recipe computing the same number on releases without the columns (the view was validated live against a running mutation, including a merge collapsing 9 pending parts mid-run), plus cross-links from `system.merges`, `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`, and the knowledge base. The stateless test asserts exact values on both engines: with merges stopped (which parks mutation tasks), `bytes_to_do` equals the active parts' total size and `progress` is 0; after completion the entry reports 0 and 1. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114850&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114850](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114850+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/series
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/series`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus clients** use **`/api/v1/series`** to discover the label sets stored for active series. This endpoint is used by **Prometheus-compatible tools** such as **Grafana** when they need to populate metric and label selectors. ClickHouse **`TimeSeries` tables** can store labels in the main **`tags` Map**, in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, or in a mixture of both layouts. The endpoint needs to expose the **same logical series** regardless of how those labels are stored. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/series` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint is available through both a **dedicated `/api/v1/series` handler** and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**. It supports **GET requests** and **`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POST requests**. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** selects series by metric name and label matchers. Repeated parameters are combined as a **union** and overlapping results are returned only once through **deduplication**. - **`start` and `end`** select series overlapping the requested **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the number of returned series and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Selector parsing:** parse Prometheus series selectors with equality, inequality, regular-expression, and negative regular-expression matchers. - **Storage compatibility:** support metric names, labels in the **`tags` Map**, dedicated tag columns, and mixed rows that use both storage layouts. - **Label normalization:** normalize missing labels to the **Prometheus empty-value semantics** and include the full logical label set in each response. - **PromQL compatibility:** support quoted label names and anchor regular expressions to the **complete label value**. - **Input validation:** validate selectors and timestamps before executing the query. - **Time ranges:** apply the time-range filter when trusted min/max data is available. When it is not available, keep the request valid and return the **compatible candidate superset** allowed by the Prometheus API. - **Result limits:** support zero and positive limits, exact-limit responses, truncation reporting, and invalid-value errors. - **Access control:** read the underlying series metadata through the **`TimeSeries` table-function path** after checking access to the configured **`TimeSeries` table**. Unknown routes are resolved before authorization, so they keep the normal **404 response**. - **Existing endpoints:** apply the configured **`TimeSeries` table access boundary** consistently to the existing Prometheus query endpoints. - **Query lifecycle:** run the generated query through the **normal query pipeline** and keep **query logging** and **query completion handling** intact. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Matcher operators:** metric-name and label selectors with all matcher operators. - **Repeated selectors:** repeated **`match[]`** parameters, selector unions, and overlapping-result deduplication. - **Storage layouts:** Map labels, dedicated tag columns, missing labels, mixed carriers, conflicting carriers, and **`__name__`**. - **Regex and names:** quoted label names and whole-value regular-expression anchoring. - **Selector validation:** invalid and unbounded selectors, including the valid **`{host!~".*"}`** case. - **Time ranges:** two-sided, one-sided, inclusive, and invalid time ranges. - **Min/max behavior:** requests with and without trusted min/max metadata. - **Limits:** zero, exact, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values. - **HTTP methods:** GET and form POST requests. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants**, access checks for all query endpoint families, and unknown-route handling. - **Observability:** query completion records and the existing query API limit behavior. Also ran **Python syntax checks** and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now covers the Prometheus handler configuration and the **`/api/v1/series` endpoint parameters**. ### Stack This is the **base PR** for the follow-up Prometheus API endpoints: - **#114868** adds **`/api/v1/labels`**. - **#114869** adds **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`**. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114867&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114867](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114867+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/labels
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/labels`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/labels`** to discover the label names available in matching series. This is useful for **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to build label selectors without fetching every series first. The endpoint follows the same **logical label model** as the series endpoint. It reads labels stored in the **`tags` Map** and in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/labels` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of label names**. It includes **`__name__`** when at least one matching series exists and supports both **unfiltered discovery** and filtering by matching series. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** filters the series used to build the label-name list. Repeated selectors are combined as a **union**. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned label names and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Label discovery:** collect distinct names from the canonical metric name, the **`tags` Map**, and configured dedicated tag columns. - **Selector support:** reuse the Prometheus series-selector and matcher behavior from **`/api/v1/series`**. - **Storage compatibility:** support both normal TimeSeries storage and **`tags_to_columns`** layouts while preserving the logical label set. - **Repeated selectors:** combine repeated **`match[]`** parameters without returning duplicate label names. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** support the dedicated endpoint and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**, with endpoint parameters kept separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Label collection:** distinct names, sorted output, **`__name__`**, Map labels, and dedicated columns. - **Selectors:** metric filters, label filters, repeated **`match[]`** unions, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the **`limit`** parameter behavior. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **Observability:** successful requests recorded as **`QueryFinish`** entries. - **Shared behavior:** the related Prometheus query and series API regression coverage. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the `/api/v1/labels` handler and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114868&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114868](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114868+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/label/<name>/values
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus-compatible clients** use **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`** to discover the values available for a label. This is used by **Grafana dashboards**, variable pickers, and integrations that need to populate label-value selectors. Prometheus also supports **escaped UTF-8 label names**. The endpoint must decode those names correctly while preserving malformed or intentionally literal values in a predictable way. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/label/<name>/values` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint returns a **sorted, distinct list of values** for one label. It supports metric names through **`__name__`**, labels from the **`tags` Map**, dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, series selectors, time ranges, and result limits. Supported parameters: - **`<name>`** identifies the label whose values should be returned, including Prometheus **`U__...` escaped names**. - **`match[]`** filters the series contributing values. - **`start` and `end`** restrict the matching series by their **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the returned values and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Value discovery:** return distinct values for ordinary labels and the special **`__name__`** metric-name label. - **Storage compatibility:** read values from the **`tags` Map** and dedicated **`tags_to_columns`** columns using the same logical label semantics as the other metadata endpoints. - **Name decoding:** decode valid Prometheus escaped label names, preserve malformed or overlong escape sequences as literal names, and reject an empty decoded label name. - **Selector support:** filter values by metric and series selectors, including unknown-label and no-match cases. - **Time ranges:** apply trusted min/max bounds when available and keep ranged requests valid with the **approximate superset** behavior allowed by Prometheus when bounds are unavailable. - **Result limits:** support empty, zero, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values, including the Prometheus truncation warning. - **HTTP handling:** add the label-values route to the **combined `/api/v1` handler** and keep endpoint parameters separate from ClickHouse settings. - **Access control:** enforce the configured **`TimeSeries` table authorization boundary** before reading the underlying target tables. - **Query lifecycle:** execute through the **normal query pipeline**, preserve query completion handling, and record the request in **`query_log`**. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Metric names:** values returned through **`__name__`**. - **Label values:** distinct Map values and values from configured dedicated columns. - **Escaped names:** valid UTF-8 decoding, malformed escape sequences, overlong escapes, and empty decoded names. - **Filtering:** selectors, unknown labels, and requests with no matching series. - **Time ranges:** matching and non-matching intervals, including empty optional parameters. - **Limits:** truncation warnings and the maximum valid **UInt64** limit. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants** on the configured `TimeSeries` table. - **HTTP integration:** the main HTTP port, routing, and query completion records. Also ran **Python syntax checks**, **XML parsing**, and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now describes the label-values handler, escaped label names, and its supported parameters. ### Stack This PR is **stacked on #114867** and includes the **`/api/v1/series`** changes. After **#114867** merges, this branch can be rebased onto `master`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114869&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114869](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114869+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: AI functions: Make quotas per query not per block
signals.text: `AIQuotaTracker` was a stack local inside `executeImpl`, so every block and every pipeline stream started with a fresh allowance. The `ai_function_max_api_calls_per_query`, `ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query` and `ai_function_max_output_tokens_per_query` limits therefore scaled with the data (one allowance per block per function) instead of bounding the query — any limit above the largest block's row count could never fire. The tracker is now a single instance owned by the query `Context` and shared by every AI function call in that context, with atomic counters for the concurrent pipeline threads. The API-call limit is claimed with an atomic bounded reservation, so it is an exact cap within a query-execution context even under `max_threads > 1`; the token limits are best-effort, since a call's token usage is known only after its response arrives. The limits are enforced per server / query fragment: a distributed query (across shards or parallel-replica fragments) enforces them independently on each, not summed globally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The AI-function quota settings (`ai_function_max_api_calls_per_query`, `ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query`, `ai_function_max_output_tokens_per_query`) were enforced per block rather than per query, letting a query exceed the configured limit in proportion to the number of blocks and threads processed. They now bound the whole query per server: the API-call limit is an exact cap (atomic reservation), and the token limits are best-effort. A distributed query enforces the limits independently on each participating server / fragment. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114885&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114885](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114885+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1732` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix AI functions under-reporting provider usage
signals.text: AI functions under-report what the provider was actually called and billed for. With the default `ai_function_throw_on_error = 1`, a failing `aiEmbed` logs an exception row showing `AIAPICalls = 0` and `AIInputTokens = 0`; flipping only that setting records the call: | `ai_function_throw_on_error` | `AIAPICalls` | `AIRowsSkipped` | |---|---:|---:| | `1` (default) | 0 | 0 | | `0` | 1 | 1 | Same query and endpoint, with `ai_function_max_retries = 0` so exactly one attempt is made. **Cause 1: counters die while unwinding.** `embedTexts` accumulated into a local `EmbeddingResult` returned by value. When a failed request rethrows, `return` is never reached: the local is destroyed and the caller's `embedding_result` is never constructed, so the caller's `ProfileEvents::increment` calls are both skipped and left with nothing to read. That defeats the intent stated at the accumulation site, which counts `api_calls` *before* issuing the request so failed calls are still counted. The providers lost their token counts the same way. **Cause 2: usage read after validation.** `call` and `embed` parsed `usage` only after validating the response body, so a `200` the provider had already billed for reported no tokens once a check rejected it. This is not only a `system.query_log` undercount: `AIQuotaTracker` never saw those tokens either, so `ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query` could not trip and a query with `ai_function_throw_on_error = 0` kept issuing billed requests past its cap. **Fix.** One rule in three places: the accumulator lives in caller-owned storage and is published from a scope guard, so every exit reports it. `embedTexts`, `IAIProvider::call` and `IAIProvider::embed` fill an out-parameter instead of returning by value, and both providers read `usage` before the checks that can reject the body. **Not covered.** `aiSimilarity` scores rows only once every batch is embedded, so its row counters are zero on a throwing exit — no row was scored, even though the first row's operands were embedded and billed. A test pins that. **Tests.** Nine integration tests. The eight regression tests were each verified to fail with the source reverted and to pass with it restored; the `aiSimilarity` one records a deliberate choice rather than a fix, so it passes either way. Two cover the quota effect rather than the reporting: a text query whose first response is billed-but-rejected stops dispatching once the cap is met, and `AnthropicProvider`, which had no coverage at all. Merged with https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111830, which introduced the throwing paths on the text side. Its guard around the text-path counters is what publishes them, so the per-attempt accounting here completes that path rather than duplicating it. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed AI functions under-reporting provider usage in `system.query_log` and in per-query quotas: counters accumulated before a failed request were dropped, and tokens for a response the provider billed for but that failed validation were never counted. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114905&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114905](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114905+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add two-model mode to continue-all-prs script
signals.text: Adds an optional two-model workflow to `continue-all-prs.sh`. A cheaper triage model checks the pull request first and can update it to the latest base branch or perform a clean base-branch merge. Work requiring source, test, or documentation changes is described in a structured handoff and continued by a fresh session using the coding model in the same worktree. The existing single-model mode remains unchanged. The status bar reports triage and coding-model spending separately, and the per-PR timeout is shared between both models, and Codex usage is priced according to the model active for each turn. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not applicable. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114909&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114909](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114909+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix an unkillable hang when dropping a low-sorting-name TimeSeries table
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114259 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a hang when dropping a `TimeSeries` table whose name sorts lexicographically below its inner tables' names, for example `` DROP TABLE `-ts` `` or dropping a materialized view declared with `ENGINE = TimeSeries`. The drop self-deadlocked on the DDL guard and could not be cancelled with `KILL QUERY`. ### Description `DROP TABLE` of a `TimeSeries` table never returned and could not be killed when the table's own qualified name sorted below its inner tables' names: ```sql SET allow_experimental_time_series_table = 1; CREATE TABLE `-ts` ENGINE = TimeSeries; DROP TABLE `-ts`; -- hung forever ``` A materialized view's inner name is `.inner_id.<uuid>`, which always sorts below `.inner_id.metrics.<uuid>`, so dropping an `MV ... ENGINE = TimeSeries` hung too. **Root cause.** `executeDropQuery` takes the DDL guard for the inner table, then synthesizes an `ASTDropQuery` for that same table without setting `no_ddl_lock`, so the nested interpreter takes the guard for the identical name again. `DDLGuard::table_lock` wraps a non-recursive `std::mutex`, so the thread deadlocks against itself. A mutex wait is not a cancellation point, so `KILL QUERY` could not land and the guard stayed held for the server's lifetime. `need_ddl_guard = true` comes from one call site, `StorageTimeSeries::dropInnerTableIfAny`, which requests the inner guard only when the parent name sorts first. That predicate is correct and is kept: guards must be taken in increasing name order. Only its comment was wrong, claiming the inner name is "almost always less", which holds for `MaterializedView` but not `TimeSeries`. **The change.** `executeDropQuery` now sets `no_ddl_lock = need_ddl_guard`, so the inner name is guarded exactly once, by the caller, across the nested execute. `InterpreterCreateQuery` sets the same field for the same reason. The fix is inert for the other ten call sites, which all take the `need_ddl_guard = false` default. The `ddl_guard` null check is pre-existing hardening. **Validation.** Both shapes time out before the fix and succeed after, while a high-sorting-name control passes on both builds. Eight concurrent drops serialize and complete and the name is reusable afterwards, so the guard is still taken and released. New test `04920` covers both shapes and asserts no inner table is left behind. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1839` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.6.7`, `26.6.4.12` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Read all summed columns for SELECT FINAL from SummingMergeTree
signals.text: `SELECT ... FINAL` from a `SummingMergeTree` table returned wrong results when the query read only a subset of the columns of the summation. A merge removes a row when the values in **all** of the columns of the summation are zero after summing. The FINAL read applied the same rule, but only over the columns the query happened to read. Two ways to misbehave follow from that: - A query reading a subset of the summed columns removed every group whose visible columns summed to zero, even though an unread summed column made the row survive a real merge — rows silently disappeared. The most common victim is bare `count()`, which reads a single smallest column (plus the internally added sorting key): on a table `(c0 Int8, c1 Int32, c3 UInt64) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree ORDER BY c3` with two overlapping parts where `c0` sums to zero for some keys, `SELECT count() FROM t FINAL` returned 10 instead of 15, and `SELECT c0, c3 FROM t FINAL` lost the same 5 rows. - A query reading none of the summed columns (e.g. only the sorting key) never removed anything, keeping rows that a real merge deletes. The fix always includes all columns that a merge would aggregate into the FINAL read set (and into the set protected from plan-level column pruning), so the removal decision is taken over the same set of columns as in a real merge. This makes `SELECT ... FINAL` agree with `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` followed by a plain `SELECT`. Note that queries over `SummingMergeTree FINAL` that previously read a subset of the summed columns now read all of them, which is the price of the correct result. Found by the nightly SQLancer `FinalMerge` oracle (`SELECT count() FROM t0 FINAL` returned 9947 before `OPTIMIZE TABLE t0 FINAL` and 9999 after it on the same data): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5c9f28ed5a2c585ad46bf74d6600cdcf3aa07a9e&name_0=NightlySQLancer&name_1=SQLancer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29&name_1=SQLancer ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results of `SELECT ... FINAL` from `SummingMergeTree` when the query reads only a subset of the columns of the summation: the decision to remove a row whose sums are all zero is now taken over all columns of the summation, as in a real merge, instead of only the columns the query reads. Previously, rows could silently disappear from the result (for example, `SELECT count() FROM table FINAL`). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115032&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115032](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115032+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
