signals.title: Add the experimental Trino SQL dialect
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental `trino` value of the `dialect` setting (gated by `allow_experimental_trino_dialect`): queries written in Trino SQL are translated to ClickHouse SQL, including Trino-specific syntax (`ARRAY[...]` literals, `TRY_CAST`, `UNNEST`, `ROW` constructors and types, `VALUES` tables, `OFFSET` before `LIMIT`, `FETCH`) and a mapping of several hundred Trino function names and argument conventions to their ClickHouse equivalents. Since Trino SQL is close to ClickHouse SQL (which already parses `AT TIME ZONE`, `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, `DATE`/`TIMESTAMP` literals, `GROUPING SETS`, `NULLS FIRST/LAST`, `WITH RECURSIVE`, ...), the dialect is not a separate grammar. It works in three stages in `src/Parsers/Trino/`: 1. **Token-level syntax translation** (`TrinoSyntaxTranslator`): `ARRAY[1, 2]` -> `[1, 2]`, `TRY_CAST(x AS t)` -> `accurateCastOrNull(x, 't')`, `ROW(...)` -> `tuple(...)` / `Tuple(...)`, `UNNEST` in `FROM` -> `ARRAY JOIN` (`LEFT JOIN UNNEST ... ON TRUE` -> `LEFT ARRAY JOIN`, `WITH ORDINALITY` -> `arrayEnumerate`, maps -> `mapKeys`/`mapValues`), `(VALUES ...)` -> a subquery over `SQLStandardValues`, `OFFSET n LIMIT m` -> `LIMIT m OFFSET n`, `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY/WITH TIES` -> `LIMIT`, `TIMESTAMP(p) [WITH TIME ZONE]` type -> `DateTime64(p)`, lambdas are parenthesized (the ClickHouse parser cannot parse a lambda after a literal argument), and backslashes in string literals are escaped (in Trino a backslash is a regular character). 2. **The standard ClickHouse parser** parses the result. If nothing needed translation, the original buffer is parsed directly, and `INSERT` statements with inline data (`VALUES`/`FORMAT`) are always delegated as-is so that the zero-copy data pointers stay valid. 3. **AST-level function mapping** (`TrinoFunctionMapper`): ~100 renames plus ~50 structural rewriters built from a review of all ~340 functions in the Trino documentation. This includes argument reordering for every higher-order function (Trino passes lambdas last, ClickHouse first: `transform(arr, f)` -> `arrayMap(f, arr)`), parametric-aggregate conversion (`approx_percentile(x, p)` -> `quantileTDigest(p)(x)`, `listagg(x, sep)` -> `groupConcat(sep)(x)`), and — most importantly — the names that resolve in ClickHouse with **different semantics** and would silently return wrong results if passed through: `to_unixtime` (an alias of `parseDateTime` in ClickHouse), `date_diff` (boundary crossings vs complete units -> `age`), `week` (non-ISO mode 0 -> `toISOWeek`), `from_unixtime(u, x)` (format string vs time zone), `rand`/`random` -> `randCanonical`, `transform`, `repeat`, `histogram`, `map(karr, varr)` -> `mapFromArrays`, `format` -> `printf`, and the varchar family (`length`, `substr`, `upper`, `lower`, `strpos`, `lpad`, ...) which is code-point-based in Trino and byte-based in ClickHouse (-> `...UTF8` variants). The feature gate follows the `polyglot` pattern: `SET` queries are handled before the gate inside the parser, so a misconfigured profile can always be recovered with `SET dialect = 'clickhouse'`. ClickHouse functions whose names do not collide with Trino names remain accessible from the dialect. Unsupported constructs (`TABLESAMPLE`, `TRY(...)`, comparator `array_sort`, ...) throw explicit `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`/`BAD_ARGUMENTS` errors instead of misbehaving, and semantics that cannot be fixed by translation at the query level (integer division `/`, `round` banker's rounding on Float, `greatest`/`least` NULL handling) are documented. The translation is observable with `EXPLAIN SYNTAX`. Note: `polyglot_dialect = 'trino'` already exists via the `polyglot` transpiler, but it performs no function mapping and passes `ARRAY[...]` through untranslated; this first-class dialect provides a much more complete translation. `BETWEEN SYMMETRIC` is translated to `BETWEEN least(a, b) AND greatest(a, b)`, and the Trino `JSON` type family is mapped to the ClickHouse `JSON` type, accepting that only objects are supported: `JSON '...'` literals and `json_parse` become casts to `JSON`, `json_format` becomes `toJSONString`, and `json_extract`, `json_extract_scalar`, `json_value`, `json_query`, `json_exists`, `json_size`, `json_array_contains` and `is_json_scalar` are translated to the ClickHouse JSON functions (the string-based JSONPath functions do not accept the `JSON` type, so casts flowing directly into them are unwrapped back to the JSON text; non-object documents are rejected when materialized as `JSON` values). Validation: the translation was exercised against four corpora derived from Trino's own tests and documentation: - **732 self-contained query/expected pairs** extracted from Trino's functional tests (`core/trino-main/src/test/java/io/trino/sql/query/Test*.java`): 206 produce identical results; of the rest, ~270 need ClickHouse engine features (`LATERAL` joins alone gate 139, plus correlated-subquery decorrelation shapes and non-integer window frame offsets) and the remainder are unsupported constructs or documented semantic differences. 75 order-deterministic pairs are committed as `05021_trino_conformance` (following the KQL conformance-test precedent), and three more conformance tests pin the adopted corpora: `05022_trino_conformance_presto_scalar` (1054 Presto scalar-function assertions), `05023_trino_conformance_tempto` (119 Tempto product-test queries running against their fixture tables inlined into the test), and `05024_trino_conformance_impala` (44 generic-SQL Impala expressions) — every adopted query verified to produce the documented result and to be stable under randomized time zones, thread counts and block sizes. - **43 convention-based Tempto product tests** (`testing/trino-product-tests` at tag 455, `.sql`/`.result` pairs): 30 of the 34 runnable ones match (using the fixed 25-row `nation`/5-row `region` TPC-H tables). - **294 `SELECT`-with-expected-result examples** from the official function documentation: 142 match. - The **22 TPC-H queries in Trino dialect** from `testing/trino-benchmark-queries`: all parse and translate. - **1689 scalar-function assertions** scraped from `prestodb/presto` unit tests (`assertFunction("expr", TYPE, value)` style) plus the **130 Tempto product tests Presto kept after the fork**, executed against real TPC-H sf0.01 data and the `datatype`/`workers` fixture tables: 1059 and 91 match respectively (most of the rest use Presto-only functions that do not exist in current Trino). The 43 Trino-era Tempto tests reach 38/43 with the data available. - **146 expression tests** from `apache/impala` as a generic-SQL cross-check (Impala is a different dialect; 44 match, and the divergences are Impala-specific by design — e.g. Impala's `LIKE` treats a backslash as an escape character while Trino treats it literally). These corpora drove another round of semantic fixes: outer joins produce NULLs (`join_use_nulls`), `sum`/`avg`/`min`/`max` over an empty set return NULL (`-OrNull` variants), `count` returns a signed bigint, `greatest`/`least` propagate NULL arguments, LIKE backslash literalness, minute-precision `TIMESTAMP` literals, `reduce` output lambdas, `bit_count` arbitrary widths, `width_bucket` over an array of bounds, and `json_array_get`. Of the 294 examples, 142 produce results matching the documentation (plus a few that differ only by printing the current time or the session time zone); most of the rest use deliberately unsupported constructs (SQL:2016 `MATCH`/`UNIQUE` predicates, `U&'...'` literals, functions with no ClickHouse counterpart, non-object `JSON` documents per the design above). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115383&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115383](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115383+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix has()/indexOf() zero-pad inconsistency for Array(FixedString)
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115311 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`/`indexOf` giving different results for `Array(FixedString)` depending on whether the array is a constant or a materialized column. Example: `has([toFixedString('V0', 3)], toFixedString('V0', 4))` was returning `0`, but the same check on a materialized array, or a plain `equals()`, returns `1`. Now both paths zero-pad `FixedString` values of different width the same way, so results are consistent. --- ### Problem `has`/`indexOf` on a constant array goes through `executeConst()` in `src/Functions/array/arrayIndex.h`. This function converts the array to `Array` (basically `std::vector<Field>`) and compares elements using `accurateEquals(Field, Field)`. The issue is `Field` does not have a separate type for `FixedString` -- it just becomes `Field::Types::String`. So once a `FixedString` value is put into a `Field`, there is no way to tell it apart from a normal `String`. And `accurateEquals` for `String` vs `String` is just plain `std::string` comparison, exact length only. No zero-padding. But the non-constant path (materialized array) works directly on `IColumn`/`ColumnFixedString`, and there zero-padding is applied correctly (same as `equals()` does, via `memcmpSmallLikeZeroPaddedAllowOverflow15`). So constant and non-constant paths give different answers for the same input. ### Fix Added a small helper `Impl::arrayIndexFieldsEqual()` in `arrayIndex.h`. It does zero-pad comparison for `Field`-level strings, but only if we already know from the *declared types* (before converting to `Field`) that one side is `FixedString`. This flag is computed once in `executeConst()` and passed down. Important: plain `String` vs `String` should NOT be zero-padded, that would be wrong behavior for normal strings. So the fix only kicks in when a `FixedString` type is actually involved. Note: `indexOfAssumeSorted` has a similar looking issue in its own binary search code (`Main::lowerBound`), but that function assumes the array is already sorted by the caller, which is a different contract, so not touching it here. Keeping this PR scoped to what the issue actually reports. ### Testing - Used a live tracer to confirm the actual code path changed, not just the output. After the fix, `accurateEquals` is not called anymore for the `FixedString` width-mismatch case (goes into new zero-pad branch instead). For plain `String` vs `String` (`has(['ab'], 'abc')`) it still calls `accurateEquals` like before -- so no unintended behavior change there. - Ran a matrix of 1791 generated cases covering different width/content combinations plus explicit `String`/`String` negative controls. Checked 4 things per case: constant result vs `materialize()`d result, constant result vs `arrayExists(x -> x = value, arr)` as ground truth, `indexOf` constant vs materialized, and `has` vs `indexOf` self-consistency. All 1791 cases passed, 0 mismatches. - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/04926_array_has_index_of_fixed_string_zero_pad.sql` covering the issue's repro, materialized/constant combinations in both directions, the `FixedString` vs `String` needle case, same-width negative controls, and `String`/`String` negative controls. Please review, happy to make changes if needed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115401&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115401](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115401+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Decompile JIT-fused functions before serializing a query plan
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115310 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112028 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111893 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a query serialized for distributed execution (`serialize_query_plan = 1`) failing with `UNKNOWN_FUNCTION` when a lambda body contains `AND` with a comparison constant wider than `UInt8`. Example: `mapExists((k, v) -> k LIKE '%2' AND v < 1000, col)` against a `Distributed` table with `serialize_query_plan = 1` used to throw `Unknown function and(UInt8, less(UInt64, 1000 : UInt16))`. Now it works correctly, and expression compilation stays fully enabled (no performance regression for `compile_expressions`). --- ### Problem `compile_expressions` (JIT) can fuse a sub-expression like `and(less(...))` inside a lambda body into a single `LLVMFunction` node. `LLVMFunction::getName()` (in `Interpreters/ExpressionJIT.cpp`) returns `dag_.dump()` -- a dump of the fused sub-expression, not a real function name. Something like `and(UInt8, less(UInt64, 1000 : UInt16))`. `ActionsDAG::serialize()` writes `node.function_base->getName()` for `FUNCTION` nodes when shipping a query plan for distributed execution. For a normal function that's fine (e.g. `and`), but for a JIT-fused node it writes the dump string instead. The receiving node tries to resolve that string as a function name via `FunctionFactory` and fails with `UNKNOWN_FUNCTION`. This looks like one of a few independent `serialize_query_plan = 1` round-trip fidelity bugs (see #112028 for a similar issue with `LowCardinality` types, #111893 for a table-resolution issue) -- different root causes, same general area of the feature still having rough edges. ### Fix First pass at this fix just disabled `compile_expressions` whenever `serialize_query_plan = 1`, gating it in `ExpressionActionsSettings`. That's correct but broader than necessary -- it costs JIT-compiled-expression performance for the *whole* query's execution (initiator and every remote shard alike, since `serialize_query_plan` stays true in the settings context throughout), not just for the specific node that needs to cross the wire. This version keeps `compile_expressions` fully enabled everywhere and instead adds `ActionsDAG::decompileFunctions()`, the reverse of the existing `compileFunctions()`: it rebuilds the original, real, resolvable sub-expression from a JIT-fused node's own `CompileDAG`. `CompileDAG::Node` already retains the real `FunctionBasePtr` for each fused sub-function plus their connectivity (`arguments`, index-based), so this is a faithful reconstruction, not a re-derivation. `serialize()` now clones the DAG and calls `decompileFunctions()` on the clone before writing it out, whenever any node is JIT-compiled -- the original (still fused, fast to execute locally) DAG is left untouched for actual execution. ### Testing - Used a live tracer to confirm `ActionsDAG::serialize()` is exercised by the repro (fires 4 times, matching the lambda's nested capture-DAG serialization). - Used a live tracer to confirm `decompileFunctions()` actually fires when JIT fusion is forced to happen (`compile_expressions = 1`, `min_count_to_compile_expression = 0`) during the repro -- and the query still returns correct results with no error. This proves fusion happened and was correctly reversed for the wire, not merely avoided. - Confirmed `serialize_query_plan = 0` still JIT-compiles normally (unaffected either way, since `ExpressionActionsSettings` no longer reads `serialize_query_plan` at all). - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/04927_serialize_query_plan_lambda_jit.sql` covering the repro, the aggressive-JIT-settings variant (deterministically forces fusion via `min_count_to_compile_expression = 0`), and the `serialize_query_plan = 0` negative control. Please review, happy to make changes if needed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115439&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115439](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115439+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support safe type conversions in correlated subquery equivalence substitution
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113407 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101863 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Correlated subqueries with an equality on columns that differ only in nullability (e.g. `Int64` vs `Nullable(Int64)` under `data_type_default_nullable = 1`, as in TPC-DS Q35), or on native-number columns having a least common type (e.g. `Int32` vs `Int64`), are now decorrelated via equivalent-expression substitution instead of falling back to a CROSS JOIN with a post-join filter, avoiding severe memory growth on such queries. Closes #113407. --- ## Motivation The equivalent-expression substitution in `PlannerCorrelatedSubqueries` recorded an equivalence only when both sides of the correlated `equals` had exactly the same type. A correlated `EXISTS` whose join condition compares `Int64` with `Nullable(Int64)` therefore decorrelated through the CROSS JOIN fallback; at TPC-DS SF100 (Q35 with `data_type_default_nullable = 1`) the cross-joined intermediate grew without bound (35+ GiB and climbing before being killed, versus 1.72 s / 1.70 GiB with aligned column types). ## Approach The exact-type guard was load-bearing: correlated columns are `PLACEHOLDER` nodes typed with the outer column's type, and every decorrelated DAG declares that type for its inputs, so a substituted column of a different runtime type is a logical error during execution. The substitution therefore cannot simply alias a column of another type, nor cast to the common supertype — it must produce exactly the placeholder's type. Equivalence classes now track `(column name, type)` pairs. The recording guard admits, besides equal types, two verified-safe families: - nullability-only differences (any base type) — the equality predicate rejects `NULL`s; - native-number pairs with a least supertype — for them `equals` is mathematically exact (`9007199254740993 :: Int64 = 9007199254740992.0 :: Float64` is `0`), the supertype exists only when every type embeds losslessly, and `accurateCastOrNull` is exactness-checking, so value equivalence is transitive across a class. At substitution the chosen equivalent column is converted to exactly the correlated type: `toNullable` / lossless `CAST` when widening, `assumeNotNull` / `accurateCastOrNull` when narrowing. For the narrowing conversions a `FilterStep` is inserted below the renaming that drops rows whose value is `NULL` or does not convert exactly — such rows can never satisfy the recorded equality (a top-level AND-conjunct of an ancestor filter), and dropping them before `assumeNotNull` is required so that its arbitrary result for non-converting values cannot leak into aggregation keys (the aggregation decorrelation appends correlated identifiers as group keys). Pairs whose comparison semantics are not consistent with `CAST` keep the previous CROSS JOIN fallback: `Decimal` vs `Float` (comparison converts to `Float` and is inexact), `String` vs `FixedString` (comparison ignores padding), and supertype-less numeric pairs such as `Int64` vs `UInt64` or `Int64` vs `Float64`. ## Verification - The issue's reproducer plans with zero `cross` nodes and returns the same result as the fallback. - New stateless test `05023_correlated_subquery_equivalence_type_conversion` (12 cases: both nullability directions, widening/narrowing/sideways/float numerics with adversarial boundary values, scalar-subquery aggregation with an outer `0` vs inner `NULL`, guarded fallbacks) passed 6/6 runs under harness setting randomization. - A cross-check over 16 type pairs compared `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` / scalar `count()` results between substitution and the CROSS JOIN fallback on value pools with boundary values (`2^31±1`, `2^32±1`, `2^53`, `2^53+1`, non-integer floats) and `NULL`s — identical everywhere, and plan probes confirmed the substitution fires exactly for the admitted pairs. - The existing `correlated` stateless subset passes (3 environment-only failures in the local scratch setup: MinIO, test cluster, writable access storage). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115493&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115493](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115493+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Reject a bare carriage return in HTTP header names and values
signals.text:
`HTTPHeaderFilter::checkAndNormalizeHeaders` rejected an embedded line feed (`
`) in HTTP header names and values, but not a bare carriage return (``). A lone `` also terminates a header line, so a value such as `tokenX-Injected: evil` could still smuggle a second header into an outgoing request (request/response splitting). This rejects `` alongside `
`, for both header names and values, in the shared filter. This covers the callers that route header names/values through `HTTPHeaderFilter` — the SQL-facing paths where headers are supplied per query: the `url` table function and engine, HTTP dictionaries, S3/Web configuration, and the DataLake/REST catalogs. Outbound HTTP clients that build headers without this filter (for example the AI providers and the BigQuery client, whose header values come from named collections, OAuth tokens, or DDL configuration) are not affected by this change; enforcing the same invariant at the shared HTTP send path for those clients is left to a separate follow-up. Deferred from #110313 to keep that pull request focused on refactoring. `), in HTTP header names and values that pass through the HTTP header filter. signals.title: Derive deterministic conditions from conditions involving the current time for the query condition cache
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): The query condition cache now serves conditions that involve the current time, e.g. `WHERE time >= now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY`, when reading from `MergeTree` tables, by deriving a deterministic condition from them with the current-time constant rounded onto a time grid. Closes #115504. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes Documented in `docs/concepts/features/performance/caches/query-condition-cache.mdx` and in the new settings' descriptions. --- A condition like `time >= now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY` reaches the storage layer with the current-time expression folded into a non-deterministic constant. It could never benefit from the query condition cache: the constant (and hence the condition hash) changes with every query, and the cache refuses non-deterministic conditions anyway (#81506, #84508). This PR derives a **deterministic** condition from such conditions by rounding the folded time constants onto a time grid: ``` time >= '2026-08-09 12:34:56' ~~~> time >= '2026-08-09 00:00:00' (rounded down) time >= '2026-08-10 00:00:00' (rounded up) ``` The grid step is proportional to the distance between the constant and the current time — one day for a condition looking back ten days, one hour for a condition looking back ninety minutes — multiplied by a configurable factor (`query_condition_cache_time_condition_grid_factor`, default 1.0) and capped at one day. This bounds the boundary error relative to the window the query looks at, and makes the cache key rotate roughly once per the same fraction of the window, balancing cache usefulness against staleness of the boundary. **Soundness.** The two sides of the cache round in opposite directions, so each cache entry stays a true statement regardless of clocks, concurrency, shards or replicas: * **Writes** (an observed "no rows of this granule match the filter") are stored under a *strengthened* condition — the derived condition implies the evaluated one, so "no rows match the evaluated condition" implies "no rows match the derived condition". This covers all three write sites: the WHERE filter (`updateQueryConditionCache`/`FilterTransform`), the PREWHERE filter (`MergeTreeSelectProcessor`), and the index-analysis granule exclusions (`ReadFromMergeTree`, under the skip-index-profiled key as before). * **Reads** (`filterPartsByQueryConditionCache`) probe a *weakened* condition — the actual filter implies the derived one, so "no rows match the derived condition" makes skipping the granule sound. Each side only needs its own implication, verified locally against its own condition; a hit is possible only when the two derived conditions are structurally identical (same rounded constant), so entries can never be misapplied. **Behavior.** When the folded constant is already aligned to the grid — `today() - 10`, `toStartOfDay(now())`, `toStartOfHour(now())` (rounding is DST-aware, in the timezone of the constant's type) — rounding up and down coincide, so the very next query already reuses the cache, and the key stays stable until the constant changes (e.g. until the end of the day). This exactly matches the issue's example: the derived condition "can be used until the end of day". For an unaligned constant like raw `now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY`, writes go to the grid point above the constant and reads probe the grid point below, so entries written during one grid cell serve the queries of the next one: yesterday's queries prime the cache for today's dashboards. The derivation understands monotone condition shapes: `AND`/`OR` chains, `NOT` (which flips the rounding direction), and comparisons of a deterministic expression with a non-deterministic constant of type `Date`/`Date32`/`DateTime`/`DateTime64`. Anything else non-deterministic (e.g. `rand()`, `__topKFilter` mixes, equality with a time constant, non-temporal folded constants such as `shardNum()` arithmetic) keeps the previous behavior: not cached. Deterministic conditions are entirely unaffected — they keep their existing hashes. Verified locally (single part of 2M rows, half of them older than the condition boundary): the second run of `SELECT sum(x) FROM tab WHERE time >= today() - 100` drops 122/245 granules through the PREWHERE consult path and 117/245 through the WHERE path. New settings: * `use_query_condition_cache_for_time_conditions` (default: `true`) * `query_condition_cache_time_condition_grid_factor` (default: `1.0`; values <= 0 disable the derivation) Possible follow-ups (out of scope here): same-cell reuse for unaligned constants by additionally evaluating the weakened condition at the write sites; applying the derivation to the object-storage read paths and to the TopK predicate-only reuse hash. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115522&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115522](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115522+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add a TOLERANCE clause to ASOF JOIN
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109034 `ASOF JOIN` matches the closest row however far away it is, so a trade can be matched against a quote from hours earlier. `TOLERANCE` bounds that distance: ```sql SELECT trades.time, trades.price, quotes.bid FROM trades ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes ON trades.symbol = quotes.symbol AND trades.time >= quotes.time TOLERANCE INTERVAL 5 SECOND ``` The bound is inclusive. With `ASOF LEFT JOIN` a row whose closest match is out of tolerance is kept with default or `NULL` values on the right, following `join_use_nulls`, which is what `pandas.merge_asof(tolerance=...)` does. With `ASOF JOIN` it is dropped, like a row with no match at all. It can be written as an `INTERVAL`, or as a plain number in the units of the `ASOF` column. For a `DateTime64(3)` column `TOLERANCE 5000` and `TOLERANCE INTERVAL 5 SECOND` are the same bound. ### Implementation notes The bound is converted into the units of the `ASOF` key once, during planning, so the join implementation compares it against key values directly with no per-probe conversion. `findAsof` already returns the closest match in the direction the inequality fixes, so if that one is out of bounds no other can be closer and the probe has no match. The interval unit is read from the result type rather than from the shape of the expression: `INTERVAL 5 SECOND` is written `toIntervalSecond(5)` but is constant folded during resolution into a constant whose value is `5` and whose type is `IntervalSecond`, so treating it as a bare number silently means five milliseconds against a `DateTime64(3)` key. ### Rejected rather than approximated - `MONTH`, `QUARTER` and `YEAR`, which are not fixed lengths of time. - An `INTERVAL` against an `ASOF` key that is not a date or time, where the unit would be undefined. - A bound finer than the key's resolution, such as `INTERVAL 1 MICROSECOND` against `DateTime64(3)`, which would otherwise round down to "exact matches only". - A negative bound, which nothing can satisfy. - `enable_analyzer = 0`, which builds `TableJoin` without the query tree the bound travels on and would silently ignore it. - `full_sorting_merge`, which matches through `IColumn::compareAt` and so has ordering but not distance. The planner falls back to another enabled algorithm; if only `full_sorting_merge` is enabled the query fails. Each of these silently returns matches further away than the query asked for if it is accepted instead, which is the failure this clause exists to prevent. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `TOLERANCE` clause to `ASOF JOIN`, bounding how far apart the left and the matched right value of the `ASOF` column may be, so that stale rows are not matched. The bound can be given as an `INTERVAL` or as a number in the units of the `ASOF` column, for example `ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes ON trades.symbol = quotes.symbol AND trades.time >= quotes.time TOLERANCE INTERVAL 5 SECOND`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115530&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115530](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115530+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Sort, filter and page a result in the Web UI
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105249 The Web UI can now sort a result by its columns, filter it by their values, and page through it, without editing the query. None of it happens in the browser. Each change re-runs the query with the corresponding query-construction setting added by #105249 — `order`, `filter`, `limit` + `page` — which the server materializes by wrapping the query as a derived table. What is on screen is therefore the sorted, filtered, paged result of the whole query, not a rearrangement of the rows the page happened to hold. And because the settings are applied to the parsed query rather than to its text, they compose with whatever the query already is: a `UNION`, a trailing `FORMAT` clause, or the query's own `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` all keep working, and the text in the editor is never rewritten. ## Sorting Two arrows in every column header. The arrow of the active direction deactivates it, the other replaces it, a plain click makes the column the only sort key, and <kbd>Shift</kbd> appends it after the keys already in effect (or only flips the direction of a key it already is, keeping its position). With more than one key, each active arrow shows its position in the `ORDER BY` as a superscript. ## Filtering A funnel in every header opens an input for a predicate on that column, with an apply button glued to it. The input opens *inside* the header cell, on the very line the filter is shown on once it is set, so a filter is edited where it is read; the header grows a line for it and shrinks back afterwards. What is typed is the part that follows the column name, so anything the server accepts there works — `> 10`, `BETWEEN 1 AND 5`, `IN (1, 2, 3)`, `% 2 = 0`. A column being filtered shows its predicate under its name for as long as it is set, with a cross to remove it, so it is never invisible that the rows on screen are a subset of the result. Selecting a cell also offers the comparisons that fit its value: `=`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` for a number or a date/time; `=`, `!=`, `contains` for a string; `=`, `!=` for an `Enum`; `true` / `false` for a `Bool`; `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` for a NULL. `contains` becomes a `LIKE` pattern with the value's own `%` and `_` escaped, so it matches literally. There is one filter per column wherever it came from, and the header always displays the one in effect. ## Pagination A result cut off at the display limit gets a pager, which lists the ten pages before the current one, the current one and the next one, plus an ellipsis that takes any page number, and ends with an editable `Per page`. The count of pages is not shown because knowing it would mean counting the rows; the next page is offered only while the current one is full, since a short page is the end of the result. The page size is capped at what the result can display at once — a larger page would return rows the table then truncates away and the next page would start beyond them, silently skipping the rows that never fit. ## Where it applies, and what it is bound to Only to the statements those settings shape, i.e. `SELECT` / `UNION` (resolved by the same CTE-aware statement-kind walk that already decides the `Run all` parallelization, so a write hidden behind a leading `WITH` is not mistaken for one). Not to `SHOW` / `DESCRIBE` / `EXISTS` / `EXPLAIN`, where the settings are silently ignored and a control would promise an order the rows do not have; and not to a multi-query run, whose statements are separate queries with separate columns. A shape belongs to the statement it was made on and is dropped by a run of anything else, so a stale sort can never put an `ORDER BY` on a column the new statement lacks. The two launch paths spell the same statement differently (with and without its trailing `;`), which the binding normalizes — otherwise a shape would be dropped by its own re-run. ## Persistence Kept per tab, and mirrored into the URL (`sort_columns`, `filters`, `page`, `page_size`), the history entry and the tab's result snapshot, alongside the existing color modes and pinned columns. Since the shape decides the rows and not only their presentation, an auto-run (`run=1`) link reproduces the result itself; Download re-runs with the same settings so the exported file matches the table. ## Header icons The pushpin and rainbow emoji became inline SVG on the same grid and stroke weight as the new funnel — they rendered visibly larger than the line art beside them, and being colour glyphs they could take no text colour. All four icons now follow one rule: muted while the feature they control is not in effect on the column, and in a colour reserved for controls in effect (magenta in the light theme, yellow in the dark one) once it is, which is also when they stay shown without hovering. Each lays the header's colour behind itself at 90% alpha so a column name running underneath does not muddle it. ## Testing - `tests/integration/test_play_result_shaping` runs the real shape helpers extracted from the served `/play` page in a Node harness, covering the sort-arrow semantics, the `ORDER BY` / `WHERE` construction and its quoting and `LIKE` escaping, the translation of a page into `limit` + `page`, the validation of a shape read back from a URL, and the statement binding. - `gtest_play_query_is_read_only` now also covers the statement-kind gate: the walk is refactored into a shared `statementKeyword`, and `queryIsShapeable` is verified to be strictly narrower than the read-only classification. - The behaviour itself was driven in a real browser (Chromium via Puppeteer) against a local server, in both themes, for each of the cases above. Documentation: `docs/concepts/features/interfaces/web-ui-result-shaping.mdx`. Written with Claude Code. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The built-in Web SQL UI (`/play`) can now sort a result by its columns, filter it by their values, and page through it, without editing the query. Sorting arrows and a filter input appear in every column header, a selected cell offers the comparisons that fit its value, and a pager with an adjustable page size appears under a result that does not fit on one screen. It is all performed by the server, using the `order`, `filter`, `limit` and `page` query-construction settings, so the whole result is shaped rather than the rows that happen to be displayed; the chosen sort, filters and page travel in the page URL, so a shared link reproduces the result. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115540&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115540](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115540+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add min_partition_age_to_force_merge_seconds to compact partitions that no longer receive inserts
signals.text: ## Summary Closes #79697. This adds an opt-in `MergeTree` setting, `min_partition_age_to_force_merge_seconds`, addressing the issue's use case in the background merge selector itself (similar in spirit to #105454). When set to a non-zero value and every part in a partition is at least that many seconds old — i.e. the partition no longer receives inserts — the `Simple` and `StochasticSimple` merge selectors waive the size-ratio requirement in `allow()` that otherwise refuses "unbalanced" merges of a large part together with small ones. That waiver is the whole of the setting's effect. It introduces no cross-heuristic relations: every other knob keeps its own meaning and its own default, and a workload that needs one of them off must turn it off explicitly through its own setting. - `window_size` still bounds which parts are examined. - `min_parts_to_merge_at_once` still sets the floor on how many parts a merge must cover. - `enable_heuristic_to_remove_small_parts_at_right` still trims a trailing small part from a selected range of three parts or more. Compacting a trailing small part is the point of #79697, and it happens out of the box: that trim only applies to ranges of three parts or more, and `min_parts_to_merge_at_once` defaults to `0`, so the cheapest candidate in an idle partition is the two-part range ending at the small tail. That follows from those settings' own defaults rather than from this one overriding them, so raising `min_parts_to_merge_at_once` deliberately still does what it says. This setting cannot be combined with `min_age_to_force_merge_seconds` + `min_age_to_force_merge_on_partition_only`, and the combination is rejected in `sanityCheck`. That pair routes a stale partition to the whole-partition merge, which is the only merge marked `final` — and a final merge is what enables `ReplacingMergeTree` `CLEANUP`. Since `selectPartsToMerge` returns as soon as a regular merge is found, forcing regular merges by partition age would pre-empt that path and silently stop cleanup from running. The two mechanisms are complementary: use the pair for partitions that fit into a single merge, and this setting for the ones that do not. Each merge still respects `max_bytes_to_merge_at_max_space_in_pool`, so a partition larger than that limit converges to a few max-size parts. Unlike `min_age_to_force_merge_seconds` with `min_age_to_force_merge_on_partition_only`, the partition does not have to fit into a single merge, and unlike plain `min_age_to_force_merge_seconds`, actively written partitions are unaffected. The default is `0` (disabled), preserving existing behavior. Merged parts start with age 0, which re-arms the threshold, so compaction of an idle partition proceeds in naturally throttled rounds. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `min_partition_age_to_force_merge_seconds` `MergeTree` setting: when every part in a partition is at least this old, the `Simple` and `StochasticSimple` merge selectors compact that partition's parts within the `max_bytes_to_merge_at_max_space_in_pool` limit. ### Documentation entry: - [x] Documentation is generated from the setting description in `MergeTreeSettings.cpp`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115547&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115547](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115547+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Map kv tokenizer minimal
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110757 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110454 Adds a `keyValuePairs` text-index tokenizer for `Map(String, String)` columns. Every `(key, value)` pair of a row becomes one token, so `WHERE m['key'] = 'value'` is answered by a single exact token lookup with direct read, instead of reading the map column. An index on `mapKeys(m)` or `mapValues(m)` cannot do this: it knows that some key exists and that some value exists, but not that they belong to the same pair. This is a minimal first increment of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110757 by @UnamedRus, split up as discussed in the review of that pull request. Only the tokenizer and `m['key'] = 'value'` are here; `m['key'] IN (...)`, `mapContainsKey`, `mapContainsValue`, the `LIKE` and prefix/suffix forms, and the new `mapContainsKeyValue` / `mapContainsKeyValueLike` functions are left for follow-ups. As a result nothing outside the tokenizer, the index aggregator and the index condition needs to change: `TextIndexAnalyzer`, `MergeTreeReaderTextIndex` and `optimizeDirectReadFromTextIndex` are untouched. The token layout is `varint((length(key) << 1) | is_rest) ‖ key ‖ value`. The length prefix keeps the key/value boundary unambiguous, so keys and values may contain arbitrary bytes, and it makes the tokens of one key a contiguous range of the sorted dictionary, which a later range scan can use. `is_rest` marks a key's non-first occurrence in a row, so the lookup matches the same occurrence as `m['key']` when a row contains duplicate keys. Restrictions, all rejected at table creation: keys and values must be `String` or `LowCardinality(String)` (`FixedString` would store padding bytes that a searched constant does not have, silently missing rows), and `preprocessor`, `postprocessor` and `support_phrase_search` are not accepted. `m['key'] = ''` is also true for rows that do not contain the key at all, so that predicate falls back to a scan. This doesn't close issue #110454, because it asks for Map text-index support broadly and this only covers exact element equality. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New text index tokenizer `keyValuePairs`, which indexes a `Map(String, String)` column directly and answers `map['key'] = 'value'` from the index without reading the map column. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115579&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115579](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115579+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix lost text index optimization for queries with ORDER BY ... LIMIT
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/issues/68580 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/93545 A query that filters on a text index and also has `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` could stop using the index to answer the filter, and read and tokenize the whole text column instead: ```sql SELECT count() FROM (SELECT id, v FROM t WHERE hasToken(s, 'error') ORDER BY v DESC, id LIMIT 10) ``` The two optimizations did not compose: the one that speeds up `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` reshaped the plan in a way the text index optimization no longer recognized, and it silently fell back to reading the column. Nothing indicated this in the query plan or the logs, and the results stayed correct, but the query got much slower and used much more memory. On a full-text search benchmark over ~30M rows the affected queries took ~300 ms and ~500 MB instead of ~30 ms and ~15 MB. Whether a query was affected depended on the order of the columns in `SELECT`, which made it look arbitrary: `SELECT v, id ... ORDER BY v` was fine while `SELECT id, v ... ORDER BY v` was not. All the settings involved are enabled by default. Both optimizations now apply together. A `TRACE` log entry was also added for the remaining cases where the text index optimization cannot be used, so a silent fallback is visible in the logs. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a performance regression where a query combining a text index filter with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` stopped answering the filter from the index and read the whole text column instead. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115586&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115586](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115586+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: CI: refuse LLVM coverage verdicts on incomplete measurements, make coverage profiles kill-safe
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112832 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The `LLVM Coverage` gate fails a PR when total line coverage drops more than 0.3 pp below the master baseline. Both totals are merged from 21 per-shard `.profdata` artifacts that are deliberately `optional=True`, and nothing verified that either side had all of them. A shard profile can vanish while every check stays green (a corrupt `.profraw` aborts the producer merge, `-failure-mode=warn` silently discards a corrupt input, a zero-length `.profraw` is accepted silently). Both error directions occur: - A short PR side fails an unrelated PR. Observed twice in the last 60 days, both times the same missing file `it-amd_llvm_coverage_4_8.profdata` with all 21 shard jobs green: [PR 110186](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110186&sha=0b33f54bc8089ea3560397c589e93dc6aec92d47&name_0=PR&name_1=LLVM%20Coverage) ("dropped 0.50 pp" on a 102-line PR) and [PR 105844](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105844&sha=66107bb44ab45a490e839225eb096e46204e5e86&name_0=PR&name_1=LLVM%20Coverage). - A short master run writes a low baseline into the CI DB, so a later real regression passes. This direction produces a PASS and is invisible in any failure count. The invariant established here: a verdict comes only from two complete measurements. - Every coverage producer (functional, integration, unit) names its profile after its own artifact (`<artifact>.profdata`), so the filename carries the shard identity. Producer merges use `--failure-mode=any` and skip zero-length `.profraw` inputs: a shard with invalid data publishes nothing instead of a silently short profile. Artifacts stay `optional=True`, so a missing profile never reddens a green test job. - The `LLVM Coverage` job compares the expected file set against what arrived and merges an explicit file list instead of a `*.profdata` glob. On a missing or invalid shard it reports `SKIPPED` naming the shard, and withholds every comparative output: no verdict, no GitHub comment, no `llvm_coverage.info` artifact, no CI DB row. A genuine tooling failure (report generation) still stays RED. - Baseline completeness needs no metadata: the diff script already selects the first master ancestor that has an `llvm_coverage.info`, and after this change such an `.info` exists only for complete runs. (Transitional: for the first ~30 master commits after merge, pre-change ancestors are still selectable, which is exactly today's behaviour.) - Under coverage, the integration sequential test phase runs regardless of how many parallel tests failed (`MAX_FAILS_BEFORE_DROP`), so a green shard cannot silently publish a profile that is short by the whole sequential phase. - Root cause of the recurring shard 4/8 loss: `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE` in merge mode writes the profile only at process exit, and integration tests `SIGKILL` servers on purpose; a kill inside that multi-second write leaves a half-written `.profraw` whose header makes `llvm-profdata` abort with `LLVM ERROR: out of memory` ([llvm/llvm-project#50970](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/50970), open since 2021). Coverage builds now compile with `-mllvm -runtime-counter-relocation` and run with `%c` (continuous mode): the counters are memory-mapped into the profile, which is valid at every instant, so a kill at any moment loses nothing and corrupts nothing. This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112832, which establishes the same invariant via a completeness sidecar published next to `llvm_coverage.info`, a manifest fingerprint, and a two-pass baseline selector. Withholding the `.info` on incomplete runs makes the sidecar unnecessary, and the profile naming plus set check shrink to ~40 lines. Accepted residuals of the simpler design: a session-timeout-truncated shard can still publish a valid short profile, and on the rare day the coverage artifact manifest itself changes, verdicts are unreliable until master republishes. Not covered here (pre-existing, unchanged): the diagnostics of the diff-report script, addressed separately by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115225. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115623&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115623](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115623+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Allow unknown settings in query plan serialization
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114184 Adding a plan setting has meant bumping `DBMS_QUERY_PLAN_SERIALIZATION_VERSION` and gating the write on it — twice already, for versions 5 and 7 — because the settings of a step were written as a name and a typed binary value. A reader that met a name it did not know could not tell where the value ended, so `QueryPlanSerializationSettings::readBinary` threw `UNKNOWN_SETTING`. That fenced off far more than the feature being added: the name goes into every plan that touches the step, so a setting a given plan cannot even use made that plan unreadable to the previous release. Fencing a feature is what the step registry does, by rejecting an unknown step. Plan settings are now written the way query settings have always travelled between client and server (`SettingsWriteFormat::STRINGS_WITH_FLAGS`): name, flags, and the value as a string of its own length. A reader steps over a name it does not know and keeps its own default for it, and rejects the plan only when the name carries `IMPORTANT` — the flag that already means "affects query results, cannot be ignored by older versions". Which form is written is decided by the version of the stream, which `QueryPlan::serialize` already negotiates as the minimum of ours and the peer's, so a peer below version 9 keeps receiving the old form and nothing changes for it. The plan settings that decide a result rather than a way of producing it are marked `IMPORTANT` accordingly: the row and byte limits of `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` with their overflow modes, the two-level aggregation thresholds, `empty_result_for_aggregation_by_empty_set`, `join_any_take_last_row`, `totals_auto_threshold`, and the two settings that decide how aggregation states are laid out. The existing per-setting gates stay — peers below version 9 still need them — but a setting added from now on needs one only when it belongs in that group. `gtest_query_plan_settings_skippable` covers the round trip of every declared setting type through its string form, the old form at the previous version, an unknown setting being skipped, and an unknown `IMPORTANT` setting being rejected. The 58 stateless tests that set `serialize_query_plan` were run against the new format locally (56 pass; two fail only for want of `s3_disk` and `https_port` in the local server config). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A query plan serialized with `serialize_query_plan = 1` no longer becomes unreadable to a peer that does not know one of the plan's settings: a setting the peer can ignore is skipped, and only one whose absence would change the query result is rejected. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115627&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115627](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115627+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add memory-pressure-adaptive read sizing to the experimental ReaderExecutor
signals.text: Brings the `MemoryPressureMonitor` from the ReaderExecutor redesign to master as a self-contained, experimental slice (gated by the existing experimental `ReaderExecutor`). The monitors form a hierarchy that mirrors the memory-tracker chain — global (server total) ← per-user ← per-query — each classifying its scope's pressure into four levels with a snap-up / sticky-cooldown state machine and escalating against its parent. The executor samples the level once per read window and shrinks its window and block size under pressure, floored at `MIN_READER_EXECUTOR_SIZE` (128 KiB). Thresholds are three shared server-wide settings, validated and applied on startup and on `SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG` (a reload takes effect on the next sample). Also raises the default `reader_executor_window_size` to 8 MiB. Prefetch-aware sizing is deferred to the later prefetch/scheduler slice. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103706 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `ReaderExecutor` now shrinks its read window and block size under memory pressure, configured via `reader_executor_memory_pressure_{elevated,high,critical}_level_pct`; its default read window is now 8 MiB. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115635&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115635](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115635+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix KeeperMap metadata compatibility with redundant parentheses
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114188 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow KeeperMap readers to accept shared metadata when equivalent primary keys differ only by redundant outer parentheses. ### Problem KeeperMap stores the table definition in Keeper and previously compared its primary-key expression as formatted text. Builds that serialize the same expression as either `key` or `(key)` therefore reject an otherwise compatible shared table definition during CREATE-against-existing-path and ATTACH/startup. ### Implementation - keep the existing writer spelling and never rewrite compatible shared metadata; - parse stored and local primary-key expressions and normalize only redundant outer parentheses that wrap one complete expression; - require the remaining input to be exact normal formatter output, preserving strict rejection of malformed, terminated, commented, or genuinely different definitions; - use the same compatibility check in CREATE-against-existing-path and ATTACH/startup; - split columns from the primary-key section using its structural newline-delimited header. This is intentionally a reader-side compatibility fix. A patched node accepts either spelling, but an unpatched node may still reject metadata serialized in the spelling it does not understand. Therefore every version participating in a rolling deployment must contain this fix; in particular, the same reader change must be backported to 26.4. Rewriting the shared znode here would not solve compatibility safely because it could replace the spelling with one rejected by another unpatched peer. The implementation uses parser and formatter APIs present in both current master and 26.4. It does not depend on `formatIgnoringRedundantParentheses()` added by #114188, so the same compatibility rule can be backported to 26.4. ### Tests The stateless SQL regression covers both directions (`key` stored with `(key)` local and `(key)` stored with `key` local), verifies that compatible CREATE and ATTACH do not rewrite the Keeper znode, and checks data access after ATTACH. It also verifies rejection of a different key, malformed `(key`, and terminated `key;` metadata, plus a primary-key expression containing the metadata header text. Red-before was reproduced with embedded Keeper on official ClickHouse 26.4.5.143 and 26.7.1.1315: after changing stored metadata from `key` to `(key)`, DETACH + ATTACH left the table in `INVALID_STATE` (Code 668). Local `git diff --check` and a snapshot-bound hostile review passed. Green-after remains a CI gate for this commit and for the future 26.4 backport. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115642&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115642](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115642+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1874` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.6.6`, `26.6.4.11` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Keep table aliases in stored query bodies when restoring under a new name
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115479 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a bug where restoring a database or table under a new name dropped the table aliases from the bodies of stored views, so reading a restored view failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. Closes #115479. ### Description Closes: #115479 A renaming restore rewrote the table references inside a stored view body but discarded the alias on each one, so the view was permanently broken: its `FROM` named a table with no alias while its projection still qualified columns by that alias. ```sql CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT a.id FROM testdb.t1 AS a; BACKUP DATABASE testdb TO Disk('backups', 'r'); RESTORE DATABASE testdb AS renamed FROM Disk('backups', 'r'); SELECT * FROM renamed.v; -- Code: 47. UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER: Unknown expression identifier `a.id` ``` Root cause: the alias is state on the reference node itself, not on the `ASTTableExpression`. `DDLRenamingVisitor::visitTableExpression` substituted a freshly built `ASTTableIdentifier` for the reference, so every field other than the name was lost, and the formatted body was persisted into the restored metadata. The fix renames the reference in place with `ASTTableIdentifier::resetTable`, so the alias, `parametrised_alias` and `prefer_alias_to_column_name` survive by construction. This is option 2 from the issue. Its `has_uuid` caveat does not apply on master: `ASTTableIdentifier` has no `formatImplWithoutAlias` override there and nothing reads `has_uuid` on the node past parse time, so a stale flag is inert; #114277 already carries the clearing line, so either merge order is correct. `resetTable` itself is untouched, and its only other caller, `InJoinSubqueriesPreprocessor`, requires a non-empty alias. Sibling carrier, so you do not have to ask: `replaceTableNameInArgument` rebuilds the reference the same way for `joinGet`/`dictGet`/`IN`. An alias does parse there but is not resolvable (`SELECT 1 IN (db.t AS a), a` already fails with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`), so dropping it has no reachable consequence and is left alone. `RESTORE TABLE db.v AS other.v` alone does not reproduce: only the view is remapped, so the visitor early-returns. Already-written backups are not repaired. signals.title: Do not treat a cast to String from a type that can hold NULL as safe
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115294 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Code: 349. Cannot convert NULL value to non-Nullable type` when a `has` or `notHas` predicate carries a NULL array element and the primary key is a `String`, `Array(String)` or `Map(String, String)`, and fixed wrong results when that element is a `Dynamic` or `Variant` holding NULL. The NULL is now dropped from the set during key analysis, as it already was for other key types. ### Description No related open issue. Reproduces on 26.7.4.55: ```sql CREATE TABLE a3 (k String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO a3 VALUES ('a'); SELECT count() FROM a3 WHERE has([CAST(NULL, 'Nullable(String)')], k); -- Code: 349. Cannot convert NULL value to non-Nullable type. ``` `ENGINE = Memory` answers `0` for the same data, and key analysis raises the error, so no rewrite avoids it. `canBeSafelyCast` declared `Nullable(X) -> String` safe, but `String` cannot hold a NULL. `tryPrepareSetColumnsForIndex` trusts that and exits early through the non-accurate `castColumn`, which throws. Every other target answers "not safe" and routes to `castColumnAccurateOrNull`, which filters unrepresentable elements out; this pair never reached it. `Array` and `Map` inherit it by recursion. The switch made the same claim for `Dynamic` and `Variant`, which carry NULL in a discriminator. There it gave wrong results rather than an error: the NULL became `''`, entered the set index and pruned away rows keyed `''`. A `Nullable` target represents it, so those two stay safe against one. That routes more targets into `castColumnAccurateOrNull`, which refuses a target it cannot wrap in `Nullable`. All four guards over such a cast tested only the outer type, so a `Tuple(Array(String))` key passed and then raised `Code: 43`; the `EmbeddedRocksDB`/`KeeperMap`/`Redis` helper had no check at all. Each now asks the cast about the target, and that helper also strips the `LowCardinality` encoding, as the key-analysis guards did. Scalar, `Nullable`, `LowCardinality` and plain `Tuple` keys keep their pruning; a container key scans when its element is Nullable-nested. Both tests fail without this change and pass with it, 50/50 under randomization. Two of my open PRs touch this. #115294 is orthogonal but appends to the same test, so the second to merge rebases it. #112890 makes two of the same `canBeSafelyCast` changes without these guards, so alone it raises that `Code: 43` for a container key. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115647&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115647](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115647+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1872` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix out-of-bounds read in `formatRowNoNewline` with empty rows
signals.text: Fixes a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline`. When a row is formatted to an empty result (for example, an empty string with the `RawBLOB` format), the newline-stripping logic could rewind the shared write buffer into the previous row's bytes, producing non-monotonic `ColumnString` offsets and a `size_t` underflow in the string size. Functions consuming the result could then return incorrect results or raise a logical error. The trailing newline is now stripped only when the current row actually emitted at least one byte, which keeps the offsets monotonic. The cursor is also kept within the current working buffer so the decrement never moves it before the buffer start after a flush. Added a regression test in `tests/queries/0_stateless/04512_format_row_no_newline_empty_row_underflow.sql`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline` that could produce incorrect results or a logical error when a row is formatted to an empty result. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115669&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115669](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115669+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.5.11`, `26.5.8.11`, `26.3.21.9`, `25.8.33.2` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix substreams cache key collision between streams of one column
signals.text: The substreams cache was keyed by the subcolumn name, which escapes nothing, so two streams of one column could share a cache slot even when their files differ: for `Array(Tuple(`size0` UInt64))` the array sizes are written to `c.size0` and the tuple element to `c%2Esize0`, and both render to the cache key `size0`. The reader then handed the wrong column to the wrong deserializer - wrong values, `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` or a logical error - and such a table could not be merged. The data on disk is correct, so existing parts read correctly after this fix. Affected are a `Tuple` element named like an automatic substream of an enclosing `Array` or of a sibling element, and a `JSON` typed path named like a substream of a sibling path or like one of `JSON`'s internal streams. The wide reader uses the cache for every read, the compact reader only for subcolumn reads. `StorageLog` and `StorageTinyLog` use the same cache and are fixed too. Both caches are now keyed by the file name rendering minus the column prefix, which is injective. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115632 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix reading a column that has two streams whose names differ only by escaping, for example a `Tuple` element named `size0` inside an `Array`, or a `JSON` typed path named like a substream of a sibling path. Such columns returned wrong values, failed with `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` or a logical error, and made the table unmergeable. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115670&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115670](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115670+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix PromQL timestamp and duration overflow at Int64 boundary
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject PromQL timestamps and durations that exceed the Int64 range.** ### Summary PromQL timestamps and durations can be passed as floating-point values. ClickHouse scales them and converts them to Int64. `INT64_MAX` is rounded to `2^63` when represented as `Float64`. The previous upper-bound check used `>` and allowed that value to reach the conversion even though `2^63` is outside the Int64 range. Converting it to Int64 is undefined behavior. The upper-bound check now rejects equality as well. ### Tests - Add a timestamp regression for the finite floating-point boundary. - Add a duration regression for the same boundary. - Compile the changed C++ translation unit. - Run `git diff --check`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115682&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115682](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115682+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Store and ingest Prometheus native histograms in the TimeSeries engine
signals.text: ## Summary First slice of Prometheus native-histogram support for the `TimeSeries` engine (storage + ingestion). Today, `timeseries[].histograms[]` in a remote-write request is parsed and silently dropped with a 204; a Prometheus sender configured with `send_native_histograms: true` loses all histogram data. This PR makes that data storable and queryable via SQL: - **Storage**: a new optional `HISTOGRAMS` target table on the `TimeSeries` engine (alongside `DATA`/`TAGS`/`METRICS`), enabled with `SETTINGS store_native_histograms = 1` or an explicit `HISTOGRAMS [db.table | INNER ENGINE ...]` clause. One row per histogram sample, mirroring the `prompb.Histogram` message for lossless round-trip: `id`, `timestamp`, `flags` (is_float / counter-reset hint / gauge / stale marker), `schema`, `zero_threshold`, `count`, `sum`, `zero_count`, positive/negative spans and bucket values, and `custom_values` for NHCB (schema −53). Bucket values are stored as absolutes (int-flavor deltas are decoded at ingest). A `timeSeriesHistograms(db.table)` table function mirrors `timeSeriesData` for introspection. - **Ingestion**: `PrometheusRemoteWriteProtocol` reads `timeseries[].histograms[]` — both the int (delta-encoded) and float flavors — validates span/bucket consistency (rejecting the request with `INCORRECT_DATA`/HTTP 400 on malformed data), preserves counter-reset hints and stale markers, updates the tags table's `min_time`/`max_time` from histogram timestamps, and counts ingested histograms in a new `PrometheusRemoteWriteHistograms` profile event. The decoding is factored so a future remote-write 2.0 message path can reuse it. The vendored protobuf gains upstream's `custom_values = 16` field. - **Backward compatibility**: tables without the `HISTOGRAMS` target work exactly as before — `CREATE`, `ATTACH`, and remote writes are unchanged; histogram samples sent to such a table are dropped with a rate-limited warning (and the profile event), so the loss is at least observable, instead of today's silent drop. Everything stays behind `allow_experimental_time_series_table`. PromQL evaluation over histograms (`histogram_quantile` etc.), the HTTP query API JSON shapes, and remote-read output are explicitly out of scope for this PR and build on this storage layer. Open design questions (called out for reviewers): whether the `flags` gauge bit should be dropped as redundant with `counter_reset_hint == GAUGE`, and whether new tables should get the `HISTOGRAMS` target by default under the experimental flag rather than opt-in. ## Tests - Stateless: `CREATE`/`SHOW CREATE` round-trip with and without the target, external histograms-table validation, `timeSeriesHistograms()` reads, `ATTACH` of a pre-histogram definition. - Integration (`test_prometheus_protocols/test_native_histograms.py`): remote-write of int, float, NHCB, and stale-marker histograms with spans, zero bucket and negative buckets, asserting every stored column; mixed float samples + histograms in one request; drop-with-warning on a 3-target table; invalid spans and negative decoded counts → 400. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `TimeSeries` table engine can now store Prometheus native histograms: a new optional `HISTOGRAMS` target table (enabled with `store_native_histograms = 1`), ingestion of native histograms from the Prometheus remote-write protocol, and a `timeSeriesHistograms` table function for reading them. Previously such samples were silently dropped. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115685&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115685](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115685+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
