signals.title: Support asynchronous inserts in the Prometheus remote-write protocol
signals.text: The Prometheus remote-write protocol handler now honors the `async_insert` setting (enabled in the user profile or passed as a URL query parameter of the handler): data from multiple concurrent remote-write requests is batched in the asynchronous insert queue before forming parts, which reduces the number of parts created in the inner tables of a `TimeSeries` table under a high rate of small remote-write requests. Since `async_insert` is enabled by default, remote-write requests are batched by default; add `async_insert=0` to the handler URL or disable the setting for the user to keep the previous synchronous behavior. A request is acknowledged only after the data is flushed to all inner tables of the `TimeSeries` table, regardless of the `wait_for_async_insert` setting, because the remote-write protocol treats an acknowledged write as durable. If the flush fails, the request returns an error instead of an acknowledgement, so the sender retries it. Deduplication on flush is forcibly disabled on this path (both `deduplicate_insert` and `async_insert_deduplicate`, since the former overrides the latter): a flushed block combines data from multiple remote-write requests, so its hash differs on every retry anyway, and the inner tables of the `TimeSeries` engine handle duplicates themselves. Verified manually with a local server and real remote-write requests: a request without settings goes through the asynchronous insert queue and the data is visible immediately after the acknowledgement; `async_insert=0` keeps the synchronous path; four concurrent requests are flushed as a single batch insert; a failing inner table (a `CHECK` constraint on an external `DATA` target table) returns HTTP 500 with no acknowledgement and no data written. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The Prometheus remote-write protocol now supports asynchronous inserts: data from multiple concurrent remote-write requests is batched before forming parts, following the `async_insert` setting (enabled by default; add `async_insert=0` to the handler URL to keep the synchronous behavior). A request is acknowledged only after the data is flushed to all inner tables of the target `TimeSeries` table. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115688&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115688](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115688+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Rename refresh dependencies when restoring under a new name
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115645 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `RESTORE ... AS <new name>` leaving the `REFRESH ... DEPENDS ON` list of a refreshable materialized view pointing at the original database. The restored view refreshed in response to a table it no longer read, ignored refreshes of its own parent, and stopped refreshing entirely once the original database was dropped. ### Description `RESTORE DATABASE db AS db_restored` rewrote every table reference in a stored refreshable materialized view definition except the `REFRESH ... DEPENDS ON` list: ``` CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW db_restored.child REFRESH AFTER 1 SECOND DEPENDS ON db.parent ... AS SELECT a FROM db_restored.parent ^^ TO/FROM rewritten, DEPENDS ON not ``` `DDLRenamingVisitor::visit` dispatches on `ASTCreateQuery`, `ASTTableExpression`, `ASTFunction`, `ASTDictionary` and `ASTStorage`; `ASTRefreshStrategy` was missing, so the node was walked but never touched. The refresh scheduler keys its dependency graph on the full table name, so a dependency naming the pre-restore database occupies a different graph slot than the restored parent. Measured: refreshing the *source* parent fired the restored child, three consecutive refreshes of its *own* parent did not, and dropping the source database left the restored view at `MissingDependencies`. The fix adds the missing visit, running the renaming map over the dependency list exactly as the existing `create.targets` loop does. `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` already visits this node to qualify the same list at CREATE time, so this is the renaming counterpart of an established pass. The visitor is the only transform applied at all four sites that rewrite a stored definition, so this covers backup-side and restore-side renaming together, and the corrected definition is what gets persisted, so later `ATTACH`es are right with no separate fixup. A dependency pointing outside the restored set is left alone, and so is one whose table is not itself renamed by a `RESTORE TABLE ... AS`; the test pins both as controls. Backups already written are not affected: the defect was in the rename transform, not the backup, so restoring an existing backup with a fixed server gives the correct dependency (verified against a backup taken by an unfixed binary). No settings or formats change; a definition without `DEPENDS ON` is untouched. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115689&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115689](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115689+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Wake idle streaming exchange sinks and sources on backward stop
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114806 When a `LIMIT` in a distributed plan is satisfied, the stop signal travels backward through the exchanges. It stalled at idle stages: a `StreamingExchangeSink` with an empty input waited only on its input port and did not read `NoMoreDataNeeded` from the socket, and a `StreamingExchangeSource` on a silent socket did not notice that its output port was closed, so it did not forward the stop upstream. Stages that no longer produce anything kept reading and computing until the query timed out. Now both wake while idle: each sink and source waits on a small epoll that holds the socket and a wakeup pipe written by `onUpdatePorts`. The sink asks for socket writability only while it has unsent bytes, so an idle socket does not cause a busy loop, and there is no periodic timer - every wake is an explicit event. This also required a fix in the sink rendezvous: it now always waits on the connection eventfd instead of extracting a ready socket in `scheduleForEvent`, where the extraction skipped the `prepare` pass that starts the rest of the fragment. The wire protocol is unchanged. Local in-memory exchanges have the same gap and are not covered here. In the new test the unfixed server hits `max_execution_time = 25` although the result is ready after ~2 s; fixed, the query ends in ~2 s and all worker tasks finish cleanly. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Distributed query plans (`make_distributed_plan`) now stop idle upstream stages promptly after a satisfied `LIMIT`: an idle exchange sink reads `NoMoreDataNeeded` as soon as it arrives, and an idle exchange source notices its closed output and forwards the stop upstream. Previously such stages kept reading and computing data that nobody consumes. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115690&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115690](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115690+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
signals.author: davenger

signals.title: Avoid deep copy of AccessRights in getGrantQueriesImpl when it is only read
signals.text: ## What's Changed `getGrantQueriesImpl` used to unconditionally deep-copy the grantee's whole `AccessRights` tree: ```cpp AccessRights access = grantee.access; ``` `AccessRights` is a radix tree, and copying it is `O(number of nodes)`. For users with a huge number of per-table grants (e.g. tens of thousands), this deep copy becomes a serious bottleneck: it is executed on **every** `GRANT`/`REVOKE` (during serialization to `DiskAccessStorage`) and on every `SHOW GRANTS`. The tree is only *modified* when `final == true` (via `unionAccessFromRoles`, which calls `AccessRights::makeUnion`). In the common case (`final == false`) the tree is only read, so we can pass a read-only reference and avoid the deep copy entirely. ## Scope - `src/Interpreters/Access/InterpreterShowGrantsQuery.cpp` — avoid the deep copy when `final == false`. ## Motivation / observed impact On a production cluster (ClickHouse 26.6.1.1193), a user with ~11.6k per-table grants in one database: - A single `GRANT ... ON <table> TO <user>` took **5–28 seconds** on some replicas. - `system.query_log` showed the grant spending **99.9% of its time in user-space CPU**, with a `MemoryAllocatedWithoutCheckBytes` of up to **~500 MB**. - `system.trace_log` showed the hot spot was the recursive `Node::operator=` deep copy inside `serializeAccessEntity -> getGrantQueriesImpl`. - The same grant completed in **~100 ms** on replicas whose in-memory `AccessRights` tree was smaller, confirming the deep copy is the bottleneck. This change removes one of the three deep copies performed per grant (the one inside `getGrantQueriesImpl`). It is a safe, behavior-preserving optimization. ## Testing - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/02536_grants_no_deepcopy.sql` + `.reference` verifying that `GRANT`, `SHOW GRANTS` and `REVOKE` behave identically. - Manual verification on the affected cluster: after applying the equivalent change, `SHOW GRANTS FOR <user>` completed in tens of milliseconds instead of seconds. ## Checklist **Changelog category (leave one):** Improvement **Changelog entry:** Avoid a deep copy of the AccessRights tree in getGrantQueriesImpl when it is only read, speeding up GRANT/REVOKE and SHOW GRANTS for users with many grants. **Unit tests pass.** **Documentation is not required** (internal implementation detail). Closes #115694 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115696&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115696](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115696+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not expose uninitialized memory in query results
signals.text: Two places where uninitialized or stale memory could end up in the result of a query: - The buffer for a binary string literal (`b'...'`) is allocated for the worst case, `ceil(bits / 8)` bytes, but when the number of bits is not a multiple of eight fewer bytes are written, and the result was built from the size of the buffer rather than from the number of bytes written. So `SELECT hex(b'000000001')` returned `01` followed by a byte of uninitialized memory. - `LZ4::decompress` returned success without writing anything when the compressed block was empty while the caller expected a non-empty result, and the caller then handed out whatever was in the destination buffer. A third one, `formatRowNoNewline` stepping the position of a shared buffer back into the previous row, was in this pull request initially; it was fixed separately in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115669, which is already in `master`, so this branch now carries the version from `master`. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115669 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Do not return uninitialized memory in the result of a binary string literal whose length is not a multiple of eight, and from the LZ4 decompressor when a compressed block has no body. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115704&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115704](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115704+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix buffer overflows on data from external servers
signals.text: Two places where a length that comes from an external server was used without checking it against the size of the destination: - `ReadBufferFromAzureBlobStorage::readBigAt` requests `n` bytes and copies `body_stream->Length()` bytes into a buffer that has room for `n`. The length is the `Content-Length` of the response, so an endpoint that returns more data than the requested range overflows the buffer. The S3 implementation caps the copy at `n`; do the same here. - The handler of a MySQL `BIT` field copies `value.size()` bytes into a `UInt64` on the stack. The length comes from the MySQL wire protocol, while a `BIT` value holds at most 64 bits. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix buffer overflows when a remote Azure Blob Storage endpoint returns more data than was requested, and when a MySQL server returns an oversized `BIT` value. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115706&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115706](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115706+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Bound the size of the PostgreSQL startup message
signals.text: The startup message of the PostgreSQL wire protocol carries its own size, which is read from the socket before any authentication, and the message is read into memory in full. The size was not bounded, so an unauthenticated peer could make the server hold an arbitrary amount of memory per connection. Bound it at 10000 bytes, the same limit PostgreSQL itself uses. The guard inside `StartupMessage::deserialize` that was meant to catch a message whose parameters run past the declared size checked the declared size itself, which is a member that never changes, instead of the remaining size. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Bound the size of the startup message of the PostgreSQL wire protocol, which is read before authentication. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115708&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115708](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115708+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix analyzer conflict between a column alias and a table expression alias
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/79966 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66143 The analyzer rejected queries where a column alias coincides with the alias of a table expression in the `FROM` section: ```sql SELECT number AS test_name FROM (SELECT * FROM numbers(1000)) AS test_name ``` ``` Code: 179. DB::Exception: Duplicate aliases test_name for table expressions in FROM section are not allowed. Try to register SELECT * FROM numbers(1000). Already registered number AS test_name. (MULTIPLE_EXPRESSIONS_FOR_ALIAS) ``` This is a regression from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66143 (25.2): `QueryExpressionsAliasVisitor` started to speculatively register aliased short identifiers from expression sections (e.g. the projection `number AS test_name`) in the table expression alias map, because such an alias can transitively name a table expression. When a table expression in the `FROM` section has the same alias, its registration in `resolveQueryJoinTreeNode` collided with the speculative entry, and the query was rejected. The same conflict also affected aliases of `ARRAY JOIN` result columns and identifier aliases defined in the `WITH` section. Now the actual table expression takes over the alias in the table expression namespace, which matches the old analyzer behavior: a column alias and a table expression alias live in different namespaces, and for table lookups the alias from the `FROM` section wins. Genuine duplicate aliases between table expressions are still rejected by `TableExpressionsAliasVisitor`, which runs before this code. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the `MULTIPLE_EXPRESSIONS_FOR_ALIAS` error in queries where a column alias coincides with the alias of a table expression in the `FROM` section (an analyzer regression in version 25.2). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115714&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115714](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115714+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Report a clean error when a table expression has no columns to read
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101005 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `LOGICAL_ERROR: No available columns` when a query reads no columns from a table expression that has no columns at all, for example `SELECT count() FROM loop(db, tbl)` where `tbl` is an `Alias` table whose target was dropped, or a parameterized view. Such a query now fails with `UNSUPPORTED_METHOD` instead of aborting the server in debug and sanitizer builds. ### Description Found by the BuzzHouse fuzzer (`BuzzHouse (amd_msan)`, STID 3938-27bd, [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115586&sha=c2aff39bbb1c833322107a522af2fd6a316adc10&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_msan%29)). No related open issue. Reproducer, deterministic, no experimental settings: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (c0 Int32) ENGINE = Memory; CREATE TABLE a ENGINE = Alias(currentDatabase(), t); DROP TABLE t; SELECT count() FROM loop(currentDatabase(), 'a'); ``` Root cause. When a query needs no columns from a table expression, the planner synthesises a cheapest column to count rows. For a table or table function it calls `chooseSmallestColumnToReadFromStorage`, which, with no column sizes available, falls through to `ExpressionActions::getSmallestColumn` -- and that treats an empty column list as a logical error. An `Alias` whose target is gone reports column-less metadata by design, `StorageLoop` copies it onto itself, and the planner hands the empty list down. The sibling branch of the same `if (columns_names.empty())` block already guards its degenerate case with `UNSUPPORTED_METHOD "Cannot read from subquery with empty projection"`. This adds the missing counterpart to the storage branch. `getSmallestColumn`'s `LOGICAL_ERROR` stays as an internal assertion and becomes unreachable from this caller. The message is cause-neutral because a parameterized view has no columns by design, so naming a missing table would be wrong. Two further carriers that also aborted are covered: a bare parameterized view, and an `Alias` to a live one. Validation. Both directions on builds of the same revision, all four carriers: unpatched aborts with the CI stack, patched returns `UNSUPPORTED_METHOD`. The new test aborts an unpatched server, so it cannot pass vacuously. Authorization ordering is unchanged and pinned by a test: without a grant the query still fails `ACCESS_DENIED` on both builds. Reading the alias directly, enumerating it in `system.tables`/`system.columns`, and `DESCRIBE` over the table function are unchanged; the existing `Alias` tests pass unmodified. 50 randomized runs, plus a matched before/after run of 399 planner, alias and table-function tests, show no new failure. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115716&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115716](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115716+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Include the peer address in deferred connect errors
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/48205 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Connect errors detected after a non-blocking connect (for example, while fetching a part from another replica) now name the peer: `Connection refused`, `Network is unreachable`, `No route to host`, and `Host is down`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes `Poco::Net::SocketImpl::connect(address, timeout)` reports connect failures in two ways: an immediate failure of `::connect` already included `address.toString()`, but an error discovered after `EINPROGRESS` via `poll()` + `SO_ERROR` — the normal outcome when the peer is a remote host, as in replicated part fetches — reaches the caller through `error(err)`, with no address argument at all. This is why logs showed bare `Connection refused` with no hint of which replica was unreachable. The message now becomes `Connection refused: <ip>:<port>`. The address reported is the endpoint that was actually dialled: the address the resolver picked for this connection (so the resolved IP is shown, which also helps diagnose stale DNS entries, as noted in the issue), or the proxy endpoint when a proxy is in use and not bypassed. An immediate failure already carries the address, so those messages are left untouched rather than repeating it. **Scope.** `Connection refused` is rethrown as a `ConnectionRefusedException` carrying the endpoint. The other deferred `SO_ERROR` failures lose the address on the same path and arrive as plain `NetException`s with Poco's bare text (`Network is unreachable`, `No route to host`, `Host is down`); those are restated as `NetException`s with the endpoint appended. `NetException` subclasses such as `SSLException`, and immediate failures whose text already names the peer, pass through untouched. The integration test uses two instances because the deferred-error path only triggers for non-loopback connects, and covers both an IP literal and a hostname, so the resolved address is asserted rather than the name from the URL. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115718&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115718](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115718+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/63082 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/70186 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/63082 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/70186 The public side of the private pull requests above. signals.title: Report accepted_rows/accepted_bytes in X-ClickHouse-Summary for async inserts
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57768 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Asynchronous INSERTs now report `accepted_rows`/`accepted_bytes` in `X-ClickHouse-Summary`, so the summary is no longer all-zero when `wait_for_async_insert = 0`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes With `wait_for_async_insert = 0` the HTTP response is sent right after the data is buffered, before anything is parsed or written, so `X-ClickHouse-Summary` was all zeros (the `wait_for_async_insert = 1` case was already fixed by #99879). Following the discussion in the issue — flush-side metrics must not be attributed to the enqueueing query, and new dedicated fields were suggested instead — this adds two fields that describe what the server *accepted* into the async-insert buffer: * `accepted_bytes` — size of the payload accepted at enqueue time; reported for both async modes. * `accepted_rows` — reported once known: after the flush result arrives, when the client waits for it. With `wait_for_async_insert = 0` the row count genuinely does not exist yet at response time (data is parsed at flush), so only bytes are reported there. The fields appear in the summary JSON only when non-zero, so summaries of non-async queries are unchanged, and they are not part of the native protocol (no revision change). `05024_async_insert_summary_accepted` covers both modes; `04046_async_insert_progress_stats` is updated for the new fields. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115721&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115721](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115721+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not overwrite files on S3Queue move destination collision
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114847 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed silent data loss in S3Queue/AzureQueue `after_processing = 'move'`: with the default `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 0`, objects sharing a basename under different prefixes mapped to the same destination key, so the second move overwrote the first object's data and then deleted its own source. Colliding objects are now left in place with an error logged; the destination guard is enforced by the object storage itself, so concurrent movers cannot both overwrite. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The move is copy-then-delete per object, and an S3/Azure overwrite is not an error, so the collision destroyed one file's bytes with no exception, no log line, and `ObjectStorageQueueMovedObjects` counting both moves as successful. The fix detects collisions at two levels and, on collision, refuses the move: the object stays at the source (it is already recorded as processed, so it is simply retained in the bucket for the operator), an error is logged, and the new `ObjectStorageQueueMoveCollisions` profile event is incremented. * **Within a processing batch** (all storages, no extra requests): destinations are computed up front and deduplicated; only the first object mapping to a given key is moved. * **Everywhere else — across batches, replicas and concurrent movers**: the copy itself carries a destination precondition (`If-None-Match: *`), so the storage refuses it rather than overwriting. This is applied on all three move paths (same-bucket, cross-bucket S3, cross-container Azure) whenever `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 0`; preserved paths cannot collide, so they are unconditional as before. It costs no extra request: the precondition rides on the request that makes the object visible. Because the guard is enforced by the storage rather than by a preflight check, there is no check-then-copy window: of two movers racing for the same destination exactly one wins, and the loser keeps its source. A rejected copy is reported as a collision (logged, counted by `ObjectStorageQueueMoveCollisions`) and never followed by the source deletion. To carry the precondition, `copyS3File`/`copyDataToS3File` and `copyAzureBlobStorageFile`/`copyDataToAzureBlobStorageFile` take an optional destination `If-None-Match`, set on the request that commits the object (`PutObject` / `CopyObject` / `CompleteMultipartUpload`, and `Upload` / `CommitBlockList` / `CopyFromUri` / `StartCopyFromUri`). The parameter defaults to "no precondition", so every existing caller is unchanged. `S3ObjectStorage::copyObject` now forwards its `WriteSettings`, which it previously discarded, so `object_storage_write_if_none_match` reaches the copy. The copy is no longer re-executed by the retry loop once it has succeeded, so a failure while removing the source cannot make the retry collide with the object this move just wrote. Setting `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 1` remains the recommended configuration when same-basename objects are possible, and the `after_processing_move_preserve_path` setting description now documents the collision behavior. Integration tests: one ingests `data/a/part.csv` and `data/b/part.csv` and asserts both survive (one archived, one left at the source, all rows still readable); another pre-creates the destination object and processes a single file, which the in-batch deduplication cannot catch, asserting for both `S3Queue` and `AzureQueue` that the source survives and the pre-existing destination bytes are untouched. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115724&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115724](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115724+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Cancel in-flight merges and mutations on server shutdown
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115732 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Cancel in-flight merges, mutations and part fetches during graceful server shutdown instead of waiting for the running step to finish. Previously a single slow merge step or a large part download could delay shutdown for its whole duration. ### Description `ContextSharedPart::shutdown` waits for the MergeTree background executors before `DatabaseCatalog::shutdown` (the reordering that fixed the SIGBUS in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85433), but nothing cancels the tasks that are already running: the executors' `wait` only prevents new steps from starting, and the per-storage `merges_blocker` cancellation happens later, in `DatabaseCatalog::shutdown`. So shutdown blocks until the currently running task step completes. This caused the `Possible deadlock on shutdown (see gdb.log)` failure in the stress test (azure, amd_msan) on master: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=a013c79d6ac80373b820381527ea85823ab03834&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_msan%29&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_msan%29 There, a background merge of `t_lwu_key_prefix` (854090 rows in 5 parts plus 3 `MergeOnKey` patch parts, left over from `04509_lwu_sorting_key_common_prefix`) spent ~37 seconds per 8192-row block inside `applyPatchesMergeOnKey` under MSan — quadratic patch application over an all-equal sorting key, tracked separately in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115732. Together with a randomized `merge_max_block_size` of ~24k rows and 5 sources to prime, the first `pull` of the merge pipeline alone needed ~8 minutes, so the executor thread never reached a step boundary, `MergeTreeBackgroundExecutor::wait` blocked the whole time, and the hung check fired: `gdb.log` shows the main thread in `ContextSharedPart::shutdown` → `MergeTreeBackgroundExecutor::wait` and the `MergeMutate` thread inside `processEqualKeyCursors` (`applyPatches.cpp:468`); the server log shows `Shutting down merges executor` at 01:27:53 and no further shutdown progress until gdb attached at 01:33:53, with `MergeWrittenRows` flat the whole time. The fix cancels the in-flight work before waiting for the executors, in three ordered steps so that the cancellation is not racy: 1. `MergeTreeBackgroundExecutor::requestShutdown` flips all four background executors into shutdown mode without joining them: new tasks are rejected by `trySchedule` and pending tasks are not started (worker threads exit at the next step boundary), so the set of running tasks cannot grow anymore. 2. `MergeList::cancelAll` and the new `ReplicatedFetchList::cancelAll` cancel everything that is currently running, and also mark entries inserted later as cancelled, so a task that is inside its first step and has not registered itself in the list yet cannot escape the cancellation. 3. The executors are joined. Merge and mutate tasks check `MergeListElement::is_cancelled` on every block through `MergeProgressCallback` (the same mechanism the OOM canary uses), so a running merge aborts with the `ABORTED` exception within one block instead of running to completion. In-flight fetches are cancelled too, checked in `ReplicatedFetchReadCallback` on every buffer refill: a replicated merge can fall back to `executeFetch` inside the same task step before any `MergeList` entry exists, and a plain `GET_PART` fetch would otherwise block the `fetch_executor` join for the whole download. The results of these merges and fetches would have been discarded after the restart anyway, so finishing them was pure waste. This also restores the pre-https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85433-fix semantics, where per-storage shutdown cancelled merges and fetches before anything waited on the executors. Also adds the `merge_tree_sequential_source_sleep_before_read` failpoint and an integration test (`test_shutdown_cancels_merges`) with two cases: a 16-part merge whose every reading step sleeps for 10 seconds, and a fetch of a ~150 MB part from a sender throttled to 1 MiB/s — in both, the server must stop within 90 seconds. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115733&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115733](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115733+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: PromQL histogram_count/histogram_sum over native histograms
signals.text: ## Summary Second slice of Prometheus native-histogram support for the `TimeSeries` engine (PromQL evaluation), building on the storage layer of #115685. Today `histogram_count`/`histogram_sum` over a native-histogram series are not implemented at all; this PR adds the end-to-end path: - **Selector + resample**: a `TimeSeries` selector over a histogram-enabled storage now produces a combined grid carrying the float arm (`values`), the histogram arm (`histogram_values`, one payload tuple per step), and a `sample_kinds` precedence oracle (`timeSeriesLastToGrid` over the sample kind). New aggregate `timeSeriesHistogramLastToGrid` resamples the histogram arm onto the query grid with the usual staleness window. - **Mixed-type instant precedence**: instant evaluation returns the newest sample of *either* type per series, matching Prometheus. The resample keeps the per-slot winner's sample and NULLs the loser's; an exact-timestamp tie resolves to the histogram (upstream rejects duplicate timestamps, so no upstream rule exists). - **Functions**: `histogram_count` and `histogram_sum` over native histograms (scalar `timeSeriesHistogramCount`/`timeSeriesHistogramSum` extracting the payload `count`/`sum`), applied per step to series whose newest sample is a histogram; float-only series are skipped, matching upstream. - **HTTP serving**: instant and range responses gain the Prometheus `histogram`/`histograms` JSON shapes, with bucket boundaries reconstructed from the stored schema (exponential + NHCB custom buckets, zero-threshold clamping) and block writers hardened so an all-stale-skipped block can never emit a leading/double comma. Everything stays behind `allow_experimental_time_series_table`. `histogram_quantile`/`histogram_fraction`, `histogram_avg`/`histogram_stddev`/`histogram_stdvar`, range functions (`rate` etc.), and the `warnings`/`infos` envelope are follow-ups. Depends on #115685 (storage); this PR is based on current master and will shrink to just the engine slice once #115685 merges. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `TimeSeries` engine can now evaluate PromQL `histogram_count` and `histogram_sum` over stored Prometheus native histograms, and serves them in the HTTP query API as `histogram`/`histograms` JSON. Instant queries over series mixing float and histogram samples return the newest sample of either type, matching Prometheus. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115685 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115734&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115734](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115734+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: PromQL histogram_avg/histogram_stddev/histogram_stdvar over native histograms
signals.text: ## Summary Third slice of Prometheus native-histogram support (PromQL evaluation), building on #115734. Adds `histogram_avg`, `histogram_stddev`, and `histogram_stdvar` over native histograms, faithful to upstream: - **Bucket helpers, one source of truth**: the span expansion and exponential-bound reconstruction used by the HTTP JSON writer are moved into `TimeSeriesNativeHistograms` and shared with the new functions. `getHistogramBoundExponential` is made bit-identical to Prometheus by porting upstream's `exponentialBounds` table verbatim (schemas 0-8), including its last-ulp deviations from the exactly-rounded values — so bucket boundaries and everything derived from them match Prometheus bit-for-bit, which the upcoming conformance testing relies on. Overflow handling also matches upstream exactly (MaxFloat64 only for the last regular bucket, +Inf beyond). - **`histogram_avg`** = `sum / count`, no special-casing (0/0 → NaN), matching upstream. - **`histogram_stddev` / `histogram_stdvar`**: variance is estimated from bucket representative values exactly as upstream — arithmetic mean for custom (NHCB) buckets, zero for the zero bucket, geometric mean (mirrored for negatives) for exponential buckets — accumulated with Kahan-Neumaier summation, then `variance / count`; stddev takes the square root. - **Lexer**: the PromQL grammar gains the three function tokens and the checked-in generated lexer is regenerated (only the serialized ATN and token table change). Series whose newest sample at a step is a float are skipped per step; float-only series are excluded from the result, matching upstream. Based on current master; the diff shrinks to just this slice as #115685 and #115734 merge. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `TimeSeries` engine can now evaluate PromQL `histogram_avg`, `histogram_stddev`, and `histogram_stdvar` over stored Prometheus native histograms, with bucket boundaries computed bit-identically to Prometheus. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115685 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115734 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115735&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115735](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115735+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: PromQL histogram_quantile/histogram_fraction over native histograms
signals.text: ## Summary Fourth slice of Prometheus native-histogram support (PromQL evaluation), building on #115735. Adds native `histogram_quantile` and `histogram_fraction`, faithful to upstream, and fixes two cross-slice defects: - **`histogram_quantile` (native)**: a new native branch of the existing applier (scalar `timeSeriesHistogramQuantile(histogram, phi)`), UNION ALL'd with the untouched classic-bucket branch. Faithful to upstream `HistogramQuantile`: out-of-range/NaN phi and `count = 0` short-circuits, forward/reverse iterator choice by `phi` (and NaN sum), rank walk over non-empty buckets, zero-bucket single-sided natural bounds, custom-bucket `-Inf`/`+Inf` short-circuits, and linear (custom / zero bucket) vs log-scale (exponential, with negative mirroring) interpolation. - **`histogram_fraction` (native)**: new applier (scalar `timeSeriesHistogramFraction(histogram, lower, upper)`), mirroring upstream `HistogramFraction` — the per-bucket rank walk with linear/exponential `FractionBelow` interpolation, `±Inf` bound handling, and `(upperRank - lowerRank) / count`. Classic-bucket `histogram_fraction` does not exist in ClickHouse and is a separate upstream task (issue #114704), so float-only input returns an empty result, consistent with the other native-histogram functions. - **Fix — `last_over_time` over a subquery on a histogram-enabled storage**: the combined grid was passed through unchanged, so an instant query threw and a range query silently returned the inner matrix on the wrong steps — for every series, including pure-float ones. Each grid arm is now resampled onto the aggregation grid via `timeSeriesFromGrid` (the histogram arm through the `-Array` combinator). - **Fix — float-only series in native-histogram functions**: `histogram_count`/`sum`/`avg`/`stddev`/`stdvar` kept float-only groups as all-NULL rows, which were still counted by the duplicate-series check after the `__name__` drop — a colliding float-only series failed the whole query where upstream skips it. They are now filtered with `has(sample_kinds, 1)`, matching the quantile/fraction appliers. Based on current master; the diff shrinks to just this slice as #115685, #115734, and #115735 merge. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `TimeSeries` engine can now evaluate PromQL `histogram_quantile` (with native interpolation) and `histogram_fraction` over stored Prometheus native histograms, alongside the classic-bucket `histogram_quantile`. Also fixes `last_over_time` over a subquery on a histogram-enabled storage. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115685 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115734 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115735 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115736&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115736](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115736+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Warm up the parser before measuring AST allocations in the parser memory profiler
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113491 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Since 2026-08-20 `Parser memory check` has failed 5 PRs across 154 test rows, every row reporting exactly `+1,280 bytes`: #115301 (37 queries), #114577 (37), #110180, #115630 and #100371 (2 each). None touches the parser. The same window credits 8 further PRs with the mirror-image `-1,280 B` improvement, so the check can both fail innocent PRs and pass one adding a genuine 1,280 byte regression. The cause is in the instrument. `parser_memory_profiler` parses one query per process with no warm-up, so lazy one-time initialization reachable from `parseQuery` is charged to that query: 2,400 bytes over five allocations on Query 64. The largest is one 1,280 byte `calloc` during the first call into the expression parser (`ParserExpressionImpl::tryParseOperand`), whose two leaf frames sit in a shared object absent from the executable's symbol table, so the profiler leaves them unresolved. Whether these land inside the window is a property of the binary, not the SQL, so the two arms, being different builds, can differ by the whole amount with identical parser source, which clears both thresholds (1,280 B, 34.7%). Parsing once before the window opens leaves only this parse's allocations. With the job's own analyzer on Query 64: 4,968 -> 2,568 bytes, the 1,280 byte stack present to absent, reverting restores it. Over all 100 queries it appears on exactly 64 and 99 before, none after; an injected per-parse 4,096 byte allocation still reports +4,112 B, so the check is not blind. @ qoega, two consequences to rule on. Reported values drop for 37 of 100 queries, and for about one master build a warmed PR arm is scored against an unwarmed baseline, inflating apparent improvements; that self-heals and I added no compensating logic. New expensive lazy initialization is also no longer visible here, which fits a per-query AST check. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113491 Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115630&sha=042aecf702d2050e274706aa20011eabedb78542&name_0=PR&name_1=Parser%20memory%20check <details> <summary>Query 64: the 2,400 bytes of one-time initialization, by allocating frame</summary> Multiset of per-stack byte diffs removed by the warm-up, attributed to the allocator frame that actually appears in the symbolized heap (not to an inlined neighbour): | bytes | allocator | initialization | |---|---|---| | 1,280 | `je_calloc` / `__libc_calloc`, two unresolved shared-object frames | during the first call into `ParserExpressionImpl::tryParseOperand` | | 608 | `operator new` / `unordered_set::insert` | `isIntegerTypeName` static set (`ParserDataType.cpp`) | | 224 | `operator new` / `unordered_set::insert` | `isArrayQuantifierPredicate` static set (`ExpressionListParsers.cpp`) | | 192 | `operator new` / `unordered_set::insert` | `isIntegerTypeName`, second allocation | | 96 | `operator new` / `unordered_set::insert` | `isArrayQuantifierPredicate`, second allocation | The 7 element `isArrayQuantifierPredicate` set and the 19 element `isIntegerTypeName` set match `sizeof(__hash_node<string_view, void*>) = 32` bytes per element (224 and 608), which is why the 1,280 byte `calloc` is not attributed to either of them. The two unresolved frames do resolve against the profile's own `MAPPED_LIBRARIES`, and on this host they are glibc's atexit registration: `libc.so.6` is mapped at `0x74e6aae00000`, and the offsets `0x470bd` / `0x47231` land in `__new_exitfn` and `__cxa_atexit+65`. The callee at `0x470b8` is `calloc(1, 0x410)`, i.e. one 1,040 byte `struct exit_function_list`, which jemalloc rounds up to its 1,280 byte size class. That is allocated once, when the first function-local static with a non-trivial destructor inside the parser registers it. The same two frames below `main` in that stack resolve to `__libc_start_main`, which is how the offsets were checked. The exact figure is a property of this glibc, so the profiler is right to leave it unnamed; the point that matters here is only that it is one-time. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115739&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115739](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115739+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1850` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Make Parquet dictionary-filter pruning cheaper: sorted hash vector, no per-value Field
signals.text: The exact dictionary filter of the native Parquet reader (`input_format_parquet_dictionary_filter_push_down`) evaluated each column chunk by hashing every dictionary value through the generic per-value `Field` path and inserting all the hashes into a per-chunk `HashSet`, probed by a handful of query constants. This did two kinds of avoidable work: - `parquetTryHashColumn` constructed a `Field` and re-dispatched on its type for every integer dictionary entry. It now hashes the data array directly, with the type check hoisted out of the loop; the digest is unchanged (widening to `Int64`/`UInt64` and narrowing to the physical type keeps the same low bits as a direct cast), and columns without a fast path (e.g. `IPv4`) fall through to the `Field` path unchanged. - `hashDictionaryValues` now keeps the hash vector itself, sorts it in place, and binary-searches the query constants, instead of building a `HashSet` whose power-of-two buffer (maximum fill factor 0.5) held up to ~4 cells per value on top of that same vector. No extra allocation, a 3-5x smaller persistent footprint charged against `input_format_parquet_memory_high_watermark`, and an exact reservation instead of a modeled one (the `HashSet` growth rule was the trickiest term of the pruning-memory accounting). The extra default-value hash under `input_format_null_as_default` is kept outside the vector so the vector stays exactly the allocation the reservation covers. Measured on a dictionary-heavy microbenchmark (64 row groups, 4M distinct `UInt64` values, absent needle, so the filter prunes everything): ~18% fewer instructions for the query. The pruning also survives a ~35% tighter memory watermark: the behavior flip on the file of `04615_parquet_v3_dictionary_filter_hash_set_budget` moves from between 6.5 and 7.0 MB down to between 4.0 and 4.5 MB. This matters on small machines, where the watermark is derived from the memory limit (about 200 MiB on a machine with 2 GiB of RAM, e.g. `t3a.small` in ClickBench): the smaller and exact footprint lets more chunks be pruned instead of falling back to a full scan, and avoids multi-megabyte transient allocations per column chunk during pruning. `04615_parquet_v3_dictionary_filter_hash_set_budget` is retuned to pin the new footprint model from both sides: a watermark that affords the hash vectors must keep pruning, one just below must fall back to a full scan. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parquet dictionary-based row group pruning (setting `input_format_parquet_dictionary_filter_push_down`) got cheaper: integer dictionaries are hashed without per-value `Field` conversions, and the value set is kept as a sorted vector instead of a hash table, several times reducing the memory footprint of the pruning stage. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115744&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115744](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115744+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Weigh the adaptive aggregation's thaw by staged bytes and add the freeze-bytes and bucket top-K settings
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111459 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115480 The behavioral half of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115480, split out so it can merge independently of the restructuring: one behavioral improvement to the adaptive aggregation's thaw, two new settings, and a latent initialization bug fix. ### The thaw verdict is weighted by bytes The thaw previously fired on the staged stream's repeat factor alone (> 12). That misses streams that repeat keys only a few times but drag wide payloads with every staged record. The verdict is now *wasted staged bytes per distinct key*: `(repeat factor − 1) × bytes per record > 300` — a key's first record is the price of storing-it-once; every repeat is bytes the baseline would have absorbed as an in-place update. Near-unique streams measure ~0 by construction and cannot fire; heavy-column streams stand down early in proportion to the damage. Only the keys and the variable-width argument columns count toward a record's bytes. Fixed-width arguments are deliberately excluded: the drain applies them with the same batch executor the scan would have used, so their staging costs about what their consumption saves — a five-`UInt64`-argument stream at repeat 10 stays engaged and is a clear adaptive win, while a bare repeat rule (or counting its fixed bytes) would thaw it away. Measured on `hits` (100M) (off → on, 16/64 threads): - `SELECT URL, min(Title) GROUP BY URL` (90-byte string key): 0.83×/0.73× → **0.99×/1.01×** - `SELECT UserID, min(URL) GROUP BY UserID` (heavy argument, +121% peak RSS before): 0.83×/0.59× → **0.97×/1.00×**, peak RSS 14.5 → 6.3 GB (matching the ordinary path) - Full ClickBench `GROUP BY` sweep within noise; winning shapes unchanged. ### New settings - **`adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold_bytes`** (default 4 MiB): the byte twin of the key-count freeze threshold — a thread's local table freezes at whichever bound is reached first. Measured as the local table's own allocated bytes (hash-table buffer plus arenas), checked between blocks like the baseline's conversion thresholds; deliberately not the query-wide tracked memory, which would freeze all the locals off each other's growth. At the default it is a guardrail: calibration on the heaviest shapes shows ordinary tables keep freezing by key count (e.g. `WatchID, min(URL)`: 14 of 16 locals unchanged, two freeze earlier by bytes, at 15582 and 8192 keys), and a full ClickBench `GROUP BY` sweep of default vs `0` is noise (geomeans 1.001 / 1.007 at 16 / 64 threads). The plan-serialization side rides version 7, since all the adaptive settings ship in the same release. - **`query_plan_aggregation_bucket_top_k`** (default true): a dedicated toggle for the bucket top-K conversion, which previously could only be disabled together with every plan rewrite via `query_plan_enable_optimizations`. The contract is worded generally (`ORDER BY` over the aggregation's outputs with `LIMIT n`, gated on provable exactness) so the planned generalization beyond the lone `count()` and a single sort column extends the rule, not the setting. The pushed flag is now visible in `EXPLAIN actions = 1` (`Bucket top-K: n ascending|descending`), which also makes the rewrite observable and testable. ### HashTable Statistics Adaptive Aggregator no longer uses previous run hash tables sizes to resize it's small buffer tables. First, buffer tables are very small so any save in runtime is negligible. Second, if buffer table is resized above `adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold_bytes`, it will freeze after first block instead storing all frequent keys eventually. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The adaptive `GROUP BY` aggregation (`enable_adaptive_aggregator`) now measures whether deferring rare keys pays off and returns to the ordinary algorithm when their keys or aggregate arguments are too wide to copy profitably, so aggregations over heavy string columns (e.g. `min(URL)` per user) run at the ordinary algorithm's speed and memory. signals.title: Activate adaptive write buffers from the number of streams a wide part writes
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115440 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed excessive memory usage when inserting into a wide `MergeTree` part that writes many more streams than it has columns, for example a table with a few bucketed `Map` columns. The `min_columns_to_activate_adaptive_write_buffer` setting is now compared against the number of streams the part writes, since one write buffer is allocated per stream. ### Description A 3-row `INSERT` into a wide part with 8 columns (7 `Map`) at `max_buckets_in_map = 100` fails with `Code: 241 ... would use 4.34 GiB (MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED)`. One `MergeTreeWriterStream` is created per substream, and each allocates its full `max_compress_block_size` up front unless `use_adaptive_write_buffer` is set. That flag was decided from `columns_list.size()` against `min_columns_to_activate_adaptive_write_buffer` (default 500). Bucketed `Map` serialization multiplies substreams per column, so this table opens 2415 streams, and because `8 < 500` every one allocated eagerly, at a measured 1.845 MiB per stream. The predicate now reads the number of streams the part will open, from the inventory the writer already builds (`columns_substreams`), counting normalized distinct names with the same already-written-offsets filter `addStreams` applies, computed once per part and cached. The setting keeps its name, default, and `= 0` means disabled behaviour. This is monotone: a column contributes at least one stream, so `streams >= columns`, the gate can only activate earlier, and adaptive buffering only reduces peak memory. For plain scalar columns the counts are equal, which is why `03770_min_columns_to_activate_adaptive_write_buffer` (300 plain columns) is unchanged. Validated on a debug build: the fixture fails at a 4.66 GiB cap before the change and passes at 200 MiB after, part shape identical at 2415 streams; with the bucket settings at their defaults the part has 25 streams and is unaffected. A `chassert` pins the count against `column_streams.size()`; counting raw inventory entries instead of distinct names makes it fire on a two-field `Nested` table, where a shared `nested.size0` gives 5 entries for 4 streams. Skip-index streams pass `query_write_settings` unmodified, so they never receive this flag. Different writer, needs its own reproducer, not addressed here. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115759&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115759](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115759+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix flaky `04628_and_compare_chain_index_hint` under randomized adaptive granularity
signals.text: The test `04628_and_compare_chain_index_hint` asserts `Granules: 1/64`, which only holds when the 65536 inserted rows are split into granules of exactly `index_granularity = 1024` rows. CI randomizes the `index_granularity_bytes` MergeTree setting, and a small value (for example `--index_granularity_bytes 14840`) makes adaptive granularity produce a different number of granules, so the check prints `0` instead of `1` and the test fails. Verified locally: with `index_granularity_bytes = 14840` the check yields `0`, with `index_granularity_bytes = 0` it yields `1`. signals.title: Make test_good_intent_size not depend on Kafka batch timing
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `test_storage_kafka/test_intent_sizes.py::test_good_intent_size` produces `message_4` and `message_5` and then waits for `Saving intent of 2 ... at offset 3`, i.e. it assumes both records land in one consuming cycle. Nothing guarantees that. `kafka_produce` flushes per message, so the two records reach the broker at different times, while the batch ends on the first of three conditions in `StorageKafka2.cpp:1224-1225`, one of which is a deadline of `kafka_flush_interval_ms` measured from a `Stopwatch` constructed per cycle at `StorageKafka2.cpp:1390`, before any message is seen. A cycle that opens before the records exist burns its window on stalled polls and closes at one row, so the engine logs `intent of 1` at offset 3 and then `intent of 1` at offset 4. `Saving intent of 2` is then never printed at all, so the test burns its full 30 s `wait_for_log_line` budget and fails. The failure reads like a too-tight wait, but no wait budget can help. Nor can a wider window: because the `Stopwatch` starts before the first poll, every finite `kafka_flush_interval_ms` still has a phase in which the produce lands too late, so widening only shrinks that phase. That was already the mitigation in 7dcb1c10eed3eed (500 to 3000 ms, by the test's author, for this same check). This stops the stream across the produce instead, so the next cycle's first poll already sees both records and a 2-row batch is guaranteed: ``` SYSTEM STOP test.kafka -> produce message_4 + message_5 -> SYSTEM START test.kafka ``` `STOP` rather than `PAUSE` because only `STOP` also cancels the in-flight cycle, and an already-open window is the hazard. The aborted cycle commits nothing (its `OffsetGuard` rolls back to committed offsets), so `at offset 3` and the final data assertion are unchanged. No assertion is relaxed. The same STOP/produce/START shape is already used by `test_system_stop.py` against this engine. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Forcing the losing interleaving deterministically (the two records produced one cycle period apart, matching the reported failure): - old test: FAILS, server log shows `Saving intent of 1 ... at offset 3` and `... at offset 4`, `grep -c "Saving intent of 2"` = 0 - old test without forcing: PASSES (control) - patched test, same forcing: PASSES, `Saving intent of 2 ... at offset 3` present - patched test with the awaited line changed to `intent of 3`: FAILS, so the assertion still discriminates 50/50 passes of the patched test (12 serial, 38 under `pytest -n 3`, the configuration the failure was seen in), and `test_intent_sizes.py` plus the whole `test_system_stop.py` suite together: 35/35. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115771&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115771](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115771+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1892` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Use PREWHERE for filters pushed down into JOIN sides
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> When a `JOIN` has OR-connected conditions in `WHERE`, ClickHouse extracts the parts that apply to a single side and pushes them down as pre-join filters, so each side reads less data: ```sql SELECT t1.k, t1.a, t2.x FROM tp1 AS t1 JOIN tp2 AS t2 ON t1.k = t2.k WHERE (t1.k IN (1, 2) AND t2.x = 100) OR (t1.k IN (3, 4) AND t2.x = 200) ``` Those pushed-down filters were never moved to `PREWHERE`, even with `optimize_move_to_prewhere` enabled. They ran as ordinary filters after all the requested columns of the row had been read, instead of being evaluated during reading so that non-matching rows skip the remaining columns. The wider the table, the more this costs. Both filters now reach `PREWHERE`. Query results are unaffected; only the plan changes, which is why one existing test reference is updated. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Filters pushed into the sides of a `JOIN` from OR-connected `WHERE` conditions are now moved to `PREWHERE`, so they are evaluated while reading instead of after it. Note: 1. This claims a performance win I have not measured. I only verified the plan and that results are unchanged. 2. A perf run would be confounded right now by the `PREWHERE` ordering bug in (#114998 still open), so if a reviewer asks for numbers, that fix needs to be in the picture first. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115772&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115772](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115772+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix quadratic reallocation while building h3 array results
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112897 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed quadratic time when the functions `h3kRing`, `h3ToChildren`, `h3PolygonToCells` and `h3PolygonToCellsWithContainment` build their result over many rows. A query over 196 000 rows spent 838 seconds copying memory in a CI stress run; it now takes about 5 seconds. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112897 (same defect class, merged) A `Stress test (amd_asan_ubsan)` hung check aborted with one query at `elapsed = 838 s` against its own `max_execution_time = 10`, having written 0 rows. Its `stacktraces` shows the working thread in `__memmove_sse2_unaligned_erms` under `asan_realloc` under `FunctionH3KRing::executeImpl`: running flat out, not stuck. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114559&sha=7698f8b0d63a71a717fb84a0ffb58a701e12223a&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29 These four functions reserve the result accumulator once per row, e.g. `dst_data.reserve(dst_data.size() + vec_size)` at `h3kRing.cpp:132`. `dst_data` is a `ColumnUInt64 &` and `ColumnVector::reserve` is `reserve_exact`, so capacity lands exactly on the current size every row and the next row reallocs, copying the whole accumulated array: `Θ(n²)`, about 11.6 TB of memmove here (peak memory was only 102 MB). Reserving through `PODArray::reserve` rounds capacity up to a power of two, making the copying amortized `O(n)`. `IColumn::reserve` affects performance only, and `reserve_exact` suits the many callers reserving a final size once, so the four per-row callers are the bug, not the primitive. Cancellation had already been delivered, but the existing per-action check cannot fire inside one `IFunction::executeImpl`; removing the quadratic factor is what lets it run. Validated under ASAN, where the defect shows (a Debug build is linear, because glibc `realloc` extends in place; every CI occurrence is a sanitizer job). Unfixed the query does not finish in 400 s; fixed it returns the same result in 4.8 s. All four functions were measured in both directions, results are byte-identical, and peak memory rises ~1.45x, the expected cost of geometric growth. The new test aborts on unfixed master with `TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED` on its first statement and passes in 1.3 s; the 59 existing h3 tests pass. Two sites share the shape with a *constant* per-row amount, which lowers the factor without bounding the total; each is left for its own change: `s2GetNeighbors.cpp:102` (4 per row) and `AggregateFunctionCategoricalInformationValue.cpp:138` (the function's arity). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115773&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115773](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115773+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1878` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fail the query when skip_unavailable_shards skipped every shard
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115646 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reading a `Distributed` or `Remote` table with `skip_unavailable_shards = 1` no longer returns an empty result when every shard was skipped. Such a query now fails with `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED`, matching what already happens when the only shard is local and when a cluster table function such as `s3Cluster` finds no reachable node. Previously an aggregate without `GROUP BY` returned zero rows instead of one, silently. Closes #115646. ### Description `skip_unavailable_shards` returns a result assembled from the shards that answered. When none answered there is no such result: `SELECT count()` gave zero rows where an aggregate without `GROUP BY` must give one. The cause is a missing contract, not the `nodes == 1` shortcut in `getQueryProcessingStage`: a skipped shard's `RemoteQueryExecutor` produces nothing, and nothing checks whether *every* shard was skipped. It is specific to neither one shard nor `count()`. The contract already holds on the local shard path (`04050`) and for cluster table functions (`03603`), so the remote path was the outlier. The check lives in `UnavailableShardTracker`, the one seam that sees both the shard total and the skip count. It counts execution units, one per logical shard plus the extra executors a custom-key parallel-replicas shard fans out to, and fires only once the topology is complete and every unit was skipped without data. A shard that answered keeps the query alive; the `max_skip_unavailable_shards_*` limits keep their behaviour and their denominator. One behaviour change needs your view. Where a shard is *itself* a `Distributed` whose own shards are all skipped, the inner layer now raises this error; coming from a reachable shard, the outer query propagates it under the default mode even with a healthy sibling, where master returned the partial result. `skip_unavailable_shards_mode = 'unavailable_or_exception_before_processing'` still tolerates it. I left `shouldIgnoreShardException` alone rather than decide this. `05031` pins all three modes. I did not take the issue's proposed guard (`stage == Complete` in `RemoteQueryExecutor`): it is per shard, so it fires for one skipped shard while siblings are healthy, and `Complete` marks neither "the only shard" nor "aggregate pushed down". It breaks `04038` and `04152`. `04665_remote_engine_settings_clause` asserted the empty result as expected. Its arms now assert `DistributedShardsSkipped`, so they still prove the storage-level setting is applied and survives a reattach. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115775&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115775](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115775+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix integer underflow in MySQL protocol handshake
signals.text: Prevent an unsigned integer underflow in the MySQL handshake handler that removes the intended bound on how much data an unauthenticated client can make the server buffer. In `MySQLHandler::finishHandshake` the first socket read may return more bytes than the client-declared packet size. When `pos > packet_size` the unsigned expression `packet_size - pos` underflows to a huge value, turning the following `copyData()` into an unbounded pre-auth read that keeps buffering socket data until EOF or the memory limit is reached. This adds a check that rejects such malformed handshake packets before the subtraction. A conforming client never sends more than the packet it announced in the header, so the check is unreachable on the normal path and introduces no regression. The MySQL interface is enabled by default (`mysql_port` 9004), so the code path is reachable without special config. This is a hardening fix, not a crash: the underflowed value is only a loop counter and is never used as a pointer offset or buffer size, so there is no memory corruption — the impact is bounded pre-auth memory pressure. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an integer underflow in the MySQL protocol handshake handler that could cause the server to buffer an unbounded amount of data from an unauthenticated client. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115776&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115776](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115776+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
