signal.title: Use text and token skip indexes for IN with `transform_null_in = 1`
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111311 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111329 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111311 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111329 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Makes the `text`, `tokenbf_v1`, `ngrambf_v1` and `sparse_grams` skip indexes apply to `IN` when `transform_null_in = 1` and the set contains no NULL, so a query no longer loses index pruning just because that setting is enabled. Previously such a query read every granule, and one using `force_data_skipping_indices` failed with `INDEX_NOT_USED`. A set that does contain NULL keeps the original predicate, since `nullIn` also matches the column's NULL rows. ### Description Follow-up to #111329, which fixed `bloom_filter` only. With `transform_null_in = 1` the analyzer rewrites `x IN (...)` to `nullIn(x, ...)` and `globalIn` to `globalNullIn`. Two skip-index condition classes decide on the function name. `MergeTreeIndexConditionText` accepted only `in`/`globalIn`, so the atom stayed unknown and the index was dropped entirely. `MergeTreeConditionBloomFilterText` (shared by `tokenbf_v1`, `ngrambf_v1` and `sparse_grams`) did admit the new names, prepared the bloom filters and then discarded them, because its body assigned an RPN function only for `notIn` and `in`. Adding the names alone would give wrong results. Set elements are materialized from the left-hand key type, and `Set::getElementTypes` strips `Nullable` only when `transform_null_in` is off, so a `Nullable` key keeps the wrapper even for a NULL-free set. Measured on a `text` index over `Nullable(String)`, `x IN ('word5', NULL)` returns 1 row at `transform_null_in = 0` and 11 at `1`; pruning the second case would drop granules holding real results. So each site now tolerates a `Nullable` wrapper in its existing type rule and refuses per row via `isNullAt` at the tokenized position only, which keeps NULL in an unindexed tuple component prunable. Two further changes are disclosed rather than advertised. `globalIn` never pruned on the token bloom filter family even at `transform_null_in = 0`; the same one-line branch fixes that, so `transform_null_in = 0` is not untouched. And a predicate that now prunes every granule no longer reaches an execution-time error it previously reached. That is a pre-existing property of pruning, observable on the primary key alone, and it already applied to `in` on these indexes; the effect here is that `nullIn` now behaves like the `in` it mirrors, where master has the two spellings disagree. The added bound check mirrors the `text` sibling and is not reachable today. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Both directions, from one worktree with only the two source files reverted: | carrier | before, `transform_null_in = 1` | after | |---|---|---| | `text` `String` / `LowCardinality(String)` / `FixedString(12)` | index dropped | `Granules: 2/250` | | `text` `Nullable(String)` / `LowCardinality(Nullable(String))`, NULL-free | index dropped | prunes | | `text` tuple set, incl. indexed component at position 1 and a `Nullable` indexed component | index dropped | prunes | | `text` map element value, JSON subcolumn via `::String` | index dropped | prunes | | `tokenbf_v1` `String` / `LowCardinality(String)` / tuple set | `250/250` | `2/250` | | `ngrambf_v1` `String` / `LowCardinality(String)`, `sparse_grams` `String` | `250/250` | `29/250` | | `force_data_skipping_indices`, all four | `INDEX_NOT_USED` | returns rows | Row counts match between the two `transform_null_in` arms in every cell, so the test asserts correctness as well as pruning. Unchanged and verified: a NULL-containing set still does not prune and still returns 11 rows, `NOT IN` still never prunes, the empty-string and tokenizes-to-nothing bail-outs still bail out, and mixed-type tuples still prune on `text` and still do not on the token bloom filter family. Six mutation arms, each reddening a specific cell set: removing the `isNullAt` refusal makes the NULL-set query fail with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`; removing only the `Nullable` tolerance reddens exactly the five `Nullable` cells while the plain `String` cells pass; reverting either site reddens exactly that site's cells; making the bound check too eager reddens every token bloom filter cell. 50 tag-free randomized runs at `--jobs 8`: 50 OK. Regression sweep over 255 tests, identical selection in both arms with the ran-test sets asserted equal: 0 new failures, 1 improvement (the new test). </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112785&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112785](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112785+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Allow Distributed and Remote tables in Replicated databases
signal.text: `database_replicated_allow_only_replicated_engine` rejects table engines that keep their own unreplicated data on disk in a `Replicated` database. Before this change, `Distributed` was also rejected because its optional background `INSERT` queue makes `storesDataOnDisk` return true, even though the queue is a transient send buffer and the table's actual data belongs to its destination shards. This change distinguishes table-owned on-disk data from auxiliary delivery state. The restriction applies to non-`ATTACH` `CREATE` queries when `database_replicated_allow_only_replicated_engine = 1`. | Engine or group | Result | Reason | |---|---|---| | `ReplicatedMergeTree` family and `SharedMergeTree` | Allow | The engine provides a replication or shared-storage contract. | | Writable non-replicated `MergeTree` with a local or remote storage policy | Reject | It owns unreplicated on-disk table data; a remote disk alone does not establish replication. | | Static read-only non-replicated `MergeTree` | Allow | It cannot create new table-owned data. | | `Log`, `TinyLog`, `StripeLog`, `Set`, `Join`, `EmbeddedRocksDB`, and database `File` | Reject | They own unreplicated on-disk table data. | | `MaterializedPostgreSQL` | Reject | It owns a local nested table. | | `Distributed`, `Remote`, and `RemoteSecure` | Allow | Their optional local queue is auxiliary delivery state rather than data of the table itself. | | `Memory`, `Buffer`, and `Null` | Allow | They do not own on-disk table data. | | `Merge`, `Alias`, and `View` | Allow | They are metadata-only. | | Views with inner tables | Depends | Each generated inner table is created and checked separately. | | External-storage engines, data lakes, external databases, and external queues | Allow | Their data is managed outside ClickHouse-owned table storage. | | Lazy `StorageTableProxy` | Reject conservatively | The nested storage is unknown without loading it. | `ATTACH` remains outside the existing gate. The `Distributed` background `INSERT` queue is local to the node accepting an insert and is not replicated. Users requiring acknowledgement only after data reaches the destination shards should set `distributed_foreground_insert = 1`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow `Distributed`, `Remote`, and `RemoteSecure` tables in `Replicated` databases when `database_replicated_allow_only_replicated_engine` is enabled, while continuing to reject writable non-replicated `MergeTree` tables using local or remote storage policies. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108820&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108820](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108820+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Resume a NATS JetStream subscription after a reconnect
signal.text: A `NATS` table reading from a JetStream stream can stop consuming for good after the NATS server restarts, while still looking subscribed and healthy. An asynchronous JetStream pull subscription asks for more messages only when one is delivered, and when the NATS client reconnects it re-sends the `SUB` line but not the pull request the broker was holding. A broker that goes away without answering that request - a hard kill, a network partition, or a graceful restart that lands in the milliseconds between a re-subscribe and its request being parked - leaves the table subscribed and permanently silent. That is what `test_nats_restore_failed_connection_without_losses_on_write` hits when the consumer is still behind at the moment the broker is stopped: all 100000 rows were published and acknowledged into the stream, but the ones not yet delivered are never fetched again, so the view stays short of them and the test fails with `ClickHouse lost some messages: 92807`. It fails this way on about 0.2% of runs since the NATS tests came back on 2026-07-30, and at the same rate before and after #112828 recovered the closed-subscription case on 2026-08-13 (88 of 46693 runs before, 27 of 15428 after), which is what points at the window that fix leaves open. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=c260929910ea94be9a359bb69bf5e33d7b3a40e4&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%204%2F4%29 Recovery so far keyed only on a subscription the NATS client had closed, which is what a graceful shutdown produces by answering the outstanding pull request. This reports a reconnect as well, by comparing the reconnect count the client keeps for the connection against the one taken when we subscribed, and re-subscribes through the same path. Only JetStream consumers do this: a core NATS subscription really is restored by the `SUB` line, and re-subscribing it would drop buffered messages nothing redelivers. The recovery is applied both by the background streaming task and by an in-flight direct `SELECT`, whose source retains its consumer until the query finishes. The window this closes is the residual documented in #112828, so `_restart_nats` no longer retries until a restart lands outside it, and a new test reaches that state deterministically with `SIGKILL`, which answers nothing and so leaves no closed subscription to fall back on. Verified locally with a release build, running the module through `ci.praktika`: - new test with the fix: passed twice (65 s, 146 s); - new test with `src/Storages/NATS` reverted to `master` and everything else unchanged: `AssertionError: consumption did not resume, view holds 10 of 20 keys` - the messages published after the restart never arrive; - the five existing restart tests plus `test_nats_restore_failed_connection_without_losses_on_write`, all six passed with the fix. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112828 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `NATS` engine table reading from a JetStream stream (`nats_stream`) silently stopping to consume messages after the NATS server restarted or the connection was re-established. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115343&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115343](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115343+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Compare array membership values the way the equals operator does
signal.text:
Compare array membership values the way the equals operator does Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112953 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104858 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`, `notHas`, `indexOf`, `countEqual`, `indexOfAssumeSorted`, `mapContainsKey` and `mapContainsValue` returning a wrong result when the element and needle types differ. A negative signed value equated with its unsigned bit-pattern twin at 32 and 64 bits, so `has([1, -1]::Array(Int32), 4294967295::UInt32)` returned 1 while `=` returns 0, and a wide integer equated with an imprecise `Float`. Over `Array(LowCardinality(T))` a needle that narrowed onto a different dictionary entry also matched it, including a `DateTime` needle against a `Date` element. `indexOfAssumeSorted` could also miss a value that is present. ### Description `executeIntegral` compared every pair of native number types with a raw C++ `==` under a suppressed `-Wsign-compare`, plus hand-rolled `static_cast` branches for a mixed integer/float pair. The usual arithmetic conversions turn the signed operand unsigned, so `int32_t(-1) == uint32_t(4294967295)` is true. `Int8` and `Int16` were correct against a same-width unsigned type, since both promote to `int` first, which is why this stayed hidden; against a wider needle they wrapped too. The float casts are lossy the same way. The helpers now call `accurate::equalsOp` and `accurate::greaterOrEqualsOp`, which is what `EqualsOp`, and therefore the scalar operator, already calls, so the two cannot disagree. Both suppressions and all six casts are deleted. `lowerBound`'s ordering moves with the equality it feeds, or the binary search descends the wrong half. Same-type pairs, which dominate, keep the identical comparison through that helper's fast path. `Array(LowCardinality(T))` with a constant needle is a second locus, since `executeArrayLowCardinality` returns before `executeImpl` strips `LowCardinality`. It resolved the needle to a dictionary index through `castColumn`, which wraps, so `UInt32(4294967295)` became `Int32(-1)` and matched that element. `dictionaryIndexForConstant` now asks `targetTypeRepresentsValue`, added by #114624 for the default slot, whether the constant survived that cast, and treats one that did not as absent. Any narrowing needle can land on a wrong entry, so it is asked at every index, including a temporal or `IPv4` element truncating a wider needle. The string family is the exception, since equality pads a shorter needle to the element width, so there it stays at the default slot. Most rows of the new test print an oracle beside the result, `arrayExists(x -> x = needle, v)`; 31 rows differ without the fix.
Reference change in 01414_low_cardinality_nullable Four lines move from `1` to `0`: `has(u8, -1)`, `has(u16, -1)`, `has(u32, -1)` and `has(u64, -1)` over `Array(LowCardinality(Nullable(UInt8/UInt16/UInt32/UInt64)))`. The second `INSERT` writes `negate(number)`, so each column stores the wrapped value (`255`, `65535`, `4294967295`, `18446744073709551615`), for which `x = -1` is false and `has` must not match. `arrayExists` with `=`, `arrayFilter` and scalar `=` all agree on `0`, and `accurateCastOrNull(-1, 'UInt32')` is `NULL`. The reference recorded the defect. The `Int8` control in the same block still returns `1`. This is the same four-line change as #112953, which fixes the `LowCardinality` half from the other side; whichever merges second resolves by taking either side of that one file.

signal.title: Add a full-featured AI agent to the client (the `?` command)
signal.text: Turns the primitive `??` "generate one SQL query" helper in the client into a full interactive AI agent, available with a single `?` (`??` is kept as an alias). The agent works over a live connection: it is given the context of the recent queries in the session (with results truncated to the first and last lines to save tokens, plus error messages) and can use tools to read the query history from `system.user_query_log`, inspect the schema (`SHOW`/`DESCRIBE`/`SHOW CREATE`), consult the embedded documentation (`system.documentation`, the same source as the `help` command), run read-only queries without confirmation under a sandbox (`readonly = 1`, a 30-second and a 10 GiB limit, no table functions reaching outside of the server's tables; if the session forbids applying these limits, the query fails instead of running without them), and run any other query after asking the user for confirmation. Queries it runs are echoed and executed on the user's connection and displayed exactly as if the user had typed them; it prints its thoughts and tool calls as it works, and the conversation keeps its context across `?` invocations within a session. When no client-side AI provider is configured (neither the `ai` section of the client configuration nor the `OPENAI_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variables), the agent falls back to the server-side `aiGenerate` function of the connected server (or of `clickhouse-local`) when it has default credentials configured for it (`ai_function_text_default_credentials`), so it works with no client-side setup when the administrator has already enabled AI functions. Implementation lives in `src/Client/AI/`: the agent loop (`AIAgent`), two model backends (`AIAgentTransport`: native tool-calling via `ai-sdk-cpp`, and a text tool-call protocol on top of `aiGenerate`), the tools (`AIAgentTools`), the read-only statement allowlist (`AIQueryValidation`), and the recent-query context buffer (`QueryContextBuffer`). Unit tests cover the tool-call protocol parsing, the read-only validation, and the context buffer; the end-to-end loop (both backends and the confirmation gate) was validated by driving `clickhouse-local` against a mock OpenAI endpoint. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The embedded AI assistant of `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local` is now a full agent, invoked with a single `?`. It sees the recent queries and their results, explores the schema and the documentation, runs read-only queries on its own (and other queries with confirmation) displayed as if you typed them, and can use the server-side `aiGenerate` function when no client-side AI provider is configured. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114043&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114043](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114043+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Implement PromQL range functions present_over_time, absent_over_time, quantile_over_time and predict_linear
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 > [!IMPORTANT] > **Depends on #115073.** `04551_promql_phase3_range_functions` runs > `absent_over_time({__name__=~"up|up2",instance="host1"}[3m])` through `--dialect promql`, and the SQL > lexer rejects `=~` before the PromQL parser sees the text: > `Code: 62 ... Unrecognized token: Syntax error: failed at position 28 (~)`. > #115073 is what lets a raw-text dialect keep tokens the SQL lexer rejects. It is the only failing > test here, and it accounts for every red check on this PR; the rest of the suite is green. Existing > PromQL tests do not hit this because they pass the expression as a string literal to > `prometheusQuery(...)`, where the lexer never sees it. > > Merge #115073 first, then a master merge here turns this green. The test is deliberately left as-is > rather than rewritten to dodge the lexer bug. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented range functions `present_over_time()`, `absent_over_time()`, `quantile_over_time()` and `predict_linear()`. ### Description Implements four PromQL functions over range vectors that were previously rejected with a not-implemented error: - `present_over_time(v range-vector)` — for each grid point, `1` if its staleness window contains at least one sample, otherwise the series is dropped. - `absent_over_time(v range-vector)` — an empty vector if the range vector has any samples, otherwise a 1-element synthetic series with value `1` and the labels inferred from the selector's equality matchers (matching Prometheus `absent_over_time` / `absent` semantics). - `quantile_over_time(phi scalar, v range-vector)` — the φ-quantile of the sample values in each grid point's window, computed with the R-7 (inclusive) method (`quantileExactInclusive`). φ outside `[0, 1]` yields ±Inf and NaN φ yields NaN, as in Prometheus. - `predict_linear(v range-vector, t scalar)` — simple linear regression over the in-window samples, extrapolated `t` seconds past the evaluation time. **Implementation** - Two new grid aggregate functions: - `timeSeriesPresentToGrid` — `1` if a window has any sample, else `NULL`. - `timeSeriesQuantileToGrid` — R-7 inclusive quantile over a window (non-invertible summary that collects window values and sorts them in `getResult`). Both are registered inline in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp`. `predict_linear` reuses the existing `timeSeriesPredictLinearToGrid` aggregate (the `is_predict` variant of the linear-regression aggregate). - `present_over_time` is wired through `applyFunctionOverRange`'s `impl_map`. `quantile_over_time` and `predict_linear` have dedicated translators because they take an extra scalar argument. - `absent_over_time` builds a per-series presence grid via `present_over_time`, then at runtime counts present series per grid point (`countForEach`) and inverts the result, so it works whether or not the metric exists (a selector on a missing metric is a runtime subquery, not a compile-time-empty one). Output labels are derived from the selector's matchers, like `absent()`. No parser changes were needed — the grammar already accepts these function names and `getFunctionResultType` already returns the correct result types. **Testing**: new parser cases in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp` for `present_over_time` and `absent_over_time` (`quantile_over_time` / `predict_linear` were already covered); new stateless test `04551_promql_phase3_range_functions.sh` exercising all four functions (present/absent, quantile at φ = 0 / 0.5 / 1, predict_linear at offsets 0 and 60) against a multi-series TimeSeries table, with values verified against Prometheus semantics. **Update: time-varying `predict_offset` / `phi`** `predict_linear`'s `t` and `quantile_over_time`'s `phi` now also accept a per-grid-point-varying PromQL scalar (e.g. `time()` in a range query), not just a constant or single-row scalar. This is handled by two new, self-contained aggregate functions, `timeSeriesPredictLinearVaryingToGrid` / `timeSeriesQuantileVaryingToGrid`, which take the varying value as a 3rd `Array(Float64)` argument instead of a fixed aggregate parameter (ClickHouse aggregate parameters are bound once per instance and can't vary per row). They're isolated from `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase` (shared by ~10 other `timeSeries*ToGrid` functions) to avoid regression risk to those. Since these are public SQL aggregate functions, not just an internal translator detail, they validate that the 3rd-argument array is identical across every row/merged state and throw `BAD_ARGUMENTS` otherwise, rather than silently using whichever array was seen first. **Scope note**: the varying value is normalized to `Array(Float64)` in the translator so it works for `Float32`-valued `TimeSeries` tables too, not just `Float64`. However, the PromQL scalar's *own* grid representation (`fromFunctionTime.cpp`'s `SCALAR_GRID` output for `time()`) is cast to `Array(scalar_data_type)`, which is the *table's value type* — for a `Float32`-valued table, that means `time()`'s own raw values (Unix timestamps, ~1.7e9) already lose precision (~128-unit rounding at that magnitude) before my code ever sees them. This is a pre-existing property of `scalar_data_type` being shared between value-precision and timestamp-scalar-precision, not something this change introduces, but this change is what makes it reachable for `predict_offset`/`phi`. It only matters when the varying value is derived from `time()` on a non-`Float64` table. A bare `time()` (also inside `scalar()`/`vector()`) is rebuilt at native timestamp precision and works; any arithmetic around it (e.g. `predict_linear(m[5m], time() - 60)` or a `phi` normalized from `time()`) would see the already-rounded evaluation time, so `makeVaryingScalarPrecisionSafe` rejects it with `CANNOT_EXECUTE_PROMQL_QUERY` instead of returning silently wrong results — this is documented in the supported-functions tables. Fixing the root cause would mean changing `fromFunctionTime.cpp`'s shared `SCALAR_GRID` representation, which has ~15 other callers — out of scope here. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112842&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112842](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112842+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Make per-key duplicate-key bookkeeping cheaper when parsing JSON objects
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113731 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improved the performance of parsing JSON objects into a `JSON` column. The per-key duplicate-key bookkeeping now keeps its two type sets as bit masks in a single map entry instead of two maps of nested sets. The gain grows with the number of keys per object, and applies whether or not the object contains a repeated key. ### Description Related: #113731 Since `ObjectJSONNode::traverseAndInsert` was split into two passes, duplicate-key bookkeeping costs two `getJSONElementType()` calls, two `unordered_map` nodes and two nested `unordered_set` allocations per traversed key, where the single-pass version paid one of each. The cost scales with key count, not byte size. The split carries backport labels, so release branches inherit it. `JSONElementType` has two enumerators, so a set of them is two bits. Both per-key sets now live in one map entry as bit masks: the types the first pass accepted, and those the second already emitted. That removes the nested-set allocations and the separate `visited_keys` map, and the second pass goes from up to four hash lookups per key to one. Measured on x86_64 release builds with `UserTimeMicroseconds`, paired interleaved, 7 runs per side, across the patch releases bracketing the split (v26.6.2.160, v26.6.3.62). The regression: **1.4772** at 1000 keys per object against **1.0398** at 10 keys per object at equal byte volume, so it tracks key count rather than a general slowdown, and **1.3277** on `json_type_parsing` query 3. Against master: **0.6604** on query 3, **0.5589** at 1000 keys, **0.5676** with the duplicated key last. Pre-scanning each object to skip the bookkeeping entirely was rejected: faster still without a repeated key, but it charges the scan to objects that have one, measuring 1.13 to 1.14 there. Duplicated literal-and-object keys are accepted by default, so that is not a rare shape. Behaviour is unchanged, so no new test is added. A differential matrix of 60 duplicated-key cases (both orderings, three-way duplicates, typed paths, shared data, escaped dots, both settings crossed) is byte-identical to master in results and error text, while diverging from a pre-split binary. Breaking either mask changes 5, 9 or 11 of the existing duplicated-key tests' queries. Root cause analysis by egor-click, who proposed the pre-scan variant. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115888&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115888](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115888+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Explain data/expected structure mismatches in INSERT parse errors
signal.text: Improves the error message shown when parsing the data of an `INSERT` fails. Previously, inserting data whose structure does not match the destination produced a confusing low-level parse error (for example `Cannot parse input: expected '\t' before ...`) with no hint about the real cause. In the linked issue, the destination's inferred schema had integer columns while the inserted `TSV` data had string columns, and the reported error pointed at a tab that was actually present. Now, on a parse failure, ClickHouse infers the structure of the data being inserted (only when the format has a data schema reader, and solely for diagnostics) and, if it does not correspond to the expected structure, appends an explanation listing both the inferred and the expected structure. For example: ``` Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected '\t' before: 'page_view... ... The structure of the data being inserted does not match the structure expected by the query, which is likely the cause of the parsing error. Inferred structure of the input data (in format `TSV`): c1 Nullable(Int64) c2 Nullable(String) c3 Nullable(String) Expected structure: c1 Int64 c2 Int64 c3 Int64 ``` The check is wired through a lazy provider on `IInputFormat` that runs only on a genuine parse error, so there is no cost on the happy path. The comparison ignores the artificial `Nullable` wrapper that schema inference adds by default, so inserting valid data into non-nullable columns is not falsely flagged. It covers the synchronous local/server path, client-side parsing, and the asynchronous insert queue (the default path now that `async_insert` is enabled by default). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110622 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): When parsing of the data being inserted by an `INSERT` fails, the error message now explains a likely structure mismatch by comparing the structure inferred from the data with the structure expected by the query. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110626&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110626](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110626+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Malformed ORC/Avro files reach `LOGICAL_ERROR` through the exception formatter (aborts on debug builds, silently, from schema inference)
signal.text: 🕵️ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour A truncated ORC file makes `clickhouse local` / `clickhouse-server` abort with **no output at all** — no error, no stack trace, nothing on stdout or stderr. The same signature is reachable from Avro. The cause is not in the ORC reader itself but in the error-handling path: schema inference catches the reader's failure and calls `getCurrentExceptionMessage()` to format it, and that function deliberately aborts when the in-flight exception derives from `std::logic_error`. The bundled parsing libraries throw `std::logic_error` subclasses for malformed input, so untrusted data reaches an assertion that is meant to catch internal bugs only. The process dies *while composing the error message*, which is why nothing is ever printed. ### How to reproduce The input is a plain truncation of a file already in the repo — no bit-level fuzzing needed: ```bash head -c 289 tests/queries/0_stateless/data_orc/orc_nested_union_type.orc > t289.orc clickhouse local --query "SELECT * FROM file('t289.orc', ORC) FORMAT Null" ``` ``` Aborted (core dumped) ``` Reproducible 3/3. Total output produced: 0 bytes. Sending the same file to a server via `SELECT * FROM file('t289.orc', ORC)` takes the server down. Note the neighbouring truncation lengths behave correctly — `head -c 100`, `-c 200`, `-c 400`, `-c 600` all return a clean `Code: 636 CANNOT_EXTRACT_TABLE_STRUCTURE`, as does the untruncated fixture. Only this length reaches the bad path. A second input with the same signature, from a different format: `SELECT count() FROM file('x.avro', Avro)` on an Iceberg manifest `.avro` fixture with four bit flips (attached, 4245 bytes) also aborts and also takes the server down. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Reproduced on 26.8.1.1599 and 26.8.1.1. **Important caveat:** both builds I have are `BUILD_TYPE = Debug`. The abort is gated on `debug_or_sanitizer_build || abort_on_logical_error`, so on a release build these inputs presumably raise a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception instead of crashing. I had no release build to confirm that. Either way a `LOGICAL_ERROR` should not be reachable from an input file. ### Expected behavior A malformed input file should produce an ordinary parse error (`CANNOT_EXTRACT_TABLE_STRUCTURE`, `INCORRECT_DATA`, …). It should never reach `abortOnFailedAssertion`, and error formatting should never be able to kill the process — least of all silently. ### Error message and/or stacktrace There is no error message; that is part of the problem. `gdb` backtrace: ``` #4 __GI_abort () #5 DB::abortOnFailedAssertion (description=..., format_string=..., trace=...) at src/Common/Exception.cpp:66 #6 DB::abortOnFailedAssertion (description=...) src/Common/Exception.cpp:72 #7 DB::getCurrentExceptionMessageAndPattern (with_stacktrace=false, ...) at src/Common/Exception.cpp:548 #8 DB::getCurrentExceptionMessage (...) src/Common/Exception.cpp:477 #9 DB::readSchemaFromFormatImpl (format_name=..., ...) src/Formats/ReadSchemaUtils.cpp:278 #10 DB::readSchemaFromFormat (...) src/Formats/ReadSchemaUtils.cpp:569 #11 DB::StorageFile::getTableStructureAndFormatFromFileImpl (...) src/Storages/StorageFile.cpp:1209 #13 DB::StorageFile::setStorageMetadata (...) src/Storages/StorageFile.cpp:1371 #21 DB::TableFunctionFile::getStorage (...) src/TableFunctions/TableFunctionFile.cpp:168 ``` The relevant code, `src/Common/Exception.cpp` (~L537-550): ```cpp if (debug_or_sanitizer_build || abort_on_logical_error.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) { try { throw; } catch (const std::logic_error &) { if (!with_stacktrace) stream << ", Stack trace:\n\n" << getExceptionStackTraceString(e); abortOnFailedAssertion(stream.str()); } catch (...) {} } ``` and its caller, `src/Formats/ReadSchemaUtils.cpp:278`: ```cpp catch (...) { auto exception_message = getCurrentExceptionMessage(false); ``` ### Root cause: which exception escapes Caught in the debugger at `abortOnFailedAssertion`, the message being formatted when the process dies is: * **ORC** — `std::exception. Code: 1001, type: orc::NotImplementedYet, e.what() = Unknown compression codec 6` * **Avro** — `std::exception. Code: 1001, type: std::domain_error, e.what() = Object end` Both are `std::logic_error` subclasses (`orc::NotImplementedYet` derives from it, and `std::domain_error` *is* one), which is precisely the branch that aborts: ```cpp // src/Common/Exception.cpp, getCurrentExceptionMessageAndPattern (~L537) if (debug_or_sanitizer_build || abort_on_logical_error.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) { try { throw; } catch (const std::logic_error &) { ... abortOnFailedAssertion(stream.str()); } catch (...) {} } ``` The truncated ORC file simply has a garbage byte where the compression codec goes; liborc reports that as `NotImplementedYet` rather than a parse error, so it sails past the guards that already exist. ### Possible fix **1. Widen the library-boundary catches (the fix that matches existing precedent).** `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/NativeORCBlockInputFormat.cpp` already wraps liborc at two points, but only for `orc::ParseError` (L1376, L1462). Per `contrib/orc/c++/include/orc/Exceptions.hh` the hierarchy splits: ```cpp class NotImplementedYet : public std::logic_error {...}; // L29 -> aborts class SchemaEvolutionError: public std::logic_error {...}; // L62 -> aborts class ParseError : public std::runtime_error {...}; // L40 -> already caught class InvalidArgument : public std::runtime_error {...}; // L51 -> not caught, but harmless ``` so the two `logic_error` branches — plus any `std::out_of_range` from bounds checks — sail past the existing guards. The comments on those catches say the intent was "instead of letting it propagate as a generic std::exception", so widening them is in keeping with the original design. Widening those catches, and adding the equivalent at the Avro boundary, follows exactly the shape used to fix #106259: ```cpp catch (const DB::Exception &) { throw; } catch (const std::exception & e) { /// liborc throws orc::NotImplementedYet / orc::SchemaEvolutionError (std::logic_error /// subclasses) on malformed input. Untranslated they reach the top level as /// LOGICAL_ERROR (code 1001) and abort via abortOnFailedAssertion. throw Exception(ErrorCodes::CORRUPTED_DATA, "Cannot read ORC data: {}", e.what()); } ``` That is the same boundary-translation used in `ThetaSketchData::read` for `datasketches` (#106260 / commit `899dd77`), and the same rationale applies. **2. Map the third-party namespaces to real error codes (complementary, not sufficient).** `getCodeForSTDException` (`src/Common/Exception.cpp` ~L189) already special-cases one library: ```cpp std::string name = demangle(typeid(exc).name()); if (name.starts_with("avro::")) return ErrorCodes::AVRO_EXCEPTION; return ErrorCodes::STD_EXCEPTION; ``` Adding `orc::`, `parquet::` and `arrow::` would at least give a meaningful code instead of `STD_EXCEPTION`. **On its own this does not stop the abort** — the abort keys off the C++ type being a `std::logic_error`, not off the error code — so it only helps alongside (1). **3. Reconsider the blanket `std::logic_error` ⇒ internal-bug assumption (broader, optional).** The assumption behind the abort is that a `std::logic_error` can only be a ClickHouse bug. Bundled parsers violate that routinely: they use `domain_error`, `out_of_range`, `invalid_argument` and `NotImplementedYet` to report *bad input*. As long as that holds, fix (1) has to be applied at every third-party parse boundary, and each new one is a fresh instance of this issue — the fuzz run reached the same abort through ORC, Avro, Parquet and ArrowStream. Narrowing the abort to exceptions that genuinely originate in ClickHouse code would fix the class rather than the instances, at the cost of losing an assertion that is presumably valuable in CI. Whichever route, a regression test in the shape of `tests/queries/0_stateless/04307_uniqTheta_corrupted_state_106259` (added by the #106260 fix) would fit — the 289-byte ORC input is deterministic and needs no fuzzing to regenerate. ### Additional context Found by a fuzzer that mutates valid Parquet/ORC/Avro/Arrow files and complete Iceberg and DeltaLake tables, then checks that reading them fails with an ordinary exception. Over the run the server went down 27 times; `ReadSchemaUtils.cpp` was by far the most frequent frame in the fatal records, and the crashing queries were Avro (28), Parquet (12) and ORC (4) — consistent with this one shared path rather than three separate parser bugs. Prior art: **#106259** / **#106260** fixed the identical pattern for `datasketches` (`std::out_of_range` from a malformed `AggregateFunction(uniqTheta)` state). The instances here are the same class in liborc / avro / arrow, which that fix did not cover. Worth noting a maintainer's comment on #106259 — *"a LOGICAL_ERROR is not a crash. It's an exception."* — which is consistent with the debug-build caveat above; on release these are bad error codes rather than aborts. One related observation from the same run, filed here for context rather than as a separate issue: * **Allocation driven by corrupted length fields.** 9 inputs pushed the reader past a 3 GB per-query memory limit; with no `max_memory_usage` set, a few corrupted bytes are a memory-exhaustion vector. Everything else behaved correctly: 55 545 corrupted inputs were rejected with ordinary errors (636 `CANNOT_EXTRACT_TABLE_STRUCTURE`, 117 `INCORRECT_DATA`, 742 `DELTA_KERNEL_ERROR`, …), and the DeltaLake and Iceberg metadata layers in particular rejected every corruption cleanly.

signal.title: HTTP: support PUT uploads to table paths
signal.text: Implements the first step from [#38775](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/38775): allow an HTTP `PUT` request to upload data to an existing table when the URL path contains the database, table, and input format. Related: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/38775 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/46925 ## What's in the box - `PUT /database/table.CSV` inserts the request body into `database.table` as CSV. - `PUT /database/table.JSONEachRow` works the same way for JSONEachRow. - Reuses the existing HTTP path parser and input format registry. - Keeps the existing GET table-as-file behavior unchanged. - Keeps PUT requests with an explicit `query` parameter read-only. - Enables the PUT mutation exception only for the built-in catch-all path handler. - Configured dynamic handlers keep their existing readonly behavior. - Requires an existing table and a request body. - Rejects missing or unknown formats, compression suffixes, and paths without a format suffix. The larger ticket also mentions schema inference/table creation and POST multipart uploads. Those are intentionally left for follow-up work. ## Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ## Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add path-based PUT uploads to existing tables in the HTTP interface. ## Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) in `docs/concepts/features/interfaces/http.mdx`. ## Tests - Added `05029_http_put_table_upload` for path uploads and validation errors. - Added keep-alive regressions for failed PUT and DELETE requests with request bodies. - Extended `test_dynamic_handler_put_delete_still_readonly` to cover the default query parameter on configured dynamic handlers. - `git diff --check` - `bash -n tests/queries/0_stateless/05029_http_put_table_upload.sh` - `python3 -m py_compile tests/integration/test_http_handlers_config/test.py` <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115849&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115849](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115849+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fail the query when skip_unavailable_shards skipped every shard
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115646 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reading a `Distributed` or `Remote` table with `skip_unavailable_shards = 1` no longer returns an empty result when every shard was skipped. Such a query now fails with `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED`, matching what already happens when the only shard is local and when a cluster table function such as `s3Cluster` finds no reachable node. Previously an aggregate without `GROUP BY` returned zero rows instead of one, silently. Closes #115646. ### Description `skip_unavailable_shards` returns a result assembled from the shards that answered. When none answered there is no such result: `SELECT count()` gave zero rows where an aggregate without `GROUP BY` must give one. The cause is a missing contract, not the `nodes == 1` shortcut in `getQueryProcessingStage`: a skipped shard's `RemoteQueryExecutor` produces nothing, and nothing checks whether *every* shard was skipped. It is specific to neither one shard nor `count()`. The contract already holds on the local shard path (`04050`) and for cluster table functions (`03603`), so the remote path was the outlier. The check lives in `UnavailableShardTracker`, the one seam that sees both the shard total and the skip count. It counts execution units, one per logical shard plus the extra executors a custom-key parallel-replicas shard fans out to, and fires only once the topology is complete and every unit was skipped without data. A shard that answered keeps the query alive; the `max_skip_unavailable_shards_*` limits keep their behaviour and their denominator. One behaviour change needs your view. Where a shard is *itself* a `Distributed` whose own shards are all skipped, the inner layer now raises this error; coming from a reachable shard, the outer query propagates it under the default mode even with a healthy sibling, where master returned the partial result. `skip_unavailable_shards_mode = 'unavailable_or_exception_before_processing'` still tolerates it. I left `shouldIgnoreShardException` alone rather than decide this. `05031` pins all three modes. I did not take the issue's proposed guard (`stage == Complete` in `RemoteQueryExecutor`): it is per shard, so it fires for one skipped shard while siblings are healthy, and `Complete` marks neither "the only shard" nor "aggregate pushed down". It breaks `04038` and `04152`. `04665_remote_engine_settings_clause` asserted the empty result as expected. Its arms now assert `DistributedShardsSkipped`, so they still prove the storage-level setting is applied and survives a reattach. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115775&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115775](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115775+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add byte-weighted bytes_to_do and progress to system.mutations
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114678 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `system.mutations` now exposes byte-weighted mutation progress: `bytes_to_do` (the on-disk size of the data parts that still need to be mutated) and `progress` (an estimated finished fraction from 0 to 1, including the live fraction of the parts currently being rewritten). Part counts are a poor work proxy — parts are unequal in size and a regular merge can retire many pending parts at once — so the byte view is the honest one; the docs gain an "Estimating mutation progress" section with an equivalent parameterized-view recipe for older releases. Implements the conclusion of the research on the issue in two layers: **Columns** (`bytes_to_do` UInt64, `progress` Float64 in `system.mutations`): derived on read like `parts_to_do` — no persisted state, no replication protocol or znode format change. For plain `MergeTree` the sizes ride along the existing per-part scan in `getMutationsStatus`; for replicated tables the queue keeps returning name-only statuses under its state lock and the storage resolves sizes afterwards, so no parts lock is ever taken under the queue mutex (parts gone by then were retired and contribute nothing). The in-flight fraction comes from the merge list (`system.merges` rows with `is_mutation = 1`). Values are estimates by nature: a merge can retire pending parts at any moment, making `progress` jump forward. **Docs**: an "Estimating mutation progress" section on the `system.mutations` page explains why part-count percentages mislead and ships a parameterized-view recipe computing the same number on releases without the columns (the view was validated live against a running mutation, including a merge collapsing 9 pending parts mid-run), plus cross-links from `system.merges`, `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`, and the knowledge base. The stateless test asserts exact values on both engines: with merges stopped (which parks mutation tasks), `bytes_to_do` equals the active parts' total size and `progress` is 0; after completion the entry reports 0 and 1. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114850&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114850](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114850+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add support for S3Queue mode='exclusive'
signal.text: This patch adds a third mode to the S3Queue engine: `exclusive` mode turns off all file tracking and synchronization in ZooKeeper. S3 file processing will be tracked only locally via in-memory structures of this ClickHouse server process. This mode is meant to support high-throughput, high-volume ingestion scenarios. In our particular case, we have a minio instance on each of our ClickHouse nodes, with S3Queue pointing to 127.0.0.1. Exclusive mode allows ingesting many terabytes of data per day while avoid file framing boundary and buffering issues. (S3 multipart uploads solve the buffering issue for ingestion clients.) We have been running our ClickHouse cluster with these patches for many years with no issues. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adds support for mode='exclusive' in S3Queue engine, for high-throughput and self-hosted scenarios. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110552&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110552](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110552+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add the `logsql` dialect: LogsQL, the query language of VictoriaLogs
signal.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental `logsql` dialect: LogsQL, the log query language of VictoriaLogs, can now be used to query ClickHouse tables with logs. Enable it with `SET allow_experimental_logsql_dialect = 1, logsql_table = '<table>', dialect = 'logsql'` (plus `logsql_database`, `logsql_time_column`, and `logsql_message_column` as needed). LogsQL queries are translated at parse time into ordinary `SELECT` queries, so text filters expect `String`-backed log columns, while the `math` pipe applies raw arithmetic and needs numeric operand columns (`String` field values are not coerced to numbers). Documentation entry for user-facing changes. - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Implementation notes: - Nearly the whole language is supported: the filters (words, phrases, prefixes, `field:value`, `:=`, `~`, comparisons, `range`, `in` with subqueries, `contains_any`/`contains_all` with subqueries, `seq`, `len_range`, `string_range`, `ipv4_range`, `ipv6_range`, `pattern_match*`, `contains_common_case`/`equals_common_case`, `json_array_contains_any`, `i()`, full `_time:` filters with `day_range`/`week_range`, `_stream:{...}` selectors), and the pipes `fields`, `delete`, `copy`, `rename`, `limit`, `offset`, `sort`/`first`/`last` (including `rank` and `partition by`), `stats` (with `by`-buckets, per-function `if`, `switch`, `rate`), `where`, `uniq`, `top`, `math`, `extract`, `extract_regexp`, `format`, `unpack_json`, `unpack_logfmt`, `join`, `union`, `unroll`, `running_stats`, `total_stats`, `len`, `hash`, `coalesce`, `decolorize`, `split`, `unpack_words`, `time_add`, `sample`, `generate_sequence`, `field_values`, `json_array_len`, `json_array_concat`, `replace`, `replace_regexp`, `pack_json`, `pack_logfmt`. On typed (non-`String`) columns, filters that emit string functions fail with a type error instead of applying VictoriaLogs' schemaless per-value matching. The numeric stats functions (`sum`, `avg`, `median`, `quantile`, `stddev`, `rate_sum`) parse the numeric value out of every field value and skip the values that are not numbers, like VictoriaLogs, which computes its stats in `float64`; a numeric column is therefore aggregated with `Float64` precision and not exactly. - The dialect is modeled on the existing `kusto`/`prql`/`promql`/`polyglot` dialects: a parser under `src/Parsers/LogsQL/` builds a ClickHouse `ASTSelectQuery` directly, so all downstream machinery (analyzer, distributed queries, query log) works as usual. Relational pipes map to real SQL constructs: `join` to `LEFT`/`INNER JOIN ... USING`, `union` to `UNION ALL`, `running_stats`/`total_stats` and the `rank`/`partition by` clauses to window functions. - The lexer and the grammar mirror the reference implementation in VictoriaLogs (`lib/logstorage` of `VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaLogs`, Apache 2.0), including Go-style string literals, compound tokens (`foo-bar.com:123/x`), comments with `#`, and the exact filter/pipe syntax. The test queries are reused from the VictoriaLogs parser tests: 675 of its 878 valid parser-test queries run end-to-end against a ClickHouse table, and 605 of its 612 invalid queries are rejected. - The implicit table is configured by the `logsql_database`/`logsql_table` settings (like `promql_database`/`promql_table`). The special fields `_time` and `_msg` are mapped to columns via `logsql_time_column`/`logsql_message_column`, so real tables (e.g. `system.text_log` with `event_time`/`message`) can be queried after setting those. - Word and phrase filters translate to `hasToken`/`match` with token boundaries, so tables with `tokenbf_v1` indexes on the message column benefit from index analysis. - Documented deviations from VictoriaLogs: word boundaries follow ClickHouse tokenization (ASCII alphanumerics; VictoriaLogs also treats `_` and non-ASCII letters as word characters); numeric comparison filters parse `String` field values per row (rows with non-numeric values do not match) and compare typed numeric columns exactly, but the per-row parsing of field values understands plain numeric text only (decimal integers, floats, scientific notation, `inf`/`nan`) - LogsQL-only spellings such as `10KiB`, `1h`, `0x10`, or `1_000` are supported in query literals but are treated as non-numeric when stored in a field value, whereas VictoriaLogs parses them there too; equality with a non-numeric value compares with the native column type instead of VictoriaLogs' string semantics; `count(field)` counts non-NULL values instead of non-empty strings; `pattern_match*` placeholders are approximated with regular expressions (VictoriaLogs uses a greedy matcher with extra boundary rules); `seq()` matches substrings in order without word-boundary checks. - The only constructs that remain `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` (with clear errors naming the construct) are the ones with no ClickHouse meaning: VictoriaLogs storage introspection (`block_stats`, `blocks_count`, `query_stats`, `value_type`, `histogram` buckets, `set_stream_fields`, `stream_context`), features that require the dynamic set of fields of a schemaless store (`facets`, `field_names`, wildcard field selectors like `foo*:filter`, stats over all fields like `sum(*)`, `unpack_json` without a `fields` list), `unpack_syslog` (a stateful wall-clock-dependent parser), and `collapse_nums` (its number-boundary rules require lookaround which RE2 lacks). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113207&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113207](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113207+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Lower PromQL predict_linear and honour stale markers in selectors
signal.text: Adds native lowering for PromQL regression and extrapolated range functions over ClickHouse `TimeSeries` data. The implementation lowers `predict_linear` through the ClickHouse time-series linear-regression aggregates, and additionally tightens PromQL selector parsing, `@`-modifier handling, and Prometheus stale-marker filtering for the range functions. Note: `increase` and `deriv` lowering landed on `master` independently - `increase` as `timeSeriesIncreaseToGrid` (which handles counter resets in the aggregate itself) and `deriv` together with a fix that scales the regression slope by the timestamp tick resolution inside `timeSeriesDerivToGrid`. When updating this branch both were resolved in favor of the `master` implementation: the local `rate`-scaled-by-range post-processing for `increase` and the per-second rescaling of `deriv` were dropped. Because `timeSeriesDerivToGrid` now returns a per-second slope, the dynamic (non-constant) `predict_linear` offset no longer converts the slope to timestamp ticks either. Split out from the integration draft #104271; shared base #104484. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added native PromQL-to-SQL lowering for `predict_linear` over ClickHouse `TimeSeries` data, and made instant selectors honour Prometheus stale markers. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=104495&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/104495](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F104495+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject a subcolumn as a UNIQUE KEY element
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114470 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114470 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `CREATE TABLE` accepting a subcolumn as a `UNIQUE KEY` element, of either a user column (for example `` UNIQUE KEY (`c.null`) ``) or a virtual one (`` UNIQUE KEY (`_partition_value.1`) ``), which produced a table that could never be inserted into, failing every `INSERT` with `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`. Such a definition is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. Closes #114470. ### Description A backticked subcolumn name parses as a single identifier, so the existing `UNIQUE KEY` DDL guard accepted it. It asks `ColumnsDescription::has`, which searches only the top-level column index, while subcolumns live in a separate one; and its fallback failed, since `getKeyFromAST` does resolve a subcolumn name. The table could then be read and dropped but never written to. The same mistake exists one level over, in the virtuals index: its lookup is exact-name, so `` `_partition_value.1` `` misses there too, while the subcolumn index only holds subcolumns of user columns. That form is reachable from any table with a `PARTITION BY`. The fix adds two predicates beside the existing virtual-column and ALIAS/EPHEMERAL checks, each asking the index that actually holds the thing. Both derive from the type's own serialization rather than a list of names, so they cover every family: I measured 13 reachable user-column ones against the report's five, and 5 virtual ones, all on `_partition_value`, the only virtual with a composite type. Both are gated on fresh definitions (`CREATE`, and full-definition `ATTACH`, which is CREATE-like user input). `UNIQUE KEY` shipped in 26.5 and this guard reached no released branch, so such tables already exist; ungated they would fail to attach and become impossible to drop. Verified with two binaries per predicate: a table from a pre-fix binary still attaches and drops under the fixed one, and with the gate removed it fails to load. The leading `has(name)` term is load-bearing and has coverage: a stored column may be named after another column's (or a virtual's) subcolumn, and a flattened `Nested` member is itself a stored column named `n.x`. All stay accepted, with an `INSERT`. For a `JSON` parent, `` `c.a` `` was already rejected and is now rejected earlier. No setting is added and no default changed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115854&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115854](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115854+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add `/dialect`, `/lang`, `/language` client commands
signal.text: Adds client-side `/dialect`, `/lang` and `/language` commands - an equivalent of `SET dialect = '...'` that is handled before parsing, so it also works when the current dialect cannot express a `SET` query (for example, to leave `kusto` or `promql`). The active non-default dialect is shown in the prompt, and a plain `SET dialect = '...'` keeps the prompt in sync. Implementation notes: - The prompt is rendered by `getPrompt` on every line from a template that keeps the `{display_name}` placeholder: the current dialect is appended to the display name in parentheses (with a separating space if the display name is non-empty), and the `:) ` smiley is appended at the end, preserving the previous behavior for the default dialect. A custom prompt without `{display_name}` gets the dialect appended at its end. - The command is interactive-only, and works in `clickhouse-client`, `clickhouse-local`, and the embedded client (SSH/web terminal). A noninteractive script is parsed as SQL from end to end, and the dialect for it is selected with the `--dialect` option or with a `SET dialect = ...` statement, as before. - A plain SQL `SET` query is now an escape hatch out of every non-ClickHouse dialect, not only out of `clickhouse_json`. It is recognized by actually parsing it with `ParserSetQuery` rather than by looking at the first token, so a valid query of the current dialect that merely starts with the word `set` (a PromQL metric named `set`) is not hijacked. - Crossing the `kusto` dialect clears the thread-local KQL `let` bindings, which the Kusto parser normally does and which the `SET` escape bypasses. - Documentation: a new "Switching the SQL dialect" section on the client page. - Test: `04892_client_dialect_command.expect`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the interactive client commands `/dialect`, `/lang`, and `/language` to `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local`, so you can switch the active SQL dialect before parsing - it also works when the current dialect cannot express a `SET` query, for example to leave `kusto` or `promql`. The current non-default dialect is now shown in the prompt, and a plain `SET dialect = ...` keeps the prompt in sync. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114568&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114568](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114568+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/metadata
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Adds Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` support for `TimeSeries` tables.** ### Description This adds the Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` endpoint backed by the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table. The endpoint returns the metric type, help text, and unit for each metadata object in the format expected by Prometheus-compatible clients. ### Why this matters - **Prometheus-compatible tools** use `/api/v1/metadata` to discover **metric types, help text, and units**. - Without this endpoint, clients need separate configuration or lose this metadata when using ClickHouse as a Prometheus-compatible endpoint. - The `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table remains the **source of truth** for this metadata. Supported parameters: - `metric` filters the response to one metric family. - `limit` limits the number of metric families. `limit=0` returns no families. - `limit_per_metric` limits the number of unique metadata objects returned for each family. Zero and negative values mean no per-family limit. Other details: - Metadata objects are unique for each metric family and returned in a stable order. - `FINAL` is used whenever the Metrics target supports it, including wrapped targets. If a remote replica rejects `FINAL` before response output starts, the metadata query retries without it. - Metadata parameters stay endpoint-local and are not treated as ClickHouse settings. - The generated query uses the normal query pipeline and is recorded in `query_log`. - Access to the configured `TimeSeries` table and related table functions is checked. - The endpoint works with dedicated handlers and the combined `/api/v1` handler. - TimeSeries target reads carry the original user and exact active-role snapshot across shards, even when `push_external_roles_in_interserver_queries=0`. - Authenticated target scopes always contain fully qualified physical `{database, table}` names. A missing database on a Distributed target is resolved before authentication, and empty or malformed scopes are rejected. - `StorageTimeSeriesTargetProxy` keeps transaction, streaming, and MergeTree capabilities visible to the planner. Planner checks also unwrap proxies so Distributed shard pruning and parallel-replica analysis continue to work. - `StorageTableProxy` remains transparent for table-function INSERT validation. Forwarding proxies are still rejected, and Buffer target-function writes fail explicitly because their destination would require separate write authorization. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - unique metadata across multiple parts and stable results after `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`. - JSON escaping for quotes, backslashes, newlines, tabs, and Unicode. - metric filtering, both limit parameters, invalid limit values, and high-cardinality metadata. - primary-key filtering, aliases, `prefer_column_name_to_alias`, and wrapped `FINAL` targets. - query logging, endpoint and table-function access control, and unknown endpoint handling. - fully qualified target scopes and role propagation with both values of `push_external_roles_in_interserver_queries`. - lazy table proxies and the explicit Buffer target-function INSERT error. - GET/HEAD, unsupported methods, dedicated handlers, and the combined `/api/v1` handler. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Documentation was added to the Prometheus protocols page. signal.title: Fix S3Queue shutdown hanging on a streaming pipeline stuck inside a blocking call
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103126 ## Problem `S3Queue`/`AzureQueue` shutdown blocks for as long as an in-flight streaming pipeline stays stuck inside a blocking call — a stalled object storage read, a mutex convoy on the shared file iterator, or an executor thread parked in `epoll_wait`. Consequences observed in production (a pipeline wedged for two hours): - A synchronous `DROP TABLE` on the queue table hangs, and everything serialized behind it hangs too. - Plain server shutdown / `DETACH TABLE` hangs the same way. Independently, the periodic metadata cleanup deletes `processing/` znodes and bucket locks older than `persistent_processing_node_ttl_seconds` (default 3600) by mtime alone, even while the owning streaming execution is still running in the same process. The execution's commit then fails with `Coordination::Exception: Transaction failed ... (No node)`, and the freed bucket lock can be acquired by another server concurrently (Ordered-mode correctness violation). ## Root cause `StorageObjectStorageQueue::shutdown` sets `shutdown_called` and calls `task->deactivate()`, which blocks until the in-flight `streamToViews` returns. The streaming pipeline runs `CompletedPipelineExecutor::execute` with no cancel callback, so all shutdown handling is cooperative at chunk boundaries inside `ObjectStorageQueueSource::generateImpl` (what #103126 merged). A pipeline parked inside a blocking call never reaches a chunk boundary, so shutdown blocks unboundedly. The cleanup TTL (`ObjectStorageQueueMetadata::cleanupPersistentProcessingNodes`) is meant to reap nodes orphaned by dead servers, but it has no notion of ownership: a node whose owner is alive in this very process is deleted just the same once its mtime passes the TTL. ## Background: why #103126's first draft dropped executor-level cancellation, and why it is safe now The first draft of #103126 used exactly this approach (`setCancelCallback` in `streamToViews`), and the review rejected it — not as wrong in principle, but because two correctness gaps had no answer at the time: 1. **Silent success after cancel → data loss** ([review comment](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103126#discussion_r3193288074): "reading is safe, but AFAICS writing the data is not"). `executor->cancel()` can land after the source finished reading but before the sink finalized; `CompletedPipelineExecutor::execute` then returns without an exception, and `commit(insert_succeeded=true)` marks files `Processed` whose rows were never written. 2. **Forced failed-commit → duplicate inserts.** The draft's counter-measures ("skip commit when `shutdown_called`", then a `cancel_was_triggered` flag) were each found racy ([1](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103126#discussion_r3195586146), [2](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103126#discussion_r3196025042)): a cancel landing between files forces an already-fully-`Processed` batch into the failed-commit path, so those files are reset and re-read — duplicating rows when deduplication is off. Two more factors sealed it: Kafka's identical fix (#100388, `setCancelCallback` + skip offset commits on cancel) had been reverted 18 days earlier (#101646) after making `test_kafka_commit_on_block_write` flaky, and the [proposed alternative](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103126#discussion_r3193311270) — a chunk-boundary throw inside `generateImpl`, where per-file state is precisely known — was much smaller to review. That is what merged. It solves "shutdown waits for the in-flight file to reach EOF" (minutes), but not "the pipeline never reaches a chunk boundary at all" (hours, this PR's production case). Both gaps are closed here, on top of the machinery the merged #103126 itself introduced: - Gap 1: when the cancel callback has fired, `streamToViews` **always** throws instead of committing success — the silent-success path no longer exists. - Gap 2: the cancel gate requires `table_is_being_dropped || is_deduplication_v2`, so a forced retry is either moot (drop — no retry) or absorbed by deduplication; the worst case is an extra read of the file, which the #103126 review itself deemed acceptable ([comment](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103126#discussion_r3213509835)). The failure direction also flips: the draft's races erred toward *not committing what was written* (loss), this PR's over-triggering errs toward *reset-for-retry under dedup* (at most a re-read). - The Kafka precedent does not transfer: Kafka's offset semantics have no deduplication, so cancellation must choose between loss and duplication; `S3Queue` since 26.2 has `deduplication_v2`, plus the `Cancelled`-not-`Failed` file state machine that the merged #103126 built — the very foundation that makes executor-level cancellation safe now. ## Solution 1. `streamToViews` installs `CompletedPipelineExecutor::setCancelCallback` (1 s poll), gated exactly like the chunk-boundary abort: `shutdown_called && (table_is_being_dropped || is_deduplication_v2)`. Without deduplication, a mid-file abort would duplicate already-inserted rows on retry, so dedup-off plain shutdown keeps processing the in-flight file to EOF, as before. `executor->cancel()` cancels the processors and wakes the polling queue, and the in-flight file lands in `Cancelled` state (reset for retry, not `Failed`) through the existing machinery. A cancelled pipeline that finishes without an exception is routed through the failed-commit path instead of being committed as successful, because the sink may not have finalized. **Scope of the cancellation.** `executor->cancel()` wakes the executor's own waits directly: `PollingQueue::finish` writes the self-pipe the driver thread sleeps on — which is exactly the shape of the two-hour production hang (the driver parked in `epoll_wait` with no worker running or blocked, frame-proven from `trace_log`). A worker inside a blocking storage call is not preempted; that call stays bounded by the client's per-socket-operation timeouts, and cancellation takes effect at the first check after it returns — what this PR removes is the previously unbounded continue-to-EOF/next-files work after that point. A blocking call that never returns (e.g. a dead connection outliving every socket timeout) needs an end-to-end per-request deadline; that is deliberately out of scope here and tracked as a follow-up. 2. Local executions register their node paths in a new `ObjectStorageQueueLocalActiveNodes` registry *before* creating them in Keeper (`trySetProcessing`, `prepareSetProcessingRequests`, bucket acquisition), backing off when registration is refused; the cleanup wraps its revalidate-and-remove window in a try-only removal lock that fails while the path is registered. Registration and the removal lock exclude each other under one mutex, so the cleanup can never delete a node owned by a live local execution, in any interleaving — the register-before-create ordering matters because a node deleted and recreated between the cleanup's revalidation read and its remove restarts at Keeper version 0, so no captured version can guard the removal; a recreated node is additionally recognized by its fresh mtime on the revalidation read. The registry is shared between sibling tables on the same keeper path, because `ObjectStorageQueueMetadataFactory` shares the whole `ObjectStorageQueueMetadata` object per `{zookeeper_name, zookeeper_path}`. Another server's cleanup can still delete a >TTL node of a live remote execution — inherent to the mtime-TTL design and unchanged here. Regression tests: a new `object_storage_queue_park_in_generate` failpoint parks a source mid-file until pipeline cancellation or failpoint disable; integration tests cover `DROP TABLE` with a stuck pipeline, both clauses of the cancel gate (`DETACH` with dedup on/off), live-node survival across TTL cleanup runs, and recreation inside the cleanup's collection-to-removal window (via a pauseable failpoint); a gtest pins the registry fencing protocol. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `S3Queue`/`AzureQueue` shutdown and `DROP TABLE` hanging for as long as a streaming pipeline stayed stuck inside a blocking call. Also fix the periodic metadata cleanup deleting the processing nodes and bucket locks of executions still running on the same server, which made their commits fail once `persistent_processing_node_ttl_seconds` elapsed. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110230&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110230](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110230+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
