signal.title: Do not overwrite files on S3Queue move destination collision
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114847 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed silent data loss in S3Queue/AzureQueue `after_processing = 'move'`: with the default `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 0`, objects sharing a basename under different prefixes mapped to the same destination key, so the second move overwrote the first object's data and then deleted its own source. Colliding objects are now left in place with an error logged; the destination guard is enforced by the object storage itself, so concurrent movers cannot both overwrite. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The move is copy-then-delete per object, and an S3/Azure overwrite is not an error, so the collision destroyed one file's bytes with no exception, no log line, and `ObjectStorageQueueMovedObjects` counting both moves as successful. The fix detects collisions at two levels and, on collision, refuses the move: the object stays at the source (it is already recorded as processed, so it is simply retained in the bucket for the operator), an error is logged, and the new `ObjectStorageQueueMoveCollisions` profile event is incremented. * **Within a processing batch** (all storages, no extra requests): destinations are computed up front and deduplicated; only the first object mapping to a given key is moved. * **Everywhere else — across batches, replicas and concurrent movers**: the copy itself carries a destination precondition (`If-None-Match: *`), so the storage refuses it rather than overwriting. This is applied on all three move paths (same-bucket, cross-bucket S3, cross-container Azure) whenever `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 0`; preserved paths cannot collide, so they are unconditional as before. It costs no extra request: the precondition rides on the request that makes the object visible. Because the guard is enforced by the storage rather than by a preflight check, there is no check-then-copy window: of two movers racing for the same destination exactly one wins, and the loser keeps its source. A rejected copy is reported as a collision (logged, counted by `ObjectStorageQueueMoveCollisions`) and never followed by the source deletion. To carry the precondition, `copyS3File`/`copyDataToS3File` and `copyAzureBlobStorageFile`/`copyDataToAzureBlobStorageFile` take an optional destination `If-None-Match`, set on the request that commits the object (`PutObject` / `CopyObject` / `CompleteMultipartUpload`, and `Upload` / `CommitBlockList` / `CopyFromUri` / `StartCopyFromUri`). The parameter defaults to "no precondition", so every existing caller is unchanged. `S3ObjectStorage::copyObject` now forwards its `WriteSettings`, which it previously discarded, so `object_storage_write_if_none_match` reaches the copy. The copy is no longer re-executed by the retry loop once it has succeeded, so a failure while removing the source cannot make the retry collide with the object this move just wrote. Setting `after_processing_move_preserve_path = 1` remains the recommended configuration when same-basename objects are possible, and the `after_processing_move_preserve_path` setting description now documents the collision behavior. Integration tests: one ingests `data/a/part.csv` and `data/b/part.csv` and asserts both survive (one archived, one left at the source, all rows still readable); another pre-creates the destination object and processes a single file, which the in-batch deduplication cannot catch, asserting for both `S3Queue` and `AzureQueue` that the source survives and the pre-existing destination bytes are untouched. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115724&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115724](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115724+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

A cheaper triage model checks the pull request first and can update it to the latest base branch or perform a clean base-branch merge. signal.title: Support quoted PromQL grouping labels
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Support quoted label names in PromQL grouping modifiers.** ### Summary Prometheus accepts quoted label names in grouping modifiers. ClickHouse previously only accepted identifier-style tokens there. Prometheus 3.x supports UTF-8 label names, and OpenTelemetry uses dotted resource attributes such as `service.name`, `deployment.environment`, and `k8s.namespace.name`. When a PromQL backend preserves these names, grouping queries need the quoted form. This comes up with OpenTelemetry-aware dashboards and backends that keep the original label names instead of converting dots to underscores. Examples: - `sum by ("service.name", "k8s.namespace.name") (http_requests_total)` - `max without ("deployment.environment") (http_request_duration_seconds)` - `http_requests_total + on ("service.name") group_left ("pod.name") target_info` - `http_requests_total / ignoring ("cluster.name") group_right ("instance.name") target_info` ### Changes - **Allow:** quoted strings in `by`, `without`, `on`, `ignoring`, `group_left`, and `group_right` lists. - **Unquote:** and validate the names before passing them to the PromQL tree. - Quote non-legacy names again when serializing the tree back to PromQL. - **Use:** PromQL-specific escaping for serialized strings, including control bytes. ### Tests - **Generated artifacts:** ANTLR output from the grammar. - **Coverage:** `gtest_PromQLParser` coverage. - **Coverage:** realistic quoted-label queries to `04131_prometheus_query_parser`. - **Coverage:** invalid empty quoted-label coverage. - **Coverage:** parse/serialization/parse round-trip coverage for an escaped NUL label. References: - [Prometheus UTF-8 in Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/guides/utf8/) - [Using Prometheus as your OpenTelemetry backend](https://prometheus.io/docs/guides/opentelemetry/) - [Prometheus query language parser](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tree/main/promql/parser) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114545&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114545](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114545+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Optimization of `GROUP BY` in the presence of `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Optimize `GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT` and `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` queries by maintaining a bounded heap during aggregation to prune groups that cannot appear in the result, significantly reducing memory usage and execution time for high-cardinality grouping. Controlled by the `enable_group_by_top_k_optimization` setting. Based on the initial implementation by [Dmitriy Terenichev](https://github.com/Dmitry909) ([#78553](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/78553)). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/72610 Query shapes that benefit from this optimization: - `SELECT key, agg() FROM t GROUP BY key ORDER BY key ASC LIMIT N` -- single key, full ORDER BY match - `SELECT key, agg() FROM t GROUP BY key LIMIT N` -- single key, no ORDER BY - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 ORDER BY k1, k2 ASC LIMIT N` -- composite keys, full ORDER BY match - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1, k2, k3 ASC LIMIT N` -- 3+ keys, full match - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 ORDER BY k1 ASC LIMIT N` -- composite keys, ORDER BY is a prefix of GROUP BY - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1 ASC LIMIT N` -- prefix 1 of 3 - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1, k2 ASC LIMIT N` -- prefix 2 of 3 - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 LIMIT N` -- composite keys, no ORDER BY - `SELECT URL, count() FROM t GROUP BY URL ORDER BY URL ASC LIMIT N` -- String keys - `SELECT URL, count() FROM t GROUP BY URL LIMIT N` -- String keys, no ORDER BY Not supported (optimization is skipped): - `ORDER BY agg()` (ORDER BY aggregate function, not a GROUP BY key) (handled by [another PR](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/98607)) - `WITH TOTALS`, `HAVING`, `GROUPING SETS`, `CUBE`, `ROLLUP` - `LIMIT WITH TIES` - ~~Non-final aggregation (distributed partial aggregation)~~ - `max_rows_to_group_by` is set - `rows_before_limit_at_least` mode (exact count) - a COLLATE on any of the matched GROUP BY keys (a COLLATE on a later ORDER BY column past the full key prefix cannot affect which groups qualify and does not disable the optimization) - ORDER BY columns that are not a leading prefix of GROUP BY keys <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=96630&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/96630](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F96630+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Native Google Cloud Storage integration (google-cloud-cpp)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental native Google Cloud Storage integration built on the Google Cloud C++ SDK (`google-cloud-cpp`, the GCS JSON API), as an alternative to the existing S3-compatibility path. Enable it with the new `use_native_gcs` setting for the `gcs` table function and dynamic `disk(...)` definitions, or configure a MergeTree storage disk with `object_storage_type: gcs`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes Documented in `docs/reference/functions/table-functions/gcs.mdx` (new "Native GCS integration" section). --- ## Description ClickHouse currently talks to GCS **only through its S3-compatible XML API** (the AWS SDK against a `storage.googleapis.com` endpoint, plus a cluster of GCS quirk-toggles in the S3 client). This PR adds a first-class native backend on top of the already-vendored `google-cloud-cpp` storage client. **Opt-in, non-breaking.** The `gcs()` table function and dynamic disks select the native backend only with the new experimental `use_native_gcs` setting (default `false`); otherwise they retain S3 compatibility and HMAC keys. `ENGINE = GCS` remains on the existing compatibility path. ### What's added - `ObjectStorageType::GCS` + `GCSObjectStorage : IObjectStorage` (`src/Disks/DiskObjectStorage/ObjectStorages/GCS/`), with `ReadBufferFromGCS`/`WriteBufferFromGCS` over the SDK's `ObjectReadStream`/`ObjectWriteStream` (ranged seeks, resumable uploads), native listing, `RewriteObject`-based copy, `DeleteObject`, `GetObjectMetadata`. - Registered as the `gcs` object-storage type + a `gcs` disk-type alias, so MergeTree data can live natively on GCS (`type: object_storage, object_storage_type: gcs`). - `StorageGCSConfiguration` (reuses `StorageS3Configuration`'s argument parsing) and a `TableFunctionGCS` selector that picks native vs S3-compat by the `use_native_gcs` setting. - Auth mirrors the compat surface on the native side: Application Default Credentials, service-account JSON, the `google_adc_*` OAuth refresh-token flow (reusing `IO/GCPOAuth`), anonymous / `NOSIGN`, and a REST endpoint override for the GCS emulator. - `USE_GOOGLE_CLOUD` is now exposed in `system.build_options`. ### Testing - Every changed/new translation unit compiles against the real headers and the vendored SDK (`USE_GOOGLE_CLOUD=1`, `USE_AWS_S3=1`). - Unit test for endpoint parsing (`gtest_gcs_endpoint`). - Stateless test for the setting wiring (`04502_use_native_gcs_setting`). - Integration test `test_native_gcs` runs against a `fake-gcs-server` emulator (a new `with_gcs` helper in `cluster.py`): `gcs()` INSERT/SELECT + glob with `use_native_gcs=1`, and a MergeTree-on-GCS-disk round trip. Note: `fake-gcs-server` speaks the GCS API (unlike minio, which is S3-only). The module is skipped on builds without the SDK. ### Known follow-ups - `GCSObjectStorage::iterate()` currently materializes the full listing (a lazy paginating iterator like S3's is a future optimization). - The `google_adc_*` refresh-token access token is minted eagerly (no auto-refresh yet for long-lived disks). - `readSmallObjectAndGetObjectMetadata` uses the base default (relevant only for a future native Iceberg-over-GCS path, which is not wired here). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109455&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109455](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109455+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Require forward progress when counting rows in Avro, MsgPack and ProtobufList
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115437 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115437 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `SELECT count()` never terminating, or returning an invented row count, on a corrupted `Avro`, `MsgPack` or `ProtobufList` file. The `optimize_count_from_files` fast path counted rows without requiring the read position to advance, so a two byte `ProtobufList` file produced billions of rows and never returned. Such input is now rejected with the same error the ordinary read path gives. ### Description Reported by @ PedroTadim, who [offered to review](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115437#issuecomment-5341268327); [I took it](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115437#issuecomment-5369600816). `IRowInputFormat::read()` re-enters `countRows()` until it returns 0, so a `countRows()` that reports a row without consuming input never terminates. Three formats could, at two layers: - **ProtobufList** discarded `readFieldNumber`'s result, which is false *without consuming* once the envelope message ends, while `reader->eof()` only reports the underlying buffer. Now honoured, throwing the read path's own `PROTOBUF_BAD_CAST` at the same guard. - **MsgPack** treated `parse_helper::execute`'s `parse_return` **enum** as a bool, so `PARSE_PARSE_ERROR (-1)` left the loop as if it had succeeded, offset unadvanced. Each status is now handled; the read path is unaffected (details below). `countRows` also discarded `readObject`'s result, counting a partial row as complete when the object count is not a multiple of the column count; it now raises the read path's own "Not enough values to complete the row". - **Avro** takes its row count from the block header, so counting without decoding the payload cannot tell a count that is present from one merely claimed. `supportsCountRows()` is therefore false and the dead `countRows()` removed, so count queries take the read path, which already rejects these inputs. Cost on 3M rows / 32MB: 0.109s to 0.136s. Beyond the report: a header declaring 10^9 rows returned `1000005000` rows from a 10KB file **as a successful answer** rather than a hang, so nothing alerted the user. Out of scope: a zero width Avro schema (only a NULL column) with a **negative** count hangs the ordinary read path too. No ClickHouse side change reaches it -- `hasMore()`/`decr()` live in `contrib/avro`, driven by `readRow` and the Iceberg manifest deserializer as well. That needs a `ClickHouse/avro` change first, where I have no write access; the patch is ready and I will follow up. <details><summary>Sibling coverage, refuted alternatives and validation</summary> MsgPack read path: `parse_error` throws before `execute()` can return `-1`, and no `MsgPackVisitor` method returns `false`, so neither error status is reachable with that visitor. Verified by measurement. Two simpler designs are refuted by measurement. A bound on the declared count by input size fails because valid Avro holds 1000 rows in 139 bytes (all NULL column) and 200000 in 797 bytes (deflate). A central guard in `IRowInputFormat::read()` fails because `Npy` and `RawBLOB` legitimately return rows consuming zero bytes. Both cases are test arms, so neither can be reintroduced silently. Also out of scope: a zero width schema declaring 10^9 rows still reports them, but the read path now agrees, so the file is self consistent rather than misreported. All 15 remaining `countRows()` implementations were swept empirically, 17 formats x 6 adversarial inputs: only the three reported formats hung, and none does now. The same sweep prints a hang on unpatched master, so it can see what it reports absent. `CapnProto`, `MySQLDump` and `RowInputFormatWithNamesAndTypes` look similar when read but consume or throw on every input tested. `Npy` and `RawBLOB` legitimately return rows consuming zero bytes and must not be guarded. Read path identity: 17 order independent oracles (`count()` plus `sum(cityHash64(...))`, sorted rows, `DESCRIBE`) at `max_block_size` 1 / 7 / 13 / 1000 / 65505, all identical before and after; 13 of 13 deliberate mutations detected, so the comparison is not blind. New test `04946_count_from_files_forward_progress.sh` asserts the error code on a bounded run, never elapsed time. signal.title: Push down string filters from PREWHERE into the scan
signal.text: Implements pushing down of string filtering into the scan phase. When a query has a substring search condition on a `String` (or `Nullable(String)`) column in `PREWHERE` (`LIKE`, `position`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, or equality with a non-empty string), and this condition does not match an empty string, the filter is pushed down into the column deserialization: every value is checked against the filter, and if it does not match, the value is read as an empty string, without copying its data into the column. This makes reading faster and lowers memory usage when the condition is selective. The result of the query does not change, because the condition is a conjunct of `PREWHERE`, which is guaranteed to filter out the rows with non-matching values, and because such conditions never match an empty string, so even a kept `PREWHERE` column is bit-identical. The optimization works for reading from `MergeTree` and from `Parquet`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added setting `apply_string_filters_during_scan` (disabled by default): substring search conditions on `String` columns (`LIKE`, `position`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`) from `PREWHERE` are pushed down into the column scan, and non-matching values are read as empty strings without copying their data. Works for reading from `MergeTree` and from the `Parquet` format. ### Implementation details - `StringValueFilter` (`src/Common/`) holds the extracted conditions (substring / prefix / suffix / equality, all with non-empty needles, so that an empty string never matches) and checks values with a bounds-safe substring searcher. A single filter object is shared by all readers of a column within one query and disables itself adaptively when the observed fraction of matching values makes the check unprofitable (more than half of the values match). - `extractStringValueFilters` (`src/Interpreters/`) walks the top-level `AND` chain of the `PREWHERE` actions and extracts filters from `like` (with fixed substrings parsed out of the pattern, honoring escaping), `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `equals` with a non-empty string, bare `position`, and comparisons of `position` with a constant that reject the zero result (e.g. `position(s, 'x') > 0`, `position(s, 'x') = 5`, but not `position(s, 'x') = 0`). - `MergeTree`: the filters are attached to `MergeTreeReaderSettings` in `ReadFromMergeTree::initializePipeline`, only when `prewhere_info->need_filter` is set (rows are guaranteed to be physically filtered). The readers apply a filter to a column only when it is a full `String`/`Nullable(String)` column with the plain serialization (not sparse), is not requested together with another column reading from the same storage column (e.g. the `.size` subcolumn, which could share deserialized data through caches), and is not overwritten by an on-fly mutation (`PREWHERE` is then evaluated on mutated values). Renamed columns are handled by keying the filter by the name in the part. Both string serialization versions are supported (`single_stream` and `with_size_stream`), for wide and compact parts. - `Parquet` (native reader): the filters are attached to the prewhere-step string leaves and applied in the plain and delta-length page decoders per value; for dictionary-encoded pages the filter is checked only once per dictionary entry, and the per-row gather materializes empty strings for non-matching entries. - New profile events: `StringValueFilterValuesChecked`, `StringValueFilterValuesReplaced`, `StringValueFilterBytesSkipped`. - The setting is added to the settings randomization in `clickhouse-test`. ### Testing - New stateless tests cover wide/compact parts, both string serialization versions, `Nullable(String)`, escaped `LIKE` patterns, conditions that must not be pushed down (`position(s, 'x') = 0`, `NOT`, `OR`, patterns matching an empty string), `AND` chains, multiple columns, and both Parquet page encodings; every query is checked with the setting enabled and disabled, plus profile events assert that the optimization actually fires. - All existing stateless tests matching `prewhere` were run locally with the setting forced on: the results are identical to the run with the setting disabled. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115848&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115848](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115848+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> ### ClickBench results Measured on the `hits` table (100M rows, 96-core aarch64, hot cache, interleaved A/B runs, query condition cache disabled to measure the scan itself). The affected queries are those with substring conditions (`URL LIKE '%google%'`, `Title LIKE '%Google%'`), written with explicit `PREWHERE`; the remaining 39 queries do not extract any filter and are unaffected. MergeTree (min of 5 runs): | Query | off, s | on, s | speedup | memory | |---|---|---|---|---| | Q20 `count() PREWHERE URL LIKE '%google%'` | 0.102 | 0.086 | 1.19× | −51% | | Q21 | 0.118 | 0.095 | 1.24× | −46% | | Q22 (`Title LIKE '%Google%'`) | 0.208 | 0.185 | 1.12× | −21% | | Q23 (`SELECT *`) | 0.134 | 0.116 | 1.16× | −59% | The filter replaces ~99.98M of 100M values and skips copying 8.4-8.8 GiB per query. The initial per-value implementation was 10-15% *slower* than the baseline on MergeTree (a substring search per short value loses to the baseline's bulk copy plus one bulk scan in `like`); the bulk-scan implementation (one scan per buffer of concatenated values) turned it into the win above. Parquet (`file('hits.parquet')`, same queries, quieter round): Q20 1.57×, Q21 1.18×, Q22 1.12×, Q23 ~1× (dominated by reading the other 100 columns). When the setting is enabled, the `WHERE` to `PREWHERE` optimization also moves suitable substring search conditions even when they use all queried columns (normally that is pointless, but with the string filter the scan itself becomes cheaper). This makes the official `WHERE`-form of Q20 use `PREWHERE` and the string filter as written: 1.25× faster (min of 5 runs, 0.119 s → 0.095 s) and −59% memory. Plain equality with a string constant is deliberately excluded from this relaxation: it is too common, and it would change the plans of too many queries where the primary key index does the job anyway. In Q23 the top-k dynamic filter occupies `PREWHERE` and the `LIKE` stays in `WHERE`, which is unaffected.

signal.title: Add SHARED REGEXP path placement policy to JSON
signal.text: Adds `SHARED REGEXP 'pattern'` to `JSON` type declarations so matching root-relative flattened paths are always stored in shared data instead of competing for dedicated dynamic-path subcolumns. This is useful for high-cardinality path families whose promotion would displace more useful paths. Matching is partial by default, like `SKIP REGEXP`. Set the persisted `JSON` type parameter `shared_regexp_use_partial_match=0` to require full-string matching. Typed paths take precedence over `SHARED REGEXP`; `SKIP` and `SKIP REGEXP` continue to discard matching data. Rules are evaluated against the complete path from the original `JSON` root, including derived sub-objects. The rules are compiled once into an immutable `RE2` matcher, with bounded rule count and pattern sizes. A single rule uses direct `RE2` matching and multiple rules use `RE2::Set`. `JSON` columns without rules keep a null matcher, their existing binary type encoding, and their existing row-placement path. Metadata snapshots are copied lazily only when retained placement provenance actually changes a type. Placement provenance is stored in part column metadata and retained by default through horizontal and vertical merges, wide and compact mutations, column renames, lightweight-update patch materialization, and `Array`/`Nullable`/`Tuple`/`Map` wrappers. Removing a rule therefore does not unexpectedly promote already-shared paths during a later rewrite. Set the `MergeTree` table setting `allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion=1` to opt into reconsidering those paths. Policy-only metadata changes inside `Variant` are documented as unsupported. The `Native` binary type encoding uses `JSON` encoding version 1 only when a policy is present; ordinary `JSON` types remain byte-identical version 0. The canonical `JSON` documentation and `Native` format specification are updated accordingly. Testing includes 18 focused unit tests and 9 stateless scenarios covering syntax, partial/full matching, root-relative sub-objects, all supported wrappers, flattened `Native` and `RowBinary` paths, horizontal/vertical merges, compact/wide mutations, renames, statistics, and both lightweight-patch application paths. An 88.6 MB real Elasticsearch `indices_stats` document produced 143,555 flattened paths; all 143,290 paths targeted by `^indices[.]` remained in shared data and none became dynamic. A one-run end-to-end smoke comparison was 1.66 s without the policy and 1.69 s with it, with a 0.055% max-RSS difference; these small differences are noise-level, not a statistical benchmark. **Scope note:** `SKIP`/`SKIP REGEXP` already applied inconsistently between array-shaped and object-shaped occurrences of the same path on `master`, independent of `SHARED REGEXP` (a path skipped when the value at that path is an object could still surface when the value is an array of objects). This PR's fix for `SKIP REGEXP` on dynamically inferred nested objects closes one instance of that inconsistency; the underlying array-vs-object gap predates this PR and is not otherwise addressed here. **Scope note:** for a value dynamically inferred as its own nested `JSON` object (an inconsistent-shape array/object under a dynamic path), a policy-only `ALTER` followed by a plain read correctly picks up the new `SHARED REGEXP`/`SKIP REGEXP` rules for that nested object. A `allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion=1` merge or mutation that rewrites such a part afterward does not: it reconstructs the nested object's dynamic-path structure from cached per-column type state that a policy change doesn't refresh, so paths inside it can still be placed according to the rule in effect when the object was first materialized. This is opt-in (`allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion` defaults to off) and not fixed by this PR. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `SHARED REGEXP` rules to the `JSON` data type to keep matching paths in shared data, with configurable full-string matching and explicit control over re-promoting paths after rules are removed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114414&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114414](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114414+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: JSON object traversal pays duplicate-key bookkeeping on every key of every object — a no-duplicate fast path removes it (json_type_parsing q3 +33%, 26.6 → 26.7, aarch64)
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the situation The JSON object-traversal loop in `src/Formats/JSONExtractTree.cpp` (`ObjectJSONNode::traverseAndInsert`) now spends a hash-map node, a nested `std::unordered_set` node and a duplicate `getJSONElementType()` call on **every key of every traversed object**, whether or not any key actually repeats. Duplicated keys inside one JSON object are rare, so for the common case this bookkeeping is provably dead work: a cheap single key-only probe per object ("does any key repeat at all?") makes the entire cost skippable with observably identical behaviour. A patch implementing that fast path is attached below; on the no-duplicate path it does strictly less work than both the current two-pass loop and the single-pass loop it replaced. The cost was found while investigating a CI dashboard step: `json_type_parsing` query 3 regressed by **+33.23%** (CI sweep step ratio **1.327**) between 26.6 and 26.7 on aarch64. Local confirmation on exact release binaries, paired interleaved A/B (client wall time), two independent sessions of 7 runs/side each: | Session | ratio (26.7 / 26.6) | bounds | median 26.6 | median 26.7 | randomization p | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | run-20260803-4cb7 | 1.2408151248527945 | [1.1495680928835508, 1.2580533451920255] | 0.53325925 s | 0.6623717499999999 s | 0.011655011655011656 | | run-20260803-34b6 | 1.2346288618234684 | [1.1209754845334359, 1.292740403757532] | 0.5427225 s | 0.67041575 s | 0.011655011655011656 | Combined significance across sessions p = 1.35e-03, direction stable. Server-side, the effect is pure CPU on the traversal path: - q3 `UserTimeMicroseconds`: 383649 → 509470 (**ratio 1.328**, delta 125821 µs); `query_duration_ms`: 390 → 516 (ratio 1.3231); client wall ratio 1.226. - Work counters are byte-identical between the binaries on q3: `SelectedRows` 100, `SelectedBytes` 24039500, `ReadBufferFromFileDescriptorReadBytes` 13044600, `IOBufferAllocBytes` 14093364, `FileOpen` 1, `ReadBufferFromFileDescriptorRead` 15, peak memory 28620878. Same work, more CPU. - q1 (same test, many-key file, dynamic paths disabled) `UserTimeMicroseconds`: 4369465 → 5976239 (ratio 1.3677). Mechanism localisation — the cost scales with the number of traversed object keys, not with input bytes: - Equal-byte-volume discriminator (~28 MB on both sides): 1000 keys per object → ratio **1.3514** [1.2685, 1.4378] (regression); 10 keys per object → ratio **0.968** [0.8434, 1.132] (no regression). A global binary slowdown cannot move two equal-byte workloads in opposite directions. - Certified controls (15 runs/side, equivalent within the ±0.05 practical band): pure-CPU long workload ratio 0.9959438444128179 [0.9828378461874818, 1.003067097796909]; reading the very same bytes as q3 but as `JSONAsString` (no object traversal) ratio 1.0102915052855355 [0.9809724047306175, 1.0428511875123037]. Stage-isolating probes: `LineAsString` 1.0248, `JSONAsString` 1.0065, pure CPU 0.9996. The culprit change rewrote the traversal into two passes: a new first pass building `key_element_types` (v26.7.1.1315-stable `src/Formats/JSONExtractTree.cpp:1952-2005`, declaration at `:1957`), plus the retained second pass with `visited_keys` at `:2010`, a duplicate `getJSONElementType` at `:2014`, and `key_element_types` lookups at `:2024` and `:2039`. All cited lines were independently re-verified at tag v26.7.1.1315-stable; the pre-PR parent had one loop with one `getJSONElementType` per key. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? - Measured: **v26.7.1.1315** regressed vs **v26.6.1.1193** (aarch64, official release binaries; binary sha256 attested in the investigation ledger). - The culprit PR was merged 2026-07-09 (merge commit `797a5a9e447305dd4d54f23f545a2d9c8266776b`); the CI series change point is 2026-07-09T22:54:43Z, so 26.7 and later. - Backport exposure: the PR carries `pr-must-backport` and `v26.2-must-backport`, and a bot comment confirms the fixed bug reproduces on 26.3/26.4/26.5/26.6 — so the fix, and this cost, are destined for those branches too. - x86_64 was not measured in this investigation; the mechanism (per-key hashing work) is not architecture-specific. ### How to reproduce Perf test `json_type_parsing`, query index 3. Setup (generates its own input under `user_files`; no CI dataset needed): ```sql INSERT INTO FUNCTION file(test_json_parsing_1.txt, Raw) SELECT toJSONString(arrayMap(x -> tuple('a' || x, multiIf(x % 6 == 0, x::UInt32, x % 6 == 1, x / 3.333333, x % 6 == 2, randomStringUTF8(16), x % 6 == 3, '2020-01-01', x % 6 == 4, '2020-01-01 10:00:00', '2020-01-01 10:00:00.000')), range(1000))::Map(String, Dynamic)) FROM numbers(10000) SETTINGS use_variant_as_common_type = 1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert = 1; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file(test_json_parsing_2.txt, Raw) SELECT toJSONString(arrayMap(x -> tuple('a' || x, [arrayMap(y -> tuple('b' || y, 'Data'), range(20))::Map(String, String)]), range(1000))::Map(String, Dynamic)) FROM numbers(50) SETTINGS use_variant_as_common_type = 1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert = 1; ``` Target query (q3): ```sql SELECT * FROM file(test_json_parsing_2.txt, JSONAsObject, 'json JSON(max_dynamic_paths=0)') FORMAT Null; ``` Compare 26.6.1.1193 vs 26.7.1.1315 with paired, strictly interleaved ABAB runs (we used 7 runs/side per session, two independent sessions with fresh server pairs and freshly generated input). The key-count discriminator, if you want the mechanism signature (equal bytes, opposite verdicts): ```sql -- many keys per object (regresses, ratio 1.3514) INSERT INTO FUNCTION file(disc_many.txt, Raw) SELECT toJSONString(arrayMap(x -> tuple('k' || x, 'abcd'), range(1000))::Map(String, String)) FROM numbers(2000) SETTINGS engine_file_truncate_on_insert = 1; -- few keys per object, same byte volume (does not regress, ratio 0.968) INSERT INTO FUNCTION file(disc_few.txt, Raw) SELECT toJSONString(arrayMap(x -> tuple('k' || x, repeat('a', 1400)), range(10))::Map(String, String)) FROM numbers(2000) SETTINGS engine_file_truncate_on_insert = 1; SELECT * FROM file(disc_many.txt, JSONAsObject, 'json JSON(max_dynamic_paths=0)') FORMAT Null; SELECT * FROM file(disc_few.txt, JSONAsObject, 'json JSON(max_dynamic_paths=0)') FORMAT Null; ``` ### Expected performance Parsing JSON objects that contain no duplicated keys — the overwhelmingly common case — should cost what it did in 26.6: on this workload, q3 at ~0.533 s client wall / 383649 µs user time rather than ~0.662 s / 509470 µs. When no key repeats, the duplicate-key bookkeeping cannot change the outcome (`visited_keys` can never report a repeat, `key_element_types[key].size() > 1` requires a repeated key, and every duplicate error/skip branch is unreachable), so it should not be paid. ### Related issues and pull requests - Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108218 ("Fix `type_json_allow_duplicated_key_with_literal_and_nested_object` not working with typed paths in JSON") - Related: query 0 of the same test (`test_json_parsing_1.txt` as plain `JSON`) also regressed in both local sessions (ratios 1.1598344332180672 and 1.157688931229005) although the CI sweep never flagged it; it is tracked as its own follow-up and not claimed here. ### Additional context **Culprit-PR intent.** PR #108218 is labelled `pr-bugfix`; its body and review discussion contain no performance statements, and its CI Performance Comparison summary was green. The measured cost is therefore undisclosed, not an intended trade-off — this issue asks to keep the bug fix and drop the constant overhead, not to revert the fix. **Proposed fix.** Probe each object once, keys only; take a fast path with zero duplicate bookkeeping when no key repeats, fall through to the current two-pass logic otherwise. The candidate improvement was measured only on two locally built binaries, so it is deliberately **not** established by this investigation (blocked at the exact-provenance gate until repeated on official builds); it is carried on a linked candidate-fix work item with its full validation bundle. The adversarial audit of the investigation confirmed the patch is one file, one hunk, purely additive (+41/−0), contains no numeric or string literals, nothing benchmark-shaped (its sole conditional keys on `!has_duplicated_key`, a universal JSON property), touches no tests or CI files, and that the culprit PR's own regression suite (`04331_*`) routes entirely through the untouched general path. Smoke on the patched build: 17/17 result-hash equality including five positive duplicate-key cases, plus 5/5 error parity on `INCORRECT_DATA`. <details> <summary>Proposed patch: skip per-key duplicate-key bookkeeping for objects with no repeated key (validated: improvement measured on locally built binaries only — G2-blocked pending official builds, not established by this report; smoke 17/17 result-hash equality + 5/5 error parity)</summary> ```diff --- a/src/Formats/JSONExtractTree.cpp +++ b/src/Formats/JSONExtractTree.cpp @@ -1949,6 +1949,47 @@ if (element.isObject() && (skip_typed_path_check || !typed_path_nodes.contains(current_path) || (format_settings.json.type_json_allow_duplicated_key_with_literal_and_nested_object && hasTypedPathWithPrefix(current_path + ".")))) { + /// Duplicated keys inside one JSON object are rare, but the bookkeeping required to + /// handle them is not free: the passes below spend a hash-map node, a nested + /// std::unordered_set node and a getJSONElementType() call on EVERY key of EVERY + /// object, whether or not any key repeats. That cost is paid per traversed key, so it + /// scales with the key count of the document and hurts wide/deeply nested JSON most. + /// + /// So first answer the much cheaper question "does this object have a duplicated key + /// at all?" with a single key-only probe (no element types, no per-key nested set). + /// When the answer is no, none of that bookkeeping can change the outcome: + /// - visited_keys can never report a repeat, so its inserts and lookups are dead; + /// - key_element_types[key].size() > 1 requires a repeated key, so skip_typed is + /// always false; + /// - every duplicate error/skip branch is unreachable. + /// The fast path below is therefore observably identical to the general path, and does + /// strictly less work than it (and than the single-pass version this replaced). + bool has_duplicated_key = false; + { + std::unordered_set<std::string_view> probed_keys; + for (auto [key, value] : element.getObject()) + { + (void)value; + if (!probed_keys.insert(key).second) + { + has_duplicated_key = true; + break; + } + } + } + + if (!has_duplicated_key) + { + for (auto [key, value] : element.getObject()) + { + String path = buildChildPath(current_path, key, insert_settings, is_root); + if (!traverseAndInsert(column_object, value, path, insert_settings, format_settings, paths_and_values_for_shared_data, current_size, error, false)) + return false; + } + + return true; + } + /// First pass: collect the set of distinct element types (LITERAL/OBJECT) per key. /// This lets us detect all duplicates upfront so we can: /// - throw errors immediately for invalid duplicates (before any data is inserted), ``` </details> **Caveats and disclosed limitations.** - All measurements are from a single dedicated aarch64 host (Linux VM); x86_64 is unmeasured. - Regression and mechanism numbers are from official release binaries (exact-release provenance, sha256-attested: 26.6.1.1193 `962fd0cc…`, 26.7.1.1315 `3057f9ff…`). Only the candidate-fix improvement involves locally built binaries, and it is explicitly not claimed here. - Unexplained observation, recorded but not claimed: `MemoryAllocatedWithoutCheckBytes` on q3 moved 183472 → 33738480 while the allocation count moved only 20 → 28; on the patched build both return to their 26.6-like values (183664 / 20). Eight extra large allocations cannot be one hash node per traversed key, so no per-key-allocation arithmetic is claimed from this counter.

signal.title: Support updating projection settings without forcing immediate re-materialization - ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY PROJECTION
signal.text: Support ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY PROJECTION <name> (<query>) WITH SETTINGS (...). Projection-level settings (index_granularity, index_granularity_bytes, and the other allow-listed settings) could previously be specified only at projection creation time via WITH SETTINGS but never modified. MODIFY PROJECTION is a metadata-only alter that replaces the stored projection settings in place: - Only the WITH SETTINGS clause may change: the projection query body must be identical to the existing definition otherwise the command is rejected with BAD_ARGUMENTS. - The new settings apply lazily: parts written by future inserts and merges use the new values, existing parts keep the old ones until they are merged or the projection is rebuilt with MATERIALIZE PROJECTION. - IF EXISTS is supported - New access type ALTER MODIFY PROJECTION under the ALTER PROJECTION group. Tests: - 04757_alter_modify_projection_settings (old part keeps old granularity while new part and merged part get the new one via system.projection_parts, plus error cases. - 04758_alter_modify_projection_settings_replicated (metadata alter replicates to a second replica). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108420 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY PROJECTION to change projection-level settings (e.g. index_granularity) of an existing projection without rebuilding it. The new settings apply lazily via merges. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113343&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113343](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113343+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Optimize aggregations of LowCardinality of 128 and 256 bit integers
signal.text: This is simply expanding what is done for narrower integers to wider ones. signal.title: Implement PromQL functions sum_over_time(), avg_over_time() and count_over_time()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `sum_over_time()`, `avg_over_time()` and `count_over_time()`. ### Description Implements three PromQL range-vector functions previously reported as not implemented. `sum_over_time`, `avg_over_time` and `count_over_time` are three different projections of the same `(sum, count)` accumulator, so they share one new header (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSumCountAvg.h`) with a single invertible `Summary{sum, count}` monoid (merge adds both fields, unmerge subtracts them), plugged into the existing generic `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSlidingSum` sliding-window fast path — the same infrastructure already proven by `rate`/`increase`/`delta`. No changes were needed to the generic grid/bucket machinery (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase.h`) or to `checkArgumentTypes` (all three take a single range-vector argument, the existing default). Registered `timeSeriesSumToGrid`/`timeSeriesAvgToGrid`/`timeSeriesCountToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the three `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`, matching `rate`/`increase`/`delta`'s convention. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0.** **Testing**: new SQL-level test (`04628_timeseries_sum_avg_count_over_time.sql`) plus cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering all three functions, an empty-window case, a window narrower than the step (grid points with no sample must be absent/NULL, not zero), and a nested `avg_over_time(rate(...)[2m:10s])` case. This flips 19 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112353&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112353](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112353+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions stddev_over_time() and stdvar_over_time()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `stddev_over_time()` and `stdvar_over_time()` (population standard deviation/variance). ### Description Implements `stddev_over_time(v range-vector)` and `stdvar_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. **Key Technical & Numerical Stability Highlights**: 1. **Welford's Algorithm & Chan's Parallel Merge**: Uses a running centered-moment `{count, mean, m2}` accumulator ($M_2 = \sum (x - \bar{x})^2$) in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesVarianceOverTime.h` updated per sample via Welford's formula and merged pairwise via Chan et al.'s parallel merge algorithm. This avoids catastrophic cancellation on large-magnitude counter series (e.g. byte counters $\sim 5 \times 10^8$, where raw $\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2 / N$ loses all precision and produces false zeroes or negative variances). 2. **Prometheus Staleness Handling**: Implements full Prometheus stale-marker (`0x7ff0000000000002`) semantics. Stale markers are flagged at ingestion (`is_stale_marker`), excluded from range-vector aggregations (`WHERE NOT is_stale_marker`) so target disappearance does not pollute range windows with NaNs, while remaining detectable by instant selectors to correctly report series absence. 3. **Non-Invertible Two-Stacks / Recompute Strategy**: Avoids floating-point `unmerge` subtraction on moments to prevent numerical cancellation and drift over long sliding windows. Registered `timeSeriesStddevToGrid`/`timeSeriesStdvarToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`. **Verified numerically against Prometheus 3.5.0**: verified bit-for-bit accuracy against Prometheus 3.5.0 live responses, including cross-architecture (ARM64 vs x86_64) ULP tolerance handling in CI. **Testing**: SQL-level test (`04628_variance_timeseries_functions.sql`) covering empty/single/multi-sample windows and `AggregatingMergeTree` round-trips, plus integration cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` (including stale-marker ingestion and instant/range evaluations). This flips 12 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112355&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112355](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112355+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: MATERIALIZE PROJECTION is a no-op after MODIFY PROJECTION, contrary to PR docs
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **After `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY PROJECTION p ... WITH SETTINGS (index_granularity = 128)`, the documented rebuild path `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE PROJECTION p` completes successfully (mutation `is_done = 1`, part version bumped) but the projection part keeps the OLD granularity - 11 marks instead of 79. A merge (`OPTIMIZE ... FINAL`) on the same data produces 79.** - **Root cause:** `MutationsInterpreter.cpp:1350` treats presence of the projection in the part as proof it is up to date. That was correct before this PR (a projection definition could never change), but this PR makes the definition mutable, so 'present' no longer implies 'built with the current settings'. The PR nevertheless states the opposite in three places: `AlterCommands.cpp:1102` ('`MATERIALIZE PROJECTION` forces a rebuild'), `docs/reference/statements/alter/projection.mdx:334` ('To rebuild existing parts with the new settings, run MATERIALIZE PROJECTION'), and the PR description. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `ALTER ... MATERIALIZE PROJECTION` -> `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` ([`src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp:1350`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a77a83b02c0de/src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp#L1350)) adds the projection to `materialized_projections` only when the source part does NOT already have it -> `MutateTask` `getProjectionsToRecalculate` ([`src/Storages/MergeTree/MutateTask.cpp:1102`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a77a83b02c0de/src/Storages/MergeTree/MutateTask.cpp#L1102)) therefore leaves the projection out of `projections_to_recalc` -> the stale projection is carried over unchanged. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/AlterCommands.cpp:1102`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a77a83b02c0de/src/Storages/AlterCommands.cpp#L1102) — comment added by this PR claiming MATERIALIZE PROJECTION forces a rebuild - [`src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp:1350`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a77a83b02c0de/src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp#L1350) — MATERIALIZE PROJECTION skipped when the part already has the projection - docs/reference/statements/alter/projection.mdx:334 — docs added by this PR pointing users at MATERIALIZE PROJECTION to rebuild existing parts **Impact:** The only rebuild path the PR documents silently does nothing: the ALTER succeeds, a mutation is recorded as done, and the projection parts keep the old settings forever. Users who lower `index_granularity` on a projection of a large table and then run `MATERIALIZE PROJECTION` will believe the change was applied. The only working path is `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL` (`OPTIMIZE ... FINAL DEDUPLICATE` is refused on tables with projections), which the docs do not mention. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `a77a83b02c0de`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/312cd816-31d2-466a-9f25-137ecb9c6572) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- Test: MATERIALIZE PROJECTION after MODIFY PROJECTION rebuilds existing parts with the new projection settings. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_modify_projection_materialize; CREATE TABLE t_modify_projection_materialize ( k UInt64, v UInt64, PROJECTION p (SELECT v ORDER BY v) WITH SETTINGS (index_granularity = 1024) ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, index_granularity_bytes = 10485760; INSERT INTO t_modify_projection_materialize SELECT number, number * 2 FROM numbers(10000); ALTER TABLE t_modify_projection_materialize MODIFY PROJECTION p (SELECT v ORDER BY v) WITH SETTINGS (index_granularity = 128); SELECT '-- MATERIALIZE PROJECTION rebuilds the projection with the new granularity'; ALTER TABLE t_modify_projection_materialize MATERIALIZE PROJECTION p SETTINGS mutations_sync = 1; SELECT name, rows, marks FROM system.projection_parts WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 't_modify_projection_materialize' AND active ORDER BY parent_name; SELECT '-- control: a merge rebuilds it'; OPTIMIZE TABLE t_modify_projection_materialize FINAL; SELECT name, rows, marks FROM system.projection_parts WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 't_modify_projection_materialize' AND active ORDER BY parent_name; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_modify_projection_materialize; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` -- MATERIALIZE PROJECTION rebuilds the projection with the new granularity p 10000 79 -- control: a merge rebuilds it p 10000 79 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` -- MATERIALIZE PROJECTION rebuilds the projection with the new granularity p 10000 11 -- control: a merge rebuilds it p 10000 79 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Either (a) make `MATERIALIZE PROJECTION` rebuild when the part's projection is stale - e.g. drop the `!source.hasProjection(...)` short-circuit for an explicitly named projection, or compare the part's stored projection metadata against the current definition; or (b) correct `docs/.../projection.mdx:334`, the `AlterCommands.cpp:1102` comment and the PR description to say that only a merge (`OPTIMIZE ... FINAL`) applies the new settings to existing parts. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - If option (a) is taken, note that `MATERIALIZE PROJECTION` on a part that already has a valid projection would then always rewrite it - a behavior change for existing users who use the command as a repair tool. Found during automated review of [PR #113343](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113343). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr113343_001` </details> cc @diegomestre2 @Michicosun (from #113343)

signal.title: Docs: clarify that use_skip_indexes_if_final stale-result risk requires exact mode to be disabled
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Documentation (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... The `use_skip_indexes_if_final` description states the stale-result risk as if it were an unconditional consequence of enabling the setting, and mentions `use_skip_indexes_if_final_exact_mode` only in a trailing clause whose `(default is enabled)` is easy to read as referring back to `use_skip_indexes_if_final` itself. Both settings default to `true` (`src/Core/Settings.cpp`, and `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` records the `0 -> 1` flip for both in 25.6). With the shipped defaults there is no stale-result risk: `use_skip_indexes_if_final_exact_mode` runs the `PrimaryKeyExpand` step (`findPKRangesForFinalAfterSkipIndex`, `src/Processors/QueryPlan/PartsSplitter.cpp`), which adds back granules in the other parts that overlap the primary key ranges the skip index selected. The "risk of missing recent updates" applies only when that setting is turned off, which is exactly what the existing sibling description says ("This setting should be disabled only if approximate results based on looking up the skip index are okay for an application"). Reworded so the conditionality and the default are explicit. Documentation only, no behavior change. Before: > Skip indexes may exclude rows (granules) containing the latest data, which could lead to incorrect results from a query with the FINAL modifier. When this setting is enabled, skipping indexes are applied even with the FINAL modifier, potentially improving performance but with the risk of missing recent updates. This setting should be enabled in sync with the setting use_skip_indexes_if_final_exact_mode (default is enabled). After: > Skip indexes may exclude rows (granules) containing the latest data, which could lead to incorrect results from a query with the FINAL modifier. When this setting is enabled, skipping indexes are applied even with the FINAL modifier, potentially improving performance. Correct results still depend on setting use_skip_indexes_if_final_exact_mode, which is enabled by default and scans the additional parts that overlap the ranges returned by the skip index. The risk of missing recent updates applies only if that setting is disabled. The rendered page (https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/settings/session-settings/use-skip-indexes) is inside `AUTOGENERATED` markers, so per `docs/reference/AGENTS.md` only the `DECLARE` doc string is edited here; the nightly docs autogeneration job regenerates the `.mdx`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115846&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115846](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115846+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Auto-retry infra failures on fork PRs
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The fork-approval gate consumes `run_attempt` 1, concluding `action_required` with zero jobs, so a fork PR's first attempt that runs anything is attempt 2. `retry_infra_failures.yml` assumed attempt 1 is the real run, leaving infra-killed fork runs invisible to the hourly auto-retry. I hit this via the slowdown #113052 fixed, which killed `Config Workflow` on ~65 PRs. **Attempt and window.** The filter widens to `.attempt <= 2`, accepting attempt 2 only if attempt 1 concluded `action_required`, so a real retry stays excluded. The cutoff compared `createdAt`, which GitHub pins to the gated attempt, while `startedAt` advances to the attempt that ran; that skew reaches p99 45.1h over 8946 runs. **Scan depth.** The listing is `createdAt`-ordered, so a gated run sits deeper than its window implies and no row cap exhausts it. The scan walks `createdAt` in 24 hour timestamp partitions over 31 days, bounding the 30 day approval expiry (observed max 26.6 days). A partition at the API's 1000 row ceiling fails the step instead of dropping rows. **Order.** The walk feeds more candidates than `MAX_RERUNS`, so their order decides who is reached. `sort -u` also sorted by the leading `databaseId`, oldest-created first, only a 0.90 pairwise proxy for `startedAt` order. Entries now lead with `startedAt` so the same dedup orders by deadline: the candidate nearest the 6 hour edge is retried on this tick or never, while a fresher one is still admitted by later ticks. Over 312 hourly clocks every clock exceeded `MAX_RERUNS`, and of the candidates on their final tick this loses 35%, against 56% and 100% for ascending and descending id. Attempt 3 stays excluded and the infra heuristic is unchanged, so this restores visibility rather than reruns. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113564&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113564](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113564+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix CAST of an Array(Map) constant sent to a remote server
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115647 A `Map` is physically an `Array(Tuple(key, value))`, and that is also how a `Map` constant is written down when the analyzer serializes a query for a remote server: `ConstantNode::toASTImpl` renders the field as an array of tuples and wraps it into `_CAST(..., 'Array(Map(K, V))')`. On the receiving side `CAST` compared the nesting depth of `Array(Array(Tuple(K, V)))` (two) with `Array(Map(K, V))` (one) and rejected the cast before ever reaching the element wrapper, which converts `Array(Tuple(K, V))` to `Map(K, V)` without trouble. So any query whose constant folds to an `Array(Map(...))` failed once it was shipped to a shard or to a parallel replica: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (m Map(String, String)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY m; INSERT INTO t SELECT map('k', toString(number)) FROM numbers(4); SELECT count() FROM remote('127.0.0.{1,2}', currentDatabase(), t) WHERE has([map('k', '3')], m); ``` ``` Code: 53. DB::Exception: Received from 127.0.0.2:9000. DB::Exception: CAST AS Array can only be performed between same-dimensional array types: In scope SELECT count() AS `count()` FROM default.t AS __table1 WHERE has(_CAST([[('k', '3')]], 'Array(Map(String, String))'), __table1.m). (TYPE_MISMATCH) ``` `CAST` now counts a `Map` as the array of tuples it stands for when comparing nesting depth, so both spellings sit at the same depth. A genuine depth mismatch, such as `Array(String)` to `Array(Array(String))`, is still rejected. This is what makes `04510_not_has_function_explain` fail in the `ParallelReplicas` job on `master`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=31e78bbbb66e018db116f4956eb25cbbc27960e6&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage%2C%20ParallelReplicas%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20parallel%29 - that test got a `has([map('k', NULL)], m)` query in #115647, and the query hits this cast whenever the filter is actually shipped to a replica. signal.title: Fix SimpleAggregateFunction Native header dropping an explicit nested aggregate version
signal.text: Fix SimpleAggregateFunction Native header dropping an explicit nested aggregate version Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading a `SimpleAggregateFunction` column whose value type holds an `AggregateFunction` declared with an explicit version `0`, such as `SimpleAggregateFunction(anyLast, AggregateFunction(0, sumMap, Array(UInt64), Array(Decimal32(2))))`. The `Native` type header omitted that version, so a reader re-parsing the announced type saw the function's default instead and could not read the data back: `SELECT` failed with `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` on `StripeLog`, and the column could not be reloaded by `Set`/`Join`, restored from a `Memory` backup, or read from a `Native` file, which was left empty. ### Description **Root cause.** `SimpleAggregateFunction(f, T)` is stored as the storage type `T` plus a custom name caching its own copy of `T`. Version `0` is never printed, so a leaf declared `AggregateFunction(0, ...)` prints a versionless spelling, and the alias rebuilds its value type by parsing that spelling back, where the missing token reads as the function's default. The version walker leaves an explicit version alone, so nothing corrects it: the header announces the default over a version-`0` payload, and for `sumMap` the two versions differ in width, so the reader over-consumes. **The change** stays at the transport boundary. `NativeWriter::write` renders the header from both type trees: syntax from the cached side, which alone remembers spellings such as `Nested(...)`, and versions from the live side. One rendering feeds the stream and index headers so they cannot drift apart. `getName()`, the type factory, the version walker and `NativeReader` are untouched, so `CREATE`, `ATTACH` and on-disk data are unchanged. **Scope after #112052.** That PR made the walker re-version the alias customization, which covers a leaf pinning no version: it is stored with the default spelled out, so header and payload already agree. What remains, and what this PR fixes, is the explicit version-`0` declaration. Verified against a master build carrying #112052 and none of this change: that case fails `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` there and round trips here. The test marks its regression arms; the wrapper and engine cases stay as round-trip coverage. **Known adjacent gap.** The same shape below a `Variant` fails identically on plain master. Covering it means mirroring the walker's discriminator-order and refuse-on-collapse semantics for an experimental type, which is a separate change; `NativeFormat.mdx` records the behaviour. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112412&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112412](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112412+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Promote exponentialTimeDecayed window-functions to aggregate-functions
signal.text: ## Motivation `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` already exist and are documented as aggregate functions, but their current implementation is a special window-function implementation in `WindowTransform`. They do not provide mergeable aggregate states that can be persisted and combined with aggregate combinators such as `-State` and `-Merge`. This prevents incremental time-decayed aggregation in engines such as `AggregatingMergeTree`: data has to be evaluated through the window path instead of being aggregated independently in multiple batches and merged later. This PR adds regular, mergeable aggregate implementations for those three names while preserving the existing window implementation and its behavior. ## What changes For the regular aggregate form, each state keeps the weighted sum and sum of weights at the greatest timestamp observed by that state, plus that timestamp. When a row or another state has an older anchor, it is moved to the newer anchor with: `exp((older_time - newer_time) / decay_length)` The existing semantics are unchanged: `decay_length` is the interval after which a contribution has weight `1/e`. It is not a half-life. With the default `exponential_time_decay_aggregate_function_calculation_budget = 0`, the state representation makes independently built states mergeable with the same calculation. Input rows do not need to be timestamp ordered, and different row orders and batch distributions produce the same mathematical result subject to normal `Float64` rounding. A positive calculation budget opts into approximate aggregation using calculation index timestamps. For sums, the index is the time when the absolute contribution or state reaches unit magnitude; counts use the corresponding total-weight index; averages consider both numerator and denominator indexes. A state more than the configured number of decay lengths behind the dominant state is discarded before evaluating `exp`. This makes the cutoff depend on remaining significance rather than source age. Approximate results near the cutoff can depend on row order or merge grouping, and signed sums that nearly cancel can have larger relative error. The aggregate forms accept numeric timestamps, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64`. ### Finalized decaying values The sum and count aggregate forms return the experimental parameterized type: `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` The decay length is part of the type. Its tuple-compatible storage is canonicalized as `(sign, signed_unit_time, decay_length)`, where `unit_time = anchor_time + decay_length * ln(abs(value))` is the timestamp at which the curve has unit magnitude and `signed_unit_time = sign * unit_time`. Zero has the canonical form `(0, 0, decay_length)`. This representation makes native sorting and relative comparisons match the curve values at any common timestamp for values with the same decay length. Comparisons across different decay lengths are rejected. The redundant decay-length marker is checked against the type parameter when a value is evaluated or combined, preventing incompatible values from being silently mixed through layout-compatible custom-tuple paths. Values can be constructed/aggregated with: `exponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)(value, time)` A finalized decaying value can be aggregated again without repeating the decay length: `exponentialTimeDecayedSum(decaying_value)` When the input is `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)`, the decay length is inferred from its type and the result has the same parameterized type. This gives the closure property required by `SimpleAggregateFunction`, so it can be stored directly in `AggregatingMergeTree`: ```sql CREATE TABLE decaying ( key UInt64, value SimpleAggregateFunction( exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(60)) ) ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree ORDER BY key; ``` The scalar helpers are: - `exponentialTimeDecayingValueAt(value, target_time)` — evaluate the same exponential curve before, at, or after its anchor, including at `now()` / `now64()`; - `exponentialTimeDecayingDecayLength(value)` — read the decay length encoded in the type; - `exponentialTimeDecayingAdd(a, b)` — combine two values at their greatest anchor. The `+` operator uses the same addition logic for two decaying values. Different decay lengths are rejected. `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg` continues to return `Float64`. All new regular-aggregate and decaying-value behavior is experimental and disabled by default behind `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. ## Effect on the existing window functions The existing window-function implementation remains in place. Window calls continue to use the previous frame-based implementation, retain their `Float64` result, and do not require `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. This PR also corrects the function documentation to consistently call the parameter `decay_length` and describe the existing `1/e` decay semantics. ## Correctness and tests Stateless tests cover: - regular aggregation and `-State` / `-Merge`; - direct aggregation of finalized `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` values; - direct `SimpleAggregateFunction(exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length))` storage and merging in `AggregatingMergeTree`; - different input orders and batch distributions, including reproducibly generated randomized inputs; - numeric, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64` time arguments; - the experimental setting in enabled and disabled forms; - forward and backward value evaluation, addition, decay-length lookup, and rejection of inconsistent/mixed decay lengths; - native sorting and all relative comparison operators, including negative, zero, and positive values; - exact-default, bounded-cutoff, and state-merge calculation-budget behavior; - signed values, empty input, nullable paths, canonical reconstruction, and large-time decay/underflow cases. The implementation uses `Float64` accumulation. As with other floating-point reductions, large signed values that nearly cancel can expose order/grouping-dependent rounding. Stronger reproducibility for that case is intentionally left for a separate improvement if feedback shows it is important in practice. ## Benchmark status There are no end-to-end ClickHouse benchmark results yet. The benchmark already posted in the PR discussion is a standalone C++ microbenchmark of the decay formulas. It showed the expected benefit from avoiding redundant `exp` evaluations in the merge/value paths, but it excludes ClickHouse aggregation, column access, serialization, scheduling, and `AggregatingMergeTree` overhead and therefore is not evidence of end-to-end query throughput. An end-to-end benchmark, preferably a ClickHouse performance test covering state creation and state merging, is still pending. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add experimental mergeable `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` aggregate forms, including a parameterized decaying-value type that can be stored directly with `SimpleAggregateFunction` in `AggregatingMergeTree`, while preserving the existing window-function behavior. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110934&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110934](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110934+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add the `Cluster` database engine
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114411 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/59304 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110975 Implement the `Cluster` database engine, a follow-up to the `Remote` database engine (#110975). It provides real-time access to tables in a configured cluster database. Each table is exposed as a `Distributed` proxy that forwards `SELECT` and `INSERT`, with the same local-shard visibility rules and remote-replica fallback as `Remote`. The cluster is resolved from server configuration by name on every access, supports macros, and follows configuration reloads. Connections use each replica's configured credentials, secure connections, compression, and inter-server secret; the engine stores no credentials. `SHOW CREATE TABLE` reports `THERE_IS_NO_QUERY` for a table of a `Cluster` database: the proxy follows configuration reloads (a reload can add shards and give the proxy an implicit `rand()` sharding key that is used only for `INSERT`, while a standalone `Distributed` table would also use it for read shard pruning), it expands macros on every access, and it falls back to a remote replica on the metadata lookup, so no standalone `Distributed` definition is equivalent to it. Best-effort paths, such as the `create_table_query` column of `system.tables`, return nothing instead of failing. `Cluster` is experimental and is enabled through `allow_experimental_database_cluster`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the experimental `Cluster` database engine, enabled via `allow_experimental_database_cluster`, which provides real-time access to the tables of a configured cluster database and forwards `SELECT` and `INSERT` queries to it. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114417&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114417](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114417+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
