signal.title: Support Variant type in aggregate functions (sum, avg, min, max, ...)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Aggregate functions that do not handle the `Variant` type natively (`sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `argMin`, `argMax`, `quantile`, `stddevPop`, ...) can now be applied to `Variant` arguments. Previously they failed, e.g. `Illegal type Variant(Decimal(7, 2), Float64) of argument for aggregate function sum`. The aggregate functions that do accept a `Variant` argument natively (`count`, `any`, `groupArray`, `groupConcat`, the `uniq` family, ...) now skip the rows where the `Variant` holds a NULL value, like they skip the NULL values of a `Nullable` argument (only the row skipping matches `Nullable`: the result type and the empty-set result of the function are preserved) -- previously `count` counted those rows, `any` could return NULL from a group that has non-NULL values, `groupArray` stored the NULLs, and the `uniq` family counted NULL as a distinct value. The `-SimpleState` combinator and declared `SimpleAggregateFunction(..., Variant(...))` columns retain the previous behavior regardless of this setting, so their raw values can be safely re-aggregated during table loading and background merges. Set `aggregate_functions_skip_variant_nulls = 0` (or `SET compatibility = '26.7'`) to restore the previous behavior for other aggregate functions. Persisted `AggregateFunction(f, Variant(...))` states (materialized views, `AggregateFunction` columns) keep the same type name, layout and serialization in both modes, so states written before and after the upgrade merge freely but mean different things -- the old ones aggregated the NULL rows, the new ones skip them -- and a merged result over the mix follows neither rule consistently. To keep the pre-`26.8` results over such data, set `aggregate_functions_skip_variant_nulls = 0` before inserting new data; the NULL rows already aggregated into the historical states cannot be removed by re-merging, only by re-inserting the data from the source. ### Description Such functions now aggregate over the least common supertype of the variants, wrapped in `Nullable`: ``` f(variant) == f(CAST(variant AS Nullable(supertype(T1, ..., TN)))) ``` `Nullable` preserves the implicit NULLs of the `Variant`, which the aggregation skips. **How it works.** `AggregateFunctionFactory::get()` resolves the function normally first; only if that fails for a `Variant` argument with an "unsupported argument type" error — `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT`, or `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` for the creators that use it instead (`rankCorr`, `mannWhitneyUTest`, `kolmogorovSmirnovTest`, `largestTriangleThreeBuckets`) — does it fall back to a new `AggregateFunctionVariantAdapter`, which casts the `Variant` argument column(s) to `Nullable(supertype)` on the fly and forwards everything else to the nested function (whose state layout it shares). If the supertype route is not possible either, the original error is reported unchanged. Functions that already accept `Variant` (`count`, `any`, `uniq`, `groupArray`, ...) are unaffected. **Supertype.** `getLeastSupertype` is strict and has no common type for e.g. `Decimal`/`Int64` ↔ `Float64` (no lossless conversion). For an aggregate whose result is a floating-point value computed by arithmetic over its input (the `sum`/`avg`/variance/... families), a mix of numeric variants with no lossless common supertype falls back to `Float64` — but only when the user has opted into the lossy numeric supertype with the `allow_lossy_numeric_supertype` setting, and under the same promotion rule that setting applies at type inference for `if`/`multiIf`/`coalesce`/`ifNull`/`array`/`map` (all-numeric variants with at least one floating-point member; an integer-only mix such as `Variant(Int64, UInt64)` is not promoted). With the setting off (the default) the adapter handles only lossless supertypes and the original `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` error — which points at the setting when enabling it would help — is reported unchanged. Reconstruction of an already declared state type such as `AggregateFunction(sum, Variant(Int64, Float64))` always allows the promotion, so a state validated when it was declared never becomes unreadable because of the setting's current value: this covers the background paths that have no query context (table load / `ATTACH` at startup, merges) and, through `from_declared_state_type`, every query-time path that names the state type explicitly — a column type, a `CAST` target, a decoded binary type, and the nested function of `-Merge` over such a state. The fallback is deliberately **not** applied to exact/order-based aggregates (`min`, `max`, `argMin`, `argMax`, `any`, `quantileExact`, ...) even under the setting: a lossy `Float64` cast would silently return wrong results for them (two distinct integers above 2^53 collapse to the same `Float64`), so they keep reporting the original `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` when there is no lossless common supertype. Whether a function is float-promoting is declared by `AggregateFunctionProperties::is_float_promoting` (set at registration, consulted through the factory), fail-closed: a function that does not set it is treated as not float-promoting. Clean supertypes are preserved regardless of the function and the setting (`Variant(UInt8, UInt32) -> UInt32`, `Variant(Int32, Float64) -> Float64`, `Variant(Date, DateTime) -> DateTime`), so `min`/`max` still work over such variants. **Combinators.** The adapter is applied as the outermost wrapper (the combinator recursion resolves nested functions without it), so combinators compose in the usual order, e.g. `Adapter(Null(If(sum)))`. `-If`, `-State`/`-Merge` and `GROUP BY` work; state serialization for `sumState` uses the supertype (`AggregateFunction(sum, Nullable(Float64))`), so distributed / two-phase aggregation is unchanged. Only the argument positions the function actually rejects are adapted: `argMin`/`argMax` (and the `*ArgMin`/`*ArgMax` combinators) accept a `Variant` in the returned "arg" position and reject it only in the comparable key, so the "arg" keeps its original `Variant` type while just the key is cast to `Nullable(supertype)`. **Examples.** ```sql SET allow_lossy_numeric_supertype = 1; SELECT sum(v), toTypeName(sum(v)) FROM values('v Variant(Decimal(7, 2), Float64)', 1.5, 2.5, NULL, 10); -- 14 Nullable(Float64) ``` **Scope.** Only top-level `Variant` arguments whose common supertype can be wrapped in `Nullable` are handled — the adapter uses `Nullable` to carry the implicit NULLs of the `Variant`. A `Variant` whose common supertype is a container type (`Array`/`Tuple`/`Map`) is therefore still rejected, even for an orderable aggregate such as `min`/`max` over `Variant(Array(UInt8), Array(UInt16))` (supporting it would require tracking the `Variant`'s NULLs separately from the value column). A `Variant` nested inside `Tuple`/`Array`, and the `Dynamic` type, are likewise still rejected as before. These are all natural follow-ups. The result is `Nullable` because a `Variant` value can always be NULL. `singleValueOrNull` is deliberately excluded from the adapter (`AggregateFunctionProperties::is_distinctness_sensitive`): its contract keys on how many distinct values there are, and the cast to `Nullable(supertype)` collapses `Variant` values that are distinct because their alternative types differ (`1::UInt8` vs `1::UInt64`, which `uniq` counts as 2), so it would silently return a non-NULL value where the contract requires NULL — including inside the `x = ALL (SELECT ...)` rewrite. It keeps reporting `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` for a `Variant` argument, unchanged from before. The `-Distinct` combinator makes any combined function distinctness-sensitive in the same way (`sumDistinct` must deduplicate the genuine `Variant` values, not their casts to the supertype), so the combinator propagates the property through `AggregateFunctionFactory::tryGetProperties` (`IAggregateFunctionCombinator::isDistinctnessSensitive`) and every `...Distinct` form over a `Variant` argument keeps its original error too. `groupArrayInsertAt` and `groupArraySorted` do not claim native `Variant` support either: their generic implementations keep the state as `Field`s, which loses the original alternative type of a `Variant` value on ingest and reinfers the first compatible one on output (`1::UInt8` and `1::UInt64` collapse), and `groupArraySorted` would order by `Field` comparison instead of `Variant` order. Like `sum` / `avg`, they go through the adapter over the least common supertype of the variants, and reject a `Variant` (or `Dynamic`) argument at resolution when there is no lossless supertype. **Error codes.** `BAD_ARGUMENTS` is deliberately not part of the "unsupported argument type" retry signal, because creators use it for genuine semantic failures — above all invalid parameters, as in `kolmogorovSmirnovTest('bogus')` — and retrying on it would report the unrelated type error of the original, unadapted call instead of the parameter error. The few creators that rejected argument *types* with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` now reject them with `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT`, like every other function, which keeps them adaptable to a `Variant` argument: `analysisOfVariance`, `studentTTest`, `studentTTestOneSample`, `welchTTest`, `meanZTest` and `boundingRatio` report `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` instead of `BAD_ARGUMENTS` when applied to an argument of an unsupported type. **`count` over a `Variant`.** `count` accepts a `Variant` natively, without the adapter, but `count(expr)` counts the not-NULL values of its argument, and a `Variant` row can hold a NULL value (`isNull` is true for it). A `Variant` is not `Nullable`, so the `Null` combinator -- and with it `AggregateFunctionCountNotNullUnary` -- is never applied to it, and the native path counted every row. `count` over a single `Variant` argument now resolves to `AggregateFunctionCountNotNullVariant`, which counts the rows whose local discriminator is not `NULL_DISCRIMINATOR`; its state is the same single counter and normalizes to `AggregateFunction(count)`, so the state forms stay byte-compatible with the plain `count` state. **The NULL-skipping contract of the natively-supported functions.** The other functions that accept a `Variant` natively are held to the same contract by `AggregateFunctionVariantNull`, a wrapper mirroring the `Null` combinator: the rows where a `Variant` argument is NULL are skipped, like the `Null` combinator skips the NULL values of `Nullable` arguments (only the row skipping is mirrored; the result-type promotion and the all-NULL-group result of the combinator are deliberately not). Without it, `any` returned NULL from a group that has non-NULL values, `groupArray` stored the NULLs its documentation promises to remove, `groupConcat` concatenated them as data, and the uniq family counted NULL as a distinct value. The wrapper is applied at the factory's leaf resolution point (`getImpl`), which every path funnels through -- the top-level native resolution as well as nested functions reconstructed from declared `AggregateFunction(f, Variant(...))` state types -- so the state layouts always match. Unlike the `Null` combinator, the wrapper never changes the result type, the state layout or the serialization of the nested function: a function that accepts a `Variant` natively already accepted it before this change, with exactly the nested result type and state representation, and both are persisted (in `AggregateFunction(f, Variant(...))` columns and in the schemas of the materialized views reading them), so changing either would break an upgrade. An all-NULL group produces the empty nested state and returns the nested function's empty-set result (`groupConcat` over a `Variant` keeps returning `String`, and an empty string for an all-NULL group); for functions whose result is the `Variant` itself (`any`, `argMin`, ...) an all-NULL group still reports NULL, because a `Variant` represents NULL on its own. Window functions keep handling their argument types themselves, so the `RESPECT NULLS` forms and `estimateCompressionRatio` still see the NULL rows, and `count` keeps its dedicated implementation above and declares `AggregateFunctionProperties::skips_variant_nulls`. **Compatibility of the NULL-skipping contract.** The functions above accepted a `Variant` argument before this change, so skipping its NULL rows is a change of their behavior and is gated by a compatibility setting: `aggregate_functions_skip_variant_nulls = 0` (implied by `compatibility` below `26.8`) restores the previous behavior, where those rows were aggregated as ordinary values. The setting only controls which rows are added to a state -- the result type, the state layout and the serialization are identical in both modes, so an `AggregateFunction(f, Variant(...))` state written by either mode stays readable and mergeable by the other. For the same reason the setting cannot change the meaning of a state that has already been written: a state written by an older version keeps the values that went into it, including the ones that came from the NULL rows, and no state-type version can retroactively tell the two apart because their bytes are identical. The consequence for existing data is spelled out in the changelog entry and in the documentation: states written before and after the upgrade merge freely but follow different accumulation rules, so a deployment that must keep the old results over persisted states has to keep writing with `aggregate_functions_skip_variant_nulls = 0` until the historical data is re-inserted. It is deliberately not consulted when there is no query context (a background operation, or a table loaded at startup). The one state that replays raw values into a nested function -- the distinct-key history of the `-Distinct` combinator -- keeps the rule by construction: the nested function of `-Distinct` over a `Variant` argument is resolved with the NULL skipping disabled, so the replay always aggregates the NULL keys a history contains (exactly like the versions that wrote states before the contract existed, so a stored `countDistinctState` over a `Variant` reads back to the same result under either value of the setting), and the NULL rows of newly aggregated data are skipped in front of the history instead, by an outer `AggregateFunctionVariantNull` over the combined function under the same setting. The aggregation of `Variant` arguments, the NULL-skipping contract and this compatibility note are documented in the `Variant` docs (the embedded documentation block in `DataTypeVariant.cpp` and `docs/reference/data-types/variant.mdx`). signal.title: Keep an Iceberg table readable after a column is dropped
signal.text: Keep an Iceberg table readable after a column is dropped <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113324 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ICEBERG_SPECIFICATION_VIOLATION` when reading an Iceberg table whose data file still physically contains a column that was dropped from the schema. The Parquet v3 reader now skips a file column whose field id is within the range the table has assigned, and still rejects an unmapped id below that range. Unrecognized ids in Iceberg's reserved metadata range are ignored, as the spec requires. Closes #113324. ### Description Closes #113324. Since 25.11 the v3 Parquet reader is the default, and reading a real column throws `Code: 743 ... Parquet file has column legacy_col with field_id 3 that is not in datalake metadata`. No setting restores the old behaviour: `input_format_parquet_use_native_reader_v3` is obsolete. Root cause: a data file written before `DROP COLUMN` still holds the dropped column with its original field id. Once the pre-drop snapshot is expired, the entry's schema resolves only from the merged manifest's header, which records the post-drop schema, so the reader gets a field-id map lacking id 3. `useColumnMapperIfNeeded` misses, finds the id outside the reserved range, and throws. Manifest merging (an Iceberg Java default) and snapshot expiry are routine housekeeping. Fix: narrow the refusal condition to what the metadata can actually decide. Iceberg's `last-column-id` is a monotonic high-water mark, so `1 <= field_id <= last-column-id` means "this table could have assigned this id", and such a column is simply not projected (Iceberg [Column Projection](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#column-projection)). An id outside that window could not belong to the table and still throws. Inside the window the bound cannot distinguish a dropped column from one never assigned, so both are skipped; deciding exactly would need the union of retained schemas, which `RemoveSnapshots` may collect. The helper now returns `std::nullopt` for a not-projected leaf, handled at both call sites. Not matching by physical column name: re-adding `legacy_col` gives a different field id, so old rows must read NULL. Name matching would serve the dropped column's values, i.e. silent wrong results. The added test pins this. The bound is attached only to mappers built from table metadata; without `last-column-id` the reader rejects as before. ORC needs no change: it uses `ColumnMapper` only when writing. The wrong schema id resolved under manifest merging is a separate defect, not addressed here. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113465&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113465](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113465+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix KeeperMap metadata compatibility with redundant parentheses
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114188 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow KeeperMap readers to accept shared metadata when equivalent primary keys differ only by redundant outer parentheses. ### Problem KeeperMap stores the table definition in Keeper and previously compared its primary-key expression as formatted text. Builds that serialize the same expression as either `key` or `(key)` therefore reject an otherwise compatible shared table definition during CREATE-against-existing-path and ATTACH/startup. ### Implementation - keep the existing writer spelling and never rewrite compatible shared metadata; - parse stored and local primary-key expressions and normalize only redundant outer parentheses that wrap one complete expression; - require the remaining input to be exact normal formatter output, preserving strict rejection of malformed, terminated, commented, or genuinely different definitions; - use the same compatibility check in CREATE-against-existing-path and ATTACH/startup; - split columns from the primary-key section using its structural newline-delimited header. This is intentionally a reader-side compatibility fix. A patched node accepts either spelling, but an unpatched node may still reject metadata serialized in the spelling it does not understand. Therefore every version participating in a rolling deployment must contain this fix; in particular, the same reader change must be backported to 26.4. Rewriting the shared znode here would not solve compatibility safely because it could replace the spelling with one rejected by another unpatched peer. The implementation uses parser and formatter APIs present in both current master and 26.4. It does not depend on `formatIgnoringRedundantParentheses()` added by #114188, so the same compatibility rule can be backported to 26.4. ### Tests The stateless SQL regression covers both directions (`key` stored with `(key)` local and `(key)` stored with `key` local), verifies that compatible CREATE and ATTACH do not rewrite the Keeper znode, and checks data access after ATTACH. It also verifies rejection of a different key, malformed `(key`, and terminated `key;` metadata, plus a primary-key expression containing the metadata header text. Red-before was reproduced with embedded Keeper on official ClickHouse 26.4.5.143 and 26.7.1.1315: after changing stored metadata from `key` to `(key)`, DETACH + ATTACH left the table in `INVALID_STATE` (Code 668). Local `git diff --check` and a snapshot-bound hostile review passed. Green-after remains a CI gate for this commit and for the future 26.4 backport. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115642&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115642](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115642+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1874` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.6.6`, `26.6.4.11` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: `timeZoneOffset` and `parseDateTime` are wrong by 24 hours for timezones that crossed the international date line
signal.text: 🕵️ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour For the seven timezones that permanently shifted their UTC offset by a whole day when they moved across the international date line, `timeZoneOffset` returns the zone's **pre-jump** offset, and `parseDateTime` (which uses it) produces an instant exactly 86400 s off. ```sql SELECT timeZoneOffset(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')); -- -36000 (-10h) WRONG -- Pacific/Kiritimati has been UTC+14 since 1995, so +50400 SELECT toUnixTimestamp(parseDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', '%Y-%m-%d %H:%i:%S', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')); -- 1750024800 WRONG -- exactly +86400; correct is 1749938400 -- (toDateTime / parseDateTimeBestEffort on the same string give 1749938400) ``` Affected zones, checked across all 597 rows of `system.time_zones` at 2010‑01‑01, 2025‑01‑01 and 2025‑07‑01 — no other zone is wrong: | zone | true offset | `timeZoneOffset` | error | jumped | |---|---|---|---|---| | `Pacific/Kiritimati` | +50400 (+14h) | −36000 (−10h) | −86400 | 1994‑12‑31 | | `Pacific/Apia` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 2011‑12‑30 | | `Pacific/Fakaofo` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 2011‑12‑30 | | `Pacific/Enderbury` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 1994‑12‑31 | | `Pacific/Kanton` | +46800 (+13h) | −39600 (−11h) | −86400 | 1994‑12‑31 | | `Pacific/Kwajalein` | +43200 (+12h) | −43200 (−12h) | −86400 | 1993‑08‑20 | | `Kwajalein` | +43200 (+12h) | −43200 (−12h) | −86400 | 1993‑08‑20 | Before its jump each zone is reported correctly (e.g. `Pacific/Apia` is right at 2010‑01‑01), which is consistent with the offset being frozen at the pre-jump value. `Pacific/Chatham` (+13:45) is **correct**, so this is not a "offset larger than +12h" problem — it is specifically the whole-day component that is lost. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Reproduced on 26.8.1.1 and 26.8.1.1599 (four local builds). Not a recent regression — the implementation below has carried this assumption for a long time. ### How to reproduce Any server or `clickhouse local`, default settings: ```sql SELECT timeZoneOffset(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')) AS reported, toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'UTC')) - toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime('2025-06-15 12:00:00', 'Pacific/Kiritimati')) AS actual; -- reported = -36000, actual = 50400 ``` Cross-checked against Python's `zoneinfo` (system tzdata), which agrees with `actual`: ```python datetime(2025,6,15,12,0,0,tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Pacific/Kiritimati")).utcoffset() # 14:00:00 ``` Sweep for all zones: ```sql -- per zone (the timezone argument must be a constant), compare SELECT toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime(D,'UTC')) - toUnixTimestamp(toDateTime(D,TZ)) = timeZoneOffset(toDateTime(D,TZ)); ``` ### Expected behavior `timeZoneOffset(t)` should return the zone's actual UTC offset at instant `t` (+50400 for Kiritimati in 2025), and `parseDateTime` should map a wall-clock string to the same instant that `toDateTime` and `parseDateTimeBestEffort` already produce. ### Additional context Root cause is in `src/Common/DateLUTImpl.h`, `DateLUTImpl::timezoneOffset`: ```cpp Time res = (lut[index].date - lut[daynum_offset_epoch].date) % 86400; /// As so far to know, the maximal DST offset couldn't be more than 2 hours, so after the /// modulo operation the remainder will sits between [-offset --> 0 --> offset] ... res = res > 43200 ? (86400 - res) : (0 - res); ... return res + offset_at_start_of_epoch; ``` It reconstructs only the *DST delta relative to the start of the epoch* and adds the zone's 1970 offset. A date-line jump changes the base offset by exactly one day, so that component is an exact multiple of 86400 and `% 86400` discards it — leaving the result anchored to `offset_at_start_of_epoch`, i.e. the pre-jump offset. Chatham is unaffected because its +13:45 has no whole-day part. `parseDateTime` inherits the error at `src/Functions/parseDateTime.cpp:581`: ```cpp if (!has_time_zone_offset) time_zone_offset = time_zone.timezoneOffset(seconds_since_epoch); seconds_since_epoch -= time_zone_offset; ``` Subtracting an offset that is 86400 too small moves the instant 86400 forward, matching the observed error. **Affected functions:** `timeZoneOffset`, `timezoneOffset`, `parseDateTime`, `parseDateTimeOrNull`, `parseDateTime64`, `parseDateTimeInJodaSyntax`. **Verified unaffected** (all agree with `zoneinfo`): `toDateTime`, `toDateTime64`, `toString`, `formatDateTime`, `toTimeZone`, `toStartOfDay`, `toHour`, `makeDateTime`, `makeDateTime64`, `YYYYMMDDhhmmssToDateTime`, `parseDateTimeBestEffort`, `parseDateTimeBestEffortUS`, `parseDateTime64BestEffort`. There is already a regression test for exactly these zones — `tests/queries/0_stateless/01252_weird_time_zone.sql` covers Kiritimati, Kwajalein, Apia, Enderbury and Fakaofo — but only via `toDateTime`, `toStartOfDay` and `toHour`, which are all correct. Extending it with `timeZoneOffset` and `parseDateTime` would cover this. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115332 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1888` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Write sampled OpenTelemetry trace context back into ClientInfo
signal.text: When a trace is started by sampling, the generated trace context existed only in the thread-local ambient. Now `executeQuery` writes the sampled context back into `ClientInfo` when the `query` span is created, so secondary query spans join the initiator's trace, parented under its `query` span. If the client supplied its own trace context, it is left untouched. No protocol or schema change. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112738 The recursive CTE also triggered a pre-existing server bug under parallel replicas, see https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115799 This is the output comparison with and without the change, now, remote query spans belong to the initiator: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A trace started by sampling (`opentelemetry_start_trace_probability`) is now written back into the query's client info, so remote and distributed secondary queries, and DDL entries, join the same trace instead of starting disjoint ones. --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115619&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115619](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115619+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]

signal.title: Push the release changelog and version bump to master directly instead of via PRs
signal.text: Direct pushes to `master` by `robot-clickhouse` are permitted (via a ruleset bypass), so the release job no longer needs a pull request and the `CH Inc sync` / merge-queue round-trip to land its changes — it pushes them straight to `master`. - Patch release: push the generated changelog artifacts (`version_date.tsv`, `docs/changelogs/<tag>.md`, `SECURITY.md`, the Docker `Dockerfile`s) directly, dropping the `auto/<tag>` changelog PR. Idempotent — skips when the changelog is already on `master`. - New release: push the post-release master version bump directly, dropping the `bump_version_<v>` PR and its enqueue. Idempotent by version string; retries on a non-fast-forward. With no release PRs left to land on `master`, the merge-queue machinery is removed (`merge_prs`, `_enqueue_release_pr`, `update_release_info`, the enqueue step), and the AutoReleases open-version-bump-PR guard drops. `--skip-docker` now skips only docker image generation and tagging, not the changelog or version bump. The release-branch Release PR (`release`/`release-lts`) is unchanged. Depends on `robot-clickhouse` being an always-bypass actor on the `master-pull-request` and `master-merge-queue-and-statuses` rulesets (clickhouse-private#66856). ## Validation Direct changelog push to `master` succeeded end-to-end: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/32500716302 — real `CreateRelease` run (`ref=v25.8.32.4-lts`), log shows `remote: Bypassed rule violations for refs/heads/master` and `docs/changelogs/v25.8.32.4-lts.md` landing on `master`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113528&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113528](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113528+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support aggregate functions in the trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114637 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true`) now also fires for projections **with aggregate functions**, e.g. ClickBench Q17 (`SELECT UserID, SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) FROM hits GROUP BY UserID, SearchPhrase LIMIT 10`), while keeping the aggregate values of the returned keys **exact**. **Why it was restricted.** The settings-based rewrite (`max_rows_to_group_by = n + offset` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`) enforces the cutoff per aggregation stream: a key kept by one stream and rejected by another loses the other stream's rows and comes out of the merge with an undercounted value. Returning an unspecified subset of the groups is fine for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`; returning wrong values is not. **How it works now (shared kept keys, zero hot-path cost).** The streams aggregate completely normally until the first one exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys (the pre-existing per-block `checkLimits`). That stream publishes a frozen seed of exactly `n + offset` kept keys with empty aggregate states (`ManyAggregatedData::SharedKeptKeys`); every stream then rebuilds its hash table to exactly that key set — keeping the states it accumulated for the kept keys, dropping the rest — and continues on the pre-existing `no_more_keys` path against a table of `n + offset` keys. Streams that finished consuming before the freeze are rebuilt by the last stream before the merge. Every row before the freeze is aggregated normally and every later row of a kept key finds its key in the rebuilt table, so the merged values are exact; the dropped keys are absent from every rebuilt table and never reach the result. The rebuild reuses the existing two-stage machinery (`convertToChunks(final = false)` + `mergeOnBlock`), so the hot aggregation loops in `Aggregator.cpp` are untouched. **Where it fires.** The cutoff is detected in the planner and enabled only when the node performs the complete aggregation itself (first and second stage): partial states sent to a remote initiator would be merged with other nodes' states, whose kept keys differ, and the values would be undercounted again — across nodes instead of across threads. On the shards of distributed queries and on the replicas of parallel-replicas reading it stays off. The settings-based rewrite of `OptimizeTrivialGroupByLimitPass` remains for aggregate-free projections (it is sound cross-shard). For the 8/16-bit key methods (fixed hash maps bounded by the key space) the cutoff stays inert and the aggregation is complete and exact. External aggregation is disabled when the cutoff is armed (spilled buckets would bypass the restriction); memory stays bounded by roughly `n + offset` keys plus one block of keys per stream. **Guards for wrong results of the existing optimization.** The shape check (shared between the pass and the planner, `getTrivialGroupByLimit`) now also rejects `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions and `arrayJoin` in the projection. These consume or filter the groups after the aggregation, and all four cases were verified to return wrong results on master with the default settings (e.g. `SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 3` returned 1 row instead of 3; `SELECT count() OVER () FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 5` returned ~100 instead of 100000). Test `04837` pins all four in both the top-level (pass) and subquery (planner) forms. The guards are also submitted separately as the minimal backportable bug fix https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 (issue https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114693); whichever merges second needs a trivial conflict resolution. **Measured** on a 96-core aarch64 box, `SELECT number % 100000000 AS k, count() FROM numbers_mt(200000000) GROUP BY k LIMIT 10`: 0.06–0.13 s with the optimization vs 0.37–0.94 s without (interleaved hot runs on a shared machine). The values of the returned keys match the full aggregation exactly (verified by the `04836` join-against-truth tests for `UInt64`/`String`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable`/two-key shapes, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`max`/`uniqExact`, with `OFFSET`, under single-stream and 16-stream execution, from aggregate projections, and over `remote()`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (setting `optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`) now also applies to queries with aggregate functions in the projection, such as ClickBench Q17: once any aggregation thread exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys, all threads are restricted to a single shared set of kept keys, so the hash tables stay small while the aggregate values of the returned keys remain exact (about 2x on ClickBench Q17). Additionally, the optimization no longer fires for queries with `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions, or `arrayJoin` in the projection, where it could return wrong results. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114690&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114690](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114690+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add VALID FOR clause for users and credentials
signal.text: We support `VALID UNTIL` for users and credentials. This adds `VALID FOR <interval>` as a convenience shorthand. Instead of an absolute date and time, `VALID FOR` accepts an interval, and the expiration deadline is computed as the current time plus that interval at the moment the query is executed. The result is stored in the `VALID UNTIL` form, so `SHOW CREATE USER` always displays the resolved absolute deadline. It can be used everywhere `VALID UNTIL` can - at the user level and per authentication method, in both `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER`. Examples: ```sql CREATE USER u1 VALID FOR INTERVAL 1 DAY; CREATE USER u2 IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x' VALID FOR INTERVAL 3 MONTH; ALTER USER u1 VALID FOR INTERVAL 1 DAY + INTERVAL 12 HOUR; ``` Implementation notes: the current time is injected as a literal (rather than using `now`, which is non-deterministic and would not fold to a constant expression), and the deadline is computed with `toDateTime64` so that large intervals saturate at the `DateTime64` upper bound instead of overflowing the year-2106 boundary of `DateTime`. Note on the system table schema: to represent deadlines beyond the year 2106 exactly, the `valid_until` column of `system.users` changes from `Array(DateTime)` to `Array(DateTime64(0))`. This is a backward-incompatible change of a documented system table for tooling that introspects the column type; the values themselves keep second precision. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `VALID FOR <interval>` clause to `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER` as a shorthand for `VALID UNTIL`. The expiration deadline is computed as the current time plus the given interval at query execution time and stored in the `VALID UNTIL` form. The `valid_until` column of the `system.users` table now has the type `Array(DateTime64(0))` instead of `Array(DateTime)`, so that deadlines beyond the year 2106 are represented exactly; tooling that reads this column should handle the new type. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110171&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110171](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110171+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Imply make_distributed_plan from distributed_plan_workers_num
signal.text: Leasing Stateless Workers only makes sense for a distributed query plan, so `distributed_plan_workers_num` no longer has to be paired with `make_distributed_plan`: a non-zero Worker count enables the plan on its own. An explicit `make_distributed_plan` still wins if provided. The implication is applied before the adjustments added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112463, so an implied plan still turns off the features it does not support yet. The derivation is judged under the session's settings constraints: any constraint that forbids enabling `make_distributed_plan` (a `const` pin, a range, a disallowed value) silently vetoes it. A derived plan leaves no trace: the compatibility overrides it applies are remembered and restored when the workers count returns to zero, while an explicitly enabled plan keeps its existing latch semantics. The memory is local to the settings object, so fragment and worker contexts cloned from the initiator keep the overrides. Client-side contexts (`clickhouse-client`, `clickhouse-benchmark`) never derive: they apply server-pushed session settings without constraints and would echo the adjustments back to the server as explicit changes. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114501 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112463 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Setting `distributed_plan_workers_num` to a non-zero value now enables `make_distributed_plan` automatically, unless that setting is set explicitly. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114504&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114504](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114504+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Less logging in the parallel replicas coordinator
signal.text: The parallel replicas coordinator logged the whole working set — every part with all of its mark ranges — at `TRACE` level on each initial announcement (`Initial request`, `Received an announcement`, `Reading state is fully initialized`), and the in-order coordinator repeated the full part list in every read request (`Got read request`). For tables with thousands of parts this produced megabytes of logs per query: ``` DefaultCoordinator(cc.pages): Initial request: replica 6, mode Default, 5148 parts: [03e19ee7d400a1ee1a85e3989e6919dd_0_6588_6[(0, 43773)], 03e19ee7d400a1ee1a85e3989e6919dd_6589_13357_6[(38, 39),(634, 635),(816, 818),... ... megabytes more ``` Now these messages log only the totals (parts, ranges, marks) at `TRACE` level via a new `RangesInDataPartsDescription::describeShort`, the detailed listing is kept under `TEST` level (as `PartsSplitter` already does), and the `describe` methods cap the number of printed elements at 100, so even test-level logs and exception messages stay bounded. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reduce the volume of logs from the parallel replicas coordinator: it no longer prints every part with all its mark ranges on each announcement and read request. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115833&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115833](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115833+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Convert only SEMI JOIN to IN in the convertJoinToIn optimization
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101698 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results with `query_plan_convert_join_to_in = 1`. The optimization replaced a JOIN with `key IN (subquery)` for `ALL` and `ANY` strictness, but `IN` only tests membership: `ALL INNER JOIN` lost rows on a duplicated right key, and `ANY INNER JOIN` returned extra rows on a duplicated left key. Only `SEMI JOIN` is converted now. Closes #101698. ### Description `tryConvertJoinToIn` rewrites a JOIN into `key IN (subquery)` over the left side, emitting each matching left row exactly once: semi-join semantics. The gate excluded strictnesses by name rather than requiring that property, so it admitted two that break it in opposite directions. - **`ALL`**, the default and the reported bug, emits `left_count(k) * right_count(k)` rows, so a duplicated right key multiplies left rows and `IN` loses them: 3 rows off, 2 on. - **`ANY`** deduplicates the *left* side at the default `any_join_distinct_right_table_keys = 0`, so `IN` adds rows: 2 off, 5 on. The gate now admits only `Semi`; `Left` joins the kind gate since `SEMI` needs `LEFT`/`RIGHT`. Six more declines, each a divergence I measured off vs on: - a `Join` engine right side, whose declared kind and strictness the rewrite stops validating: `Join(ANY, LEFT, id)` threw `INCOMPATIBLE_TYPE_OF_JOIN` off, returned rows on; - an active join or transfer size limit: the join bounds its stored right side, the set only its hash table, so a limit could stop being enforced; - a key whose type has dynamic structure, which `IN` rejects; - a key-value prepared right side (dictionary, `EmbeddedRocksDB`, any `IKeyValueEntity`), which the planner probes by key: `DirectKeyValueJoin` off, a 2000000-element set on. The `Join` engine check covers both, testing the whole `PreparedJoinStorage`; - an algorithm the planner would pick ahead of hash, since being enabled is not being chosen: `partial_merge`, `prefer_partial_merge`, `grace_hash` or `auto` listed first streams or spills the right side the set materializes (1 off, 0 on each). Position decides: `hash,partial_merge` still converts. - a key expression consuming a left column the projection needs, throwing `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`. #104809 has since merged that predicate, so master carries it and this branch no longer duplicates it. Master's `03918` regression asserted its conversion arm through an implicit `ALL INNER JOIN`, now declined, so it moves to `SEMI LEFT JOIN` with the algorithm and limits pinned. Its reference is unchanged and both plan arms still discriminate. Requested by @ PedroTadim in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101698#issuecomment-5254250810 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114422&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114422](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114422+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix out-of-bounds write on a long codec chain
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a server crash and an out-of-bounds write when inserting into a column with a long chain of compression codecs, for example `CODEC(FPC, FPC, ..., FPC)`. `CompressionCodecMultiple` compounded each stage's reserved size in a `UInt32` without checking for overflow, so a long enough chain wrapped the reserved size below its own input and the destination buffer was then sized from the wrapped value while the real payload kept growing. Such a chain is now rejected with `CANNOT_COMPRESS`. A chain of more than 255 codecs, which used to write a part that could not be read back, is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` when the codec is created, unless `allow_suspicious_codecs` is set. ### Description `CompressionCodecMultiple::getMaxCompressedDataSize` compounds each stage's reserve in a `UInt32` with no overflow check (`CompressionCodecMultiple.cpp:38`). Every codec reserves at least its own input, so the reserve grows each stage and eventually wraps below its own input. The payload keeps growing too, but more slowly, so from the wrap onward the destination buffer is sized from a small wrapped number while the real data is hundreds of megabytes. `doCompressData`'s unguarded `memcpy(&dest[1 + codecs.size()], ...)` (`:64`) then writes past the end of it. Measured on a plain `MergeTree` table with an ordinary `INSERT` and **no settings**. For `Float32`/FPC the reserve wraps at stage 105 and the payload overtakes it around 135 stages: at 140 ASAN reports a `heap-buffer-overflow` with `WRITE of size 2940232275`, and at 150 the server dies with a SIGSEGV. All of these are now `CANNOT_COMPRESS`; 104 stages still works unchanged. The guard is a per-stage monotonicity check: a stage whose reserve comes back below its own input has wrapped. It is applied at both sites that consume a per-stage reserve. A second check compares the actual post-loop size against the bound, immediately before the `memcpy`; being computed from real output rather than from a bound, it holds wherever inside a codec the arithmetic overflowed. Widening the accumulator does not help: `getCompressedReserveSize` returns `UInt32` and hands back an already-wrapped value. This mirrors the `doDecompressData` hardening in the same file from #60731, making the two directions symmetric. **Behaviour change:** chains of 105-134 stages currently return correct results and are now rejected. Their reserve is already a wrapped, meaningless bound; they avoid overflowing only because the payload has not yet caught up. Not FPC-specific: `DoubleDelta` and `Gorilla` chains wrap the same way, and `Nullable(Float32)` behaves like `Float32`. <details><summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, `clickhouse local` and a real server. The crash arms need the memory limit lifted, since a limit masks the crash as `Code: 241`. | `CODEC(FPC x N)` | before | after | |---|---|---| | 104 | works | works, unchanged | | 105-134 | works, but the reserve has already wrapped | `CANNOT_COMPRESS` | | 140 | ASAN `heap-buffer-overflow`, `WRITE of size 2940232275` | `CANNOT_COMPRESS` | | 150 | SIGSEGV / `span:522` assertion | `CANNOT_COMPRESS` | Chain length is capped at 255 separately: the codec count is stored in one byte, so 256 codecs used to write a part whose count read back as 0 (`Code: 246` on read). 255 codecs round-trips; 256 is now rejected at `CREATE`/`ALTER` with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`, and on the write path with `CANNOT_COMPRESS` for metadata stored earlier. - Both directions, pristine master `25d677a44eb4be59` vs the fix: FPC x150 / 2 rows is `rc=139` SIGSEGV before and `CANNOT_COMPRESS` after; FPC x104 is byte-identical on both. - ASAN (`master-asan-build`, same base): pre-fix `heap-buffer-overflow`, `WRITE of size 2940232275`, `0 bytes after 2147483648-byte region`. - Mutation arms: removing either guard alone still rejects the chain (the other catches it); removing both reproduces the SIGSEGV. With only the outer bound removed, the inner check reports `Compressed data of size 2940232416 does not fit the reserved buffer of size 1622428514`, the exact write ASAN flags. - New test `04812_codec_chain_reserve_overflow`: 50/50 runs pass with randomized settings and 50/50 with randomization off. - `codec`/`compress` suite (188 tests, identical population on both arms): 20 pre-existing environmental failures on both, identical failure sets, **0 regressions**. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113877&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113877](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113877+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread`
signal.text: Each thread accumulates up to `max_untracked_memory` (4 MiB by default) of allocations before reporting them to the server-wide `MemoryTracker`. With many threads, this unreported memory can sum to a large amount, causing the server's tracked memory usage to under-count actual consumption and leading to OOM. This PR introduces a server-level setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) and speculatively charges this amount to the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. The global tracked memory becomes a tighter upper bound on actual consumption when `max_untracked_memory` for those workers does not exceed this setting; operators that permit a larger per-query value must raise the server setting accordingly. The reservation is charged on the server-wide (total) tracker only — deliberately not through the query's tracker chain. Query-level accounting feeds heuristics that compare memory deltas against byte thresholds (conversion of aggregation hash tables to two-level via `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes`, spill-to-disk decisions), and phantom reservations of `num_threads * 4 MiB` trip those thresholds immediately: an earlier revision of this PR that charged the query tracker showed consistent slowdowns of GROUP BY queries in performance tests for exactly this reason. The reservation itself does not alter query-level or user-level accounting (`max_memory_usage`, `memory_usage` in `system.processes`); however, every pipeline worker flushes its pending real allocation reports before releasing its outermost reservation, so those counters and memory-based heuristics can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. The speculative reservation uses the throwing path of the memory tracker, so when it would exceed the server memory limit the corresponding job is treated as failed with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — the same behavior as if the job itself had exceeded the limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) which speculatively reserves this amount on the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. When it is at least the workers' `max_untracked_memory`, it makes server-wide tracked memory a tighter upper bound on actual consumption and reduces the risk of OOM with many concurrent pipeline workers. The reservation does not alter query-level or user-level accounting, but workers flush pending real allocation reports before releasing their outermost reservation, so those counters can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - signal.title: Scale the lldb stacktrace budget by build flavor, keep timed-out dumps
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109455 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109455 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `clickhouse-test` collects C-side backtraces with `lldb -o 'thread backtrace all'` under a hard 30s timeout. On a debug server the attach needs longer, the timeout fires, and the partial dump was discarded too, leaving no C stacks for the wedged process. CIDB, 90 days: 181 `suspiciously small stacktraces` rows over 118 PRs, 80 `timed out after 30 seconds` over 59 PRs, 78 carrying both. Two causes: 1. The 30s budget assumed the backtrace "should finish in seconds even on a debug build". Measured on a 174-thread debug server in the CI stress image, a healthy attach takes 44-118s and returns a complete dump: the cost is symbolization. 2. `shell_get_output` honoured `keep_output_on_error` only for `CalledProcessError`; `TimeoutExpired` is not a subclass, so a timeout returned `""`, discarding what lldb wrote. The per-PID budget now scales with the build flavor, reusing the `slow_build` predicate (debug, TSan/ASan/UBSan/MSan, coverage) that `MergeTreeSettingsRandomizer` uses: 120s on a slow build, 30s unchanged on release (`Stress test (arm_debug)` is 51 of those 80 rows, so the driver is debug). The flavor comes from `args.build_flags`, not the module globals a spawned worker resets; the startup-failure caller runs before those flags exist, so there it is read from the binary via `clickhouse local`, like `is_asan_build`. A separate aggregate ceiling bounds the pid loop and reports skipped pids. The per-test timeout handler keeps 30s, running inside its own fired alarm. A timed-out dump is now kept, decoded and marked truncated. Validated against a live debug server with real lldb: before, 30.8s and a 0-byte dump called suspiciously small; after, 63.6s and 834KB with 348 headers. Forcing the budget below the attach cost keeps 48.7KB where master keeps 0. Reverting each change reddened one of twelve arms, run as a throwaway script since master no longer carries the `ci/tests` file that held them. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114565&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114565](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114565+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support DEFAULT expressions inside Tuple data types
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/2797 `DEFAULT` expressions are now supported for named elements of `Tuple` data types, e.g.: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt8, c Tuple(a UInt8, s String DEFAULT 'Hello')) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; ``` Such defaults exist only at the syntax level: they are pulled up to the column level (for `CREATE TABLE` as well as `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` / `MODIFY COLUMN`), so the stored schema is normalized without any `DEFAULT` inside the data type. The column above is stored as type `Tuple(a UInt8, s String)` with a column-level `DEFAULT tuple(defaultValueOfTypeName('UInt8'), 'Hello')`. A default expression may reference other columns, but not other elements of the same tuple/nested; a reference that collides with an element name is rejected as ambiguous. Building an actual data type while a default is set throws. `DEFAULT` inside `Nested` (which is `Array(Tuple(...))`) or `Array` is not supported yet and is rejected with a clear `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` error, because a scalar element default cannot be represented as a static array column default. Note this is why issue #2797 (which asks specifically for `DEFAULT` on `Nested` elements) is linked as `Related` rather than `Closes`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `DEFAULT` expressions inside `Tuple` data types, e.g. `Tuple(a UInt8, s String DEFAULT 'Hello')`. The default is normalized away from the type and pulled up to the column level. Works for `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER TABLE ... ADD`/`MODIFY COLUMN`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108090&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108090](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108090+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108090&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108090](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108090+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix quadratic reallocation while building h3 array results
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112897 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed quadratic time when the functions `h3kRing`, `h3ToChildren`, `h3PolygonToCells` and `h3PolygonToCellsWithContainment` build their result over many rows. A query over 196 000 rows spent 838 seconds copying memory in a CI stress run; it now takes about 5 seconds. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112897 (same defect class, merged) A `Stress test (amd_asan_ubsan)` hung check aborted with one query at `elapsed = 838 s` against its own `max_execution_time = 10`, having written 0 rows. Its `stacktraces` shows the working thread in `__memmove_sse2_unaligned_erms` under `asan_realloc` under `FunctionH3KRing::executeImpl`: running flat out, not stuck. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114559&sha=7698f8b0d63a71a717fb84a0ffb58a701e12223a&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29 These four functions reserve the result accumulator once per row, e.g. `dst_data.reserve(dst_data.size() + vec_size)` at `h3kRing.cpp:132`. `dst_data` is a `ColumnUInt64 &` and `ColumnVector::reserve` is `reserve_exact`, so capacity lands exactly on the current size every row and the next row reallocs, copying the whole accumulated array: `Θ(n²)`, about 11.6 TB of memmove here (peak memory was only 102 MB). Reserving through `PODArray::reserve` rounds capacity up to a power of two, making the copying amortized `O(n)`. `IColumn::reserve` affects performance only, and `reserve_exact` suits the many callers reserving a final size once, so the four per-row callers are the bug, not the primitive. Cancellation had already been delivered, but the existing per-action check cannot fire inside one `IFunction::executeImpl`; removing the quadratic factor is what lets it run. Validated under ASAN, where the defect shows (a Debug build is linear, because glibc `realloc` extends in place; every CI occurrence is a sanitizer job). Unfixed the query does not finish in 400 s; fixed it returns the same result in 4.8 s. All four functions were measured in both directions, results are byte-identical, and peak memory rises ~1.45x, the expected cost of geometric growth. The new test aborts on unfixed master with `TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED` on its first statement and passes in 1.3 s; the 59 existing h3 tests pass. Two sites share the shape with a *constant* per-row amount, which lowers the factor without bounding the total; each is left for its own change: `s2GetNeighbors.cpp:102` (4 per row) and `AggregateFunctionCategoricalInformationValue.cpp:138` (the function's arity). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115773&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115773](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115773+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1878` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: CI: bound each docker buildx invocation in the Docker image jobs
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `Docker server image` and `Docker keeper image` wedged with no output for about five hours, then died on the praktika 18000s job cap: four times on 2026-08-05 on four unrelated PRs, producing no image and no usable log. No related open issue found. The stall is inside `apt-get update`. apt cannot bound it: `Acquire::http::Timeout` is an **inactivity** timeout, not a wall-clock one. Measured locally, a mirror trickling **a byte per second** runs unbounded past a 700s cap, and `Acquire::Retries=5` does not change that. The failing jobs show that shape. And the retry configured here could never run: both call sites pass `retries` and `retry_errors`, but `Result.from_commands_run` never forwards a `timeout`, so a command that never returns is never retried. All four logs show zero `Retryable error` lines. Both invocations are now wrapped in GNU `timeout`, so an expiry is retried while a real build error still fails fast. The bound starts at 2700s, above the slowest healthy single attempt over 90 days (1819.1s). A fixed bound would not bound the *job*: `main()` loops over os variants and tags, so the invocation count is not fixed, and nine successful builds at 2700s exceed the cap alone. Each invocation instead gets what remains of the cap after a 3600s reserve, divided by the retry count: the scheduled shape's worst case is then 16334s against 18000s. That division is also why the retry count drops from 5 to 2: five attempts fit only up to a 255s bound, seven times below the slowest healthy attempt, where two attempts leave 881s above it. Being one count for all of `Shell.run`'s tokens, it applies to the registry and mirror signatures too. `ci/tests/test_docker_buildx_timeout.py` pins that arithmetic against the job's own cap, and the sentinels arming a real retry by attempt count rather than membership. <details> <summary>Validation (click to expand)</summary> An expiry is recognised on 124, and on the escalated 137 only when `timeout` logged its own KILL diagnostic, so an OOM or an external kill is not mistaken for one: the same discrimination `clickhouse_proc.py` makes with `_TIMEOUT_KILL_DIAG`, with `LC_ALL=C` pinning that translated string. `Acquire::Retries` is deliberately not re-added to the published Dockerfiles, which would revert 7cb40723f9ef632. The `git clone` of `docker-library/official-images` stays unbounded: not the apt layer, never observed wedging. Retry behaviour through the real `Shell.run` at the shipped count of 2: | arm | rc | attempts | verdict | |---|---|---|---| | expiry, child honours SIGTERM | 124 | 2 | retried | | expiry, child ignores SIGTERM (escalated) | 137 | 2 | retried | | succeeds | 0 | 1 | no retry | | real error `exit 7` | 7 | 1 | fails fast | | bare 137 (`kill -9`) | 137 | 1 | no retry | The last two are the discriminating controls. Replacing the KILL diagnostic with a string `timeout` never prints drops the second arm to one attempt, proving the token is read rather than merely present in a list. Quoting is pinned against an unwrapped baseline: the brace group reproduces every argument byte-for-byte, while `bash -c` returns rc=0 and truncates a `--build-arg`. The worst case walks `main()`'s own loop, allowing a wedge in every variant/tag group rather than one per job, since nothing breaks between groups; it is exact by construction, merging combinations that reach the same elapsed. Restoring five retries, or cutting the reserve to 600s, reddens it at 18510s and 18246s. One extra os variant stays green at 17180s, since a shrinking deadline absorbs it, while thirty redden it. A separate arm pins the single tag both scheduled commands request: unreachable `--tag-type release` would build four tags and not fit (23948s). signal.title: Re-land aggregate function `gini` in the `sum` family
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113868 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112280 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New aggregate function `gini`, which calculates the [Gini coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient) of a column of finite, non-negative numeric values. The result ranges from `0` (all values equal) towards `1` as inequality grows; for a sample of `n` values the maximum is `(n - 1) / n`. `NaN` values are skipped, while infinite and negative values are rejected. The function returns `Float64` and consumes `O(n)` memory. ### Description Re-lands the `gini` function that #113868 reverted, following the option-2 spec @ Manerone gave in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763#issuecomment-5217284116. `gini` now registers and folds exactly like `sum`. Relative to #112280 it drops the `getArgumentsThatCanBeOnlyNull` override, `.returns_default_when_only_null = true`, and the `argument_type->onlyNull()` branch in the creator, and touches no file under `src/AggregateFunctions/Combinators/`. The property was doing the work: it made `AggregateFunctionFactory::getImpl` skip its only-null guard and build a real `gini` over `Nullable(Nothing)`, so `gini(NULL)` returned `Float64` `nan` where every `sum`-family function folds to `Nullable(Nothing)`. Without it the fold happens in the `Null` combinator first, which is why `createAggregateFunctionSum` has no equivalent. It also drops `getOwnNullAdapter`, at @ Manerone's request in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114643#issuecomment-5354588069. Keeping it left `gini` the only function in the family whose plain and wrapped forms disagreed on nullability: the `Null` combinator consults that hook only on the object it wraps directly, and for `giniIf` / `giniDistinct` that is `AggregateFunctionIf` / `AggregateFunctionDistinct`, whose own adapters win. So `gini(x)` stayed `Float64` while `giniIf(x, c)` became `Nullable(Float64)`. Dropping it gives parity on the runtime axis too: over a `Nullable` column every form returns `Nullable(Float64)`, `NULL` when no non-`NULL` value qualifies and `nan` when fewer than two do. Non-nullable input is unchanged. Validated against `sum` on the same binary: every literal-`NULL` and `Nullable`-column cell matches its `sum` counterpart, and non-nullable results are unchanged from #112280. Docs: `gini.mdx` plus its slug-map, navigation and redirect entries are restored from their merged state in #114314, which #113868's revert had removed as collateral; the generated region is regenerated from the `FunctionDocumentation` block by `ci/jobs/scripts/docs/autogenerate/autogenerate_docs.py` (`--check` clean) and the page keeps its hand-written header. The slug-map row is needed, not cosmetic: without it the nightly generator resolves no Mintlify destination and fails for this page. The `pr-autogenerated-docs` label is what lets a page carrying the markers pass the generated-region guard, as the guard's own message asks for. cc @Manerone <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114643&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114643](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114643+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix logical error in optimize_or_like_chain with aggregate/window function on LIKE LHS
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a logical error (`Function node with name '...' is not resolved as ordinary function`) that could occur with `optimize_or_like_chain` enabled when an aggregate or window function appeared on the left-hand side of a `LIKE`/`ILIKE`/`match` inside an `OR` chain. ### Description Found by the BuzzHouse fuzzer (STID 3477-117d) on [this CI run](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107567&sha=16ccfffe167f14e51996ce4ec16384f92e4d15d0&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_msan%29). Not caused by that PR — it is a trunk analyzer bug the fuzzer happened to surface there. `isExpressionNonDeterministic` in `ConvertOrLikeChainPass` guarded its `getFunctionOrThrow()` call with `FunctionNode::isResolved()`. `isResolved()` returns true for aggregate and window functions too (it only checks that the function pointer is set), but `getFunctionOrThrow()` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` when the function kind is not `ORDINARY`. So a resolved aggregate (e.g. `count()`) or window function nested under a `LIKE` argument in an `OR` chain tripped the assertion — an exception in release builds, an abort in debug/sanitizer builds. Fix: guard with `isOrdinaryFunction()` instead, matching the existing correct guard in `PlannerExpressionAnalysis`. Aggregate/window functions are never non-deterministic-in-scope-of-query at this point, so recursing into their children is sufficient. Minimal reproducer (aborts before the fix on a debug build): ```sql SET optimize_or_like_chain = 1; SELECT toString(count()) LIKE '%1%' OR toString(count()) LIKE '%2%' FROM numbers(3); ``` Covered by `tests/queries/0_stateless/04545_optimize_or_like_chain_aggregate_lhs.sql` (aggregate and window variants, plus an ordinary-function control that must still collapse). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110641&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110641](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110641+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1882` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
