signal.title: Fix lazy materialization OOB and a Merge LOGICAL_ERROR from unused text index virtual columns
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an out-of-bounds read (release) / logical error (debug) in the lazy materialization optimization, and a logical error in `Pipe::unitePipes` for `Merge` tables, when the direct-read-from-text-index optimization leaves an unused index virtual column in the read header of a `MergeTree` table with multiple `text` indexes. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 `TextIndexDAGReplacer::replace` rewrites text-search predicates into `__text_index_*` virtual columns, recording one per rewritten node, then runs `removeUnusedActions()`. When the rewrite keeps a different index's virtual column (or the original expression), the first virtual's input becomes unreferenced, but `result.added_columns` was not re-filtered, so `createReadTasksForTextIndex` still appended that orphaned column to the `ReadFromMergeTree` output header. `removed_columns` was already reconciled against the surviving inputs; `added_columns` was not, and that asymmetry is the bug. The fix collects the rewritten virtuals as candidates while walking the DAG and only populates `added_columns` after `removeUnusedActions()`, keeping a candidate when its input is in the surviving-inputs set already computed for `removed_columns`. The reading step's header then matches what the plan consumes, and a redundant index read goes away. One orphaned column causes two user-visible failures, both fixed: 1. **Lazy materialization out-of-bounds read** (the reported issue). `optimizeLazyMaterialization2` builds its `required_columns` mask positionally from the input headers above the reading step, which never contain a read-only virtual column. The mask ends up shorter than that step's header and the pass indexes a `std::vector<bool>` past its end: out-of-bounds read in release, `cols.size() == required_columns.size()` assertion in debug. 2. **`Merge` table logical error.** With `text` indexes on both `mapKeys(map)` and `mapValues(map)`, the `mapKeys` virtual wins the predicate and the `mapValues` one is left registered but unreferenced. Under `SELECT count()` nothing else is read, so the dead virtual becomes the indexed child's only output column while a non-indexed sibling's header stays empty. `Pipe::getCommonHeader` picks the first non-empty header and `unitePipes` asserts the empty sibling against it: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream`, a server abort in debug and sanitizer builds. `02346_text_index_bug111422` covers the first shape. The new `04563_text_index_merge_heterogeneous_children` covers the second, which the first cannot reach (no `merge()`, no bare `count()`). It pins the two runner-randomized settings it depends on per setting, not with a blanket tag. <details> <summary>Validation of the new test</summary> Debug build of this branch, memory-capped server, per-slot ports. | arm | build id | result | |---|---|---| | master `f9801d5649` (no fix) | `c29b56ab…` | aborts: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream: different number of columns` (`Block.cpp:308` <- `Pipe.cpp:316` <- `QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:263`) | | this branch, reconciliation loop removed | `fd96fd28…` | aborts: `Column __text_index_idx_map_values_equals_… already added for reading` (`ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4765`); via the test runner: `ClickHouse server died` | | this branch, unmodified | `a0a422da…` | passes byte-for-byte, and 50/50 randomized runs | The pre-fix signature differs between the two bases because this branch's merge-base predates the `already_has_direct_read` re-entry gate (`optimizeDirectReadFromTextIndex.cpp`, `6253632d8da4`): without that gate the pass visits the step twice and the same over-registration trips the duplicate guard before a pipe is united. Same defect, two assertions. Both pinned settings were verified load-bearing and effective: with the pins removed, a client injecting `query_plan_direct_read_from_text_index=0` or `query_plan_text_index_add_hint=0` turns the `EXPLAIN` assertion vacuous (`1 0` -> `0 0`); with the pins present the test matches the reference under either injection and under both together. Full `text_index` suite on this branch, base vs with the new test: 157 -> 158 tests, 7 -> 6 failures, **zero new failures**. All shared failures are environmental on a bare slot server (missing stateful `test.hits` dataset, no `localhost:9000`, and four debug-build 600s timeouts). </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111467&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111467](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111467+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Avoid per-row heap allocations in blocked Myers edit distance
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improved the performance of `levenshteinDistance` (and `editDistance`) for medium-length strings on ARM by avoiding per-row heap allocations in the blocked Myers code path. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 Fixes the ARM regression reported in #106595: `string_similarity` query `0` (`SELECT avg(levenshteinDistance(randomString(300), randomString(300))) FROM numbers(10000)`) was about +12.6% slower on Neoverse-V2. Root cause: the blocked Myers path (`BlockMyersEditDistance`, used for byte needles of 257..8192 bytes) allocated its per-row scratch buffers on the heap once per row through `VectorWithMemoryTracking`: the pattern-mask table `tbl` and the `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` bit vectors. Each allocation pairs a `malloc`/`free` with a `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomic update. On ARM those atomic updates are comparatively expensive, so this per-row churn showed up as the regression. Only this path was affected: the single-word Myers widths (`ByteEditDistanceMyersImpl`, needles up to 256 bytes) already use fixed stack scratch, which is why the other `string_similarity` queries did not regress. Fix: hold the per-row buffers in `PODArrayWithStackMemory`. It keeps an allocation up to its inline capacity in an inline buffer (no heap allocation, no `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomics) and transparently spills to a tracked allocation above it. The per-row allocation is therefore eliminated across each buffer's inline range, and the buffer management is a single idiomatic type instead of a hand-rolled stack-array + tracked-vector + raw-pointer split (suggested by @ nikitamikhaylov). The inline range differs per buffer because their shapes differ: - `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` hold one `Word` per block (1 KB each), so a 128-block inline buffer covers the full 8192-byte blocked-Myers range. - `tbl` is the ASCII pattern table, `256 * num_blocks` words (one row per byte value), so it is 256x larger per block. Its inline buffer covers needles up to 8 blocks (512 bytes, 16 KB); a full-range inline table would be about 256 KB, so longer needles transparently spill `tbl` to a tracked allocation while the bit vectors stay inline. The reported regression (300-byte needles, 5 blocks) is fully on the inline path for every buffer. Correctness: distances are unchanged. `02884_string_distance_function`, `03369_function_arrayLevenshtein` and `04125_array_levenshtein_types` pass, and a differential check of `editDistance` and `editDistanceUTF8` against a brute-force DP reference (1392 random pairs) matches exactly, including the block and inline/spill boundary lengths (64/128/192/256/512/8192). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108185&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108185](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108185+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1883` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Reject a table reference in the IN operator of a constraint expression
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107424 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A constraint whose `IN` operator had a bare identifier on the right-hand side, such as `CONSTRAINT c CHECK a IN (b)`, silently rewrote it into a table reference `default.b` and persisted it. The resulting table rejected every `INSERT` with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`, and the server refused to start once the referenced column was dropped. Such a constraint is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` when it is supplied by `CREATE TABLE`, a full-definition `ATTACH TABLE`, or `ALTER TABLE ... ADD/MODIFY CONSTRAINT`, and when it is copied by `CREATE TABLE ... AS` or `CLONE AS`. Existing tables keep loading. ### Description `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` turns an `IN` right-hand side into a table identifier. Correct in a SELECT, where `x IN t` is shorthand for `x IN (SELECT * FROM t)`, but wrong for a constraint, evaluated against the inserted row. The rewritten AST is persisted. Measured on master, for `CHECK a IN (b)` with `b` a column: `SHOW CREATE` reports a constraint the user never wrote (`IN (default.b)`), and every `INSERT` fails `Code: 47 UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. Dropping that column makes the metadata unloadable, fatal at startup. Found on `Stress test (amd_msan)` in three unrelated PRs, as the fuzzer's operand-swapped mutation of `02841_not_ready_set_constraints`. This adds `checkConstraintExpressionIsValid`, mirroring #107424's key-expression check, applied only to user-supplied DDL. The recursion stops at subquery boundaries, so `IN <table>` inside a subquery keeps working. **Cases found in review.** `CREATE TABLE ... AS src` and `CLONE AS src` parse no declaration; they copy the source constraints, so a legacy source could seed the shape into a new table. Copied constraints go through the same gate. An `ALTER` command that stores nothing (`ADD ... IF NOT EXISTS` on an existing name, `MODIFY ... IF EXISTS` on a missing one) stays accepted as on master, judged against the commands preceding it in the same statement. **What this removes.** Where the identifier names an existing table the constraint did work, but only in the process that parsed the DDL: the load path never applies that visitor, so after a restart `INSERT` fails `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. I reject it rather than keep a form that write-deads a table at the next restart. Tell me if you would rather keep it. Unlike #107424 I do not reject at load time: such metadata exists in the wild. Existing tables keep loading, stay ALTER-able including `DROP CONSTRAINT`, and Replicated databases still recover them. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112992&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112992](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112992+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Report why the stress script failed, not just its exit code
signal.text:
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113857 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `Stress test (*)` and `Upgrade check (*)` wrap the stress script like this: ```sh ... && echo -e "Test script exit code$OK" \ || echo -e "Test script failed$FAIL script exit code: $?" ``` The script's output is never redirected, so it reaches only the job console; the only thing written into `test_results.tsv`, which `stress_job.py::read_test_results` parses into result rows, is the exit status. In the 30 days to 2026-08-09, all **152** `Test script failed` rows (133 pull requests, 6 on master, 11 flavours) had a byte-identical `info` cell of ` script exit code: 1`. Reading three of those job logs gave two unrelated causes, so the family cannot be triaged from the CI database. This captures the output and puts its tail into the `info` cell of the row the wrapper already emits, outside `/test_output` (uploaded wholesale) so a passing run gains no artifact. The script is redirected there and mirrored to the console with `tail --pid`, not piped: `prepare_for_hung_check` drops databases with a fire-and-forget `Popen(..., shell=True)` inheriting the wrapper's stdout, and a pipe reader waits for those clients long after the script exits. The exit code is `$?` after `wait`. Those clients can also append after the script exits, while the mirror ends with it, so the wrapper waits for the capture to stop growing and then prints the bytes the mirror missed. The wait is a bounded size poll, never a wait on the descriptor, since that is what deadlocked the pipe form, and the offset is the mirror's own byte count rather than the file size, which can already include unmirrored bytes. A writer slower than that bound would leave its bytes in `/tmp`, which is not collected, while master printed them at any delay, so the wrapper looks once more when the job ends, from an `EXIT` trap covering the early exits after the row too. The offset advances, so nothing prints twice, and a failing run keeps the capture as `stress_script.log` with the other artifacts. `escaped_tail` is a single-level sibling of `escaped`, which pre-compensates its terminator for `echo -e`; `escaped` is untouched. The reader decodes `\t`, `\r` and `\n` only, so a byte the `Escaped` rule encodes but it does not keeps a visible backslash, and #113857 makes the codec reversible. This fixes visibility, not the trigger: verify with `length(test_context_raw) > 20`, not by the rows disappearing.
Validation (click to expand) Every arm extracted the real wrapper block from each runner by content anchor and drove it with a stub, asserting through the real `read_test_results`. `ci/tests/test_stress_job.py` is byte-identical to master: the executable harness was removed at the reviewer's request, so this is evidence rather than coverage this branch ships. Row content: master gave a 20-byte `info`, this gives 517 bytes with the exception line, one parsed row either way, and the same for a tab, CR, NUL, quote, backslash, embedded `\n`, a cut mid-UTF-8, 708 KB / 40001 lines, an empty capture and three replayed job logs. Late writers, with a console pipe that ends with the container and survivors killed, as the job log behaves: the piped form times out with an empty `test_results.tsv`; a child printing 2 s or later lost the line from row and console before the drain and keeps it after; at 20 s and 30 s the console and the artifact keep it where the previous head lost both, on both runners and when the epilogue aborts early, matching master's console at every delay. A descriptor never closed bounds the wait at 16 s instead of hanging. Each line appears once, exit codes 0/1/42/143 are unchanged with an empty capture, a non-empty capture and an unwritable artifact directory, where preservation warns, and a passing run adds about 6 s and no artifact. Mutations each reddened the relevant arm: inverting the exit-code comparison, deleting `set +e` or the restoring `set -e`, capturing to `/dev/null`, `echo -e` for `printf`, the counted offset for the file size (console 20/20 to 0/20 at a 1.0 s child), and removing the trap. A passing run leaves the `/test_output` file set unchanged, and the `shellcheck -x` finding set matches master on all three files.

signal.title: SQL interface for creating clusters
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse Inc. ### Use case In some deployment modes, it is not possible to change a configuration file to fill in the `<remote_servers>` section, yet it is still desirable to be able to define a cluster for use with a Distributed table. ### Describe the solution you'd like Create a new entity called `CLUSTER`, which is in fact a collection of named collections. Each named collection would represent a shard. Overall it would look like ``` CREATE NAMED COLLECTION shard1 AS user = 'Nikita', password = 'p@s$w0rd', replicas = 'hostname1:9000|hostname2:9000|hostname3:9000', weight = 42, internal_replication=false; CREATE NAMED COLLECTION shard2 AS user = 'default', password = 'qwerty123', replicas = 'hostname4:9000|hostname5:9000|hostname6:9000', weight = 1, internal_replication=false; CREATE CLUSTER remote_cluster (shard1, shard2); ``` After that it will be available for use in the distributed table. Funnily it seems possble to support a command like `CREATE CLUSTER cluster ON CLUSTER another_cluster`

signal.title: Size parallel replicas mark_segment_size by active replica count
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107805 --> Related: #107805 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parallel replicas now size the automatic `parallel_replicas_mark_segment_size` by the number of active replicas, consistent with the reading coordinator, so registered-but-inactive replicas no longer skew segment sizing. ### Description Follow-up to #107805 (the optional `total_nodes_count` / `mark_segment_size` alignment noted in review). #107805 made the parallel replicas reading coordinator size itself by the number of *active* replicas (excluding registered-but-inactive ones), so mark segments are not assigned to replicas that never participate. The automatic `mark_segment_size` heuristic in `ReadFromMergeTree`, however, still derived its work-distribution denominator from `getAllNodeCount()` (the *registered* count via `ParallelReadingExtension::total_nodes_count`). When a replica was registered but inactive the two sizings disagreed. This sources `ParallelReadingExtension::total_nodes_count` from the active replica count through a shared `ClusterProxy::getActiveReplicasCountForParallelReplicas` helper that mirrors the coordinator's sizing exactly: the active count when liveness is known, the registered count when it is not (or when it does not line up with the cluster definition), and a zero-active safety net that falls back to the registered count. `total_nodes_count` feeds only `chooseSegmentSize`, whose result is clamped to `{128, 1024, 16384}` and is never used for indexing, so this cannot go out of range (replica numbering stays bounded by the registered count) and can only make segments smaller, which balances work no worse. The existing integration test `test_parallel_replicas_skip_inactive_replicas` is extended to assert the segment-sizing heuristic sees the active replica count (2), not the registered count (3), when one of three replicas is stopped. Verified the added assertion fails before this change and passes after; the `all_groups` sibling test is unaffected. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109377&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109377](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109377+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

Catalog metadata is stored in Keeper, replicated across nodes that share a replica group, and materialized for use with `Distributed` tables, the `cluster` table function, and `ON CLUSTER` DDL. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Docs added under `docs/en`:** - Guide: [`operations/sql-clusters.md`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/feature-sql-cluster-interface/docs/en/operations/sql-clusters.md) — motivation, `<cluster_metadata>` settings (Keeper `path`, `replica_group`, encryption, `imports`), privileges, `SYNC` / `ON CLUSTER`, coexistence with `remote_servers` / cluster discovery, and end-to-end examples. - SQL reference: `CREATE` / `ALTER` for `ENDPOINT`, `SHARD`, and `CLUSTER`; `DROP` / `SHOW CREATE` updates. - System tables: `system.endpoints`, `system.shards`; `system.clusters` description updated for SQL catalog clusters. **Example use:** ```sql CREATE ENDPOINT replica_01 PROPERTIES (host = 'ch1.example.com', port = 9000, user = 'default', password = 'secret'); CREATE ENDPOINT replica_02 PROPERTIES (host = 'ch2.example.com', port = 9000); CREATE SHARD shard_01 REPLICA (replica_01, replica_02) PROPERTIES (weight = 1, internal_replication = true); CREATE CLUSTER analytics (shard_01) PROPERTIES (secret = 'interserver-secret', allow_distributed_ddl_queries = true); SHOW CREATE CLUSTER analytics; -- Use `analytics` with Distributed / cluster() / ON CLUSTER like a remote_servers cluster

signal.title: Parquet: fuse dictionary-index decoding with the dictionary gather
signal.text: Dictionary-encoded Parquet data pages were decoded in two passes: expand the RLE/bit-packed indexes into a temporary `UInt32` column, then gather the dictionary values at those indexes into the output column (`Dictionary::index`). In `hits.parquet`, ~74% of all values sit in RLE runs of a repeated index (average run length 91 — the stats are quoted in a comment in the decoder), so most of that work was expanding runs into explicit indexes only to gather the very same dictionary value again and again — plus a full write + read pass over the temporary indexes column for everything else. This fuses the two passes (`PageDecoder::decodeAndIndex`, overridden by `BitPackedRLEDecoder`): - an RLE run becomes a single dictionary lookup and a bulk fill of the value; - bit-packed runs are unpacked into a small stack buffer — with the bounds check hoisted out of the inner loop to once per batch, so the loop body is branch-free — and gathered from there; - `Mode::Column` dictionaries keep the old path (`IColumn::index` needs the indexes as a column anyway), as does anything else through the base-class fallback in the reader. On ClickBench Q3 (`SELECT SUM(AdvEngineID), COUNT(*), AVG(ResolutionWidth) FROM hits`) over `hits.parquet` on 2 cores this is 21% faster (0.46 s → 0.36 s, best of 3, interleaved A/B of otherwise identical builds); in the profile, the dictionary gather that took 27% of the query's CPU disappears, closing about half of the gap to DuckDB on this query (0.25 s). Results are bit-identical on checksums over seven dictionary-encoded `hits` columns (including strings) and on nullable dictionary-encoded columns; the Parquet dictionary-filter, prewhere, filter-pushdown and preserve-order stateless tests all pass. The existing `clickbench_parquet_short.xml` performance test covers these query shapes. Profiling context, for the record: after this change the remaining CPU of such queries is snappy decompression, the (now leaner) bit-unpacking, and the aggregation itself. Possible future refinements: SIMD bit-unpacking and batching the per-run `insertRawUninitialized` bookkeeping. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reading dictionary-encoded Parquet data got faster: the dictionary indexes are now decoded and resolved to values in one fused pass, turning runs of a repeated value into bulk fills instead of per-row gathers (~20% faster scans of dictionary-encoded numeric columns). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115819&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115819](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115819+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add experimental support for reading Iceberg v3 deletion vectors

Supported: - Read Iceberg v3 deletion vector metadata from manifest entries: - `referenced_data_file` - `content_offset` - `content_size_in_bytes` - Read Puffin deletion vector blobs from object storage. - Validate DV blob length, magic bytes, and CRC. - Decode Roaring64 deletion vectors. - Apply deletion vectors during reads. - Support mixed reads with: - v2 parquet position delete files - v3 Puffin deletion vectors - Support table functions and table engines through the common Iceberg read path, including local/S3/Azure object storage. - Add an experimental setting: - `allow_experimental_iceberg_deletion_vectors` Not supported: - Writing Iceberg v3 deletion vectors. - Updating existing deletion vectors. - Compaction/rewrite of deletion vectors. - Container-level lazy decoding of Roaring bitmaps. - Hard memory limit on decoded Roaring bitmap memory. - Full Iceberg v3 feature support beyond deletion vector reads. signal.title: Report accepted_rows/accepted_bytes in X-ClickHouse-Summary for async inserts
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57768 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Asynchronous INSERTs now report `accepted_rows`/`accepted_bytes` in `X-ClickHouse-Summary`, so the summary is no longer all-zero when `wait_for_async_insert = 0`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes With `wait_for_async_insert = 0` the HTTP response is sent right after the data is buffered, before anything is parsed or written, so `X-ClickHouse-Summary` was all zeros (the `wait_for_async_insert = 1` case was already fixed by #99879). Following the discussion in the issue — flush-side metrics must not be attributed to the enqueueing query, and new dedicated fields were suggested instead — this adds two fields that describe what the server *accepted* into the async-insert buffer: * `accepted_bytes` — size of the payload accepted at enqueue time; reported for both async modes. * `accepted_rows` — reported once known: after the flush result arrives, when the client waits for it. With `wait_for_async_insert = 0` the row count genuinely does not exist yet at response time (data is parsed at flush), so only bytes are reported there. The fields appear in the summary JSON only when non-zero, so summaries of non-async queries are unchanged, and they are not part of the native protocol (no revision change). `05024_async_insert_summary_accepted` covers both modes; `04046_async_insert_progress_stats` is updated for the new fields. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115721&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115721](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115721+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: `DESCRIBE FILESYSTEM CACHE` refused on the introspection port that lists DESCRIBE as allowed
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **On an introspection port, `DESCRIBE FILESYSTEM CACHE 'x'` fails with `QUERY_IS_PROHIBITED` and a message that itself names DESCRIBE as an accepted kind. The same statement works on a regular port.** - **Root cause:** [`src/Parsers/ASTDescribeCacheQuery.h:9`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Parsers/ASTDescribeCacheQuery.h#L9) - the class has no `getQueryKind` override, so `DESCRIBE FILESYSTEM CACHE` reports `QueryKind::None` instead of `QueryKind::Describe`. The PR added `Kind` to the four `ASTQueryWithOutputImpl` instantiations it needed but did not sweep the remaining kind-less read-only statements that the new allow-list now gates. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `executeQueryImpl` -> `checkQueryIsAllowedOnIntrospectionPort` ([`src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp:2186`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp#L2186)) -> `isAllowedOnIntrospectionPort` ([`src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp:1224`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp#L1224)) switches on `ast.getQueryKind()`. `ASTDescribeCacheQuery` derives from `ASTQueryWithOutput` and never overrides `getQueryKind`, so it falls through to `IAST::getQueryKind`'s `QueryKind::None` ([`src/Parsers/IAST.h:516`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Parsers/IAST.h#L516)) and lands in the `default: return false` arm. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Parsers/ASTDescribeCacheQuery.h:9`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Parsers/ASTDescribeCacheQuery.h#L9) — ASTDescribeCacheQuery has no getQueryKind override -> QueryKind::None - [`src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp:1224`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp#L1224) — isAllowedOnIntrospectionPort switches on getQueryKind; None hits the default arm - [`src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp:2186`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp#L2186) — checkQueryIsAllowedOnIntrospectionPort throws QUERY_IS_PROHIBITED listing DESCRIBE as allowed **Impact:** An operator diagnosing a server stuck in startup or shutdown - exactly the window this port exists for, and the window in which filesystem-cache load is a plausible cause - cannot inspect cache state. The error message actively misleads by listing DESCRIBE as permitted. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `d8bf9a01b85be`). ### How to reproduce ```python cd tests/integration && CLICKHOUSE_TESTS_SERVER_BIN_PATH=<build>/programs/clickhouse CLICKHOUSE_TESTS_CLIENT_BIN_PATH=<build>/programs/clickhouse CLICKHOUSE_TESTS_BASE_CONFIG_DIR=<repo>/programs/server python3 -m pytest test_introspection_port/test.py -v -s --timeout=500 (after appending the two assertions above to test_introspection_port) ``` ### Expected behavior ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Received from 172.18.0.2:9010. DB::Exception: There is no cache by name: nonexistent. ... (BAD_ARGUMENTS) (query: DESCRIBE FILESYSTEM CACHE 'nonexistent') -- i.e. the same error the regular port 9000 returns ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 392. DB::Exception: Received from 172.18.0.2:9010. DB::Exception: Only diagnostic queries are allowed on the introspection port: SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE, EXPLAIN, EXISTS, KILL QUERY, SYSTEM, SET and USE. ... (QUERY_IS_PROHIBITED) (query: DESCRIBE FILESYSTEM CACHE 'nonexistent') ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Add `QueryKind getQueryKind() const override { return QueryKind::Describe; }` to `ASTDescribeCacheQuery` (src/Parsers/ASTDescribeCacheQuery.h). This also fixes `system.query_log.query_kind` for the statement. Alternatively, if the exclusion is intended, qualify both the docs table and the `QUERY_IS_PROHIBITED` message. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `ASTExecuteAsQuery` is the only other `ASTQueryWithOutput` subclass without a `getQueryKind` override; it is correctly refused (EXECUTE AS impersonates in the session), so no second finding. Audit performed with `for f in $(grep -rln "public ASTQueryWithOutput\b" src/Parsers/); do grep -q getQueryKind $f || echo $f; done` - exactly two hits. Found during automated review of [PR #110838](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110838). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr110838_001` </details> cc @mstetsyuk @alexey-milovidov @evillique (from #110838)

signal.title: Fix optimize_functions_to_subcolumns rewriting onto the wrong subcolumn
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115632 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115394 `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` rewrites a function to a subcolumn of its argument (`length(arr)` to `arr.size0`, `isNull(n)` to `n.null`, `mapKeys(m)` to `m.keys`, ...) and hardcodes the type that subcolumn has. It only checked that a subcolumn with that name exists, which is wrong in two independent ways, both giving wrong results. A `Tuple` element or a `JSON` path can claim the name with the same type, and declaration order decides which one a read returns: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (c Tuple(`a.size` UInt64, `a` String)) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO t VALUES ((99, 'abc')); SELECT length(c.a) FROM t SETTINGS optimize_functions_to_subcolumns = 0; -- 3 correct SELECT length(c.a) FROM t SETTINGS optimize_functions_to_subcolumns = 1; -- 99 wrong ``` The same shape affects `empty`, `notEmpty`, `isNull`, `isNotNull`, `count`, `mapKeys`, `mapValues`, `mapContains` and `m['key']`. An enclosing `Nullable` wraps the subcolumn without changing which substream it is - `c.a` is a bare `Array` while `c.a.size0` is `Nullable(UInt64)`, because `Array` cannot be inside `Nullable`. Only `length` lacked the guard the other rewrites already had: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (c Nullable(JSON(`a` Array(Int64)))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t VALUES ('{"a":[1,2]}'), (NULL); SELECT length(c.a) FROM t SETTINGS optimize_functions_to_subcolumns = 0; -- 2, 0 correct SELECT length(c.a) FROM t SETTINGS optimize_functions_to_subcolumns = 1; -- 2, \N wrong ``` To tell these apart, subcolumn resolution now reports the substreams path identifying the resolved subcolumn, not just its data (`getSubcolumnData` becomes `getSubcolumnInfo`). Subcolumns resolved from the data get a synthesized path too, so all of them are identifiable the same way. The optimizer asks the serialization owning the substream whether the resolved subcolumn is the one the rewrite means, and additionally requires the exact type; neither check catches the other's case. Subsumes `subcolumnIsNullableInStorage` and `nestedTypeHasNullSubcolumn`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results from `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns`. A `Tuple` element or a `JSON` path named like an automatic subcolumn claimed it, so for example `length(c.a)` on ``Tuple(`a.size` UInt64, `a` String)`` returned the element instead of the length; `empty`, `notEmpty`, `isNull`, `isNotNull`, `count`, `mapKeys`, `mapValues`, `mapContains` and `m['key']` were affected the same way. Separately, `length` on an `Array` or `Map` inside a `Nullable` (for example ``Nullable(JSON(`a` Array(Int64)))``) returned NULL instead of 0 for a NULL row. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115777&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115777](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115777+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Speed up `IN (subquery)` set building by pre-deduplicating each `MergeTree` partition independently
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108326 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105126 The set for `IN (subquery)` is built by a single `CreatingSetsTransform`: all streams of the subquery are merged into one and every row is hashed serially, no matter how many threads read the data. If the partition expression of the subquery's table is a function of the subquery's output columns (the set is keyed on all of them), the reading will now emit each partition through a single port and each stream is deduplicated independently before the filling transform. Because a key then lives in exactly one stream, per-stream deduplication is complete, and the single filling transform only hashes unique rows — the serial part of the build shrinks from all rows to distinct rows, and the deduplication itself runs in parallel. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() PARTITION BY a % 8; INSERT INTO t SELECT number % 1000000 FROM numbers(100000000); OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL; EXPLAIN PIPELINE SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t) SETTINGS allow_creating_set_partitions_independently = 1, max_threads = 8; ``` ```response (CreatingSets) DelayedPorts 9 → 8 (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (Aggregating) Resize 1 → 8 AggregatingTransform (Expression) ExpressionTransform (Filter) FilterTransform (ReadFromSystemNumbers) NumbersRange 0 → 1 (CreatingSet) CreatingSetsTransform <- the single filling transform now hashes ~1M unique rows instead of 100M Resize 8 → 1 DistinctTransform × 8 <- new: parallel pre-deduplication on partition-disjoint streams (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (ReadFromMergeTree) MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder) × 8 0 → 1 <- per-partition reading (8 partitions → 8 streams) ``` On the table above (100M rows, 1M distinct keys, 8 balanced partitions; 64-core machine, average of 3 runs after 2 warm-ups): | query | off | on | speedup | |------------------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|---------| | `SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t)` | 0.643s | 0.113s | 5.7× | ### Adaptive abandonment of the preliminary deduplication The per-stream `DistinctTransform` in front of the set fill pays off only when it removes rows: the set deduplicates anyway, so on mostly-unique input the transform removes almost nothing while its hash tables hold roughly a second copy of the unique keys next to the set being built. To keep the optimization strictly non-regressing, the pre-deduplication observes its own effectiveness and gives up when it is not helping (`DeduplicationAbandonController`): * It accumulates, over all chunks seen so far, how many rows survived deduplication. The rate is first checked after 5 chunks — or earlier, once the observation itself retains 16 MiB of hash table, so wide keys (e.g. long strings) cannot hold multiples of that just to finish the window. From then on it is checked after every chunk, so duplicates concentrated at the head of a stream do not keep a useless hash table alive through a unique tail. * When at least 90% of the observed rows survive, the transform abandons: it frees its hash table and passes the remaining chunks through untouched. This is correct only because the consumer deduplicates anyway, so abandoning is allowed by an explicit constructor flag that only the set-fill call site enables. * The 0.9 threshold is calibrated on per-partition set builds over uniform data: keeping the deduplication is ~8–11x at ~1% uniqueness and ~1.2x at 10%, turns time-neutral but memory-negative once only about a quarter of the rows are duplicates — which the observation sees as a unique rate of about 0.9, because a stream's duplicates concentrate in its partition and repeat within the window. The transform also mirrors the set fill's `NULL` handling: with the default `transform_null_in = 0` the fill drops every row with a `NULL` in any key component, so the pre-deduplication drops them too (using the same `extractNestedColumnsAndNullMap` helper, plus the dictionary `NULL` entry for `LowCardinality(Nullable)` keys) instead of hashing them and letting them distort the abandon decision. Chunks fully resolved by the `LowCardinality` dictionary mask are likewise counted as duplicate rows. Together this keeps the abandon decision based on exactly the row population the fill would hash. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up set building for `IN (subquery)` on partitioned `MergeTree` tables by keeping each partition's rows within a single stream and deduplicating each stream independently, so the single set-filling transform — previously hashing every row serially — only sees unique rows. This applies when the partition expression is a deterministic function of the subquery's output columns. The optimization is not applied when the largest partition holds more than twice the rows of the average partition; the new setting `force_creating_set_partitions_independently` (disabled by default) bypasses this check. Controlled by the new setting `allow_creating_set_partitions_independently` (enabled by default). --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114645&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114645](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114645+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]

signal.title: AI functions: Make quotas per query not per block
signal.text: `AIQuotaTracker` was a stack local inside `executeImpl`, so every block and every pipeline stream started with a fresh allowance. The `ai_function_max_api_calls_per_query`, `ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query` and `ai_function_max_output_tokens_per_query` limits therefore scaled with the data (one allowance per block per function) instead of bounding the query — any limit above the largest block's row count could never fire. The tracker is now a single instance owned by the query `Context` and shared by every AI function call in that context, with atomic counters for the concurrent pipeline threads. The API-call limit is claimed with an atomic bounded reservation, so it is an exact cap within a query-execution context even under `max_threads > 1`; the token limits are best-effort, since a call's token usage is known only after its response arrives. The limits are enforced per server / query fragment: a distributed query (across shards or parallel-replica fragments) enforces them independently on each, not summed globally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The AI-function quota settings (`ai_function_max_api_calls_per_query`, `ai_function_max_input_tokens_per_query`, `ai_function_max_output_tokens_per_query`) were enforced per block rather than per query, letting a query exceed the configured limit in proportion to the number of blocks and threads processed. They now bound the whole query per server: the API-call limit is an exact cap (atomic reservation), and the token limits are best-effort. A distributed query enforces the limits independently on each participating server / fragment. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114885&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114885](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114885+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1732` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Check the query cancellation while filling `system.parts` and its siblings
signal.text: The tables based on `StorageSystemPartsBase` (`system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`) build the whole result eagerly in `initializePipeline`, so a cancelled or timed out query kept building rows over every storage and part until the very end. In a stress test with ThreadFuzzer this took minutes and tripped the hung check: a `SELECT` over `system.parts_columns` (with a filter matching every active part on the server) stayed in the process list for 252 seconds with `is_cancelled = 1` and `max_execution_time = 10`. Check the query status per storage and per part, following the pattern of `system.zookeeper` and `system.remote_data_paths`. The check also covers the storage-discovery prepass in `StoragesInfoStream` (the eager enumeration of all databases and tables), the analogous prepass in `StoragesDroppedInfoStream` (so `system.dropped_tables_parts` is interruptible as well), the skip loop in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::next`, and the per-storage part enumeration itself: the `MergeTreeData` helpers (`getDataPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllDataPartsVector`, `getProjectionPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllProjectionPartsVector`) take an optional `need_stop` callback that is checked periodically while the parts snapshot is being built. The two column-oriented tables additionally check the query status inside their column-enumeration loops and their metadata prepass, so a very wide table does not create a long uninterruptible stretch inside a single storage. The return value of `checkTimeLimit` is honored, so with `timeout_overflow_mode = 'break'` the eager build stops at the soft deadline and returns the rows collected so far. The table-lock acquisition in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::tryLockTable` is interruptible as well: instead of a single wait inside `RWLockImpl::getLock` for the whole `lock_acquire_timeout`, the lock is acquired in 100 ms slices with a query-status poll between the attempts (the total timeout and the `DEADLOCK_AVOIDED` semantics are preserved), so a killed or soft-timed-out query does not sit in the lock wait while a concurrent DDL query holds the drop lock. The test `04869_system_parts_lock_wait_cancellation` pins this with a share lock held by a long `SELECT` and a `DROP TABLE` in an `Ordinary` database queued behind it. The test uses the new `slowdown_system_parts_enumeration` failpoint, which only affects the specially named test tables (so concurrently running tests are unaffected). It sleeps 500 ms on every enumerated part, so building the full result for a 20-part table takes at least 10 seconds, and it sleeps 1 second per `COLUMNS_CANCELLATION_CHECK_PERIOD` (128) enumerated columns of a part, so building the full `system.parts_columns` / `system.projection_parts_columns` result over a single part with 1,025 columns (and a projection over all of them) takes at least 8 seconds. The test asserts that queries with a 1 second deadline in the `break` mode finish well under that (the elapsed time is taken from `system.query_log`, because the startup of `clickhouse-client` alone takes seconds in the debug and sanitizer builds), which is only possible by stopping at the per-part and per-column cancellation checkpoints. Timed assertions are needed because a plain row-count assertion cannot distinguish a build with the fix from one without: in the `break` mode the executor drops the eagerly built result after the deadline in both cases. The test also asserts partial row counts under a pre-expired deadline for all five tables, including `system.dropped_tables_parts` over a deterministic dropped-table fixture. The pre-expired-deadline checks also run under the failpoint, so the fewer-rows assertion is deterministic even on a machine fast enough to build the whole result in under a millisecond. For tables with the `_snap` name marker, the failpoint additionally slows down the parts-snapshot walks inside `MergeTreeData` (500 ms per enumerated part) and makes them poll the stop callback on every element, and for tables with the `_meta` name marker it slows down the column-metadata prepass of the column-oriented tables (1 second per 128 enumerated metadata columns), so the timed checks also prove that the snapshot materialization and the prepass are interruptible: all six of these checks fail against a binary with the `need_stop` polls and the prepass checkpoints disabled. Caught by `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113722&sha=ceedb772f6aa36e221d25ce48f9af71f032a7b08&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113722 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Queries over `system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`, and `system.dropped_tables_parts` now react to cancellation and `max_execution_time` while the result is being built. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113909&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113909](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113909+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add the experimental Trino SQL dialect
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental `trino` value of the `dialect` setting (gated by `allow_experimental_trino_dialect`): queries written in Trino SQL are translated to ClickHouse SQL, including Trino-specific syntax (`ARRAY[...]` literals, `TRY_CAST`, `UNNEST`, `ROW` constructors and types, `VALUES` tables, `OFFSET` before `LIMIT`, `FETCH`) and a mapping of several hundred Trino function names and argument conventions to their ClickHouse equivalents. Since Trino SQL is close to ClickHouse SQL (which already parses `AT TIME ZONE`, `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, `DATE`/`TIMESTAMP` literals, `GROUPING SETS`, `NULLS FIRST/LAST`, `WITH RECURSIVE`, ...), the dialect is not a separate grammar. It works in three stages in `src/Parsers/Trino/`: 1. **Token-level syntax translation** (`TrinoSyntaxTranslator`): `ARRAY[1, 2]` -> `[1, 2]`, `TRY_CAST(x AS t)` -> `accurateCastOrNull(x, 't')`, `ROW(...)` -> `tuple(...)` / `Tuple(...)`, `UNNEST` in `FROM` -> `ARRAY JOIN` (`LEFT JOIN UNNEST ... ON TRUE` -> `LEFT ARRAY JOIN`, `WITH ORDINALITY` -> `arrayEnumerate`, maps -> `mapKeys`/`mapValues`), `(VALUES ...)` -> a subquery over `SQLStandardValues`, `OFFSET n LIMIT m` -> `LIMIT m OFFSET n`, `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY/WITH TIES` -> `LIMIT`, `TIMESTAMP(p) [WITH TIME ZONE]` type -> `DateTime64(p)`, lambdas are parenthesized (the ClickHouse parser cannot parse a lambda after a literal argument), and backslashes in string literals are escaped (in Trino a backslash is a regular character). 2. **The standard ClickHouse parser** parses the result. If nothing needed translation, the original buffer is parsed directly, and `INSERT` statements with inline data (`VALUES`/`FORMAT`) are always delegated as-is so that the zero-copy data pointers stay valid. 3. **AST-level function mapping** (`TrinoFunctionMapper`): ~100 renames plus ~50 structural rewriters built from a review of all ~340 functions in the Trino documentation. This includes argument reordering for every higher-order function (Trino passes lambdas last, ClickHouse first: `transform(arr, f)` -> `arrayMap(f, arr)`), parametric-aggregate conversion (`approx_percentile(x, p)` -> `quantileTDigest(p)(x)`, `listagg(x, sep)` -> `groupConcat(sep)(x)`), and — most importantly — the names that resolve in ClickHouse with **different semantics** and would silently return wrong results if passed through: `to_unixtime` (an alias of `parseDateTime` in ClickHouse), `date_diff` (boundary crossings vs complete units -> `age`), `week` (non-ISO mode 0 -> `toISOWeek`), `from_unixtime(u, x)` (format string vs time zone), `rand`/`random` -> `randCanonical`, `transform`, `repeat`, `histogram`, `map(karr, varr)` -> `mapFromArrays`, `format` -> `printf`, and the varchar family (`length`, `substr`, `upper`, `lower`, `strpos`, `lpad`, ...) which is code-point-based in Trino and byte-based in ClickHouse (-> `...UTF8` variants). The feature gate follows the `polyglot` pattern: `SET` queries are handled before the gate inside the parser, so a misconfigured profile can always be recovered with `SET dialect = 'clickhouse'`. ClickHouse functions whose names do not collide with Trino names remain accessible from the dialect. Unsupported constructs (`TABLESAMPLE`, `TRY(...)`, comparator `array_sort`, ...) throw explicit `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`/`BAD_ARGUMENTS` errors instead of misbehaving, and semantics that cannot be fixed by translation at the query level (integer division `/`, `round` banker's rounding on Float, `greatest`/`least` NULL handling) are documented. The translation is observable with `EXPLAIN SYNTAX`. Note: `polyglot_dialect = 'trino'` already exists via the `polyglot` transpiler, but it performs no function mapping and passes `ARRAY[...]` through untranslated; this first-class dialect provides a much more complete translation. `BETWEEN SYMMETRIC` is translated to `BETWEEN least(a, b) AND greatest(a, b)`, and the Trino `JSON` type family is mapped to the ClickHouse `JSON` type, accepting that only objects are supported: `JSON '...'` literals and `json_parse` become casts to `JSON`, `json_format` becomes `toJSONString`, and `json_extract`, `json_extract_scalar`, `json_value`, `json_query`, `json_exists`, `json_size`, `json_array_contains` and `is_json_scalar` are translated to the ClickHouse JSON functions (the string-based JSONPath functions do not accept the `JSON` type, so casts flowing directly into them are unwrapped back to the JSON text; non-object documents are rejected when materialized as `JSON` values). Validation: the translation was exercised against four corpora derived from Trino's own tests and documentation: - **732 self-contained query/expected pairs** extracted from Trino's functional tests (`core/trino-main/src/test/java/io/trino/sql/query/Test*.java`): 206 produce identical results; of the rest, ~270 need ClickHouse engine features (`LATERAL` joins alone gate 139, plus correlated-subquery decorrelation shapes and non-integer window frame offsets) and the remainder are unsupported constructs or documented semantic differences. 75 order-deterministic pairs are committed as `05021_trino_conformance` (following the KQL conformance-test precedent), and three more conformance tests pin the adopted corpora: `05022_trino_conformance_presto_scalar` (1054 Presto scalar-function assertions), `05023_trino_conformance_tempto` (119 Tempto product-test queries running against their fixture tables inlined into the test), and `05024_trino_conformance_impala` (44 generic-SQL Impala expressions) — every adopted query verified to produce the documented result and to be stable under randomized time zones, thread counts and block sizes. - **43 convention-based Tempto product tests** (`testing/trino-product-tests` at tag 455, `.sql`/`.result` pairs): 30 of the 34 runnable ones match (using the fixed 25-row `nation`/5-row `region` TPC-H tables). - **294 `SELECT`-with-expected-result examples** from the official function documentation: 142 match. - The **22 TPC-H queries in Trino dialect** from `testing/trino-benchmark-queries`: all parse and translate. - **1689 scalar-function assertions** scraped from `prestodb/presto` unit tests (`assertFunction("expr", TYPE, value)` style) plus the **130 Tempto product tests Presto kept after the fork**, executed against real TPC-H sf0.01 data and the `datatype`/`workers` fixture tables: 1059 and 91 match respectively (most of the rest use Presto-only functions that do not exist in current Trino). The 43 Trino-era Tempto tests reach 38/43 with the data available. - **146 expression tests** from `apache/impala` as a generic-SQL cross-check (Impala is a different dialect; 44 match, and the divergences are Impala-specific by design — e.g. Impala's `LIKE` treats a backslash as an escape character while Trino treats it literally). These corpora drove another round of semantic fixes: outer joins produce NULLs (`join_use_nulls`), `sum`/`avg`/`min`/`max` over an empty set return NULL (`-OrNull` variants), `count` returns a signed bigint, `greatest`/`least` propagate NULL arguments, LIKE backslash literalness, minute-precision `TIMESTAMP` literals, `reduce` output lambdas, `bit_count` arbitrary widths, `width_bucket` over an array of bounds, and `json_array_get`. Of the 294 examples, 142 produce results matching the documentation (plus a few that differ only by printing the current time or the session time zone); most of the rest use deliberately unsupported constructs (SQL:2016 `MATCH`/`UNIQUE` predicates, `U&'...'` literals, functions with no ClickHouse counterpart, non-object `JSON` documents per the design above). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115383&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115383](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115383+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add native Version data type (proof of concept)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adds a native `Version` SQL data type for semantic-version-style values (`major.minor.patch.build`), enabling correct numeric ordering instead of lexicographic string comparison. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes: The new `Version` type stores versions of up to 4 components, such as `major.minor.patch.build`. Comparisons between these values correctly evaluate numeric size, meaning `toVersion('1.2') < toVersion('1.10')` is true. `Version` values parse 1-4 dot-separated non-negative integer components, zero-padding missing trailing components (`1.2` is equal to `1.2.0`). ### Description **Summary** Adds a native `Version` SQL data type for semantic-version-style values (`major.minor.patch.build`), so comparisons use correct numeric ordering instead of lexicographic string comparison: ```sql SELECT '1.2' < '1.10'; -- 0 (wrong, string comparison) SELECT toVersion('1.2') < toVersion('1.10'); -- 1 (correct) SELECT toVersion('1.2') = toVersion('1.2.0'); -- 1 (padding equality) ``` Stored as a packed `UInt128` (`(major<<96)|(minor<<64)|(patch<<32)|build`), so `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `!=` all work natively via plain integer comparison — no custom operator overloads needed. Parsing (`toVersion`/`toVersionOrNull`/`toVersionOrZero`/`toVersionOrDefault`) accepts 1–4 dot-separated non-negative integer components, zero-pads missing trailing components, and rejects more than 4 components or any non-numeric component. Leading zeros parse numerically (`01` → `1`). Pre-release/build-metadata suffixes (`-beta`, `+build1`) are intentionally out of scope for this first pass. **Design decision: numeric-only model, not full semver** Per review discussion (thanks @groeneai), `1.0.0-alpha`-style pre-release ordering was considered and deliberately rejected: the 4 `UInt32` components already fill the `UInt128` with no spare bits, and semver's ordering rule (`0.9.9 < 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0`) has no integer to sit between two adjacent packed values, so supporting it would require replacing the fixed integer-packing model with a comparison-based one, giving up free integer ordering. `Version` therefore stays a 4-component numeric-only scheme — closer to `ClickHouse`'s own version scheme (`24.3.1.2672`) than to semver — and text with a pre-release/build-metadata suffix is rejected with `CANNOT_PARSE_VERSION` rather than silently truncated. This is now documented directly on the type in `base/base/Version.h`/`DataTypeVersion.h`. **Caveats** This is exploratory. I've verified it manually end-to-end against a real build via `clickhouse local` (parsing, padding-equality, numeric ordering, and both rejection cases all confirmed), but: - It has **not** been run through the full functional/stateless test suite, only the two new test files included here. - The wire-format tag byte choices (`FieldBinaryEncoding.cpp` uses `0x16`, `DataTypesBinaryEncoding.h` uses `0x38`) are new protocol constants — once shipped these are effectively permanent for backward compatibility, so they deserve explicit maintainer review before being treated as final. - No prior design discussion/RFC happened before writing this — I'd like feedback on whether a type like this is wanted at all, and on the packing/validation choices, before investing further in edge cases and full test coverage. **Test plan** - [x] `tests/queries/0_stateless/04614_data_type_version_basic.sql` — parsing/round-trip/padding - [x] `tests/queries/0_stateless/04615_data_type_version_comparison.sql` — ordering + rejection cases - [x] Manual verification via `clickhouse local` against a full local build - [x] Full stateless/functional test suite (not run) - [x] Style/clang-tidy pass 🤖 Generated with heavy AI assistance (agentic exploration + implementation), per [AI_POLICY.md](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/AI_POLICY.md) — disclosing since this was a substantial, multi-file core-engine change built through an unusually AI-heavy process, not just a docs tweak.

The engine defect is old and is not what I change here. The stress profile sets `ast_fuzzer_runs = 5` and `ast_fuzzer_any_query = true` (`tests/docker_scripts/stress_tests.lib`), so the server-side AST fuzzer re-runs mutated copies of every statement of every stateless test, `CREATE` included. In `04870` it retypes the fixture's `Merge` parent and substitutes the clone into a `SELECT`, and a `Merge` parent whose column type differs from its child's is the precondition for the assertion. My test is the amplifier, and this PR removes only that. The defect itself is #113242, still open. The change is one statement, `SET ast_fuzzer_runs = 0;`, pinning the setting to its own declared default. It weakens nothing: all seven arms still run and still assert, and the `.reference` file is unchanged. Nine stateless tests already pin it, several for this same reason. It is file-level rather than per-query because the chain needs both a fuzzed `CREATE`, to mint the clone, and a fuzzed `SELECT`, to substitute it in. `-- Tags: no-stress` is not an option, `clickhouse-test` rejects it. Validation, one debug binary differing only in the test file: with the fuzzer armed the unpinned test fails 6 of 30 runs and the pinned test passes 30 of 30. I also reproduced the abort on a hand-built mistyped fixture, with a stack matching CI. 50 randomized runs, and 50 with the fuzzer armed, pass. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115839&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115839](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115839+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Lazy materialization OOB: cols.size() mismatch (debug) + release vector<bool> out-of-bounds read with Map subscript + two text indexes
signal.text: # Lazy-materialization OOB — `cols.size()` mismatch and release `vector<bool>` out-of-bounds read with Map subscript + text indexes ## Summary A `MergeTree` `SELECT` with **two `text` skip indexes** on `mapValues(map)` and `mapKeys(map)`, plus `PREWHERE` and `WHERE` clauses each referencing a **different** Map subscript, plus `LIMIT` (which triggers the lazy-materialization pass), aborts on both build modes: - **Debug/sanitizer:** `Logical error: 'cols.size() == required_columns.size()'` at `src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/optimizeLazyMaterialization.cpp:544` (`optimizeLazyMaterialization2`). - **Release:** libc++ hardening detects `vector<bool>::operator[] index out of bounds` at `contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__vector/vector_bool.h:297` — a **genuine out-of-bounds read**, not masked. Both symptoms are the same underlying bookkeeping bug in the lazy-materialization pass: the optimizer's column-count arithmetic desynchronizes from the actual `required_columns` set when the plan mixes Map subscripts with text-index-covered predicates, then indexes a `vector<bool>` past its end. Found by the AST-fuzzer-oracle campaign (PR #99980), snapshot `runs/merged15/crashes/inst-02-20260720-200503` (old master, surfaced as `verbose_abort:62`); rechecked + reduced on current master **`4c1b7ef9edcd`** (2026-07-22). ## Reproduction — self-contained, verified on both debug and release ```sql CREATE TABLE tab ( id UInt32, map Map(String, String), INDEX idx_mv mapValues(map) TYPE text(tokenizer = 'array') GRANULARITY 100000000, INDEX idx_mk mapKeys(map) TYPE text(tokenizer = 'array') GRANULARITY 100000000 ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS index_granularity = 1, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO tab VALUES (1, {'127.0.0.1':'a', '::1':'b'}), (2, {'x':'y'}), (3, {'(':'z'}); SELECT id FROM tab PREWHERE '(' IN (map['127.0.0.1']) WHERE map['::1'] IN '(' ORDER BY ALL LIMIT 681; ``` Debug output: ``` Logical error: 'cols.size() == required_columns.size()' src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/optimizeLazyMaterialization.cpp:544 ``` Release output (with libc++ hardening enabled, as in the release fuzz build): ``` vector<bool>::operator[] index out of bounds contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__vector/vector_bool.h:297 ``` ## Path ``` InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer::buildQueryPipeline → QueryPlan::optimize → optimizeTreeSecondPass → optimizeLazyMaterialization2 (optimizeLazyMaterialization.cpp:544) ``` The optimizer's column-count bookkeeping desynchronizes: it computes a `required_columns` set of size N based on the pre-optimization plan (Map-subscript virtual columns + text-index synthetic columns), but produces a `cols` vector of size ≠ N when it walks the actual index-read plan. The subsequent `cols[i]` accesses index a `vector<bool>` past its end — caught by the assert on debug and by libc++ hardening on release. ## Minimization / load-bearing conditions - **BOTH text indexes are required.** With only `idx_mv` (mapValues) or only `idx_mk` (mapKeys) the query runs clean. - **PREWHERE and WHERE must reference DIFFERENT Map subscripts.** Dropping either the PREWHERE or the WHERE — or using the same subscript in both — makes it clean. - **`LIMIT` is required** (it's what triggers the lazy-materialization pass). Removing `LIMIT` is clean. - **The three-row dataset shown is sufficient** (a Map with 2 entries, one with 1 entry, one with the `'('` key). The `'('` value/key in row 3 is what the PREWHERE / WHERE constants match against. - `GLOBAL` is not needed (plain `IN` works). Any constant `SELECT` decoration is not needed either. - `index_granularity = 1` reproducibly triggers the mark bookkeeping; larger granularity may not. ## Environment - ClickHouse `26.7.1.1`, git hash `4c1b7ef9edcd` (master + 868 commits over the fuzz base), aarch64. - Reachable via ordinary user SQL — `text` skip index and `Map` are supported features, no experimental gate needed at the SQL level. ## Suggested fix direction `optimizeLazyMaterialization2` must reconcile its `required_columns` vs. `cols` arithmetic when the plan includes text-index-covered Map subscripts. Either (a) exclude text-index-covered virtual columns from the lazy-materialization eligibility, or (b) recompute the bit-vector size to match the post-optimization column layout. The release out-of-bounds read is only visible because our release build has libc++ hardening enabled. Downstream users on release builds without hardening would see silent undefined-behavior reads (potentially returning garbage rows), so a fix on release is more urgent than the debug assertion alone would suggest.

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/series
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/series`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus clients** use **`/api/v1/series`** to discover the label sets stored for active series. This endpoint is used by **Prometheus-compatible tools** such as **Grafana** when they need to populate metric and label selectors. ClickHouse **`TimeSeries` tables** can store labels in the main **`tags` Map**, in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, or in a mixture of both layouts. The endpoint needs to expose the **same logical series** regardless of how those labels are stored. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/series` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint is available through both a **dedicated `/api/v1/series` handler** and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**. It supports **GET requests** and **`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POST requests**. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** selects series by metric name and label matchers. Repeated parameters are combined as a **union** and overlapping results are returned only once through **deduplication**. - **`start` and `end`** select series overlapping the requested **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the number of returned series and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Selector parsing:** parse Prometheus series selectors with equality, inequality, regular-expression, and negative regular-expression matchers. - **Storage compatibility:** support metric names, labels in the **`tags` Map**, dedicated tag columns, and mixed rows that use both storage layouts. - **Label normalization:** normalize missing labels to the **Prometheus empty-value semantics** and include the full logical label set in each response. - **PromQL compatibility:** support quoted label names and anchor regular expressions to the **complete label value**. - **Input validation:** validate selectors and timestamps before executing the query. - **Time ranges:** apply the time-range filter when trusted min/max data is available. When it is not available, keep the request valid and return the **compatible candidate superset** allowed by the Prometheus API. - **Result limits:** support zero and positive limits, exact-limit responses, truncation reporting, and invalid-value errors. - **Access control:** read the underlying series metadata through the **`TimeSeries` table-function path** after checking access to the configured **`TimeSeries` table**. Unknown routes are resolved before authorization, so they keep the normal **404 response**. - **Existing endpoints:** apply the configured **`TimeSeries` table access boundary** consistently to the existing Prometheus query endpoints. - **Query lifecycle:** run the generated query through the **normal query pipeline** and keep **query logging** and **query completion handling** intact. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Matcher operators:** metric-name and label selectors with all matcher operators. - **Repeated selectors:** repeated **`match[]`** parameters, selector unions, and overlapping-result deduplication. - **Storage layouts:** Map labels, dedicated tag columns, missing labels, mixed carriers, conflicting carriers, and **`__name__`**. - **Regex and names:** quoted label names and whole-value regular-expression anchoring. - **Selector validation:** invalid and unbounded selectors, including the valid **`{host!~".*"}`** case. - **Time ranges:** two-sided, one-sided, inclusive, and invalid time ranges. - **Min/max behavior:** requests with and without trusted min/max metadata. - **Limits:** zero, exact, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values. - **HTTP methods:** GET and form POST requests. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants**, access checks for all query endpoint families, and unknown-route handling. - **Observability:** query completion records and the existing query API limit behavior. Also ran **Python syntax checks** and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now covers the Prometheus handler configuration and the **`/api/v1/series` endpoint parameters**. ### Stack This is the **base PR** for the follow-up Prometheus API endpoints: - **#114868** adds **`/api/v1/labels`**. - **#114869** adds **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`**. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114867&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114867](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114867+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Use actual codec to estimate compressed column sizes for dataflow statistics
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Take a column's CODEC into account when estimating how many bytes a query reads from compact parts. The estimate compressed a sample with the default codec (`LZ4`) no matter how the data is really stored, so a column stored with a stronger codec was overestimated, which inflates `effective_max_reading_threads` and can make automatic parallel replicas distribute a query that is cheaper to run on a single node. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114535&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114535](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114535+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
