signal.title: Make SQL SECURITY views an optimization barrier
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A view with `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` or `SQL SECURITY NONE` is now an optimization barrier, so an expression in the query reading the view is never evaluated on rows that the view itself filters out. Previously such an expression could observe the hidden rows through an exception, and a view used to restrict which rows a user may see did not actually restrict them. --- ## The problem `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` is widely used to build a view that restricts which rows a user may see: ```sql CREATE VIEW user_query_log DEFINER = default SQL SECURITY DEFINER AS SELECT * FROM system.query_log WHERE user = currentUser(); GRANT SELECT ON user_query_log TO alice; ``` `alice` has no grant on the source table, only on the view. But the outer `WHERE` and the view's own `WHERE` are merged into a single filter over the source table, and nothing guarantees which of the two decides first. Any function that can signal through a side channel therefore observes the rows the view is supposed to hide: ```sql -- as alice, whose only grant is SELECT ON user_query_log SELECT event_time FROM user_query_log WHERE throwIf(query LIKE '%some probe%', 'DISCLOSED'); -- DB::Exception: DISCLOSED ... While executing MergeTreeSelect ``` That is a one-bit oracle per query. Exception messages carry the offending value, which turns it into a plain read of the hidden rows: ```sql SELECT * FROM v_secrets WHERE if(owner = 'alice', 1, toUInt8(secret)) = 1; -- DB::Exception: Cannot parse string 'TOP-SECRET-BOB-42' as UInt8 ``` Both work on `SQL SECURITY NONE` as well, and both work with `enable_analyzer = 0`. Row policies are *not* affected: a row policy is a separate `row_level_filter` that the reading step always applies before PREWHERE and before any pushed-down filter. This PR gives a view's own filtering the same standing. ## The fix `IQueryPlanStep` gets a `security_barrier` flag. After `StorageView::readImpl` builds the view's subplan, every step that can drop rows is marked, and optimizations that move a step down the plan refuse to cross a marked step: - `tryMergeExpressions`, `tryMergeFilters`, `tryPushDownFilter` and `tryMergeFilterIntoJoinCondition` refuse when the child is a barrier; - `optimizePrewhere` refuses to pull an outer filter into a barrier source — conditions are combined into the prewhere DAG with `and`, which gives no ordering guarantee — and transfers the barrier onto the source when it absorbs the view's own filter; - `trySplitFilter` moves the flag onto the new lower `FilterStep`, which is the one that still drops rows. - `tryPushDownLimit` refuses to move the invoker's `LimitStep` below a barrier step: once across the seal it would seed `DistinctStep::limit_hint` or a sorting limit inside the view's subplan, and `optimizeLimitForAggregationInOrder` walked through the seal to seed `AggregatingStep::limit_hint` the same way — hints that stop reading the source once enough visible rows are produced, so `read_rows`, progress and timing depended on the rows the view drops or collapses. Both walks, and `pushLimitByIntoSort`, fail closed on a barrier step. Blocking the steps that evaluate expressions is not enough on its own, because index analysis reaches the source by a different route and skips granules by the values of the rows the view hides — `read_rows` then tells the invoker whether such a row exists, with no exception needed. Ten walks are fenced as well: - `optimizePrimaryKeyConditionAndLimit` walks up from the reading step and hands every `FilterStep` it meets to the source's key condition; it now stops once it has consumed a barrier. The barrier's own condition still reaches the source — it is the definer's, and it is what decides which rows exist for the view — but nothing above it does. - `StorageView::readImpl` forwarded `query_info.filter_actions_dag` into the view's inner analyzer, where `Planner::collectFiltersForAnalysis` injects it into the inner plan and the filters it collects reach the inner tables' index analysis. It is no longer forwarded for a barrier view, which costs such a view over `Distributed` its shard skipping on the outer predicate. - `buildSortingDAG` in the read-in-order analysis descended through the view subplan and pulled outer `FilterStep` predicates into the fixed columns and the merged DAG, so an outer `ORDER BY` / `GROUP BY` / `DISTINCT` / `LIMIT BY` could still shape how the source below the barrier reads. It now reports a barrier in the chain and every consumer (sorting, aggregation, `DISTINCT`, `LIMIT BY`, the normal-projection choice, top-K, and the `Merge` child-plan walk) skips the analysis for that chain. Unlike the primary-key walk, the barrier step cannot be consumed here: the sort description belongs to the top of the chain, and a DAG missing the steps above the barrier could resolve a renamed column by name to the wrong source column and change the result order — so the analysis is skipped entirely, which is fail-closed and keeps correctness because the sorting step stays in the plan. - `tryOptimizeTopK` rewrites an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` into a dynamic `__topKFilter` PREWHERE and minmax-skip-index granule pruning on the source, walking `LimitStep` → `SortingStep` → `ExpressionStep` → `FilterStep` → `ReadFromMergeTree` — and both rewrites are on by default. The walk now fails closed on the first barrier step it meets, including a reading step that carries the barrier after `optimizePrewhere` absorbed the view's own filter. - `tryTopKThroughJoin` peels the expression chain between the invoker's `Sorting` and a `Join` and grafts the invoker's `Sort + Limit` onto the join's preserved input, re-running the optimization passes on that subtree. For a barrier view whose inner query is a join, the graft landed below the seal — verified live pre-fix on both analyzers. The pass now fails closed on a marked `Limit`/`Sorting` (the pattern lies inside a view), a marked peeled expression (the seal), and a marked join (a join of a barrier view is always marked, not being row-preserving). Grafting above the seal of the invoker's own join input stays allowed: the inserted `Sort` consumes its whole input and the re-run passes are individually fenced. - `registerLeftSideIndexAnalysisSecondPass` of the join runtime filters walked from the `__applyFilter` step (which the fenced filter pushdown correctly keeps above the seal) down through every single-child expression or filter step — sealed or not — to the `ReadFromMergeTree` inside the view, and registered the invoker's build-side keys for granule pruning there. The walk now fails closed on the first barrier step. A live disclosure could not be constructed — the descriptor's key name has to match the read's namespace and the consumption path declined in every configuration tried — so this fence makes the contract structural rather than incidental. - The vector search rewrites — the vector-similarity-index pass and the quantized-codes shortlist — walk the same chain and prune the source to the top-N candidates of the invoker's `ORDER BY`. Both now fail closed on a barrier step the same way. - Projection planning: `QueryDAG::build` in `projectionsCommon.cpp` collects every filter of the chain below the aggregation — the invoker's predicates together with the view's own filtering — and both `optimizeUseAggregateProjections` (including `minmax_count_projection`) and `optimizeUseNormalProjections` prune parts and marks with it, so a projection-enabled table under a filtering barrier view still let the invoker's predicate shape the read. The DAG build now fails closed on the first barrier step, which makes the projection optimizations decline the read entirely. - Join reordering: `addChildQueryGraph` in `optimizeJoin.cpp` peeled the sealing step — as a trivial pass-through step, or by merging it into the child join, which `query_plan_merge_expression_into_join` enables by default — and then flattened the join inside the view into the join graph of the invoker, where the relations are reordered by their estimated sizes. A sealed subplan is now one opaque relation of the graph: the seal is neither peeled nor merged, a barrier child join is neither flattened nor pre-optimized for statistics, and the two walks that mirror this one (the overlapping-column-name pre-check and the exposed-column check) are fenced identically so that they keep agreeing with it. - `optimizeJoinByShards` (setting `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges`) merged the expression and filter DAGs of the chain through the seal and could then make the reading inside the view emit one output port per primary-key range of the invoker's join keys. The walk now produces no result for a barrier step, so nothing propagates above the seal; the sharding of the joins the view itself contains, which the invoker does not control, is still applied. One more family reaches the source without going through its index analysis at all. `optimizeDistinctPerPartition`, `optimizeLimitByPerPartition` and `optimizeAggregationPerPartition` walk down through the sealing step and ask the reading to output each partition through a separate port, and `applyStreamDisjointness` carries the resulting partition disjointness back up across the seal, so the invoker's `DISTINCT` / `LIMIT BY` / `GROUP BY` skips its stream merging as well. Read scheduling, progress and resource consumption below the view then depend on how the rows the view drops are spread over the partitions, and all three `allow_*_partitions_independently` settings default to `1`. Both directions now fail closed on a barrier step. Four passes endanger the barrier by rebuilding steps rather than by walking past them, and each now fails closed on a barrier step: - lazy materialization splits every `Expression` / `Filter` step of the chain into a main and a lazy half, and the rebuilt steps do not carry the barrier flag, so the post-lazy `tryMergeExpressions` / `tryMergeFilters` passes saw an unmarked chain and could merge an invoker predicate into the view's own filtering — reopening the exception oracle itself, not just the read-shaping one; - `tryLiftUpUnion` rebuilds the `UnionStep` and clones the parent step into the branches as fresh unmarked steps, so a barrier view over `UNION ALL` lost its seal and `tryPushDownFilter` could then duplicate an invoker predicate into the branches; - `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` replaces the expression under a `SortingStep` with two new unmarked steps, which would strip the seal of a wrapper view and let the read-in-order and top-K walks descend through it again. - `tryLiftUpArrayJoin` splits the expression or filter above an `ArrayJoinStep`, moves one half below the `ARRAY JOIN`, and rebuilds both halves as fresh unmarked steps. When the parent is the seal of a view whose plan contains `ARRAY JOIN` (the seal is non-trivial whenever the view declares explicit column names or types), the invoker's predicate descended below the `ArrayJoinStep` and was evaluated on rows hidden by empty arrays — a live disclosure through the exception oracle, on both analyzers. Measured on a `DEFINER` view that exposes no row, over 100000 rows sorted by `key`, reading `WHERE key = <a key only a hidden row has>` against `WHERE key = <a key nothing has>`: 576 rows read against 0 without this, and 1000000 against 1000000 with it, on both `enable_analyzer = 1` and `enable_analyzer = 0`. `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` is left alone. It builds `InterpreterSelectQuery` with `only_analyze`, whose plan reads from `ReadNothingStep`, so no expression of the outer query is ever evaluated on a row and the view is still inlined for the diagnostic. Two paths substitute the view into the outer query before a plan exists, so a plan-level barrier cannot see them, and both are closed the same way — such a view is not inlined and is read through `StorageView::read`, which keeps the outer predicate in a step above it: - with `enable_analyzer = 0`, `InterpreterSelectQuery` replaces the view with a subquery and `TreeRewriter` merges the predicates; - with `analyzer_inline_views = 1`, `QueryAnalyzer::inlineViewSubqueryIfNeeded` does the same in the query tree. Without this, `SET enable_analyzer = 0` or `SET analyzer_inline_views = 1` would bypass the fix entirely. The flag also travels with a serialized query plan. A distributed worker deserializes a fragment and optimizes it again, so a barrier it does not know about is a barrier it will optimize across. `QueryPlan::serialize` writes the flag per step and fails closed when the negotiated query plan serialization version predates it (the version is bumped to 7), rather than sending a plan that silently loses its protection. ## Views that hide nothing are left alone Only a view that can actually drop rows becomes a barrier. A step is row-preserving if it is an `ExpressionStep`, a `SortingStep` without a limit, or a source step without PREWHERE; if none of the view's steps is anything else, nothing is marked and the plan is what it is today. The pre-plan paths make the same distinction. `StorageView::canHideRows` proves over the view's definition that the inner query preserves every row of a plainly readable source, and only a view for which that proof fails loses inlining and the forwarded outer filter. The proof fails closed: filters, limits, aggregation, `DISTINCT`, joins, `ARRAY JOIN`, `SAMPLE`/`FINAL`, multi-select unions, table functions, and a `FROM` that is itself a view or a view-wrapping engine (`Merge`, `Buffer`, anything remote) all count as able to hide rows. The proof classifies the storage that actually serves the read, not the object the name resolves to: proxy layers (a lazily loaded table of a database with `lazy_load_tables = 1`, or a table created from a table function) and `Alias` tables are unwrapped first, failing closed on a chain that cannot be resolved, and a storage that rewrites its own reads with `FINAL` and a `_sign` filter (`MaterializedPostgreSQL`) counts as able to hide rows even without another wrapper. So a projection-only `DEFINER` view produces exactly the plan of the same view declared `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` on every path, which the test pins byte-for-byte. Measured on 20M rows with `SELECT sum(length(payload)) FROM v WHERE tag = 'RARE'`, from `system.query_log`: | view | barrier | read_rows | read_bytes | ms | |---|---|---|---|---| | `DEFINER`, filters rows | on | 20 000 000 | 1.43 GiB | 35 | | `DEFINER`, filters rows | off | 1 638 400 | 82.84 MiB | 14 | | `DEFINER`, projection only | on | 1 638 400 | 82.84 MiB | 9 | | `DEFINER`, projection only | off | 1 638 400 | 82.84 MiB | 11 | A projection-only view is unaffected. A filtering view does pay: PREWHERE then holds only the view's own condition, so it no longer skips granules on the outer predicate. That is the inherent price of the guarantee — PostgreSQL's `security_barrier` views behave the same way — and it applies only to views that restrict rows, which are exactly the ones where it matters. The new server setting `sql_security_views_are_optimization_barriers` (default `1`) turns it off. It is deliberately a **server** setting and not a user setting: a user setting would be turned off by the very query that is trying to read the hidden rows. ## Testing `04758_sql_security_view_barrier_read_rows` covers the `read_rows` oracle through index analysis, on both analyzers, and prints `DISCLOSED` on both with the setting off. `04670_sql_security_view_barrier` covers the leak on `DEFINER` and on `NONE`, with `enable_analyzer = 1`, with `enable_analyzer = 0` and with `analyzer_inline_views = 1`, the value leak through a cast error message, the same oracle through a shard with `serialize_query_plan = 1`, that a projection-only `DEFINER` view and an `INVOKER` view still have the outer predicate merged into the view's own filter, and that a projection-only view keeps PREWHERE. `04813_sql_security_view_barrier_read_in_order` pins the read-in-order fence: the `INVOKER` twin and a projection-only `DEFINER` view read `InOrder`, a filtering `DEFINER` view does not, under both analyzers, with unchanged results. `04817_sql_security_view_barrier_top_k` pins the top-K fence: the `INVOKER` twin gets the `__topKFilter`, the filtering `DEFINER` view does not, and `read_rows` of an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` over twin views is identical whether or not the hidden row holds the extreme minimum of the sort column that minmax pruning would rank first. `04818_sql_security_view_barrier_lazy_materialization` pins the lazy-materialization fence the same way and checks that an invoker predicate over the view is never evaluated on the hidden row. `04821_sql_security_view_barrier_projections` pins the projection fence: the `INVOKER` twin uses both a normal and an aggregate projection, the filtering `DEFINER` view uses neither, and `read_rows` of a predicate probe over twin views is identical whether or not the hidden row matches it. `04825_sql_security_view_barrier_union` pins that an outer predicate over a filtering `DEFINER` view on `UNION ALL` stays in a single filter above the union — before the `tryLiftUpUnion` fix it was duplicated into the branches — while the `INVOKER` twin keeps the pushdown. `04826_sql_security_view_barrier_functions_after_sorting` pins that an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` over a wrapper `DEFINER` view (a `Merge` table over a nested filtering view) produces no in-order reading and no `__topKFilter` with `query_plan_execute_functions_after_sorting` on, while the `INVOKER` twin exploits the source order. `04827_sql_security_view_barrier_masked_wrappers` pins that the classification survives engine masking: a `DEFINER` view over a `Merge` wrapper behind a lazy `TableProxy` (re-masked before every round, since planning materializes the proxy) or behind an `Alias` table plans differently from its `INVOKER` twin on both analyzers and with `analyzer_inline_views = 1`. `04832_sql_security_view_barrier_limit_pushdown` pins the LIMIT fence: over a `DISTINCT` `DEFINER` view the invoker's `LimitStep` stays above the sealing step on both analyzers — before the fix it crossed the seal and sat directly on the `DistinctStep`, where it seeds the hint — and `read_rows` of an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` over twin in-order `GROUP BY` views is identical whether the first group holds one raw row or almost all of them. `04837_sql_security_view_barrier_per_partition` pins the per-partition fence, with the `allow_*_partitions_independently` settings left at their defaults: an outer `DISTINCT` / `LIMIT BY` over a filtering `DEFINER` view produces none of the `Skip stream merging` / `Read each partition through separate port` markers its `INVOKER` twin gets, and the disjointness of a view whose own inner `DISTINCT` legitimately requests per-partition reading does not propagate across the seal into the invoker's `GROUP BY` / `LIMIT BY` — before the fix every `DEFINER` case was identical to its twin. `04840_sql_security_view_barrier_array_join` pins the `ARRAY JOIN` lift-up fence with an exception oracle on both analyzers: the `INVOKER` twin's predicate legitimately descends below the `ARRAY JOIN` and throws on the row an empty array hides, while the `DEFINER` view counts without throwing and its plan keeps every `throwIf` line above the `ArrayJoin` step — before the fix the `DEFINER` view threw as well. `04891_sql_security_view_barrier_top_k_through_join` pins the top-K-through-join fence: the `INVOKER` twin of a view over a `LEFT JOIN` gets the preserved-side `Sort + Limit` graft below the join, the `DEFINER` twin keeps its join input untouched — before the fix the `DEFINER` plan got the graft below the seal. `04892_sql_security_view_barrier_join_runtime_filter` pins the join-runtime-filter contract: with `enable_join_runtime_filters_index_analysis = 1`, twin filtering `DEFINER` views over tables identical except for the hidden row's primary-key value read exactly the same number of rows, while the `INVOKER` control is pruned by the build-side key. Every setting the plan shape depends on is pinned, because the test also runs with randomized settings. `04893_sql_security_view_barrier_join_reorder` pins the join-reordering fence: with `query_plan_merge_expression_into_join = 1` and no overlapping column names between the relations, the `INVOKER` twin of a view over an `INNER JOIN` with a `WHERE` is flattened and reordered into a three-relation graph with no step left converting the view subquery result, while the `DEFINER` twin keeps that step and stays one relation, with equal results. `04894_sql_security_view_barrier_join_shard_by_pk` pins the join-sharding fence: with `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges = 1` and `join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge'`, plain tables, a `DEFINER` view that hides nothing and the `INVOKER` twin of the filtering view all get a `Sharding` line, while the filtering `DEFINER` view gets none, with equal row counts. Those two fences are contract-made-real rather than live leaks: with the fence removed the `DEFINER` twin behaves the same, because a neighbouring fence of this PR happens to block the pass first — which is exactly why the barrier is checked explicitly. With `sql_security_views_are_optimization_barriers = 0` every one of those lines changes, so none of them passes vacuously. Ran 542 existing tests matching `view`, `prewhere`, `push_down`, `pushdown`, `row_policy`, `sql_security` and `definer`. 60 fail in my local environment, and the identical 60 fail with the barrier disabled on the same binary, so this introduces no regressions among them. ## Not covered here - The serialized-plan fence is defensive. With the serialization change reverted I could not make the barrier loss observable — neither the `throwIf` nor the failing-cast oracle leaks through `serialize_query_plan = 1`, `make_distributed_plan = 1`, or a `Distributed` table, because the initiator optimizes the fragment before shipping it. The flag is serialized so that the guarantee does not depend on that. - A separate hole remains: `additional_table_filters` and `additional_result_filter` from the invoker are copied verbatim into the definer's context by `StorageInMemoryMetadata::getSQLSecurityOverriddenContext`. Keyed on the view's *inner* table, the filter lands inside the view and its expression — which may contain scalar subqueries and table functions — is evaluated with the definer's privileges. That is a privilege escalation rather than a row disclosure, it is unaffected by this PR, and it needs its own fix. Until then it can be mitigated with a constraint on the definer's profile (`CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE p SETTINGS additional_table_filters = '' CONST TO <definer>`), which does not help for `SQL SECURITY NONE`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112847&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112847](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112847+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Keep a read with pinned block numbers local in plan-based parallel replicas
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112723 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when plan-based parallel replicas shipped a read pinned by `select_sequential_consistency`. Follower replicas rebuilt the read without the pinned block-number boundary and returned rows the insert quorum never confirmed. Such a read is now executed locally. ### Description `select_sequential_consistency` clamps a `ReplicatedMergeTree` read to the parts the initiator saw confirmed by the insert quorum, via `max_block_numbers_to_read`. That pin is not serialized: `ReadFromMergeTree::deserialize` rebuilds a shipped read with `max_block_numbers_to_read = nullptr`. `mergeTreeReadCanBeShipped` did not consult it, so the read was split and each follower read its own unclamped part set. The result is wrong results with no exception. On a two-replica quorum fixture whose correct answer is `(45, 10)`, a remote-only plan-based execution returns `(435, 30)`: the 20 unconfirmed rows leak in. A join whose broadcast side reads the pinned table returns 30 rows where the pinned truth is 10. This adds `hasPinnedBlockNumbers()` to `mergeTreeReadCanBeShipped`, mirroring the existing rejection for the same property in `make_distributed_plan` (`checkDistributedReadSupported`). The predicate gates both `collectReadsToDistribute` (the coordinated read) and `subtreeHasUnshippableRead` (the broadcast side of a lifted join), so one check covers both carriers. Returning `false` rather than throwing matches how this path already keeps a refreshable-MV target read local: `make_distributed_plan` is an explicit opt-in, plan-based parallel replicas falls back to a local read. The test asserts row sets and step order, not step presence, since refusing the lift leaves the split below the join. Reverting only this guard flips four of its seven assertions while the unpinned controls stay unchanged. 50/50 randomized runs pass. The fix and its regression test are @ alexey-milovidov's, from commit b305123a8f79 on #112723. That PR was closed unmerged in favour of #114242, which does not carry this guard, so it was lost. `checkDistributedReadSupported` has three further predicates with no counterpart here (`input_order_info`, `isStream()`, and the `_part_index` / `_part_starting_offset` virtual columns). I could not demonstrate any of them diverging, so I left them alone; `isStream()` is also unreachable here, because the planner disables parallel replicas for a `STREAM` table expression before these settings are built. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114263&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114263](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114263+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Bound the integration-test job's post-run archiving so it cannot starve the result upload
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 An integration-test shard can publish a job-level `ERROR` with `results: []` even though every test produced a result. **What breaks.** On `6cdf4dfaea6e071cddeea4daeb74ea26e0d96e19`, `Integration tests (amd_asan_ubsan, db disk, old analyzer, 5/6)` reported `ERROR` with no children and is absent from the CI database, while its five siblings uploaded 600-1300 test rows each. Its job log holds 502 per-test outcome lines: the results existed and were discarded. Correcting the report: the harness survived both timeouts, then hung ~80 min in archiving. **Root cause.** `main` collects every result but dumps it only after unbounded post-processing. `Utils.compress_files_gz` sits in between with no timeout, archiving whole `tests/integration/<suite>` trees, so an archive that never returns costs a report already in memory. `Runner._get_result_object` runs the `on_error_hook` the same way, even earlier (comment: `# Add hook timeout once it's needed`). **The change.** Both paths are bounded at 30 minutes and fail non-fatally, so an overrun costs the tarball, not the report. `compress_files_gz` returns failure instead of raising, publishes by rename from a per-writer temporary, uses a direct `tar -czf` instead of `tar -cf - | gzip`, and judges the archive by reading it back, not by `tar`'s exit code; all four load-bearing, see below. Bounding needs a working watchdog, so `Shell._check_timeout` waits on an event set when the attempt's child is reaped, not sleeping the timeout out. `main` also checkpoints the results first. **Scope limits.** The checkpoint does not recover the job above, where the runner died, nor an externally cancelled job. 30 minutes comes from healthy shards' 4491-5747s of 18000s. **Validation.** 37 tests, each shown to fail against a mutation of what it pins: a 37-case matrix reddening exactly its predicted arms, plus a probe for the four it did not reach. Empty failure-set diff over `ci/tests/`, as host user and as root. <details> <summary>Why each detail of the change matters</summary> Four measured properties beyond the bound. * **Must not raise.** `Shell.check(..., strict=True, timeout=N)` raises `RuntimeError`, so merely adding `timeout=` turns the hang into an exception that still skips the dump. Nor an absent declared input (`Result.from_pytest_run` registers its log and report before running pytest) or a failed publish. * **Must not publish a partial archive.** A timed-out `tar` leaves a large truncated archive and the upload only checks the file exists. The temporary is per writer: both target one `ci/tmp/logs.tar.gz`, so sharing it lets the loser write into the published file. * **Must not reject a usable archive over `tar`'s exit code.** Two reachable cases exit non-zero with a complete, listable archive: 1 for a member appended to while read, which every archive here holds (`job.log`, the dockerd log, live `_instances` trees), and 2 for an unstattable input, which the hook hits whenever its `_instances*` glob is unexpanded because no cluster started. Rejecting on the code discards both, timeout unfired. So 0 and 1 are accepted and any other code is settled by `tar -tzf`: 0 on those, non-zero on every truncated archive (~1.6s for 367MB). * **Must see `tar`'s status at all.** `Shell.run` uses bash without `pipefail`, so the old `tar -cf - | gzip > out` reported only gzip's status: a `tar` failing part-way exited 0. The watchdog event is per attempt (a shared one is already set when attempt 2 starts waiting), and all three of its liveness tests - before SIGTERM, in the grace loop, at the SIGKILL gate - ask about the process GROUP. A descendant holding the inherited pipes keeps the readers blocked, so the event is unset while the leader is already reaped, and a leader-only `poll()` signals nothing or skips the SIGKILL. Only the first was a regression; a SIGTERM-ignoring descendant was unbounded on master too, so that part is a hardening. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112972&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112972](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112972+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Model IPv4/IPv6 as their substituted integer in plus/minus/multiply monotonicity
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112156 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long` (`BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD`) raised during primary key analysis of valid queries using `plus`, `minus` or `multiply` with an `IPv4` or `IPv6` operand, and restored primary key pruning for `multiply` over an `IPv4`/`IPv6` key. ### Description `plus`, `minus` and `multiply` substitute an `IPv4`/`IPv6` operand with `UInt32`/`UInt128`, so the arithmetic works, but `FunctionBinaryArithmeticWithConstants::getMonotonicityForRange` reasoned about the raw `Field`s, which keep their IP tag. Two IP `Field`s compare through the visitors' same-type branch, but an IP `Field` against a numeric zero matches no arm, since `is_arithmetic_v<IPv4>` is false. Two defects follow, both on `master`: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a SETTINGS index_granularity = 1; INSERT INTO t VALUES (10); SELECT count() FROM t WHERE plus(a, toIPv4('0.0.0.2')) > 0; -- Code: 169. DB::Exception: Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long. (BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD) ``` Without a key the query answers correctly. `plus`/`minus` fail only when a granule has `min == max`; `multiply` fails at any granularity, either side. `Nullable`/`LowCardinality` constants and `plus(1, ip_key)` fail alike. Second, `multiply` over an IP key silently loses pruning: the overflow check converts endpoints via `Field::dispatch`, instantiated on the runtime `Field`'s type, so an `IPv4` endpoint hits `is_integer<IPv4> == false` and counts as overflow. Results stay correct, but `multiply(a, 2) > 6000000000` reads `Granules: 4/4` against `2/4` for an identical `UInt32` key. The divisor-zero checks in the equal-endpoints branch now run only for `divide`/`intDiv`; the `if` below them was their only consumer, so no verdict changes. In the `multiply` arm the constant and both endpoints are normalized through `castColumn`, the order-preserving conversion the arithmetic itself applies to IP operands, keeping the monotonicity claim sound. Gating on the declared type would instead have dropped the pruning. The test compares keyed reads against an `ENGINE = Log` oracle and pins granule counts against a numeric control holding identical bit values, so a degraded optimization also fails. Genuine overflow still rejects monotonicity. `divide`/`intDiv` reach this class through other mechanisms, handled in #112156 and a follow-up adding a byte-identical `substituteIPField`; whichever merges second drops its copy. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112400&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112400](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112400+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fsync backup files and directories when writing a backup to local disk
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111320 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `BACKUP ... TO File(...)` / `Disk(...)` now fsyncs the backup data files, the `.backup` manifest and the containing directories before reporting `BACKUP_CREATED`, so an acknowledged backup to local storage survives power loss. The guarantee covers `backups.allowed_path` and everything the backup writes below it. Controlled by the new backup setting `fsync_backup_files` (default `true`). Object-storage destinations (`S3`/`Azure`) are unaffected. ### Description Fixes #111320. `BACKUP ... TO File()/Disk()` returned `BACKUP_CREATED` without issuing any `fsync`/`fdatasync` at the destination: not the data files, not the `.backup` manifest, not the directories (there was no `fsync` anywhere in `src/Backups/`). On power loss after the acknowledgement the backup could be lost entirely or left torn, even though `BACKUP_CREATED` is what an operator relies on before dropping the source data. Only local `File()`/`Disk()` were affected; object-storage destinations were already durable. Report URL: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111320 (reproduced 3/3 with a `dm-flakey` power-loss simulation). Fix, gated on the new backup setting `fsync_backup_files` (default `true`), following the durability audit family (#68958 -> #111346, #111269 -> #111335): - Two writer hooks with a no-op default on `IBackupWriter`, overridden only by the local `File`/`Disk` writers (`S3`/`Azure`/`Memory`/`Null` inherit the no-op): `syncFileToDisk(file_name)`, called right after each data file is written in `BackupImpl::writeFile` (each call fsyncs its own file, so the concurrent write path is safe), and `syncDirectoriesToDisk()`, which fdatasyncs every directory the backup created, deepest-first. - In `BackupImpl::finalizeWriting` the `.backup` manifest (or, for archives, the archive file) is synced last, after all data files, so a persisted manifest never precedes its payload. Directory syncing runs for every writer, including the internal writers of `BACKUP ON CLUSTER` which write their own data files. Regression test `tests/queries/0_stateless/04412_backup_to_file_fsync.sh` asserts the `FileSync`/`DirectorySync` ProfileEvents of the `BACKUP` query, present with `fsync_backup_files=1` and absent with `0`; integration coverage adds the `Disk`, archive and `ON CLUSTER` internal-writer cases. Guarantee boundary, stated rather than left implicit: `backups.allowed_path` and everything written below it are synced in a loop that propagates failures. Ancestors above it are best-effort, because `fsyncBackupDirectory` needs `O_DIRECTORY` (read permission) while writing a backup only needs them searchable: measured with the area inside a `0311` directory, writing succeeds and `open(O_DIRECTORY)` on the ancestor fails `EACCES`, so throwing there would newly fail backups that work today. So if a directory above `backups.allowed_path` was itself created without being made durable, a power loss can still take the whole tree. The setting's docs row now says this. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111394&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111394](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111394+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Choose IEJoin key conditions by estimated selectivity
signal.text: When the `JOIN ON` expression contains more inequality conditions between the joined tables than the two the IEJoin algorithm uses as its key conditions, pick the two with the smallest estimated joint selectivity instead of the first two in syntax order. The conditions not chosen as keys are evaluated per pair of rows passing both key conditions (a filter over the join result for `ALL INNER JOIN`, a residual condition inside the operator for the other kinds), so the least selective key pair minimizes that work: on an adversarial three-condition query (50k×50k rows, marginal selectivities 0.5 / 0.5 / 0.0005) the planner-chosen order now runs in ~0.015 s instead of ~5.5 s, matching a manually reordered `ON` clause. Selectivity is estimated from the column min/max statistics (the `basic` type, collected by default) under a uniformity assumption. To make the estimates reachable at planning time: `ColumnStats` now carries `min_value`/`max_value`/`null_fraction` (resolving the TODO in `ConditionSelectivityEstimator.h`), `remapColumnStats` keeps them only across value-preserving hops, and `estimateReadRowsCount` is declared in `joinOrder.h` and called on the join inputs. Conditions reading the same column on one side (the band shape `lo < x AND x < hi`) are correlated, so such pairs are scored with the sharp Frechet bound `P(A) + P(B) - 1` instead of the independence product, which also preserves the band-join fast path. When any estimate is unavailable (no statistics, `use_statistics = 0`, expression keys, non-MergeTree inputs), the previous syntax order is kept. Pairwise scoring is capped at 64 candidates; beyond that the two smallest marginal selectivities are chosen in linear time. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The IEJoin algorithm now chooses which two `JOIN ON` inequality conditions to use as its key conditions by their estimated selectivity from the column min/max statistics, instead of taking the first two in syntax order. The remaining conditions are evaluated per candidate pair, so picking the most selective pair can speed up such joins by orders of magnitude. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115790&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115790](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115790+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: PromQL: speed up duplicate series zero scan
signal.text: ### TL;DR Use `memoryIsZero` to return early for all-zero PromQL condition vectors. Keep the existing scalar fallback for other values. The local 10M-row microbenchmark is up to 26.8x faster. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up duplicate-series checks for all-zero PromQL condition vectors. ### Summary PromQL duplicate-series detection calls `timeSeriesThrowDuplicateSeriesIf` with a condition column. The function used to scan the whole column value by value even when every value was zero. This change uses `memoryIsZero` as an all-zero check. If the bytes are all zero, the function returns immediately. Otherwise, it keeps the existing scalar scan. This preserves the behavior for non-zero values and special floating-point values such as `-0.0`. ### Benchmark Local arm64 macOS. 10M preallocated values. Median of 7 runs. The old path is the existing scalar scan. | Input | Old path | New path | Speedup | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | UInt8, all zero | 7.393 ms | 0.275 ms | 26.8x | | Float64, all zero | 3.442 ms | 2.246 ms | 1.53x | | Float64, `-0.0` | 3.676 ms | 3.440 ms | 1.07x | The `-0.0` case does not take the early return because its sign bit is set. It still uses the scalar fallback and returns the same result. ### Tests - Add all-zero vector coverage to `03779_time_series_tags_functions`. - Add `-0.0` fallback coverage. - Add non-zero vector error coverage. - Add a performance fixture for 1M and 10M rows. - Compile the changed C++ translation unit. - Run `git diff --check`.

signal.title: Query cache on disk, backed by the filesystem cache
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115361 The query cache can now additionally store its entries on disk, backed by a preconfigured filesystem cache (an entry of the `filesystem_caches` section of the server configuration), selected per query with the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`. Compared to the in-memory query cache, this gives the entries more space, makes them survive server restarts, and (with a distributed filesystem cache) provides a way to share them between servers. Design, following the RFC in the issue: - The entries are ordinary filesystem cache entries, indistinguishable from other data in the same filesystem cache: they are not held from deletion, they are evicted by the same rules, and there are no specific limits on their total size or number other than the limits of the filesystem cache itself. The keys are hashed with a salt so that they cannot intersect with other keys in the filesystem cache. - No extra in-memory state is kept: all metadata needed to validate an entry (TTL, user id, roles, the shared flag) is serialized into the entry itself, followed by the result payload in `Native` format, compressed with the codec from the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_codec` (default `ZSTD(3)`; reading is independent of the setting because the compressed frames are self-describing). - The on-disk cache works independently of the in-memory cache and can separately be enabled for reads and/or writes with the new settings `enable_reads_from_query_cache_on_disk` and `enable_writes_to_query_cache_on_disk` (both `true` by default, activated by setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`). If both caches are enabled for reads, the lookup is attempted first from memory and only on a miss from disk. If both caches are enabled for writes, the result is written to both. A result served from memory is not written to disk. - A stale (expired TTL), partially evicted, corrupt, or inaccessible (another user's non-shared) entry is treated as a cache miss; stale entries are overwritten on the next write. - Introspection of the on-disk entries in `system.query_cache` is out of scope, per the issue. New profile events: `QueryCacheOnDiskHits`, `QueryCacheOnDiskMisses`, `QueryCacheOnDiskReadBytes`, `QueryCacheOnDiskWrittenBytes`. Tests: `05019_query_cache_on_disk_local` proves persistence across process restarts (separate `clickhouse-local` invocations sharing one filesystem cache directory, including a cached non-deterministic result, TTL expiry, and disabled reads); `05020_query_cache_on_disk` covers the server path with user isolation, sharing via `query_cache_share_between_users`, and error cases (unknown cache name, invalid codec). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The query cache can now store its entries on disk, backed by a preconfigured filesystem cache: this gives the entries more space, makes them survive server restarts, and (with a distributed filesystem cache) provides a way to share them between servers. Select the filesystem cache with the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`; see also the new settings `query_cache_on_disk_codec`, `enable_writes_to_query_cache_on_disk`, and `enable_reads_from_query_cache_on_disk`. Closes [#115361](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115361). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115382&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115382](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115382+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add a release-pipeline dry-run PR check
signal.text: Add a digest-gated PR job that rehearses the release pipeline in `--dry-run` so a change to the release code is caught before it can break a real release. `Release Dry Run (new)` runs `release_job.py --ref master --release-type new --dry-run --skip-repo --skip-docker`. It's gated (via `digest_config`) to the release files, so it only runs when they change. It runs on the small PR pool (not `amd-release-maker`, which the PR workflow's `pr-` label prefix can't resolve) and authenticates `gh` with a minted PR token (`enable_gh_auth`) — a dry run pushes nothing, so no robot PAT is needed. `Release Dry Run (patch)` uses `--ref auto`, which picks the newest unreleased release-branch commit (a pass when none exists); release branches are sorted version-aware (`25.10` after `25.9`). Both checks exercise the generic prepare/setup path — the changelog-push-to-`master` and the R2/package/docker steps are real-only (gated by `not dry_run` / `not skip_repo`), so a dry run never reaches them; those are validated by real release runs. Supporting changes in `release_job.py`: skip the SSM robot token on a dry run; make `master` a local branch when the checkout is detached (the PR case); don't apply the skip-repo/skip-docker recovery-misuse guard on a dry run; and the `--ref auto` candidate scan. Split out of #113528 to keep that PR focused on the direct-push conversion. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):

signal.title: _sample_factor pinned to 1 only in the materialized arm; on-the-fly arm still samples
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **A pending mutation whose expression names `_sample_factor` is evaluated with the *reading query's* sample factor when `apply_mutations_on_fly = 1`, but with the constant 1 once materialized. `ALTER TABLE t DELETE WHERE _sample_factor > 1` - a no-op after materialization - makes `SELECT count() FROM t SAMPLE 0.5` return 0 while the mutation is pending and 100 after it lands.** - **Root cause:** [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp:339`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/68d548f854a5b/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp#L339) fixes only the materialized arm. The on-the-fly arm reuses the SELECT's `shared_virtual_fields`, so the mutation predicate sees the query's `SAMPLE` factor instead of the constant the PR chose. The PR's stated justification - 'no `SAMPLE` clause reaches this path' - holds for the sequential source but not for the on-the-fly evaluation of the same mutation. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** Two independent evaluations of the same mutation expression: the materialized arm goes `MutationsInterpreter.cpp:2416` -> `createMergeTreeSequentialSource` -> `MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp:339`, which now pins 1.0. The on-the-fly arm goes `MergeTreeData.cpp:12663` (`need_data_mutations = apply_mutations_on_fly`) -> `ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4747`, which publishes `result.sampling.used_sample_factor`, copied into every read task at `MergeTreeReadPoolBase.cpp:280` and looked up at `IMergeTreeReader.cpp:154`. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp:339`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/68d548f854a5b/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp#L339) — materialized arm pins _sample_factor to 1.0 - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4747`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/68d548f854a5b/src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp#L4747) — on-the-fly arm publishes the reading query's used_sample_factor - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeReadPoolBase.cpp:280`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/68d548f854a5b/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeReadPoolBase.cpp#L280) — shared_virtual_fields copied into every read task, reaching the on-the-fly mutation steps **Impact:** With `apply_mutations_on_fly = 1`, a sampled read of a table with a pending `_sample_factor` mutation returns data that disagrees with the same read after the mutation materializes - and, on a replicated table, with a replica that has already materialized it. In the DELETE shape above every row disappears from the sampled query. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `68d548f854a5b`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test that a pending mutation referencing _sample_factor does not change what a sampled query sees. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_otf_sf; CREATE TABLE t_otf_sf (c0 UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY c0 SAMPLE BY c0; INSERT INTO t_otf_sf SELECT number FROM numbers(100); SYSTEM STOP MERGES t_otf_sf; SET mutations_sync = 0; -- _sample_factor is 1 in a mutation, so this deletes nothing. ALTER TABLE t_otf_sf DELETE WHERE _sample_factor > 1; SELECT 'pending plain', count() FROM t_otf_sf SETTINGS apply_mutations_on_fly = 1; SELECT 'pending sampled', count() FROM t_otf_sf SAMPLE 0.5 SETTINGS apply_mutations_on_fly = 1; SYSTEM START MERGES t_otf_sf; SET mutations_sync = 2; ALTER TABLE t_otf_sf DELETE WHERE 0; SELECT 'materialized plain', count() FROM t_otf_sf; SELECT 'materialized sampled', count() FROM t_otf_sf SAMPLE 0.5; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_otf_sf; ``` ### Expected behavior ``` pending plain 100 pending sampled 100 materialized plain 100 materialized sampled 100 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` pending plain 100 pending sampled 0 materialized plain 100 materialized sampled 100 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Pin `_sample_factor` to 1.0 for the mutation steps in the on-the-fly path as well (the `need_data_mutations` branch reached from `MergeTreeData.cpp:12663`), so both arms agree; alternatively reject `_sample_factor` in mutation expressions at analysis time, which is what the guard this PR removed did. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `_table` and `_database` remain unseeded in the sequential source, so a mutation naming them still fails per part forever - pre-existing, and the PR's test pins the current behaviour. Found during automated review of [PR #109813](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109813). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr109813_001` </details> cc @groeneai @alexey-milovidov (from #109813)
signal.author: clickgapai

signal.title: Early short-circuit guard calls getResultType on IN's subquery arg: UNSUPPORTED_METHOD
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With `enable_function_early_short_circuit = 1`, a valid query whose decided `and`/`or` has an `IN`/`NOT IN`/`GLOBAL IN` argument over a bare `SELECT count()` subquery fails with `Code: 1 ... Method getResultType is supported only for correlated query node. (UNSUPPORTED_METHOD)`. The same query returns a result with the setting off.** - **Root cause:** resolveFunction.cpp:287 assumes every argument of a resolved `FunctionNode` has a result type. Set-producing arguments (`QueryNode`/`UnionNode` under `in`-family functions) do not. The unguarded call sits outside the fallback try/catch, so instead of declining the optimization the analyzer aborts the whole query. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `QueryAnalyzer::resolveFunction` (resolveFunction.cpp:1186-1188) computes `post_resolution_is_safe` OUTSIDE the try/catch at :1166-1184 -> `hasFunctionNotSuitableForEarlyShortCircuit` walks the resolved clone -> for the resolved `in` node it builds `DataTypesWithConstInfo` at :287 by calling `argument->getResultType()` on every argument -> `in`'s second argument is still a `QueryNode` -> `QueryNode::getResultType` throws `UNSUPPORTED_METHOD` (QueryNode.cpp:172). Confirmed by server stack trace frames 4-8. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Analyzer/Resolve/resolveFunction.cpp:287`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/342d96b5c63d3/src/Analyzer/Resolve/resolveFunction.cpp#L287) — hasFunctionNotSuitableForEarlyShortCircuit: getResultType on every argument of a resolved function - [`src/Analyzer/Resolve/resolveFunction.cpp:1186`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/342d96b5c63d3/src/Analyzer/Resolve/resolveFunction.cpp#L1186) — post_resolution_is_safe computed outside the try/catch that is meant to make speculative analysis fall back - [`src/Analyzer/QueryNode.cpp:172`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/342d96b5c63d3/src/Analyzer/QueryNode.cpp#L172) — QueryNode::getResultType throws UNSUPPORTED_METHOD for a non-correlated query node **Impact:** Users who enable `enable_function_early_short_circuit` get a hard failure with an internal-sounding error on legitimate SQL. There is no workaround other than turning the setting back off or rewriting the query. Because the setting is a plain analyzer toggle, enabling it globally (or via a profile) breaks any query of the shape `<decided constant> OR/AND (expr IN (SELECT count() FROM <local table>))`. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `342d96b5c63d3`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/25b6a847-621d-4c4c-8042-1957686d7a41) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- Test: a decided AND/OR whose other branch is an IN subquery must still resolve. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_05028; CREATE TABLE t_05028 (x UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO t_05028 VALUES (1); SET enable_function_early_short_circuit = 1; SELECT 1 OR (1 IN (SELECT count() FROM t_05028)); SELECT 0 AND (1 IN (SELECT count() FROM t_05028)); SELECT 1 OR (1 NOT IN (SELECT count() FROM t_05028)); DROP TABLE t_05028; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` 1 0 1 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Received exception from server (version 26.8.1): Code: 1. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:19010. DB::Exception: Method getResultType is supported only for correlated query node. (UNSUPPORTED_METHOD) (query: SELECT 1 OR (1 IN (SELECT count() FROM t_05028));) Having 1 errors! 0 tests passed. ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Skip arguments without a result type when building `DataTypesWithConstInfo` (bail out with `return true` for any argument whose node type is `QUERY`/`UNION`), and move the `post_resolution_is_safe` computation inside the existing try/catch so any unexpected throw degrades to a fallback instead of failing the query. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - The same `getResultType`-on-every-argument pattern would also fire for any future resolved function that keeps a non-expression node as an argument; only the `in` family is reachable today (UNION arguments are rejected earlier by `hasScopeDependentNodesForEarlyShortCircuit`). Found during automated review of [PR #83505](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/83505). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr83505_001` </details> cc @fhw12345 @novikd @alexey-milovidov (from #83505)
signal.author: clickgapai

signal.title: minmax/set skip index on mortonEncode(x,y): any query on x or y throws Code 10
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **A table with `INDEX i mortonEncode(x, y) TYPE minmax` (or `TYPE set(N)`, or `hilbertEncode`) accepts `CREATE` and `INSERT`, but every `SELECT` whose `WHERE` mentions `x` or `y` fails with `Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column x in block. There are only columns: mortonEncode(x, y). (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK)`. Queries on the curve expression itself (`WHERE mortonEncode(x,y) > 100`) still work, as does the same query with `use_skip_indexes = 0` or `analyze_index_with_space_filling_curves = 0`.** - **Root cause:** [`src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp:3108`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/57516b9fe4de3/src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp#L3108) assumes every space-filling-curve argument name is present in the key expression's sample block. That holds for the primary-key and partition-key expressions (which keep their input columns) but not for a skip-index expression, whose sample block contains only the index expression results. `getAllSpaceFillingCurves` registers the curve without checking that its arguments are resolvable in that sample block. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `MergeTreeIndexMinMax::createIndexCondition` -> `buildCondition` ([`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexMinMax.cpp:201`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/57516b9fe4de3/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexMinMax.cpp#L201)) builds `KeyCondition{filter_dag, context, index.column_names, index.expression}`. The constructor calls `getAllSpaceFillingCurves`, where the curve node IS the index column, so the `key_columns.find` guard added by this PR succeeds and the curve is registered with `arguments = {x, y}`. Later, `extractAtomFromTree` -> `isKeyPossiblyWrappedByMonotonicFunctions` -> `isKeyPossiblyWrappedByMonotonicFunctionsImpl` matches the atom column `x` against `curve.arguments` and calls `sample_block.getByName("x")` at [`src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp:3108`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/57516b9fe4de3/src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp#L3108). For a skip index, `sample_block = info.key_expr->getSampleBlock()` (KeyCondition.cpp:3075) is the index sample block, which holds only `mortonEncode(x, y)` - the source columns are projected out. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp:3108`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/57516b9fe4de3/src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp#L3108) — curve-argument branch of isKeyPossiblyWrappedByMonotonicFunctionsImpl - unguarded sample_block.getByName(name) - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp:1414`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/57516b9fe4de3/src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp#L1414) — getAllSpaceFillingCurves registers the curve without checking that its argument names exist in info.key_expr->getSampleBlock() - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexMinMax.cpp:201`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/57516b9fe4de3/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexMinMax.cpp#L201) — buildCondition passes index.column_names + index.expression, whose sample block omits the source columns - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexSet.cpp:374`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/57516b9fe4de3/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexSet.cpp#L374) — same construction for TYPE set(N) - same failure **Impact:** A table whose DDL ClickHouse accepted becomes effectively unreadable: any predicate on a column that is an argument of the indexed curve aborts the query during query-plan optimization. Same user-visible shape as the bug this PR fixes (create + insert succeed, reads fail), reached through the skip-index construction site the PR description names as one of the three it covers. Workarounds are `SETTINGS analyze_index_with_space_filling_curves = 0` or `use_skip_indexes = 0` per query, or dropping the index. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `57516b9fe4de3`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/ab664c4c-8f38-4973-8780-589551b21d47) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- Test: a minmax/set skip index over a space-filling curve must not break queries on the curve's arguments. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_curve_minmax_idx; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_curve_set_idx; CREATE TABLE t_curve_minmax_idx (x UInt32, y UInt32, INDEX i mortonEncode(x, y) TYPE minmax GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t_curve_minmax_idx SELECT number % 100, number % 37 FROM numbers(1000); SELECT count() FROM t_curve_minmax_idx WHERE x = 5; SELECT count() FROM t_curve_minmax_idx WHERE x >= 10 AND x <= 20 AND y >= 5 AND y <= 15; CREATE TABLE t_curve_set_idx (x UInt32, y UInt32, INDEX i hilbertEncode(x, y) TYPE set(100) GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t_curve_set_idx SELECT number % 100, number % 37 FROM numbers(1000); SELECT count() FROM t_curve_set_idx WHERE y = 5; DROP TABLE t_curve_minmax_idx; DROP TABLE t_curve_set_idx; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` 10 33 27 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` [1 / 1] 05028_space_filling_curve_skip_index_arg: [ FAIL ] 0.09 sec. Reason: return code: 10 Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column x in block. There are only columns: mortonEncode(x, y). (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) (version 26.8.1.1841 (official build)) (query 5, line 9) (in query: SELECT count() FROM t_curve_minmax_idx WHERE x = 5;), Stack trace: 4. DB::Block::getPositionByName(String const ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> In `getAllSpaceFillingCurves`, alongside the new `key_columns.find` guard, also require that every curve argument is resolvable in the key expression's sample block before registering the curve - e.g. treat `!info.key_expr->getSampleBlock().has(child->result_name)` the same way a non-`INPUT` child is treated (clear `curve.arguments` and break). That keeps primary-key and partition-key pruning untouched (their sample blocks contain the source columns) and turns the skip-index case into a plain no-op instead of an exception. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/ManifestFilesPruning.cpp:137` constructs `KeyCondition(inverted_dag, context, {name_and_type->name}, expression)` with a single column name and an arbitrary expression; if that expression can ever contain a curve whose arguments are projected out, it hits the same line. I could not construct an Iceberg table with a space-filling-curve min/max expression in this environment, so it is untested. Found during automated review of [PR #114233](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114233). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114233_001` </details> cc @groeneai @al13n321 (from #114233)
signal.author: clickgapai

signal.title: DatabaseMySQL::getTablesIterator throws: one unreachable MySQL DB breaks system.tables
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With a `MySQL` database engine attached to an unreachable server, `SELECT ... FROM system.tables` and `SELECT ... FROM system.columns` fail server-wide with `Code: 279 ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED` under default settings. Any query whose identifier fails to resolve also answers 279 instead of `UNKNOWN_TABLE`, because the hint lookup iterates every database.** - **Root cause:** `DatabaseMySQL::getTablesIterator` calls `fetchTablesIntoLocalCache` with no try/catch, unlike its sibling `DatabasePostgreSQL::getTablesIterator`, which wraps the same work and states the invariant in a comment: 'Do not allow to throw here, because this might be, for example, a query to system.tables. It must not fail on case of some postgres error.' ([`src/Databases/PostgreSQL/DatabasePostgreSQL.cpp:160-161`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Databases/PostgreSQL/DatabasePostgreSQL.cpp#L160-L161), catch at :171-174). Predates this PR; the PR touches the tolerated-failure handling in both files and leaves the asymmetry in place. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `StorageSystemTables` -> `IDatabase::getLightweightTablesIterator` -> `DatabaseMySQL::getTablesIterator` ([`src/Databases/MySQL/DatabaseMySQL.cpp:184`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Databases/MySQL/DatabaseMySQL.cpp#L184)) -> `fetchTablesIntoLocalCache` (:299) -> `mysqlxx::PoolWithFailover::get` throws `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED` ([`src/Common/mysqlxx/PoolWithFailover.cpp:294-296`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Common/mysqlxx/PoolWithFailover.cpp#L294-L296)). Nothing on that path catches. The typo path is `IdentifierResolver::tryGetTableNameHint` -> `TableNameHints::getAllRegisteredNames` -> `IDatabase::getAllTableNames` -> the same iterator. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Databases/MySQL/DatabaseMySQL.cpp:184`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Databases/MySQL/DatabaseMySQL.cpp#L184) — getTablesIterator calls fetchTablesIntoLocalCache with no catch - [`src/Databases/MySQL/DatabaseMySQL.cpp:299`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Databases/MySQL/DatabaseMySQL.cpp#L299) — fetchTablesIntoLocalCache — borrows from mysql_pool, propagates ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED - [`src/Databases/PostgreSQL/DatabasePostgreSQL.cpp:171`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d8bf9a01b85be/src/Databases/PostgreSQL/DatabasePostgreSQL.cpp#L171) — sibling that does catch, stating the invariant this violates **Impact:** One unreachable MySQL remote makes `system.tables` and `system.columns` unusable for every user and every tool on the server (BI introspection, client autocompletion, monitoring). It also poisons CI: a stateless test that attaches such a database and aborts before its DROP leaves it attached for the rest of the run. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `d8bf9a01b85be`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Tag justification, matching 04210_show_remote_databases_in_system_tables: -- no-fasttest: depends on libmysql (MySQL database engine), not built in fast test. -- no-parallel: the database created here points at an unreachable host and is visible in -- system.tables, so a concurrent scan without a database filter would connect there too. -- An unreachable MySQL database must not break an unfiltered system.tables / system.columns scan. DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS {CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE_1:Identifier}; SET send_logs_level = 'fatal'; ATTACH DATABASE {CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE_1:Identifier} ENGINE = MySQL('127.0.0.1:1', 'fake_db', 'user', 'password') SETTINGS connect_timeout = 1, connection_max_tries = 1; SELECT count() > 0 FROM system.tables; SELECT count() > 0 FROM system.columns; DROP DATABASE {CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE_1:Identifier}; ``` ### Expected behavior ``` 1 1 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Received exception from server (version 26.8.1): Code: 279. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:19020. DB::Exception: Connections to mysql failed: fake_db@127.0.0.1:1 as user user, ERROR 2002 : mysqlxx::ConnectionFailed: Can't connect to server on '127.0.0.1' (115) ((nullptr):0). signal.title: CHECK TABLE returns 0 instead of failing when the check is aborted by a partial shutdown (Keeper session loss) — a false corruption alarm on healthy data
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong When a `ReplicatedMergeTree` replica has lost its Keeper session and entered partial shutdown, `CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=1` returns `0` — the result that is documented to mean "the check detected an error in the table data" — even though the data is perfectly healthy and nothing was actually checked. The window is deterministic. In the first seconds of a Keeper outage (session still alive but unresponsive), the query correctly fails with `KEEPER_EXCEPTION` / `Connection loss`. Once the session expires and the restarting thread calls partial shutdown, the same query flips from erroring to *certifying failure*: the storage check throws `ABORTED` ("Table shutdown was called"), and `TableCheckTask::checkNext` in `src/Interpreters/InterpreterCheckQuery.cpp` deliberately refuses to rethrow `ABORTED`, converting it into a `CheckResult` row with `success=false` and an empty `part_path`, and marks the task finished — so the remaining parts are never checked and the single-value aggregation latches `0`. With `check_query_single_value_result=0` the output is a single row with an empty part path and the message `Table shutdown was called` — clearly not a per-part data verdict, yet in the single-value form it is indistinguishable from real corruption. Any monitoring or automation that runs `CHECK TABLE` and alerts (or quarantines, or re-replicates) on `0` fires a false alarm on every Keeper flap. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Reproduces on 26.8.1.1068 (official build) and on current master 26.8.1.1833 (official build). ### How to reproduce 1. Start a ClickHouse server with a standalone (or embedded) Keeper and create a small `ReplicatedMergeTree` table with a few parts: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt16) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/t', 'r0') PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, number, number % 4 FROM numbers(1000); ``` 2. Verify the baseline: `CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=1` returns `1`. 3. Pause the Keeper process (`kill -STOP <keeper pid>`) and wait for the session to expire so the replica enters partial shutdown (the table becomes readonly). 4. Run the check repeatedly. Observed timeline: ``` t+30s CHECK -> Code: 999. Coordination::Exception: ... Connection loss ... (KEEPER_EXCEPTION) -- correct: the query fails t+35s CHECK -> 0 -- wrong: certifies data failure ``` With `check_query_single_value_result=0` the `0` case returns one row: empty part path, `is_passed=0`, message `DB::Exception: Table shutdown was called`. 5. Resume the Keeper (`kill -CONT <keeper pid>`); after the session is re-established, `CHECK TABLE` returns `1` again. ### Expected behavior `CHECK TABLE` should fail with an error (as it already does for the session-loss window) whenever the check could not be executed. A result of `0` should only ever mean that at least one part actually failed its data check. ### Error message and/or stacktrace `is_passed=0` row produced without any part being read: ``` 0 DB::Exception: Table shutdown was called ``` ### Additional context The conversion happens in the `catch` block of `TableCheckTask::checkNext` (`src/Interpreters/InterpreterCheckQuery.cpp`): `ABORTED` is excluded from the retryable-exception rethrow, turned into a failed `CheckResult` with an empty path, and `is_finished` is set so the remaining parts are skipped. The same window also reproduces on `SharedMergeTree`.

signal.title: Fix integer underflow in MySQL protocol handshake
signal.text: Prevent an unsigned integer underflow in the MySQL handshake handler that removes the intended bound on how much data an unauthenticated client can make the server buffer. In `MySQLHandler::finishHandshake` the first socket read may return more bytes than the client-declared packet size. When `pos > packet_size` the unsigned expression `packet_size - pos` underflows to a huge value, turning the following `copyData()` into an unbounded pre-auth read that keeps buffering socket data until EOF or the memory limit is reached. This adds a check that rejects such malformed handshake packets before the subtraction. A conforming client never sends more than the packet it announced in the header, so the check is unreachable on the normal path and introduces no regression. The MySQL interface is enabled by default (`mysql_port` 9004), so the code path is reachable without special config. This is a hardening fix, not a crash: the underflowed value is only a loop counter and is never used as a pointer offset or buffer size, so there is no memory corruption — the impact is bounded pre-auth memory pressure. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an integer underflow in the MySQL protocol handshake handler that could cause the server to buffer an unbounded amount of data from an unauthenticated client. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115776&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115776](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115776+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
