signal.title: Derive deterministic conditions from conditions involving the current time for the query condition cache
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): The query condition cache now serves conditions that involve the current time, e.g. `WHERE time >= now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY`, when reading from `MergeTree` tables, by deriving a deterministic condition from them with the current-time constant rounded onto a time grid. Closes #115504. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes Documented in `docs/concepts/features/performance/caches/query-condition-cache.mdx` and in the new settings' descriptions. --- A condition like `time >= now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY` reaches the storage layer with the current-time expression folded into a non-deterministic constant. It could never benefit from the query condition cache: the constant (and hence the condition hash) changes with every query, and the cache refuses non-deterministic conditions anyway (#81506, #84508). This PR derives a **deterministic** condition from such conditions by rounding the folded time constants onto a time grid: ``` time >= '2026-08-09 12:34:56' ~~~> time >= '2026-08-09 00:00:00' (rounded down) time >= '2026-08-10 00:00:00' (rounded up) ``` The grid step is proportional to the distance between the constant and the current time — one day for a condition looking back ten days, one hour for a condition looking back ninety minutes — multiplied by a configurable factor (`query_condition_cache_time_condition_grid_factor`, default 1.0) and capped at one day. This bounds the boundary error relative to the window the query looks at, and makes the cache key rotate roughly once per the same fraction of the window, balancing cache usefulness against staleness of the boundary. **Soundness.** The two sides of the cache round in opposite directions, so each cache entry stays a true statement regardless of clocks, concurrency, shards or replicas: * **Writes** (an observed "no rows of this granule match the filter") are stored under a *strengthened* condition — the derived condition implies the evaluated one, so "no rows match the evaluated condition" implies "no rows match the derived condition". This covers all three write sites: the WHERE filter (`updateQueryConditionCache`/`FilterTransform`), the PREWHERE filter (`MergeTreeSelectProcessor`), and the index-analysis granule exclusions (`ReadFromMergeTree`, under the skip-index-profiled key as before). * **Reads** (`filterPartsByQueryConditionCache`) probe a *weakened* condition — the actual filter implies the derived one, so "no rows match the derived condition" makes skipping the granule sound. Each side only needs its own implication, verified locally against its own condition; a hit is possible only when the two derived conditions are structurally identical (same rounded constant), so entries can never be misapplied. **Behavior.** When the folded constant is already aligned to the grid — `today() - 10`, `toStartOfDay(now())`, `toStartOfHour(now())` (rounding is DST-aware, in the timezone of the constant's type) — rounding up and down coincide, so the very next query already reuses the cache, and the key stays stable until the constant changes (e.g. until the end of the day). This exactly matches the issue's example: the derived condition "can be used until the end of day". For an unaligned constant like raw `now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY`, writes go to the grid point above the constant and reads probe the grid point below, so entries written during one grid cell serve the queries of the next one: yesterday's queries prime the cache for today's dashboards. The derivation understands monotone condition shapes: `AND`/`OR` chains, `NOT` (which flips the rounding direction), and comparisons of a deterministic expression with a non-deterministic constant of type `Date`/`Date32`/`DateTime`/`DateTime64`. Anything else non-deterministic (e.g. `rand()`, `__topKFilter` mixes, equality with a time constant, non-temporal folded constants such as `shardNum()` arithmetic) keeps the previous behavior: not cached. Deterministic conditions are entirely unaffected — they keep their existing hashes. Verified locally (single part of 2M rows, half of them older than the condition boundary): the second run of `SELECT sum(x) FROM tab WHERE time >= today() - 100` drops 122/245 granules through the PREWHERE consult path and 117/245 through the WHERE path. New settings: * `use_query_condition_cache_for_time_conditions` (default: `true`) * `query_condition_cache_time_condition_grid_factor` (default: `1.0`; values <= 0 disable the derivation) Possible follow-ups (out of scope here): same-cell reuse for unaligned constants by additionally evaluating the weakened condition at the write sites; applying the derivation to the object-storage read paths and to the TopK predicate-only reuse hash. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115522&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115522](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115522+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Delete Iceberg table files on DROP with iceberg_delete_data_on_drop
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108524 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `DROP TABLE` on an Iceberg table with `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop = 1` not deleting the table's files, which made re-creating a table at the same path fail with `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS`. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108524 Long-standing (reproduces at least down to v25.9), not a recent regression. Two independent bugs, both in the self-managed Iceberg drop path: 1. `IcebergMetadata::drop` passed the table path as both the listing base and the prefix. `listFiles` keys on `path / prefix`, so it looked under `table_path/table_path` and matched nothing. Fixed with an empty prefix, matching the existing `create` and `Hudi` callers. 2. `StorageObjectStorage::drop` runs in a background pool and read `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop` from the global context, always the default `false`, so deletion never ran even with bug 1 fixed. The value is now captured from the query context in `checkTableCanBeDropped` and applied to the context passed to the background drop, the same `mutable`-flag pattern `StorageNATS`/`StorageRabbitMQ` use for drop-time state. The `DataLakeCatalog` path needed separate work: `DatabaseDataLake::dropTable` re-resolves a fresh storage instance, so it never saw the `checkTableCanBeDropped` snapshot and its uninitialized metadata made `configuration->drop()` a no-op. It now replays `checkTableCanBeDropped` with the query context, and `drop()` initializes metadata only when deleting data. With the setting off (default) files are left in place, as before. Failure handling is per owning database (`DropCleanupPolicy`): reattaching databases never get a partially deleted table back, async-retry databases keep their retry metadata, and the catalog path keeps its row and metadata anchor so a failed DROP stays retryable. Known residual, catalog-backed path only: a DROP failing midway is retryable but not atomic. If a later data delete throws, or the catalog removal does, the table stays visible with part of its data deleted. Atomicity needs the reverse ordering (trading this for orphaned files with no SQL retry path) or a persisted drop intent, both outside this fix. Regression tests `04365_iceberg_delete_data_on_drop_108524` and `04366_iceberg_drop_best_effort_cleanup_109071` fail without the fix and pass with it, plus catalog-path coverage in `test_database_iceberg`. Default-off behavior is checked unchanged. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109071&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109071](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109071+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add a notebook mode to the Web UI
signal.text: Adds a notebook mode to the Web SQL UI (`/play`): a tab can become an ordered sequence of cells, each either a query with its own result or a block of Markdown text — the shape of document Jupyter, Observable, Hex and Deepnote use, and for the same purpose: keeping a chain of queries, and the reasoning between them, on one page. ## How it works A tab starts as a single query cell and looks exactly as it always has — no headers, no cell chrome, no notebook. Once a query has produced a result, a large muted `[+]` appears under it and expands into the two kinds of cell that can be added, query or text. Adding the second cell is what turns notebook mode on, and it is per tab: one tab can be a notebook while another stays a plain single-query editor, and each tab remembers its own notebook across reloads. From two cells on, each cell gets a header with its position and kind (`1. Query`, `2. Text`) and the editing actions: run, edit, insert a cell before, move up/down, delete. There is still exactly one query editor on the page — the full one, with its highlighting backdrop, autocompletion and query-parameter inputs. In notebook mode it is docked into whichever query cell is active, and shown only while it has the focus; as soon as focus leaves, that cell collapses to its query on a single line, syntax highlighted, whitespace runs reduced to one space, fading out on the right. The Run / progress / copy / download row docks under the query being edited, between it and its result, and appears and disappears with the editor. Results are more compact: a smaller font with the cell padding scaled to match, and a table of at most a quarter of the viewport that is its own scroll container on both axes, so its (thin) scrollbars sit at its own edges and a long or wide result neither pushes the notebook down the page nor widens it. Results and Markdown editors can be resized by dragging their bottom edge, as the query editor already could. A text cell shows its Markdown source with the markers highlighted while it is being edited, and the rendered result once editing finishes. Raw HTML is escaped and link targets are restricted to `http`, `https`, `mailto` and relative URLs. ## Implementation The query text, parameters and result snapshot moved from the tab to a cell. `tab.query` / `tab.result` / `tab.resultEl` and the rest are now accessors onto the cell the editor is docked in, so the editor, history, URL and persistence code is unchanged and always means "the cell in front of the user". A run captures its own cell, so moving on to another cell mid-run does not redirect the response. The Logs/Metrics view and the resource meters follow the cell whose result they describe. The whole notebook is persisted in IndexedDB alongside the rest of the workspace, and history entries record the cell they belong to so Back/Forward cannot push one cell's query into another. A tab holding a single cell renders exactly as before — verified by screenshot diff against `master`: 51 pixels differ, all on one row, all by 1 in a single channel. ## Testing Driven in headless Chrome against a local server: cell creation and deletion, moving and inserting cells, collapsing and expanding, per-tab independence, tab duplicate/close with a docked editor, query parameters inside a cell, per-cell errors, reload restore from IndexedDB, "Run all" inside a cell, the Logs and Metrics views per cell, column and result resizing, the theme switch and download menu inside the docked Run row, Markdown rendering and backdrop alignment, and light and dark themes. Two pre-existing issues were fixed along the way: the download drop-down positioned itself without accounting for `#main`'s scroll offset, and the `#run` submit button needed `form="controls"` once it could be moved out of the form's subtree. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a notebook mode to the Web UI (`/play`). After a query is run, a `[+]` button under the result adds further cells, each either a query with its own result or a block of Markdown text, turning the tab into a notebook in the style of Jupyter or Observable. Cells can be run, reordered, inserted and deleted individually; the query editor collapses to a single line when it is not focused, results are bounded and scroll inside themselves, and the whole notebook is restored on reload. Notebook mode is per tab, so a tab that has only one cell looks and behaves exactly as before. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115378&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115378](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115378+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support UPDATE of sorting/partition key columns via a server-side insert-then-delete
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Use case Today `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE` and lightweight `UPDATE` both refuse any column that participates in the sorting key, the primary key, the partition key, or the `sign`/`version` columns: ``` DB::Exception: Cannot UPDATE key column `x`. (CANNOT_UPDATE_COLUMN) ``` The common real-world need is not "update the key at scale", it is a one-off correction or backfill of a value that happens to be part of `ORDER BY` — a mis-ingested `tenant_id`, a device id that was recorded wrong for a range of rows, a category that has to be re-mapped after a schema decision changed. These are rare, bounded, and not latency-sensitive. The only options right now are to rebuild the affected data by hand (`INSERT INTO ... SELECT` into a new table, or `INSERT` the corrected rows and then `DELETE` the originals, keeping the two consistent yourself), or to drop and reload a partition. Both are error-prone precisely because the user has to get the atomicity right, which is the part the server is in a much better position to handle. I want to be upfront that this cannot be made cheap. It is a full rewrite of the affected rows and it temporarily stores them twice. The value here is that the operation becomes *possible and safe*, not that it becomes fast. ### Describe the solution you'd like Rather than trying to make mutations able to update key columns in place, implement `UPDATE` on key columns as a **server-side insert-then-delete**: 1. Read the rows matching the `WHERE` clause. 2. Apply the assignments. 3. Write the modified rows back through the ordinary insert path. 4. Retire the original rows with a lightweight delete. The appeal is that ClickHouse already has both halves, and they already solve the two hard problems by construction: * `MergeTreeDataWriter::writeTempPart` sorts each block by the sorting key (`stableGetPermutation`), so the resulting parts are correctly ordered no matter how the key values changed. * `MergeTreeDataWriter::splitBlockIntoParts` routes rows to the partition their new key values actually belong to, so a changed partition key lands in the right place instead of staying in the wrong part. * `_row_exists` retires the originals without rewriting the source parts. So the primary index, the part min/max key bounds, partition pruning and merge inputs all stay correct without any new machinery for maintaining sort order. The engineering that remains is real but bounded and well-understood: * **Atomicity** — a reader must not observe both the old and the new copy of a row, nor neither. This is the core of the work. * **Replication ordering** — the insert and the delete have to reach replicas as one logical step. * **`ReplacingMergeTree` / deduplication** — the new rows must not be collapsed against, or deduplicated away by, the originals. * Behaviour when the `UPDATE` touches both key and non-key columns (the whole row is rewritten either way, so this is mostly a question of which path is chosen). Two consequences worth stating in advance, because they are user-visible: * `_part_offset` and `_block_number` change for the affected rows. Anything that depends on them (including patch parts for the same rows) has to account for that. * Cost is proportional to the rows matched by `WHERE`, not to the columns assigned — this is a row rewrite, not a column rewrite. A reasonable shape would be to keep the current error by default and put this behind an explicit setting, so nobody pays for it accidentally. ### Describe alternatives you've considered **Re-sorting the part inside the mutation.** `MutateTask` contains no sorting at all today — it streams a part's rows through in stored order and writes them back, and it never recomputes the partition id. Adding a sort there would handle the sorting key, but: * it would not help the partition key at all, since the row has to physically move to a different part in a different partition, while a mutation is 1 source part → 1 result part with the same partition id; * it would break the "mutations preserve row order" invariant that patch parts rely on — v2 patches address rows by `(_block_number, _block_offset)` and are sorted by the storage sorting-key prefix (see `getEffectivePatchSortingKeySize`) precisely so that `RangesInPatchParts` can locate rows by key range. If a key value changes, a patch's key no longer matches its target. **Just lifting the check.** This is not viable: nothing anywhere validates that a part is sorted (`checkDataPart` does not), so violating the invariant is silent wrong results rather than an error. #78655 is a live example of the same failure mode arriving through a different door — a rollup `TTL ... GROUP BY ... SET` legitimately changes a partition-key column, and afterwards partition pruning filters out the rows that were rolled up, so `SELECT ... WHERE <partition expr>` silently returns nothing. Related: #99647 refuses materializing columns used in sort key expressions for the same underlying reason. **Leaving it to the user.** This is the status quo. It works, but the atomicity is exactly the part that is easy to get wrong and that the server could do properly. ### Additional context Where the restriction lives, as of 26.8: * `validateUpdateColumns` in `src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp` raises `CANNOT_UPDATE_COLUMN`. * The forbidden set comes from `getKeyColumns` in the same file, and is broader than the documentation sentence "It isn't possible to update columns that are part of the primary or sorting key" suggests — it is partition key columns ∪ sorting key columns ∪ `sign` ∪ `version`. * Lightweight `UPDATE` is subject to the same rule, because `MergeTreeData::updateLightweightImpl` builds a `MutationsInterpreter` too. The `sign`/`version` case is worth separating from the other two. Those columns decide what a `Collapsing`/`Replacing`/`VersionedCollapsing` merge collapses, so changing them changes row identity rather than row content. It may well be right to keep rejecting those even if sorting-key and partition-key updates become possible. I am happy to prototype this if the direction seems acceptable — including the narrower first step of proving out what the insert-then-delete path breaks in the existing test suite before any of the atomicity work.

signal.title: Fix vector search with `arrayJoin` below the sort and with a row policy
signal.text: Fixes for the vector search `ORDER BY <distance> LIMIT` optimization. **`arrayJoin` below the sort.** `arrayJoin` changes the number of rows - an empty array drops its base row - so the rewrite must not shortlist base rows before it runs. `optimizeTopK` rejects `arrayJoin` for this reason (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82279), but the vector search optimization did not, so the rows that a later base row would have contributed were never produced: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt32, tags Array(UInt32), vec Array(Float32), INDEX idx vec TYPE vector_similarity('hnsw', 'cosineDistance', 2)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS index_granularity = 4; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, if(number < 16, [], [number]), [toFloat32(number), toFloat32(number + 1)] FROM numbers(64); SELECT arrayJoin(tags) FROM t ORDER BY cosineDistance(vec, [0., 1.]) LIMIT 1; -- returned nothing; with `use_skip_indexes = 0` it returns 16 ``` **A row policy is an additional filter.** A row policy restricts rows inside the reader just like a `WHERE` or a `PREWHERE`, but it did not participate in `additional_filters_present`, so a query filtered only by a policy was treated as unfiltered: the `vector_search_filter_strategy = 'prefilter'` bailout was skipped, so an explicit request for exact search was ignored, and the index fetched only `LIMIT` neighbours without the `vector_search_index_fetch_multiplier` compensation, which the policy can then discard. **Filters that read the vector column broke the non-rescoring rewrite** (found during review). The rewrite drops the physical vector column from the read list and replaces it with the virtual `_distance` column, so any filter that still needs the column was left without its input and the query failed with `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` (an exception, pre-existing on master). The rewrite is now skipped - the same treatment as the vector column in `SELECT` - when the column is read by: - a row policy (including a policy carried in the deferred filter under `FINAL` with `apply_row_policy_after_final`), - a plain `WHERE` filter below the sort, e.g. `WHERE length(vec) > 0` (reachable with default settings, because the implicit `PREWHERE` optimization is disabled for vector-search candidates). The quantized-codes rewrite (`useVectorSearchWithQuantizedCodes`) is not affected by these problems: it splices the shortlist above the whole `Expression`/`Filter` chain, so the expansion and the filters run below it, and its reader-side filters prefilter the approximate ranking. This was checked with the same queries. `FINAL` with an explicit `PREWHERE` is covered by a separate regression test. `FINAL` can defer a `PREWHERE` until after the merge, but the deferral copies the filter and clears `query_info.prewhere_info` only when the pipeline is built, i.e. past every query plan optimization, so the existing `getPrewhereInfo` bailout still fires and the physical vector column survives for the deferred filter. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82279 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110188 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed vector search returning too few rows for a query with `arrayJoin` below `ORDER BY <distance> LIMIT`. A row policy now counts as an additional filter for vector search, so `vector_search_filter_strategy = 'prefilter'` is honored and the index fetch multiplier is applied for a query filtered by a row policy. Fixed `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` for a non-rescoring vector search query when a `WHERE` filter or a row policy reads the vector column. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114074&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114074](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114074+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix JSON/XML format statistics race condition with parallel replicas
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `rows_read` and `rows_before_limit_at_least` reported as 0 or stale in JSON/XML format output when a query with `LIMIT` reads from remote connections (parallel replicas or the `remote` table function). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) No documentation changes needed — this is a bug fix with no user-facing API changes. --- ## Summary - When parallel replicas are used with `LIMIT`, `rows_read` in JSON/XML output is reported as 0 - Root cause: race condition where `finalizeImpl` writes statistics BEFORE `PipelineExecutor::finalizeExecution` collects remaining progress from connection draining - Fix: two-phase output format finalization — statistics are written AFTER all progress has been collected - The same drain also delivers late `ProfileInfo` packets that update the `rows_before_limit_at_least` / `rows_before_aggregation` counters, so the deferral covers the whole trailer, and the native-protocol `ProfileInfo` sent to the client is refreshed from the post-drain counters ## Approach Split the output format's finalization so statistics are written AFTER `finalizeExecution` collects all remaining progress: - **Phase 1** (during pipeline, in `finalizeImpl`): Write everything EXCEPT the trailer after the `rows` field (`rows_before_limit_at_least`, `rows_before_aggregation`, the `"statistics"` section) and closing delimiter - **Phase 2** (after `finalizeExecution`): Re-read the rows-before-* counters, write the trailer and close the document via a finalize callback ### Key changes: - `IOutputFormat`: Added `hasDeferredStatistics`, `writeDeferredStatisticsAndFinalize`, `completeDeferredStatistics` mechanism; `snapshotRowsBeforeCounters` re-reads the shared counters before the deferred trailer is written - `PipelineExecutor`: Added `setFinalizeCallback` called at end of `finalizeExecution` after progress collection - `CompletedPipelineExecutor`: Sets the finalize callback to invoke `completeDeferredStatistics` - `JSONRowOutputFormat`, `XMLRowOutputFormat`, `JSONColumnsWithMetadataBlockOutputFormat`: Override deferred statistics methods; the whole trailer (`rows_before_limit_at_least`, `rows_before_aggregation`, `statistics`) is deferred to phase 2 (`JSONUtils::writeRowsBeforeAndStatistics` factors out the shared writer) - `ParallelFormattingOutputFormat`: Propagates deferred statistics through the parallel formatting pipeline - `LazyOutputFormat` / `PullingOutputFormat`: `getProfileInfo` re-snapshots the rows-before-* counters, so the `ProfileInfo` packet sent to native-protocol clients (TCP `clickhouse-client`, gRPC, `LocalConnection`) carries the post-drain values — by the time it is sent, the executor thread has been joined and the counters are final - New failpoint `tcp_handler_sleep_before_secondary_query_trailing_packets` delays a secondary query's trailing `Totals` / `Extremes` / `ProfileInfo` / `Progress` / `EndOfStream`, making the race deterministic for tests Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85785 ## Test plan - [x] Build succeeds (Release) - [x] Test `00365_statistics_in_formats` passes - [x] JSON format tests pass (`00159_parallel_formatting_json_and_friends_1/2`, `00378_json_quote_64bit_integers`, `00685_output_format_json_escape_forward_slashes`, `01447_json_strings`, `01449_json_compact_strings`, `01486_json_array_output`, `02554_format_json_columns_for_empty`) - [x] XML format tests pass (`00307_format_xml`, `02122_parallel_formatting_XML`) - [x] `03918_statistics_in_formats_parallel_replicas` — forward guard: parallel-replicas `rows_read` matches the single-node value - [x] New deterministic reproducer `04603_rows_before_limit_parallel_replicas_late_packets` — fails without the fix (failpoint forces the trailing packets into the drain window); checks `rows_read` under parallel replicas and `rows_read` + `rows_before_limit_at_least` through the `remote` table function, over HTTP (server-side formatting) and native TCP (client-side formatting), across `JSON`, `JSONColumnsWithMetadata`, and `XML` - [ ] CI: Run with parallel replicas to verify `rows_read` is no longer 0 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches query pipeline execution, cancellation, and output formatting/finalization paths; while scoped to statistics/progress reporting, it changes timing and thread-synchronization and could affect query completion/cancellation behavior under parallel replicas. > > **Overview** > Fixes a race where JSON/XML output could report `rows_read=0` with parallel replicas + `LIMIT` by ensuring final `Progress` packets (drained after cancellation/early completion) are incorporated before statistics are emitted. > > This introduces **two-phase output finalization**: `IOutputFormat` can defer writing statistics/closing delimiters (`hasDeferredStatistics`/`writeDeferredStatisticsAndFinalize`), and `PipelineExecutor` now supports a `setFinalizeCallback` invoked at the end of `finalizeExecution()` after collecting remaining progress; `CompletedPipelineExecutor` wires this to `IOutputFormat::completeDeferredStatistics()`. > > Cancellation/draining logic is tightened to preserve trailing progress and avoid blocking hard cancels: `PipelineExecutor` triggers a `PartialResult` cancel on normal completion, `ISource::cancel` skips `onCancel` for `PartialResult` but allows later escalation, `RemoteSource` adds explicit cancel-reason upgrades and aborts drain via `RemoteQueryExecutor::abortDrain`, and `RemoteQueryExecutor::finish()` drains until all replica connections complete while swallowing expected cancel exceptions. Adds a stateless regression test `03918_statistics_in_formats_parallel_replicas` to assert `rows_read > 0` across JSON/XML formats over TCP/HTTP. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 5818266286a7645dcf1b57212bf9b3214cfd2ec8. signal.title: Fix has()/indexOf() zero-pad inconsistency for Array(FixedString)
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115311 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`/`indexOf` giving different results for `Array(FixedString)` depending on whether the array is a constant or a materialized column. Example: `has([toFixedString('V0', 3)], toFixedString('V0', 4))` was returning `0`, but the same check on a materialized array, or a plain `equals()`, returns `1`. Now both paths zero-pad `FixedString` values of different width the same way, so results are consistent. --- ### Problem `has`/`indexOf` on a constant array goes through `executeConst()` in `src/Functions/array/arrayIndex.h`. This function converts the array to `Array` (basically `std::vector<Field>`) and compares elements using `accurateEquals(Field, Field)`. The issue is `Field` does not have a separate type for `FixedString` -- it just becomes `Field::Types::String`. So once a `FixedString` value is put into a `Field`, there is no way to tell it apart from a normal `String`. And `accurateEquals` for `String` vs `String` is just plain `std::string` comparison, exact length only. No zero-padding. But the non-constant path (materialized array) works directly on `IColumn`/`ColumnFixedString`, and there zero-padding is applied correctly (same as `equals()` does, via `memcmpSmallLikeZeroPaddedAllowOverflow15`). So constant and non-constant paths give different answers for the same input. ### Fix Added a small helper `Impl::arrayIndexFieldsEqual()` in `arrayIndex.h`. It does zero-pad comparison for `Field`-level strings, but only if we already know from the *declared types* (before converting to `Field`) that one side is `FixedString`. This flag is computed once in `executeConst()` and passed down. Important: plain `String` vs `String` should NOT be zero-padded, that would be wrong behavior for normal strings. So the fix only kicks in when a `FixedString` type is actually involved. Note: `indexOfAssumeSorted` has a similar looking issue in its own binary search code (`Main::lowerBound`), but that function assumes the array is already sorted by the caller, which is a different contract, so not touching it here. Keeping this PR scoped to what the issue actually reports. ### Testing - Used a live tracer to confirm the actual code path changed, not just the output. After the fix, `accurateEquals` is not called anymore for the `FixedString` width-mismatch case (goes into new zero-pad branch instead). For plain `String` vs `String` (`has(['ab'], 'abc')`) it still calls `accurateEquals` like before -- so no unintended behavior change there. - Ran a matrix of 1791 generated cases covering different width/content combinations plus explicit `String`/`String` negative controls. Checked 4 things per case: constant result vs `materialize()`d result, constant result vs `arrayExists(x -> x = value, arr)` as ground truth, `indexOf` constant vs materialized, and `has` vs `indexOf` self-consistency. All 1791 cases passed, 0 mismatches. - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/04926_array_has_index_of_fixed_string_zero_pad.sql` covering the issue's repro, materialized/constant combinations in both directions, the `FixedString` vs `String` needle case, same-width negative controls, and `String`/`String` negative controls. Please review, happy to make changes if needed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115401&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115401](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115401+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not use a non-deterministic expression as a join key when rewriting a comma or `CROSS` join
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112965 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results for a comma or `CROSS` join whose `WHERE` compares columns of two tables through a non-deterministic expression such as `rand`. Such a query could return rows that contradict its own `WHERE` clause, because rewriting the join into an `INNER` join moved the expression into the join key, where it is evaluated again per row of each side. ### Description At default settings this query returns rows where `r.a` is not `3`: ```sql CREATE TABLE l (a UInt64) ENGINE = Memory; CREATE TABLE r (a UInt64) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO l SELECT number % 16 FROM numbers(500); INSERT INTO r SELECT number % 16 FROM numbers(500); SELECT uniqExact(r.a), countIf(r.a != 3) FROM l, r WHERE rand(l.a) % 16 = r.a AND rand(l.a) % 16 = 3; ``` Expected `1 0`. Master returns `10 29`: the second conjunct pins the key to `3`, yet 29 of the returned rows hold a different `r.a`. Only the new analyzer is affected, with `enable_analyzer = 0` the same query returns `1 0`. `CrossToInnerJoinPass` moves an `equals` conjunct out of the `WHERE` into the join `ON` and rebuilds the `WHERE` from the conjuncts it did not take. In the key position the expression is evaluated per row of each joined side instead of once per cross-product row, so the key a row was hashed under is unrelated to the value the surviving conjunct checked. The fix refuses a condition as a join key when its subtree holds a window function, a stateful function, one that is not deterministic in the scope of the query, or one fixed per executing node. A refused condition stays in the `WHERE`, exactly as `cross_to_inner_join_rewrite = 0` leaves it. The predicate is `isDeterministicInScopeOfQuery`, so `now`, `currentUser` and `randConstant` keep their rewrite. Several functions of that class did not declare the property and now do, so the pass compares no function names. `query_plan_merge_filter_into_join_condition` moves the same class of predicate into a join key and is fixed separately in #112965. No issue is linked because there is no existing report: I found this while auditing the pass. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112938&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112938](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112938+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Bind the parallel replicas shard scope to the cluster that produced it
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/81738 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results and a `LOGICAL_ERROR` when a query reads with parallel replicas inside a distributed sub-query whose `cluster_for_parallel_replicas` numbers its shards differently from the cluster the query is distributed over, for example a `VIEW` carrying its own `SETTINGS cluster_for_parallel_replicas`, or a read through `clusterAllReplicas` of that same cluster. The shard number shipped by the initiator was applied to the other numbering and selected the wrong shard. Parallel replicas are now declined for such a read. ### Description `prepareClusterForParallelReplicas` indexes the `_shard_num` scalar into `cluster_for_parallel_replicas` as if both described the same cluster. They are independent: `_shard_num` is shipped over the wire by a distributed query's initiator, while `cluster_for_parallel_replicas` is a per-query setting any nested `SETTINGS` clause can change, including inside a `view(...)`. - Above the other cluster's shard count, the read throws `LOGICAL_ERROR: Shard number is greater than shard count`, aborting debug and sanitizer builds. - In range, no check fires and the read silently returns **the wrong shard's data**: `10000090` where `90` is correct. `21ef1f1d1c9ba39` removed a `_cluster_for_parallel_replicas` scalar, reasoning that the setting alone identifies the cluster; a view with its own `SETTINGS` falsifies that. This restores the provenance as a second column of the `_shard_num` block, so overwriting the number replaces it atomically. A scope is honoured only when its provenance identifies the same shard *numbering*, not merely the same cluster name: `clusterAllReplicas` derives a renumbered cluster that keeps the name. Otherwise parallel replicas are declined at every admission site, giving the same results as `enable_parallel_replicas = 0`. No assertion is weakened: with admission gated, the `LOGICAL_ERROR` becomes correct rather than misapplied. Absent provenance means "trust the shard number", so mixed-version clusters keep today's behaviour. Each consequence reproduces on unpatched master and passes here. Added a stateless test, an integration test for the wrong-shard read, and gtests for wire cases SQL cannot build. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101325 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113589&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113589](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113589+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support safe type conversions in correlated subquery equivalence substitution
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113407 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101863 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Correlated subqueries with an equality on columns that differ only in nullability (e.g. `Int64` vs `Nullable(Int64)` under `data_type_default_nullable = 1`, as in TPC-DS Q35), or on native-number columns having a least common type (e.g. `Int32` vs `Int64`), are now decorrelated via equivalent-expression substitution instead of falling back to a CROSS JOIN with a post-join filter, avoiding severe memory growth on such queries. Closes #113407. --- ## Motivation The equivalent-expression substitution in `PlannerCorrelatedSubqueries` recorded an equivalence only when both sides of the correlated `equals` had exactly the same type. A correlated `EXISTS` whose join condition compares `Int64` with `Nullable(Int64)` therefore decorrelated through the CROSS JOIN fallback; at TPC-DS SF100 (Q35 with `data_type_default_nullable = 1`) the cross-joined intermediate grew without bound (35+ GiB and climbing before being killed, versus 1.72 s / 1.70 GiB with aligned column types). ## Approach The exact-type guard was load-bearing: correlated columns are `PLACEHOLDER` nodes typed with the outer column's type, and every decorrelated DAG declares that type for its inputs, so a substituted column of a different runtime type is a logical error during execution. The substitution therefore cannot simply alias a column of another type, nor cast to the common supertype — it must produce exactly the placeholder's type. Equivalence classes now track `(column name, type)` pairs. The recording guard admits, besides equal types, two verified-safe families: - nullability-only differences (any base type) — the equality predicate rejects `NULL`s; - native-number pairs with a least supertype — for them `equals` is mathematically exact (`9007199254740993 :: Int64 = 9007199254740992.0 :: Float64` is `0`), the supertype exists only when every type embeds losslessly, and `accurateCastOrNull` is exactness-checking, so value equivalence is transitive across a class. At substitution the chosen equivalent column is converted to exactly the correlated type: `toNullable` / lossless `CAST` when widening, `assumeNotNull` / `accurateCastOrNull` when narrowing. For the narrowing conversions a `FilterStep` is inserted below the renaming that drops rows whose value is `NULL` or does not convert exactly — such rows can never satisfy the recorded equality (a top-level AND-conjunct of an ancestor filter), and dropping them before `assumeNotNull` is required so that its arbitrary result for non-converting values cannot leak into aggregation keys (the aggregation decorrelation appends correlated identifiers as group keys). Pairs whose comparison semantics are not consistent with `CAST` keep the previous CROSS JOIN fallback: `Decimal` vs `Float` (comparison converts to `Float` and is inexact), `String` vs `FixedString` (comparison ignores padding), and supertype-less numeric pairs such as `Int64` vs `UInt64` or `Int64` vs `Float64`. ## Verification - The issue's reproducer plans with zero `cross` nodes and returns the same result as the fallback. - New stateless test `05023_correlated_subquery_equivalence_type_conversion` (12 cases: both nullability directions, widening/narrowing/sideways/float numerics with adversarial boundary values, scalar-subquery aggregation with an outer `0` vs inner `NULL`, guarded fallbacks) passed 6/6 runs under harness setting randomization. - A cross-check over 16 type pairs compared `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` / scalar `count()` results between substitution and the CROSS JOIN fallback on value pools with boundary values (`2^31±1`, `2^32±1`, `2^53`, `2^53+1`, non-integer floats) and `NULL`s — identical everywhere, and plan probes confirmed the substitution fires exactly for the admitted pairs. - The existing `correlated` stateless subset passes (3 environment-only failures in the local scratch setup: MinIO, test cluster, writable access storage). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115493&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115493](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115493+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Declarative function signatures, continuation of #3775
signal.text: This is an experimental continuation of [#3775 (2018)](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/3775) by @alexey-milovidov, which proposed a declarative way to describe function signatures so that argument validation and return-type inference can be driven by a small DSL instead of hand-written `getReturnTypeImpl` logic per function. ### What's in this branch A `getSignatureString()` method on `IFunction` and `IFunctionOverloadResolver`. When a function exposes a non-empty signature, the base `getReturnTypeImpl(ColumnsWithTypeAndName)` parses and applies it via a small grammar of type **matchers** (`UInt`, `Number`, `Array(T)`, `MaybeNullable(T)`, `Function((args), R)`, `T : Any` capture, …) and type **functions** (`leastSupertype`, `nativeNumber`, `aggregateFunctionReturnType(AggregateFunction(name, …))`, `subcolumnTypeOf`, `typeFromString`, `DateTime64(scale, tz)`, …). The DSL supports variadic positions (`…`), ellipsis grouping for repeated argument units (`T1, V1, …` repeats the pair), `OR` between alternatives, optional positions `[T]`, const-value capture (`const name String`), lambdas, etc. The grammar / parser / type matchers / type functions live under `src/DataTypes/FunctionSignature.h`, `FunctionSignature.cpp`, `TypeMatchers.cpp`, `TypeFunctions.cpp`. ### Coverage ~191 commits on top of master, each is a small per-family round titled `Function signatures: round N — …`. Current state on this branch: ``` SELECT count(*) AS total, countIf(signature != '') AS with_sig, round(countIf(signature != '') * 100.0 / count(*), 1) AS pct FROM system.functions WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND alias_to = '' AND origin = 'System'; 1416 1395 98.5 ``` (With \`allow_experimental_nlp_functions = 1\`; the few remaining unset ones are setting / config-gated functions like \`aiClassify\`, \`region*\`, \`synonyms\`, whose \`create\` throws unless the relevant config block / setting is present, so \`system.functions.tryGet\` returns null even though the signature is in source. With the right config + setting they all surface — verified in tmp/ test config.) Roughly: - **Authoritative** (DSL drives type-check and return type, the legacy `getReturnTypeImpl` is either gone or bypassed): higher-order array functions (`arrayMap`, `arrayFilter`, `arrayFirst*`, …), `toIntervalX`, comparison, `multiSearch*` / `multiMatch*`, vector L-norms / distances / dot product, `UUIDv7ToDateTime`, `arrayReduce` / `arrayReduceInRanges`, `reverse`, `mapKeys` / `mapValues`, `getSubcolumn`, the `least` / `greatest` resolver, paired-variadic `timeSeriesTagsToGroup` / `timeSeriesStoreTags`, … - **Documentation-only** (signature surfaced via `system.functions` but the legacy `getReturnTypeImpl` still runs because the result type uses promotion / widening / setting-dependent dispatch the current DSL can't express): arithmetic (`plus`, `minus`, `multiply`, `divide`, modulo / intDiv family), array widening (`arraySum` / `arrayCumSum*` / `arrayDifference`), `mapContains*Like`, `dateTrunc`, `toStartOfWeek`, `parseDateTime*`, `transform`, `range`, `toX` conversions, etc. There is a `signature_documentation` opt-in alongside `signature` in the binary-arithmetic, unary-arithmetic, FunctionArrayMapped, and FunctionMapToArrayAdapter families specifically so a function can advertise a signature without the DSL accidentally hijacking the legacy widening logic. ### Status Draft / experimental. - This is an experiment — I'm not asking for it to be merged. There's significant disruption (191 commits touching every function family), and the gain is mostly documentation: today only ~30% of the converted functions are actually DSL-authoritative; the rest are decorative. The arithmetic promotion matrix and the per-Op widening rules in particular would need a richer type-function vocabulary (or new matchers) before they can be expressed declaratively. - The branch has been kept rebased on master throughout and builds cleanly. I've run the stateless test suite on each round. The pre-existing-on-master test failures I hit are listed in commit messages of the rounds where I encountered them (none introduced by this work). - The original PR has been open since 2018 — this branch is intended as a concrete data point on \"what fraction of ClickHouse functions can be reasonably described by a declarative signature, and what would the DSL need to grow to cover the rest.\" That's the question I'd love feedback on. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=104948&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/104948](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F104948+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix compiled `if`/`multiIf` on a negative `Time` value
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `if` and `multiIf` returning a large positive value instead of a negative one when a `Time` branch is combined with `Time64`, `DateTime` or `DateTime64` and the expression is JIT-compiled. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115381 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114168 (found there in review; a separate mechanism) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/103390 A negative `Time` value read through a JIT-compiled `if`/`multiIf` comes back as a huge positive number: ```sql SELECT if(number % 2 = 0, toTime('-01:00:00'), toTime64('00:00:00', 3)) FROM numbers(1); -- executions 1-3: -01:00:00.000 -- execution 4+: 999:59:59.000 ``` No `SETTINGS` clause is needed to hit this: `compile_expressions` defaults to `1` and `min_count_to_compile_expression` to `3`, so the 4th execution of the expression in a session silently changes the answer. `enable_time_time64_type` also defaults to `1`. The wrong value is ticks `4294963696` = `2^32 - 3600`, i.e. the negative `Int32` tick count zero-extended to 64 bits. Root cause: `typeIsSigned` in `src/DataTypes/Native.cpp` did not list the `Time` family, so the widening cast emitted by `FunctionIfBase::compileImpl` asked whether `Time` is signed, got `false`, and LLVM emitted `zext` where `sext` was required. `Time` is `DataTypeNumberBase<Int32>` and is the only member of the date/time family that widens on this path, which is why the defect is specific to it. `Time64` is included in the same predicate for correctness of the contract: `isDecimal()` matches only `TypeIndex::Decimal32..256` and so does not cover `TypeIndex::Time64` - the same reason `isDateTime64()` is listed separately. No wrong-result carrier reaches the `Time64` half today, so it is not given a test that could not fail. Validation: five wrong-result carriers plus a `Nullable(Time)` case are covered by the new test. The reference values were taken from the non-compiled path on an unpatched binary, so the oracle is independent of this change. With the predicate token removed the test fails on 7 of 13 lines; non-negative `Time`, large-negative `Time`, and `DateTime64` controls are unchanged. 50/50 runs under settings randomization pass. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1864` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Add arrayPermutations, arrayPartialPermutations, and arrayCombinations
signal.text: Closes #43175 ### Changelog category: - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added new array combinatorics functions: `arrayPermutations`, `arrayPartialPermutations`, and `arrayCombinations`. These functions generate permutations and combinations by element indexes (so equal values may produce duplicate rows), validate argument `k`, and enforce result-size limits via `function_range_max_elements_in_block`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written in code Motivation: - Add built-in SQL functions for common combinatorics tasks on arrays without using external logic. Parameters: - `arrayPermutations(arr)`: - `arr`: source array, returns all full permutations. - `arrayPartialPermutations(arr, k)`: - `arr`: source array. - `k`: selection length, must be non-negative and not exceed array length. - `arrayCombinations(arr, k)`: - `arr`: source array. - `k`: combination length, must be non-negative and not exceed array length. - Result size is limited by `function_range_max_elements_in_block`. Example use: - `SELECT arrayPermutations([1, 2, 3]);` - `SELECT arrayPartialPermutations([1, 2, 3], 2);` - `SELECT arrayCombinations([1, 2, 3], 2);` <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101135&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101135](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101135+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support the NetCDF format
signal.text: Adds support for the [NetCDF](https://www.unidata.ucar.edu/software/netcdf/) format, a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays that is the standard way climate, weather, oceanographic and other scientific data is distributed. There is a lot of public data in it (ERA5, CMIP, NOAA, Copernicus), and until now the only way to query it with ClickHouse was to convert it first. Reading is supported for the three "classic" versions of the format: CDF-1, CDF-2 (64-bit offset) and CDF-5 (64-bit data), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. The files are parsed directly, so there is no new dependency. A NetCDF-4 file, which is an HDF5 file with a different data model on top, is recognized and reported with a message that says how to convert it. **Data model.** Every variable of a file becomes a column, and the rows enumerate the Cartesian product of all the dimensions that the variables use; a variable that does not use some of them is repeated along them. The `to_dataframe` method of `xarray` produces a table with the same columns and the same set of rows, though possibly in a different order: `to_dataframe` puts the dimensions in alphabetical order by default, while ClickHouse keeps the order of the dimensions of the variables. So a file with the dimensions `time`, `lat`, `lon` and the variables `time(time)`, `lat(lat)`, `lon(lon)`, `temperature(time, lat, lon)` reads as a table with four columns and `time * lat * lon` rows. The classic format has no string type, so a `char` variable is read as a String whose length is the last dimension of the variable, when that dimension serves only as the length of the strings; a dimension that anything else in the file uses as a real axis stays in the row space, and such a `char` variable is read as one character per row. Only the variables that a query needs are read, the number of rows comes from the header (so `count()` does not read any data), and an input that cannot be seeked is read into memory instead. **Writing.** Every column becomes a variable over a single dimension named `row`, so a file written by ClickHouse is read back with the same column names and the same rows; the types come back as the closest types of the classic format (a `FixedString` as a `String`, an `Enum` or a `LowCardinality` column as the type it wraps, dates and times as plain numbers, a `Nullable` column as its base type unless read with `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null`). The version of the format is chosen automatically: CDF-5 when a column needs a type that only CDF-5 has or takes more than 4 GiB, CDF-2 otherwise. A `Nullable` column is written with the `_FillValue` attribute, and a column with dates or times gets the `units` attribute of the CF conventions, so `xarray` decodes it back into timestamps. **Settings.** `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null` reads the values equal to the `_FillValue` (or `missing_value`) attribute of a variable as NULL, which is how the CF conventions mark missing data such as sea surface temperature over land. `input_format_netcdf_add_dimension_columns` adds a column with the index along every dimension that has no coordinate variable of the same name, for the files that have none. **Testing.** The test files in `tests/queries/0_stateless/data_netcdf` were written by the netCDF C library, not by this code. Beyond the two functional tests, during development the reader was compared value by value against an independent reference implementation for all three format versions, the output was checked by opening it with the netCDF C library for every supported type family, and 321 truncated and bit-flipped files were fed to the reader — all of them either parsed or failed with a clean error, with no crashes. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support the `NetCDF` format for both reading and writing. It is a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays, widely used for climate, weather and other scientific data. Reading supports all three classic versions of the format (CDF-1, CDF-2 and CDF-5), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111932&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111932](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111932+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix lost text index optimization for queries with ORDER BY ... LIMIT
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/issues/68580 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/93545 A query that filters on a text index and also has `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` could stop using the index to answer the filter, and read and tokenize the whole text column instead: ```sql SELECT count() FROM (SELECT id, v FROM t WHERE hasToken(s, 'error') ORDER BY v DESC, id LIMIT 10) ``` The two optimizations did not compose: the one that speeds up `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` reshaped the plan in a way the text index optimization no longer recognized, and it silently fell back to reading the column. Nothing indicated this in the query plan or the logs, and the results stayed correct, but the query got much slower and used much more memory. On a full-text search benchmark over ~30M rows the affected queries took ~300 ms and ~500 MB instead of ~30 ms and ~15 MB. Whether a query was affected depended on the order of the columns in `SELECT`, which made it look arbitrary: `SELECT v, id ... ORDER BY v` was fine while `SELECT id, v ... ORDER BY v` was not. All the settings involved are enabled by default. Both optimizations now apply together. A `TRACE` log entry was also added for the remaining cases where the text index optimization cannot be used, so a silent fallback is visible in the logs. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a performance regression where a query combining a text index filter with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` stopped answering the filter from the index and read the whole text column instead. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115586&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115586](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115586+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115766 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115221 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104631 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115036 `ci/tests/test_build_profile_diff_scheduling.py::test_registry_edits_do_not_schedule_a_run_without_profile_data` fails on current master, so the `CI Tests` job is red for every pull request that touches `ci/`. The test (added in #115221) asserts that a registry-only edit schedules no build; `Parser memory check` (added to the PR workflow in #104631) digests `ci/defs/defs.py`, `ci/defs/job_configs.py` and `ci/workflows/pull_request.py` while requiring `CLICKHOUSE_EXAMPLES`, so a registry-only edit marks it affected and the rescue pass in `_filter_unaffected_jobs` schedules `Build (arm_release)` just to produce the artifact. Each PR was green on its own — #115221's branch predates #104631's merge, and #104631 could not run the not-yet-existing test — the combination on master is what breaks. Fix: drop the registry paths from the job's `digest_config`, keeping its own script and `utils/parser-memory-profiler/`. No other job digests the registry, so this also restores the convention. `python3 -m pytest ci/tests/test_build_profile_diff_scheduling.py` passes with the change (37/37; the failing test plus the rest of the module). signal.title: Web UI: bring back the color highlight of high read speeds
signal.text: The progress line of the Web UI wraps the outstanding numbers of the read stats - huge row and byte counts and high read speeds - in `<b>`, and a CSS rule used to paint them in a color, so an extreme speed stood out: ``` Read 240.00 G rows, 5.12 TB (1.71 T/sec, 36.57 TB/sec) ``` The rule was lost when the progress line was reworked to paint its text through a `background-clip: text` gradient mask keyed to the `--progress` custom property. Since then the numbers were only bold - the computed color of `#stats b` is `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`. Restore the highlight, painting it in the top tier of the rate palette that the metrics table already uses, so that an extreme speed reads the same way in both places. Two deliberate deviations from the original rule: - the mask makes the text of the whole line transparent and `-webkit-text-fill-color` is inherited, so the highlight has to set that property as well - a rule setting only `color` is silently ignored; - the color is no longer the progress color: the read stats now sit over the bar, and the bar is painted in the progress color, so the old highlight would have blended into it at high progress. Checked in a headless browser in both themes, while the query runs (at 60% and at 99% of the bar) and after it finishes. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Web UI: bring back the color highlight of high read speeds and huge row and byte counts in the progress line. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115830&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115830](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115830+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Use PREWHERE for filters pushed down into JOIN sides
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> When a `JOIN` has OR-connected conditions in `WHERE`, ClickHouse extracts the parts that apply to a single side and pushes them down as pre-join filters, so each side reads less data: ```sql SELECT t1.k, t1.a, t2.x FROM tp1 AS t1 JOIN tp2 AS t2 ON t1.k = t2.k WHERE (t1.k IN (1, 2) AND t2.x = 100) OR (t1.k IN (3, 4) AND t2.x = 200) ``` Those pushed-down filters were never moved to `PREWHERE`, even with `optimize_move_to_prewhere` enabled. They ran as ordinary filters after all the requested columns of the row had been read, instead of being evaluated during reading so that non-matching rows skip the remaining columns. The wider the table, the more this costs. Both filters now reach `PREWHERE`. Query results are unaffected; only the plan changes, which is why one existing test reference is updated. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Filters pushed into the sides of a `JOIN` from OR-connected `WHERE` conditions are now moved to `PREWHERE`, so they are evaluated while reading instead of after it. Note: 1. This claims a performance win I have not measured. I only verified the plan and that results are unchanged. 2. A perf run would be confounded right now by the `PREWHERE` ordering bug in (#114998 still open), so if a reviewer asks for numbers, that fix needs to be in the picture first. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115772&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115772](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115772+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix ANY/SEMI RIGHT JOIN with OR conditions emitting rows twice or losing matches
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112640 `ANY RIGHT JOIN` and `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` emit every row of their right table at most once, and exactly once when the row has a match. With several OR-ed conditions in `ON` the claim for that was taken with a single CAS on the head row of the matched key's `RowRefList`, while `addFoundRowAll` then emitted every row of that list and discarded the result of the per-row `setUsedOnce` it called afterwards. With `OR` a right row is reachable through several keys in several hash maps, so a per-key claim does not partition the right rows: a list whose head row was claimed through another condition was skipped whole, orphaning its other rows, and a list whose head row was still free re-emitted rows another left row had already taken. Some right rows then appeared twice and others lost their match — padded with defaults for `ANY RIGHT JOIN`, dropped entirely for `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` — varying from run to run with the probe order under `max_threads > 1`. The claim is now taken per emitted row: `addFoundRowAll` claims a row before appending it and skips the rows whose CAS it loses, and returns whether it appended anything so the left row is filtered in only then. A single disjunct keeps the per-key claim, which is exact there, since one key owns all of its rows. The residual-condition path (`joinRightColumnsWithAdditionalFilter`) already claimed per row and is unchanged. Besides writing `ANY RIGHT JOIN` / `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` directly, this is reached by a plain `ANY LEFT JOIN` whenever the planner swaps the tables (`query_plan_join_swap_table`, `auto` by default), which is how the issue was reported. Measured on the reported query before and after, at `max_threads = 8`: 20 of 60 runs returned 5 or 6 rows for a 4-row left table, now 60/60 return 4. On a 1000-row shape, `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` returned 200 rows instead of 1000; `ANY LEFT JOIN` padded 416–736 rows with defaults although they had a match, and with `max_joined_block_size_rows = 7` also returned 1008 rows for 1000 left rows. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ANY RIGHT JOIN` and `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` with several `OR`-ed conditions in the `ON` section returning some rows of the right table twice and losing the matches of others. A written `ANY LEFT JOIN` was affected too, because the planner may swap the tables and execute it as `ANY RIGHT JOIN`.

signal.title: Text index written by 26.6 is unreadable by older replicas in the same cluster — breaks rolling upgrades
signal.text: ### Company or project name Nebius ### Describe what's wrong Since 26.6, ClickHouse writes the `text` skip index with sparse index version 1, which no earlier version can read. An older replica that receives such a part through normal replication fails every query that uses the index: ``` Code: 246. DB::Exception: Unsupported version of sparse index (1): While reading part all_0_0_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CORRUPTED_DATA) ``` **This is not a downgrade problem.** It breaks the upgrade itself. During a rolling restart of a replicated cluster, an already-upgraded replica writes parts with a v1 text index, replication delivers them to replicas that have not been restarted yet, and those replicas start failing reads — while both versions are running normally and no data directory has been touched. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Three files and six commands. This runs **one ReplicatedMergeTree cluster with both versions live at the same time** — the state a rolling upgrade passes through. Nothing is downgraded and no data directory is moved. ```bash mkdir ch-textindex && cd ch-textindex cat > keeper.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <listen_host>0.0.0.0</listen_host> <keeper_server> <tcp_port>9181</tcp_port> <server_id>1</server_id> <log_storage_path>/var/lib/clickhouse-keeper/log</log_storage_path> <snapshot_storage_path>/var/lib/clickhouse-keeper/snapshots</snapshot_storage_path> <raft_configuration> <server><id>1</id><hostname>keeper</hostname><port>9234</port></server> </raft_configuration> </keeper_server> </clickhouse> EOF cat > repl.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <zookeeper><node><host>keeper</host><port>9181</port></node></zookeeper> <macros> <shard>1</shard> <replica from_env="REPLICA"/> </macros> </clickhouse> EOF cat > docker-compose.yml <<'EOF' services: keeper: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper:26.6.2.160 volumes: [./keeper.xml:/etc/clickhouse-keeper/keeper_config.xml:ro] old: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-server:26.3.10.60 environment: {REPLICA: old} volumes: [./repl.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/repl.xml:ro] new: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-server:26.6.2.160 environment: {REPLICA: new} volumes: [./repl.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/repl.xml:ro] EOF docker compose up -d for r in old new; do until docker compose exec -T $r clickhouse-client -q "SELECT 1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done; done # 1. the same replicated table on both replicas for r in old new; do docker compose exec -T $r clickhouse-client -q " CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, s String, INDEX idx s TYPE text(tokenizer = array)) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/1/t', '{replica}') ORDER BY id"; done # 2. write on the already-upgraded replica, let replication carry the part over docker compose exec -T new clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number, hex(number) FROM numbers(20000)" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SYSTEM SYNC REPLICA t" # 3. the old replica only fetched that part, it never wrote one docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SYSTEM FLUSH LOGS" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SELECT DISTINCT event_type FROM system.part_log WHERE table = 't'" # 4. the same query on each replica docker compose exec -T new clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t WHERE s = '3039'" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t WHERE s = '3039'" docker compose down -v ``` Output of the last three steps: ``` DownloadPart <- step 3: fetched, not written locally 1 <- step 4 on the new replica Code: 246. DB::Exception: Unsupported version of sparse index (1): While reading part all_0_0_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CORRUPTED_DATA) <- step 4 on the old replica ``` No special settings are needed — the optimizer chooses the index on its own, which is how we hit it in production. `hasToken(s, '3039')` fails identically. `SELECT count() FROM t` still works, so only queries that touch the index break. [ch-textindex-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31214857/ch-textindex-repro.zip) ### Expected behavior Either of: 1. A reader that meets a sparse index version it does not understand skips the index and reads the granules, instead of failing the query. Skip indexes are an optimisation; an unreadable one should not be fatal. 2. Failing that, the format bump is called out as backward-incompatible in the changelog with a "drop the text index before upgrading" note, as was done for the 25.12 v3 change in #91518. Currently it is neither: the query fails, and the 26.6 changelog does not mention it. Related: #91518 introduced the sparse-index version header in 25.12 and *was* flagged backward-incompatible. #111550 (open) received review feedback describing this same hazard for a later layout change — *"older binaries misparse new ones, so rolling upgrades/downgrades ... have no safe migration path"* — recommending a versioned reader that migrates or throws an explicit rebuild-required error. The 26.6 bump shipped without either. ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests A search for the error text (`"Unsupported version of sparse index"`, `"version of sparse index"`) returns no existing report. - **#91518** — *Inverted Text Index v3* (merged, 25.12). Introduced the version header for the text index sparse index. It was explicitly flagged backward-incompatible, with a changelog note telling users to drop the index before upgrading and rebuild it. The 26.6 bump changes the same field with no equivalent note. - **#111550** — *Text index: introduce new storage layout for positions* (open). Review feedback on it describes this exact hazard for a later layout change: *"older binaries misparse new ones, so rolling upgrades/downgrades on tables that already use `support_phrase_search` have no safe migration path"*, and recommends giving the layout a new persisted version while keeping a reader that either migrates or throws an explicit rebuild-required error. That is the same remedy this issue asks for. - **#103398** — *Upgrade from 25.x to 26.x ends with CORRUPTED_DATA* (closed). The same failure shape in a different subsystem: rolling upgrade of a replicated cluster, error 246, `Unknown version of serialization infos (1). Should be less or equal than 0`. It was resolved by manual intervention (`SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA`) rather than by making the reader tolerant, so the pattern of a version field that older binaries reject outright is recurring. - **#94494** — *Fix text index mrk file incompatibility* (merged 26.1, backported 25.12.4.32). A different text index format problem (`.mrk` with non-adaptive `index_granularity`, triggered by merges). Listed to distinguish it: it is not this bug. - **#84606** — *Text index: remove multi format versions handling* (merged, July 2025, not-for-changelog). Consolidated `Format::v2` into `v1` and removed multi-version handling. Predates the version header, so it is not the cause, but it is context for how format-version tolerance in this index has been treated. ### Additional context **Workaround** On the not-yet-upgraded replicas, `SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0` makes the query succeed; `ALTER TABLE ... DROP INDEX` also works. Both give up the index for the duration. - Reproduced on `clickhouse/clickhouse-server` and `clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper` docker images, linux/aarch64. - Single shard, two replicas, one keeper. Nothing else required.
