signal.title: JSON -> text serialization is ~4.4x slower since 26.4 (`getDefaultSerialization` is called per value and now goes through the global serialization pool)
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe the situation Every read path that writes a `JSON` column as text became about 4.4x slower in 26.4. Read paths that write the same column in **binary** form did not change. The cause is a per-value call in `SerializationDynamic`: ```cpp // src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationDynamic.cpp:971 (master) nested_serialize(*dynamic_column.getVariantInfo().variant_type->getDefaultSerialization(), variant_column, row_num, ostr); ``` The shared-variant branch of the same function does the same thing at line 964. `SerializationJSON::serializeTextImpl` calls this once **per JSON path, per row**. `IDataType::getDefaultSerialization()` has never been cached, so this call was always hot. Before 26.4 it only allocated a `SerializationVariant`. Since [#96563](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/96563) ("Added a serialization object pool") it goes through a process-wide pool: `getDefaultSerialization()` -> `DataTypeVariant::doGetSerialization()` -> `SerializationVariant::create()` -> `ISerialization::pooled()` -> `SerializationObjectPool::getOrCreate()` `getOrCreate` takes a `std::shared_lock` on one global `SharedMutex`, does an `absl::flat_hash_map::find`, and calls `weak_ptr::lock()`. The `shared_ptr` it returns is released immediately after the value is written, which runs the custom deleter and can take the **write** lock to erase the map entry. The pool does not remove the construction cost that it is meant to avoid. `DataTypeVariant::doGetSerialization()` must first build the `serializations` and `variant_names` vectors (one `IDataType::getName()` string per variant, plus a recursive `getDefaultSerialization()` per nested type) to compute the pool key. So the pool adds a hash, a lock, a map lookup and atomic `weak_ptr` traffic **on top of** the work that 26.2 did, on a path that runs about 10^7 times for a 1M-row scan. Because the pool is global and the reference counts are shared, the added cost is contended state. It should get worse as core count goes up. **Why the binary paths are not affected.** They resolve the serialization once per column per block and keep it. `SerializationObject::serializeBinary` uses the `dynamic_serialization` member, and Native's bulk path caches `dynamic_state->variant_serialization`. Only the text path re-acquires the serialization for every value. The asymmetry is also visible in `SerializationDynamic.cpp` itself. The row-level **binary** serializer already avoids the global pool with a thread-local cache: ```cpp // line 762 — binary, not regressed getDataTypesCache().getSerialization(variant_type_name)->serializeBinary(...); ``` `serializeForHashCalculation` does the same at lines 786 and 797. The **text** path at lines 964 and 971 is the one that still goes to the global pool. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? 26.4 and later, including `master`. Measured on official Docker images: | Version | Regressed | | --- | --- | | 26.2.18.8 | no | | 26.3.19.3 | no | | 26.4.5.143 | **yes** | | 26.7.3.19 | **yes** |. ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE json_bench (id UInt64, payload JSON) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO json_bench (id, payload) SELECT number AS id, CAST( ( number, ['info', 'warn', 'error', 'debug'][(number % 4) + 1], map('user', randomPrintableASCII(8), 'session', randomPrintableASCII(12), 'region', randomPrintableASCII(4)), [randomPrintableASCII(5), randomPrintableASCII(6), randomPrintableASCII(4)], CAST( (randomPrintableASCII(6), (toInt64(rand64() % 180000000) - 90000000) / 1000000.0, (toInt64(rand64() % 360000000) - 180000000) / 1000000.0) AS Tuple(country String, lat Float64, lon Float64) ), (number % 2) = 0 ) AS Tuple(user_id UInt64, event String, props Map(String, String), tags Array(String), geo Tuple(country String, lat Float64, lon Float64), active Bool) )::JSON AS payload FROM numbers(1000000); OPTIMIZE TABLE json_bench FINAL; ``` The payload has 10 leaf paths. All of them are dynamic paths, well below the `max_dynamic_paths` default of 1024, so nothing goes to shared data. **Query A — text output (regressed):** ```sql SELECT sum(length(toString(payload))) FROM (SELECT payload FROM json_bench LIMIT 200000); ``` `toString()` is used to keep the measurement free of output-format, socket and compression cost. `FORMAT TSV`, `FORMAT JSONEachRow`, and `FORMAT RowBinary` with `output_format_binary_write_json_as_string = 1` all show the same regression. **Query B — binary output (control, not regressed):** ```sql SELECT * FROM json_bench LIMIT 200000 FORMAT Native; ``` **Results.** `max_threads = 4`, server-side `query_duration_ms` from `system.query_log`, 10 interleaved rounds per version in shuffled order, all four servers holding an identical 1M-row single-part table: | Version | Query A median | Query A range | vs 26.2 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 26.2.18.8 | 766 ms | 739–951 | 1.00x | | 26.3.19.3 | 698 ms | 643–925 | 0.91x | | 26.4.5.143 | 3347 ms | 3217–3461 | **4.37x** | | 26.7.3.19 | 3592 ms | 3491–3683 | **4.69x** | The ranges do not overlap, in either direction. 26.7 is also reliably worse than 26.4 (26.7 min 3491 > 26.4 max 3461). Query B (`FORMAT Native`) stays at a 69–80 ms median on all four versions. ### Expected performance The 26.2 and 26.3 result: about 770 ms for Query A, that is ~4.4x faster than 26.4+. ### Additional context **Profile.** `query_profiler_cpu_time_period_ns = 1000000` on `SELECT * FROM json_bench LIMIT 200000 FORMAT TSV`, `max_threads = 4`, symbol sample counts from `system.trace_log`: 26.2.18.8 (386 root samples): ``` 297 SerializationJSON<SimdJSONParser>::serializeTextEscaped 240 SerializationDynamic::serializeTextJSON 154 DataTypeVariant::doGetDefaultSerialization <-- 40% of the query 65 SerializationVariant::SerializationVariant ``` 26.7.3.19 (915 root samples): ``` 840 SerializationJSON<SimdJSONParser>::serializeTextEscaped 737 SerializationDynamic::serializeTextJSON 713 IDataType::getDefaultSerialization <-- 78% of the query 523 DataTypeVariant::doGetSerialization 363 ISerialization::pooled 333 SerializationObjectPool::getOrCreate 275 SerializationVariant::create 163 <pool deleter> __on_zero_shared 102 SerializationObjectPool::getOrCreate::$_0::operator() 100 SerializationVariant::~SerializationVariant ``` 26.4.5.143 shows the same symbols in the same order. Serialization acquisition went from 40% of the query to 78%, while the query itself became 4.4x slower. In absolute terms that call is about 7x more expensive than it was. **Ruled out.** `output_format_parallel_formatting` is not involved: on 26.4 the query is slow with the setting both on (12976 ms) and off (10175 ms). Nothing in the window changes `SerializationJSON::serializeTextImpl`, `SerializationDynamic::serializeTextImpl`, `writeJSONString` or `writeEscapedString`. There is no relevant JSON/object default change in the 26.3 or 26.4 entries of `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp`. Shared data is not involved, since 10 paths stay well below `max_dynamic_paths`. **Possible directions.** Use the existing thread-local `getDataTypesCache().getSerialization(...)` at lines 964 and 971, which is what the binary serializer two functions above already does. Alternatively, hold the resolved serialization in `SerializationJSON` / `SerializationDynamic` for the duration of the block. Either way the pool lookup leaves the per-value loop. **Related work.** This fix pattern is already accepted for other call sites of the same problem: * [#113344](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113344) (open) — "Use cached serializations for `Dynamic` fields". Replaces `getDefaultSerialization()` with `getDataTypesCache().getSerialization(...)` in `SerializationDynamic::serializeBinary(const Field &)` and `deserializeBinary(Field &)` (lines 718 and 730), for the same reason: those calls "enter the globally locked `SerializationObjectPool` for every value". It reports up to 122% improvement. It does **not** touch the text path, so it does not fix this issue. * [#112264](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112264) (closed) — names the same `getDefaultSerialization()` -> `SerializationObjectPool` cost as the expensive part of `ColumnDynamic::serializeValueIntoArena` in the aggregation prefetch path. Together with this report, that is three separate hot call sites paying the global pool per value. It may be worth checking the remaining `getDefaultSerialization()` calls that sit inside row loops rather than fixing them one at a time.

signal.title: Optimize min/max aggregates using column statistics
signal.text: ## Summary This PR adds an optimization that answers filterless `min()` and `max()` aggregation queries from per-part column statistics without reading column data, avoiding full scans. ## How it works When a query like `SELECT min(x), max(x) FROM t` runs on a `MergeTree` table with column statistics configured (via `auto_statistics_types = 'basic'`), the optimizer checks whether the aggregate results can be obtained from the per-part `StatisticsBasic` metadata. If all conditions are met, the query plan replaces the `ReadFromMergeTree` step with a `ReadFromPreparedSource` that produces the answer directly from statistics without reading column data. The optimization applies when: - All aggregates are `min()` or `max()` - The table has `auto_statistics_types = 'basic'` and statistics have been materialized for the relevant columns - The table has no active mutations, patch parts, or lightweight deletes that would make stored statistics stale - For GROUP BY queries, the GROUP BY keys must map to partition key columns - If a filter is present, it must be computable from partition-level expressions and virtual columns If any check fails the query silently falls back to a normal `ReadFromMergeTree` read. ## SQL Examples ```sql -- Create a table with column statistics CREATE TABLE t ( key UInt64, value Int32 ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY key SETTINGS auto_statistics_types = 'basic'; -- Insert data (statistics are materialized on insert) SET materialize_statistics_on_insert = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toInt32(rand() % 1000) FROM numbers(10000000); -- This query is answered from per-part statistics — no column data is read SELECT min(value), max(value) FROM t; -- GROUP BY partition key is also supported CREATE TABLE t2 ( p UInt8, v UInt32 ) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY p ORDER BY tuple() SETTINGS auto_statistics_types = 'basic'; INSERT INTO t2 SELECT number % 10, number FROM numbers(10000000); SELECT p, min(v), max(v) FROM t2 GROUP BY p ORDER BY p; ``` The optimization can be disabled via `SET use_statistics_for_min_max_aggregation = 0`. ## Related PRs Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/93037 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Optimize `min()` and `max()` aggregate functions by utilizing per-part column statistics (`basic`) metadata when available, avoiding full data scans for queries. Controlled by the new setting `use_statistics_for_min_max_aggregation`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105197&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/105197](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F105197+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix logical error for RIGHT JOIN with parallel replicas
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113292 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108645 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the logical error `Can't determine table for parallel replicas` for a `RIGHT JOIN` whose right side has no table eligible for parallel replicas, and made such a `RIGHT JOIN` materialize a left side that is not a `MergeTree` instead of letting every replica read it independently. ### Description Master-only logical error thrown at `findParallelReplicasQuery.cpp:637`: release builds reject the query, debug and sanitizer builds abort, reddening Stress and fuzzer jobs. **Root cause.** For `JoinKind::Right` the side read with replicas is the right one, because `buildQueryTreeForShard` materializes the left table expression into a temporary table. `getSupportingParallelReplicasQueries` descended the left expression instead, so a query was accepted for its left side, the rewrite materialized that same side, and the lookup on the rewritten tree threw. `88b22b8fb66c115` (#108645) flipped the target while renaming `getRightTableExpression`; `26.2` through `26.7` still descend right, so the defect is confined to master. **The fix** descends the right expression again (`RIGHT SEMI`/`ANTI` were affected too), then corrects three places that had the materialized side wrong, each of which let every replica read its own copy of data it must not: - `rewriteJoinToGlobalJoin` decided locality from the right side for every kind; it now requires the materialized side of a `RIGHT JOIN` to be eligible for parallel replicas, not merely `MergeTree`. - That question was asked about the raw storage, so an eligible `View`/`MaterializedView` lost its local join; the wrapper is resolved to the table it reads first. - The global-join collector skipped each global join's right child, so a nested global join in the offloaded subtree never got a temporary table. The last two were reported by `clickhouse-gh[bot]`. No backport is requested: every release branch already decides locality from the right side while descending right, so that half is pre-existing there and no repro was measured on a release binary. **Validation.** New stateless test, untagged and parallel-safe. It fails on unmodified master with the logical error, and reverting any hunk reddens only that hunk's own assertions. At the current head it passes 30/30 sequentially and 12/12 at four-way concurrency, and is identical across the `join_use_nulls` and `compatibility` values Stress randomizes. The 127 `parallel_replicas` tests show no regression. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113515&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113515](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113515+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject Delta Lake partition column absent from the table schema
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114462 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` when reading a Delta Lake table whose `metaData.partitionColumns` names a column that `metaData.schemaString` does not declare. Such metadata is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` on the delta-kernel reader and `INCORRECT_DATA` on the legacy reader, whenever the table or its schema is read from a snapshot, not only when the query carries a predicate. ### Description Requested by @ PedroTadim in #114462. `partitionColumns` and `schemaString` are independent fields of externally supplied metadata and nothing cross-checked them, so a mismatch was reported as `LOGICAL_ERROR`, which aborts on debug and sanitizer builds. Paimon already threw `BAD_ARGUMENTS` here. - delta-kernel reader: validate in `TableSnapshot::initOrUpdateSchemaIfChanged`, where both values first exist, beside the existing empty-schema rejection. Previously an unfiltered `SELECT *` succeeded and only a predicate threw, since `PartitionPruner` is built only when a filter exists. That site keeps `LOGICAL_ERROR`, now a genuine internal invariant. - legacy reader: `LOGICAL_ERROR` -> `INCORRECT_DATA` where an `add` action's `partitionValues` names an undeclared key, in the JSON-log and checkpoint branches. It also validates `partitionColumns` where `metaData` is loaded, in both branches, so a snapshot with no `add` action to resolve is rejected too. That check compares logical names: a parsed legacy schema is keyed by column-mapping physical names, so comparing against it would reject well formed column-mapped tables. Iceberg is unaffected: it resolves partitions by numeric `source_id` field ids, not by name. Change-data-feed reads go through `TableChanges`, which resolves no partition name, and are out of scope. Behaviour change: such a table was readable without a predicate, and on the legacy reader also with no `add` action; it is now rejected for every query that reads it. It is malformed per the Delta protocol. One case is left alone, unchanged from master: on a table with an explicit column list a bare `count()` is answered from transaction-log row counts, which resolve no column name, so it is not rejected, while reading any column from it is. Validated with the new stateless test `04877`: every failure arm fails on a targeted revert of the line it covers, including a well formed column-mapped control that must keep reading. Also 50/50 randomized runs and the `delta_lake` suite. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1554` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Quadratic complexity of applying MergeOnKey patch parts with long equal-key runs
signal.text: Applying `MergeOnKey` patch parts has quadratic complexity when the effective sorting key contains long equal-key runs: `applyPatchesMergeOnKey` is called for every result block (8192 rows during merges) and rebuilds the cursors and the per-run hash map (`EqualRunScratch::run_map` in `processEqualKeyCursors`) over **all** patch rows of the equal-key run every time. When the key is constant for the whole table — for example after `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY ORDER BY` shrinks the sorting key, as in the third scenario of `04509_lwu_sorting_key_common_prefix` — every result block re-inserts the entire patch into the hash map, so the total work is `O(result_blocks × patch_rows)`. Observed in a master stress test run (MSan): a background merge of `test_7.t_lwu_key_prefix` (854090 rows in 5 parts, 3 `MergeOnKey` patch parts of comparable size, effective key `k` equal to `0` for all rows) spent **~37 seconds per 8192-row block**, all inside patch application. The whole merge would have needed well over an hour. `gdb` caught the merge thread here: ``` #14 DB::(anonymous namespace)::processEqualKeyCursors (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:468 #15 DB::(anonymous namespace)::applyCursorsHeap (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:670 #16 DB::(anonymous namespace)::applyPatchesMergeOnKey (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:769 #17 DB::applyPatchesToBlock (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/PatchParts/applyPatches.cpp:818 #18 DB::MergeTreeReadersChain::applyPatches (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeReadersChain.cpp:861 #22 DB::MergeTreeSequentialSource::generate (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp:228 #33 DB::MergeTask::execute (...) at ./src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTask.cpp:2631 ``` Because server shutdown waited for this merge, the stress check reported `Possible deadlock on shutdown (see gdb.log)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=a013c79d6ac80373b820381527ea85823ab03834&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_msan%29&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_msan%29 (the shutdown side is addressed separately by cancelling in-flight merges on shutdown; this issue is about the complexity itself). The same pattern affects `SELECT` with `apply_patch_parts = 1`, not only merges: patch application runs per read block through `MergeTreeReadersChain`, with the same per-block rebuild of the run map. A possible fix: reuse the built run map across consecutive result blocks of the same equal-key run. The patch side of a run does not change between result blocks (the incremental patch readers keep all overlapping patch chunks resident), so the map built by `processEqualKeyCursors` could be cached in a small state object owned by `MergeTreeReadersChain` (per stream, single-threaded) and invalidated when the run key or the set of patch blocks changes. That makes the total work linear: build the map once per run, probe it with the result rows of each block. Reproducer (the merge is minutes-long in a release build already; scale `numbers(...)` up for more): ```sql SET enable_lightweight_update = 1, apply_patch_parts = 1; CREATE TABLE t_lwu_quadratic (k UInt64, u UInt64, v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree PRIMARY KEY k ORDER BY (k, u) SETTINGS enable_block_number_column = 1, enable_block_offset_column = 1, patch_parts_version = 'v2'; INSERT INTO t_lwu_quadratic SELECT 0, number, number FROM numbers(2000000); UPDATE t_lwu_quadratic SET v = v + 1 WHERE 1; ALTER TABLE t_lwu_quadratic MODIFY ORDER BY k; -- the effective key is now constant for the whole table OPTIMIZE TABLE t_lwu_quadratic FINAL; -- quadratic patch application ```

signal.title: Fix flaky `04628_and_compare_chain_index_hint` under randomized adaptive granularity
signal.text: The test `04628_and_compare_chain_index_hint` asserts `Granules: 1/64`, which only holds when the 65536 inserted rows are split into granules of exactly `index_granularity = 1024` rows. CI randomizes the `index_granularity_bytes` MergeTree setting, and a small value (for example `--index_granularity_bytes 14840`) makes adaptive granularity produce a different number of granules, so the check prints `0` instead of `1` and the test fails. Verified locally: with `index_granularity_bytes = 14840` the check yields `0`, with `index_granularity_bytes = 0` it yields `1`. Observed in, for example, https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112928&sha=8506897e0a968cd59d1cf10a3f2eb0bf8cd41eee&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20parallel%29 (Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112928); the same test also failed on https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106734 and https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115767&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115767](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115767+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: short-circuit in SELECT OR/AND clause
signal.text: ### Describe the situation Hi, ClickHouse developers, please consider such queries: ```sql SELECT TRUE OR (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0)>1; SELECT FALSE AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0)>1; ``` For the first query, there are two conditions in the `WHERE` clause, connected by `OR`, which means that if any one of the conditions is met, it is `TRUE`. Therefore, when we calculate two conditions, if we calculate one of the conditions to be `TRUE`, we can short-circuit the `OR` expressions, which can avoid unnecessary calculations. For the Second query, similarly, if we calculate one of the conditions to be `FALSE`, we can short-circuit the `AND` expressions. However, ClickHouse does not short-circuit to optimize such queries. Especially, short-circuiting is necessary when the computation of the condition is expensive. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? I ran the following case on the last two versions: 25.4.2 and 25.5.1: ### How to reproduce ```sql SET default_table_engine = 'Log'; CREATE DATABASE test; USE test; CREATE TABLE t0(c0 Int64); INSERT INTO t0 SELECT * FROM generate_series(1, 1000000000);-- 1 billion rows SELECT TRUE OR (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0)>1 AS bool; ┌─bool─┐ 1. │ true │ └──────┘ 1 row in set. Elapsed: 2.896 sec. Processed 1.00 billion rows, 8.00 GB (345.30 million rows/s., 2.76 GB/s.) Peak memory usage: 63.68 MiB. SELECT FALSE AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0)>1 AS bool; ┌─bool──┐ 1. │ false │ └───────┘ 1 row in set. Elapsed: 2.918 sec. Processed 1.00 billion rows, 8.00 GB (342.70 million rows/s., 2.74 GB/s.) Peak memory usage: 63.87 MiB. ```` Moreover, If there is a subquery in the `EXPLAIN` statement, the `EXPLAIN` statement will performs actual execution. ```sql EXPLAIN SELECT TRUE OR (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0)>1 AS bool; ┌─explain─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ 1. │ Expression ((Project names + (Projection + Change column names to column identifiers))) │ 2. │ ReadFromStorage (SystemOne) │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 2 rows in set. Elapsed: 2.855 sec. Processed 1.00 billion rows, 8.00 GB (350.30 million rows/s., 2.80 GB/s.) Peak memory usage: 63.83 MiB. EXPLAIN SELECT FALSE AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0)>1 AS bool; ┌─explain─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ 1. │ Expression ((Project names + (Projection + Change column names to column identifiers))) │ 2. │ ReadFromStorage (SystemOne) │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 2 rows in set. Elapsed: 3.059 sec. Processed 1.00 billion rows, 8.00 GB (326.87 million rows/s., 2.61 GB/s.) Peak memory usage: 63.78 MiB. ``` <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #83505 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1856` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix MaterializedPostgreSQL database/table with ON CLUSTER
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58726 A `MaterializedPostgreSQL` database or table created with `ON CLUSTER` gets the *same* ClickHouse UUID on every replica, because the UUID is generated once on the initiator and shipped in the DDL. With `materialized_postgresql_use_unique_replication_consumer_identifier = 1` the replication slot name was derived from that UUID and the publication name from the PostgreSQL database/table name, so every replica computed the same names and fought over one PostgreSQL slot and publication: a single replica replicated, the others failed in the background with `pqxx::unique_violation` or could not hold the slot, leaving divergent data. The fix hashes the persistent per-server `ServerUUID` together with the object UUID (via `makeUUIDv4FromHash`, which keeps the result within PostgreSQL's identifier length limit) and derives both the slot and the publication name from it, so each replica gets its own pair and replicates independently. Both UUIDs are persistent, so `ATTACH` keeps reusing the same slot. The default behaviour (setting disabled) is unchanged, and since the change is in the shared `PostgreSQLReplicationHandler` it covers both the database and the table engine. A user-managed `materialized_postgresql_replication_slot` has one fixed name that every replica would share, so combining it with this setting is contradictory and is now rejected for a freshly supplied engine definition — a `CREATE`, or an `ATTACH` that carries a full definition, so it cannot be bypassed through `ATTACH ... ON CLUSTER`. A replay of an already stored definition (startup, `RESTORE`, short-syntax `ATTACH`) still accepts it, so existing deployments keep starting. ## Upgrade of existing deployments Salting the names is a rename of the generated identity, so `adoptLegacyReplicationIdentityIfNeeded` — the mechanism that already handles the schema-aware rename — now also adopts the pre-salt slot and publication when the salted ones do not exist. Replication resumes from the same slot position: no re-snapshot into the already-populated nested tables, nothing orphaned. The pre-salt slot name embeds the object's own ClickHouse UUID, so its existence proves ownership. The publication name is schema-blind and does not, so it is adopted only when it publishes *exactly* the tables this engine replicates: the configured `materialized_postgresql_tables_list`, or otherwise the tables the engine actually replicated in the previous run (their nested tables exist on disk) — not the live PostgreSQL schema, which may have grown since `CREATE DATABASE` with tables that are never replicated without an explicit `ATTACH TABLE`. Adoption is skipped for a database that never materialized a single nested table: there is nothing to preserve and its empty on-disk set cannot prove any publication's ownership, so it synchronizes under the current identity and the legacy objects are named in the log for the operator. ## Fail-closed attach paths `pgoutput` resolves publication membership from the historic catalog snapshot at each change's LSN, so streaming through a publication that was created or narrowed after those changes were written silently drops them — unrecoverably, once `confirmed_flush_lsn` advances. Attach therefore no longer papers over a broken PostgreSQL-side state; it fails with a retryable error, so startup keeps retrying and an operator can repair the conflict or rebuild the replica. This holds for every identity, not only for the pre-salt rename: - **Publication gone behind a surviving slot** — previously recreated silently, skipping every change committed while it was missing. - **Slot gone behind a surviving publication**, as after `pg_upgrade` (it keeps publications but not replication slots) or an operator dropping the slot — previously an in-place re-snapshot, whose rows are materialized with `_sign = 1` and `_version = 1` and therefore neither delete rows that disappeared from PostgreSQL nor override rows already at a higher version, silently leaving the replica stale. A clean rebuild recovers every row. A user-managed slot is excluded, since a missing one is already reported as a configuration error. - **Both gone** while the replica already holds data from a previous run. - **Publication drift under the current identity** — `ALTER PUBLICATION ... DROP TABLE`, an altered `publish` set (`CREATE PUBLICATION` defaults to `insert, update, delete, truncate`), or, on PostgreSQL 15 and newer, a row filter or a column list on a published table. The published set is compared by exact `(schema, table)` pair, because in the single-schema modes both the publication table list and the WAL consumer key tables by bare name, so a publication rewritten from `foo.a` to `bar.a` would otherwise resume and replay `bar.a`'s changes into the ClickHouse table for `foo.a`. Extra published tables stay tolerated — the identity already owns the publication name — unless a foreign-schema table's bare name collides with a replicated one. A database that has not materialized a single nested table is exempt throughout: there is nothing a snapshot could make stale, so it bootstraps through whatever survived. If an interrupted first synchronization left both the publication and the slot behind, the leftover slot is dropped so the initial synchronization can run instead of resuming and then failing forever with `UNKNOWN_TABLE` on a nested table that was never created (a user-managed slot, which this engine may not recreate, is refused with an explicit message). Relatedly, the set of tables to materialize on attach now comes from the existing publication — the engine's persisted table set, which the code always claimed to assume correct — instead of the live schema. Previously a PostgreSQL table created after `CREATE DATABASE` made every attach retry fail with `UNKNOWN_TABLE` on its missing nested table, so a whole-schema database could never resume replication after a restart; this reproduces on master with the setting disabled. Published-but-not-materialized tables are reported in a warning that names the recovery (`ATTACH TABLE`), because that state is indistinguishable from a table that was in the original definition but never completed its first snapshot; persisting the configured table set is deferred to the separate persistent-replication-state change, together with the `rebuild required` marker discussed in the review. ## Tests The new `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine_on_cluster` suite covers the fix — two-node `ON CLUSTER` databases and tables, each replica getting its own slot and publication and synchronizing independently, and both removed by `DROP ... ON CLUSTER` — the adoption of a reconstructed pre-salt identity (including a whole-schema database whose PostgreSQL schema has grown, and foreign publications that must not be adopted), every fail-closed case above, the bootstrap paths for never-synchronized runs and for a fresh full-definition `ATTACH TABLE`, and the rejection of a user-managed slot on `CREATE` and on a full-definition `ATTACH ... ON CLUSTER` of either engine. It also covers the `ATTACH TABLE` paths: a failed attach leaves no persisted table-list entry, no cached wrapper and no publication entry behind; an attach of a table the publication already publishes reuses that membership instead of issuing a duplicate `ALTER PUBLICATION ... ADD TABLE`; and an attach is refused when the publication already publishes a foreign-schema table with the same bare name. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `MaterializedPostgreSQL` databases and tables created with `ON CLUSTER`. When `materialized_postgresql_use_unique_replication_consumer_identifier` is enabled, the PostgreSQL replication slot and publication names are now unique per server, so replicas no longer collide on a shared replication slot and publication, which previously left all but one replica unable to replicate. Also fixed a whole-schema `MaterializedPostgreSQL` database failing to resume replication after a server restart when a new table had been created in PostgreSQL, and made the attach fail closed instead of silently losing changes when the publication or the replication slot is missing. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110493&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110493](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110493+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Per-shard OpenTelemetry spans for distributed SELECT queries
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112738 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114813 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115619 Every remote shard read of a distributed `SELECT` is now covered by a span that identifies the query fragment. Until now the trace of a distributed query showed the remote side (`TCPHandler`, remote `query` span) but nothing on the initiator identified *which shard of which cluster* a subtree belonged to, or where the query was actually sent. On the asynchronous connection paths the span covering the read context fiber becomes the per-shard fragment span renamed to `RemoteQueryExecutor::execute`. The synchronous sending path gets an equivalent `RemoteQueryExecutor::sendQuery` span. * `clickhouse.cluster`, `clickhouse.shard_num` — filled on the classic distributed path (`ReadFromRemote`) * `clickhouse.processed_stage` — the stage requested from the shard * `clickhouse.query_id`, `clickhouse.initial_query_id` * `clickhouse.target_host` — the established connection addresses, added once known Implementation: * `AsyncTaskExecutor` accepts initial span attributes and provides a thread-safe `addSpanAttribute` for attributes that become known only during task execution. * Attributes are only built when the query is traced; when tracing is off the cost is an empty vector per executor. * New test `05025_opentelemetry_remote_query_executor_shard_spans` checks both shards' spans and all attributes over `test_cluster_two_shards` for all combinations of `async_socket_for_remote`/`async_query_sending_for_remote`, and pins the attribute flush on cancellation (`KILL QUERY` while the fiber is suspended). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/uidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Distributed `SELECT` queries now produce a per-shard OpenTelemetry span (`RemoteQueryExecutor::execute`, or `RemoteQueryExecutor::sendQuery` on the synchronous path) with attributes identifying the fragment: `clickhouse.cluster`, `clickhouse.shard_num`, `clickhouse.processed_stage`, `clickhouse.query_id`, `clickhouse.initial_query_. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115784&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115784](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115784+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: DataLakeCatalog: aws_external_id setting leaks in plaintext in SHOW CREATE DATABASE / system.databases.engine_full (masked everywhere else)
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** A `DataLakeCatalog` database masks every credential-bearing setting in `SHOW CREATE DATABASE` and `system.databases.engine_full` **except `aws_external_id`**, which is shown in plaintext — at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0` and without the `displaySecretsInShowAndSelect` privilege. Any user who can run `SHOW CREATE DATABASE` or read `system.databases` sees it. `aws_external_id` is the external ID passed to AWS STS `AssumeRole`, matching the `sts:ExternalId` condition on the role's trust policy (its own setting description in `src/Databases/DataLake/DatabaseDataLakeSettings.cpp` notes it is for roles owned by a third party, such as ClickHouse Cloud). ClickHouse already treats this value as a secret in the *inline* `s3()` / `extra_credentials` form: `external_id` is a member of `s3_secret_keys` in `src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.h`, whose own comment calls it "the shared secret of the assume-role triple". So the identical value is masked in one surface and leaked in another. The cause is that the `SETTINGS_TO_HIDE` masking map in `src/Databases/DataLake/DataLakeConstants.h` lists `catalog_credential`, `auth_header`, `aws_access_key_id`, `aws_secret_access_key`, the `storage_*` variants, `onelake_*`, `google_adc_client_secret` / `google_adc_refresh_token`, and `dlf_*`, but has no entry for `aws_external_id`. (`aws_role_session_name` is likewise absent from the map, but that is an operator-chosen session label rather than a secret; the concern here is `aws_external_id`.) **How to reproduce** Any ClickHouse build with the Glue `DataLakeCatalog` backend. The Glue catalog is constructed lazily, so no live endpoint is needed to observe the masking: ```sql SET allow_database_glue_catalog = 1; CREATE DATABASE ge ENGINE = DataLakeCatalog('https://glue.us-east-1.amazonaws.com') SETTINGS catalog_type = 'glue', region = 'us-east-1', aws_access_key_id = 'AKIAEXAMPLE', aws_secret_access_key = 'SECRET', aws_role_arn = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/r', aws_external_id = 'my-external-id-value'; SELECT engine_full FROM system.databases WHERE name = 'ge'; ``` Output (note `aws_secret_access_key` is `[HIDDEN]` but `aws_external_id` is verbatim): ``` DataLakeCatalog('https://glue.us-east-1.amazonaws.com') SETTINGS catalog_type = 'glue', region = 'us-east-1', aws_access_key_id = '[HIDDEN]', aws_secret_access_key = '[HIDDEN]', aws_role_arn = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/r', aws_external_id = 'my-external-id-value' ``` `SHOW CREATE DATABASE ge` shows the same unmasked value. **Expected behavior** `aws_external_id` should be masked as `'[HIDDEN]'` in `SHOW CREATE DATABASE`, `system.databases.engine_full`, and any other formatted-with-secrets-hidden surface, consistent with how the inline `external_id` argument is masked via `s3_secret_keys` and with the other credential settings in `SETTINGS_TO_HIDE`. **Which ClickHouse server versions are incompatible** Reproduced on master (26.8). By code inspection the gap exists on every version whose `SETTINGS_TO_HIDE` map omits `aws_external_id`.

signal.title: Validate IN tuple/subquery column count mismatch in analyzer
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/74442 The analyzer (`resolveFunction`) now validates that the number of elements on the left side of `IN` matches the number of columns in the right-side subquery. Previously, constant folding could optimize away the `IN` expression and silently hide the mismatch: for example, `(1, 1) IN (SELECT 1)` wrapped in a subquery with a constant-false outer `WHERE` succeeded silently. Now it correctly throws `NUMBER_OF_COLUMNS_DOESNT_MATCH` during analysis. A single `Tuple` column on the right side is still accepted, since `FunctionIn` compares the whole left-side value against it; `LowCardinality` and `Nullable` wrappers are unwrapped before the check. Covered by the new test `03380_in_tuple_subquery_column_count`, including the original reproducer from the issue. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Detect column count mismatch between a tuple and a subquery in the `IN` clause during analysis, preventing constant folding from silently hiding the error. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=97540&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/97540](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F97540+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Wake idle streaming exchange sinks and sources on backward stop
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114806 When a `LIMIT` in a distributed plan is satisfied, the stop signal travels backward through the exchanges. It stalled at idle stages: a `StreamingExchangeSink` with an empty input waited only on its input port and did not read `NoMoreDataNeeded` from the socket, and a `StreamingExchangeSource` on a silent socket did not notice that its output port was closed, so it did not forward the stop upstream. Stages that no longer produce anything kept reading and computing until the query timed out. Now both wake while idle: each sink and source waits on a small epoll that holds the socket and a wakeup pipe written by `onUpdatePorts`. The sink asks for socket writability only while it has unsent bytes, so an idle socket does not cause a busy loop, and there is no periodic timer - every wake is an explicit event. This also required a fix in the sink rendezvous: it now always waits on the connection eventfd instead of extracting a ready socket in `scheduleForEvent`, where the extraction skipped the `prepare` pass that starts the rest of the fragment. The wire protocol is unchanged. Local in-memory exchanges have the same gap and are not covered here. In the new test the unfixed server hits `max_execution_time = 25` although the result is ready after ~2 s; fixed, the query ends in ~2 s and all worker tasks finish cleanly. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Distributed query plans (`make_distributed_plan`) now stop idle upstream stages promptly after a satisfied `LIMIT`: an idle exchange sink reads `NoMoreDataNeeded` as soon as it arrives, and an idle exchange source notices its closed output and forwards the stop upstream. Previously such stages kept reading and computing data that nobody consumes. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115690&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115690](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115690+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix out-of-bounds read in `formatRowNoNewline` with empty rows
signal.text: Fixes a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline`. When a row is formatted to an empty result (for example, an empty string with the `RawBLOB` format), the newline-stripping logic could rewind the shared write buffer into the previous row's bytes, producing non-monotonic `ColumnString` offsets and a `size_t` underflow in the string size. Functions consuming the result could then return incorrect results or raise a logical error. The trailing newline is now stripped only when the current row actually emitted at least one byte, which keeps the offsets monotonic. The cursor is also kept within the current working buffer so the decrement never moves it before the buffer start after a flush. Added a regression test in `tests/queries/0_stateless/04512_format_row_no_newline_empty_row_underflow.sql`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline` that could produce incorrect results or a logical error when a row is formatted to an empty result. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115669&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115669](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115669+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.5.11`, `26.5.8.11`, `26.3.21.9`, `25.8.33.2` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix gRPC and Arrow Flight listeners for wildcard listen hosts
signal.text: `gRPC` treats `::` and `0.0.0.0` as one family-agnostic wildcard: for either of them it binds a dual-stack `::` socket, and falls back to `0.0.0.0` only on a host without IPv6 (see `add_wildcard_addrs_to_server` in `contrib/grpc`). Listing both wildcard addresses in `listen_host` therefore made ClickHouse create two listeners that bind the very same socket address, and the second one either - failed with `EADDRINUSE`, because the Arrow Flight transport disables `SO_REUSEPORT`, and the exception terminated the whole server: ``` <Error> grpc: Failed to add port to server: No address added out of total 1 resolved for '0.0.0.0:9110' (Failed to add any wildcard listeners: Error in bind for address '[::]:9110': Address already in use Error in bind for address '0.0.0.0:9110': Address already in use) <Error> Application: Code: 1002. DB::Exception: Failed init Arrow Flight Server: Unknown error: Server did not start properly. ``` - or silently shared the port with the first one, because plain gRPC keeps `SO_REUSEPORT` enabled, so each of the two independent servers ended up serving a random half of the connections, and a listener configured for `0.0.0.0` accepted IPv6 connections as well: ``` <Information> Application: Listening for gRPC protocol: [::]:9100 <Information> Application: Listening for gRPC protocol: 0.0.0.0:9100 LISTEN 0 4096 *:9100 users:(("clickhouse",pid=3851032,fd=55)) LISTEN 0 4096 *:9100 users:(("clickhouse",pid=3851032,fd=56)) ``` Only one gRPC and one Arrow Flight listener is created for a group of wildcard `listen_host` values now, which is what the transport does internally anyway. Also, `listen_try` is honored for the protocols that bind their listening socket when they are started rather than when they are created. `EADDRINUSE` from gRPC or Arrow Flight was reported from the plain `server.start()` loop, outside of the `createServer` handler that implements `listen_try`, so it was fatal even with `listen_try` (and with `listen_reuse_port`) enabled - which contradicts the documented behavior of listening to at least one of the addresses without quitting. Not addressed here: plain gRPC still keeps `SO_REUSEPORT` enabled, so a gRPC port that is already taken by a different process is silently shared instead of reported. Making that consistent with `listen_reuse_port` for both gRPC and Arrow Flight is a possible follow-up. For the record, gRPC and Arrow Flight are not available as composable protocols (the `protocols` section): the composable stack is a Poco `TCPServer` with a chain of `TCPServerConnectionFactory` layers that receive an already accepted socket, while gRPC and Arrow Flight own the listening socket, the HTTP/2 framing, TLS and their own event loop, so they can neither be a layer nor sit under `tls` / `proxy1`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the server failing to start when `listen_host` contains both `::` and `0.0.0.0` and `arrowflight_port` is configured, and fix two gRPC listeners silently sharing one port in the same configuration. `listen_try` now also covers the gRPC and Arrow Flight protocols, which bind their listening socket when they are started. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115074&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115074](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115074+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add pointwise and global min/max functions to `NumericIndexedVector`
signal.text: <!---AI changelog entry and formatting assistance: false--> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added pointwise min/max operations and global min/max value functions for NumericIndexedVector. Also improved and refactored the internal implementation of `pointwiseLess` for better correctness, performance, and code reuse across signed and unsigned numeric types. Resolves #88274 ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes #### Motivation: These additions extend the NumericIndexedVector family with commonly used numerical comparison and reduction capabilities, enabling more expressive analytical queries and feature computation over vectorized numeric aggregates. This work also addresses user requests for richer NumericIndexedVector operators — see [issue #88274](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/88274). #### New functions: - numericIndexedVectorPointwiseMax(v1, v2) — pointwise maximum between two numeric indexed vectors. - numericIndexedVectorPointwiseMin(v1, v2) — pointwise minimum between two numeric indexed vectors. - `numericIndexedVectorPointwise*`— functions now accept a Bitmap as the second argument. - numericIndexedVectorGetMaxValue(v) — returns the maximum value stored in a single numeric indexed vector. - numericIndexedVectorGetMinValue(v) — returns the minimum value stored in a single numeric indexed vector. All functions are compatible with both signed and unsigned numeric types, as well as floating-point vectors. #### Other changes: - Reimplemented and refactored pointwiseLess that correctly handles signed two's-complement representations. - Unified common bitmap selection logic to enhance code reuse and reduce redundant Roaring bitmap operations. - Introduced shared helpers for efficient bit-slice accumulation and extrema computation. #### Example usage: ``` SQL WITH numericIndexedVectorBuild(mapFromArrays([1, 2, 3], [10.0, -2.5, 5.5])) AS vec1, numericIndexedVectorBuild(mapFromArrays([1, 2, 3], [3.0, -8.0, 7.2])) AS vec2 SELECT numericIndexedVectorToMap(numericIndexedVectorPointwiseMax(vec1, vec2)) AS max_result, numericIndexedVectorToMap(numericIndexedVectorPointwiseMin(vec1, vec2)) AS min_result, numericIndexedVectorGetMaxValue(vec1) AS global_max, numericIndexedVectorGetMinValue(vec1) AS global_min;\G ``` #### Result: ``` SQL Row 1: ────── max_result: {1:10,2:-2.5,3:7.199999988079071} min_result: {1:3,2:-8,3:5.5} global_max: 10 global_min: -2.5 ``` <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=88840&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/88840](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F88840+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix cardinality underestimation when join column NDVs are unknown
signal.text: Restore the join-step row count estimation (originally #97114, reverted in #99957 because of regressions reported) and add a trust-propagation mechanism that prevents fabricated estimates from leaking into decisions where they cause regressions. **Trust-propagated cardinality** - `DPJoinEntry` / `RelationStats` carry a `rows_estimate_trusted` flag. It is `true` only when every NDV along the DP path came from real column statistics. - The NDV-unknown fallback in `computeSelectivity` (`1 / max(rows)` for both direct and transitive predicates) still gives the DP a usable estimate, but marks the entry untrusted. - `JoinStepLogical` exposes two accessors: - `getResultRowsEstimation` — raw DP estimate; used by `EXPLAIN` for visibility. - `getTrustedResultRowsEstimation` — returns `nullopt` when untrusted, so outer-scope `estimateReadRowsCount` does not feed a fabricated number upstream (equivalent to master's behavior for join steps). **Guards against fabricated estimates** - Build-side swap (`swap_on_sizes`) is gated by `sides_trustworthy` so a fabricated smaller side cannot flip `HashJoin` onto a huge relation. - When `HashTablesStatistics` returns a `source_rows` below the current estimate, trust is demoted (used in the swap gate) but `estimated_rows` is **not** clamped. Clamping made the DP read different leaf sizes on cold vs warm runs, which flipped greedy ordering and caused degradation in some cases; keeping source upper bounds keeps the plan shape stable across runs. **Regression tests** - `04103_join_build_side_no_stats` — without stats the 100-row dim still builds, fact probes, outer `ResultRows: unknown`. - `04104_join_trust_boundary_propagation` — nested `JoinStepLogical` exposes its result estimate only when trusted. - `04105_plan_stability_hash_table_stats_cache` — cold and warm EXPLAINs of the same query are identical both with and without stats. - `04106_join_plan_stats_toggle` — same 3-table star-join run twice with `SETTINGS use_statistics = 0` and `= 1`; contrasts the left-deep fallback plan against the right-deep pre-joined-dimensions plan. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Restore join-step row count estimation with trust propagation: when column NDVs are available, join cardinality and column stats flow through the DP and to the outer optimizer, enabling better build-side and multi-join ordering decisions; when NDVs are unavailable, an untrusted fallback keeps the DP working but does not drive structural decisions or propagate to upstream joins. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. At a minimum, the following information should be added (but add more as needed). - Motivation: Why is this function, table engine, etc. useful to ClickHouse users? - Parameters: If the feature being added takes arguments, options or is influenced by settings, please list them below with a brief explanation. - Example use: A query or command. --> <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **High Risk** > Changes core join-order optimization cardinality/selectivity estimation and build-side swapping logic, which can alter query plans and performance across many workloads despite added safeguards and tests. > > **Overview** > Restores and extends join cardinality estimation in the join-order optimizer, adding end-to-end **trust propagation** so only estimates derived from real table/column statistics influence upstream optimizers and structural decisions. > > When join key NDVs are missing, selectivity now falls back to a row-count-based heuristic but marks the result *untrusted*; untrusted estimates are hidden via `JoinStepLogical::getTrustedResultRowsEstimation()` and are prevented from driving hash-join build-side swapping, while still being usable internally for DP cost comparisons. > > Also adjusts handling of hash-table statistics cache hints to demote trust (instead of clamping row counts) to keep join plans stable between cold and warm runs, and adds several stateless tests covering trust boundaries, build-side choice without stats, and plan stability/statistics toggling. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 255b598d8cc841a84129519a67b7c04ec8aa916c. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Add INSERT ... RETURNING (non-atomic, user-supplied SELECT)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `INSERT ... RETURNING (SELECT ...)` to run a user-supplied SELECT after INSERT and return its result in one round-trip. Closes #21697. **Backward-incompatible change:** `RETURNING` is now a reserved keyword and can no longer be used as an unquoted implicit column alias (e.g. `SELECT 1 returning`). Use `AS returning` or a quoted identifier instead. --- Closes #21697 ## Summary Draft implementation of `INSERT ... RETURNING` for ClickHouse. The INSERT runs first using the existing pipeline; if it succeeds, a parenthesized `RETURNING (SELECT ...)` subquery runs in the same session and its result set is returned to the client in one round-trip. This is intentionally **not** Postgres-style atomic `RETURNING`. The user supplies the trailing SELECT and owns the `WHERE` clause used to identify inserted rows. ## Syntax For `INSERT VALUES` and `INSERT FORMAT`, `RETURNING` appears **before** the data clause (parser constraint: bytes after `VALUES`/`FORMAT` are raw input): ```sql INSERT INTO t (id, name) RETURNING (SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 123) VALUES (123, 'foo'); INSERT INTO t RETURNING (SELECT count() FROM t WHERE batch_id = 'X') FORMAT JSONEachRow {"batch_id":"X", ...} ``` For `INSERT SELECT`, `RETURNING` appears **after** the source query: ```sql INSERT INTO t SELECT * FROM src RETURNING (SELECT count() FROM t WHERE batch_id = 'X'); ``` The parenthesized subquery is required (distinct from Postgres column-list `RETURNING id, name`). ## Semantics - INSERT runs first with its existing pipeline untouched. - If INSERT throws, the RETURNING SELECT does not run. - If INSERT succeeds, a select interpreter is built for the trailing subquery using the same Context; its pipeline is returned as the statement result. - The trailing SELECT inherits session, user, and settings. It can reference any table and use the full SELECT grammar. - Client receives **one result set** (the RETURNING SELECT's), not an INSERT ack plus a result set. ## Limitations (documented, not bugs) - **Not atomic.** Concurrent writers can land rows between INSERT completion and SELECT execution. - **No automatic "the rows I just inserted."** User provides the SELECT and owns its `WHERE`. - **Replication lag is visible** on Replicated tables unless consistency settings are used. - **Incompatible with `async_insert=1`.** Returns `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. - **No special MV interaction.** MVs fire on INSERT; RETURNING SELECT is a normal SELECT. - If INSERT succeeds but RETURNING SELECT fails, inserted data is **not rolled back**. ## Backward-incompatible change `RETURNING` is added to the parser's reserved-keyword list (same list as `FROM`, `WHERE`, `SETTINGS`, etc.) to prevent it from being consumed as an implicit table alias in `INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM tablename RETURNING (...)`. As a side-effect, `RETURNING` can no longer be used as an unquoted implicit alias anywhere in ClickHouse SQL: ```sql -- Before: worked (returning was a plain identifier) SELECT 1 returning SELECT * FROM t returning -- After: must use AS or quoting SELECT 1 AS returning SELECT * FROM t AS returning ``` ## Implementation - **Parser** (`ParserInsertQuery.cpp`): parse `RETURNING` + parenthesized SELECT; placement rules above. - **AST** (`ASTInsertQuery.h`): `returning_select` field; clone/format updated. - **Interpreter** (`InterpreterInsertQuery.cpp`): reject `async_insert`; wrap completed INSERT pipeline with RETURNING via `DelayedSource`. - **Pipeline** (`buildInsertReturningPipeline.cpp`): run INSERT to completion, then build SELECT pipeline; native push inserts swap to RETURNING SELECT after data is received. - **executeQuery** / **TCPHandler** / **LocalConnection** / **ClientBase**: inlined-data wrap, native-protocol push path, query-log accounting, process-list propagation. - **Docs**: section added to `insert-into.md` ## Tests added - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04266_insert_returning_21697.sql` — core `INSERT ... RETURNING` semantics, delayed planning/failure behavior, query-cache rejection paths, transactional rollback checks (`implicit_transaction=1` + explicit transaction), and parser keyword regression coverage (`SELECT 1 returning` rejected; explicit/quoted alias accepted). - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04267_insert_returning_native_format.sh` — native TCP `INSERT FORMAT` + external data + `RETURNING`, including `input(...)` + `FORMAT` placement/round-trip stability. - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04410_insert_returning_trailing_settings.sql` — source-side trailing `SETTINGS` scoping/precedence, nested source settings handling, source-side query-cache settings rejection (`NOT_IMPLEMENTED`), and a plain `INSERT ... SELECT` regression proving nested source subquery settings stay local (non-`RETURNING`). ## Alternatives considered - **`AND SELECT` / `THEN SELECT` keywords** — parser ambiguity or poor discoverability for Postgres migrants. - **Atomic Postgres-style RETURNING** — much larger surface (formats, MVs, distributed, async); deferred as a possible follow-up. - **Multi-statement `;`** — out of scope. ## Open questions for maintainers 1. Is the non-atomic, user-supplied-SELECT model the right v1 framing? 2. Confirm canonical placement rules (before data for VALUES/FORMAT, after source for INSERT SELECT). 3. Restrict trailing SELECT to read-only queries only? (Current implementation: yes, via SELECT parser.) 4. Confirm single-result-set protocol behavior across HTTP/native/JDBC. ## Test plan - [x] Stateless test `04266_insert_returning_21697` - [x] `INSERT VALUES` + `RETURNING` with row filter - [x] `INSERT SELECT` + `RETURNING` with aggregate - [x] `RETURNING` against a table other than INSERT target - [x] INSERT failure prevents `RETURNING` subquery from running - [x] `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` when `async_insert=1` - [x] Native TCP `INSERT FORMAT` + `RETURNING` (`04267_insert_returning_native_format`) - [x] `input(...)` source with `FORMAT` before `RETURNING` (parser/formatter round-trip + execution) - [x] Source-side `SETTINGS` precedence and nested-source scoping (`04410_insert_returning_trailing_settings`) - [x] Plain `INSERT ... SELECT` keeps nested source subquery `SETTINGS` local (no non-`RETURNING` leakage) - [x] Source-side query-cache settings rejection in `INSERT ... RETURNING` source `SETTINGS` - [x] `02310_profile_events_insert` local `clickhouse-local` profile-events check is non-fatal in CI (`InsertedRows` is not emitted consistently there) - [x] Transactional rollback when delayed `RETURNING` planning fails (`implicit_transaction=1` and explicit transaction) - [x] `RETURNING` keyword parser regression (`SELECT 1 returning` rejected; `SELECT 1 AS returning` and quoted alias accepted) - [x] `04266` rollback subtests stabilized by avoiding fixed database-name collisions in flaky/parallel runs (use `t_insert_returning_tx` in the current test DB) - [ ] Replicated-table non-atomic behavior (integration test, future)

signal.title: Add per-user filesystem cache disk usage metrics
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105020 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added opt-in Prometheus gauges for current filesystem cache usage (`filesystem_cache_size_bytes` and `filesystem_cache_elements`), labeled by `cache_name` and `user_id`. The gauges are exposed through `system.dimensional_metrics` and the Prometheus endpoint and controlled by the `expose_prometheus_cache_usage_metrics_per_user` cache setting, which is disabled by default. --- ### Description Adds two gauges exposed through `system.dimensional_metrics` and the Prometheus endpoint: | Name | Labels | |---|---| | `filesystem_cache_size_bytes` | `cache_name`, `user_id` | | `filesystem_cache_elements` | `cache_name`, `user_id` | **Motivation.** Operators can identify which users currently occupy filesystem cache space, measured both in bytes and in file segments, for each cache. **Mechanism.** Each enabled cache owns a `FileCacheUsageTracker` containing shared per-user atomic counters. Main cache-priority entries retain the corresponding counters and update them together with the existing cache size and element accounting. `ServerAsynchronousMetrics` periodically obtains a per-user snapshot through `getUsageStatPerClient` and updates the dimensional gauges. This keeps `DimensionalMetrics` updates out of cache mutation paths. Composite LRU, SLRU, and split-cache priorities share the same tracker, including during SLRU queue transitions. Counters use shared ownership so inactive users can be reclaimed safely. When a user no longer has cache entries and its counters are zero, the next snapshot removes it from the tracker. Stale dimensional metric label combinations are also removed. **Sampling.** The metrics reflect the most recent asynchronous metrics update. **Cardinality.** In-process cardinality is bounded by users currently retained by each cache, plus labels awaiting the next asynchronous metrics update. Stale `(cache_name, user_id)` label combinations are removed. The feature remains disabled by default because enabling per-user metrics can still create significant Prometheus time-series cardinality. ### Documentation entry: - [x] Documentation is updated.

signal.title: Exact-size parallel_hash build to avoid rehashing on cold builds
signal.text: Resolves https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111268 Builds `parallel_hash` hash tables exactly sized to the number of *distinct keys* so that cold builds (when no hash-table statistics are cached) avoid rehashing as the hash maps grow. Sizing now uses the distinct key count rather than the total number of buffered rows. This is the portion of #107189 focused on exact-size table builds, split out as requested by maintainers. The PR for compact index-based row references is a sibling update and not dependent on this one. ### Motivation Previously, when executing a cold build (no cached hash-table size statistics—e.g. first query run or stats collection off), `parallel_hash` would fill two-level maps incrementally, causing repeated rehashes as they expanded. However, by the end of the build phase, the count of distinct right keys per slot is essentially available, so we can size the maps exactly once and fill them in a single pass, skipping intermediary rehashing steps. ### What changed **Exact-size `parallel_hash` build (avoids rehashes on cold build).** In the absence of statistics hints, each `ConcurrentHashJoin` slot buffers its corresponding right-hand blocks during build. After build completion (`onBuildPhaseFinish`), the two-level buckets are pre-sized and populated in one go. This path is skipped if a reliable hint exists, for `any_take_last_row`, or for simple single-level `FixedHashMap` maps. These changes are tracked under `HashJoinDeferredPreallocatedElementsInHashTables` to keep the statistics-driven `HashJoinPreallocatedElementsInHashTables` event limited to that code path. **Table pre-sizing by distinct keys (using HLL), not buffered row count.** While buffering rows, each slot uses a HyperLogLog (precision 12, the `uniqHLL12` estimator) on the scatter hashes of its rows (with `intHash64`, since the scatter hash is a 32-bit CRC). Since slots are keyed by hash, the total distinct-key estimate is the sum of all per-slot HLL estimates. Both preallocation and spill projections are computed from this total, so builds with many duplicate rows no longer over-allocate memory by the redundancy factor. This eliminates the peak memory regression observed during initial test runs (see below for resolution details). **Deferred two-phase spill check.** During `SpillingHashJoin::addBlockToJoin`, live byte usage is checked per block (since no map exists during buffering), and a single projection-based check occurs during `onBuildPhaseFinish` just prior to replay and allocation. The projection (`getProjectedTotalByteCount`) covers post-replay table buffer sizes (based on the distinct key count), arena key copies, and a nearly exact bound for the `RowRefList::Batch` arena, allowing the final spill decision to compare directly to the cap. The allocation uses the full distinct-key count after this check passes, ensuring the replay will not trigger a rehash. **Skip deferred HLL-based sizing when a trusted statistics NDV is available.** If the query planner provides a reliable, uniq-backed NDV (number of distinct values) for the right join key (from `JoinStepLogical::result_column_stats`), there is no need to buffer and estimate; `deferred_build` is disabled and the streaming build preallocates hash maps to that count as with warm `ht_size` builds. A trust flag ensures that only real, `uniq`-backed values are used (never estimates like `0.1 × rows`). For composite/expression keys or non-MergeTree/non-subquery data sources, the deferred path remains active and uses HLL sizing. Correctness with `SpillingHashJoin`/`GraceHashJoin` and limits: - **Spill → grace transition based on projected byte usage.** During buffering the maps are empty; spill checks use `getProjectedTotalByteCount` (which includes buffered blocks, maps to be built, and the arena). If a spill is needed, it occurs before any replay that would overstep `max_bytes_before_external_join`, and buffered blocks are sent to `GraceHashJoin` instead of being built in-memory. - **Enforcement of size limits after replay.** Under `throw`, deferred building remains enabled and post-replay the real maps are validated against `max_rows_in_join` / `max_bytes_in_join` (row count is distinct key cells, bytes include arena), along with an early byte-cap check during buffering for fast failure. When `join_overflow_mode = 'break'` the deferred path is disabled since a truncated build can’t be replayed; the streaming build path enforces limits instead. - **Kill/cancellation during replay.** During map replay, `onBuildPhaseFinish` checks query status between buffered block replays, so `KILL QUERY` and `max_execution_time` will interrupt a large cold build. ### Limits and user-visible behavior Query results remain unchanged. Peak cold-build memory consumption is no longer artificially high for keys with many duplicates, since reserve sizing is based on the estimated distinct key count. The estimator (HLL) may undercount by many-sigma in rare cases, but such misses only result in bounded, correctness-safe rehashing. ### Known follow-ups (not part of this PR) - **Gate deferred path for tiny cold builds.** With the duplicate-aware (distinct-key) preallocation, prior issues in TPC-H Q16 are resolved. If performance regressions remain for small builds, consider directly gating the deferred buffer-then-replay path using an estimated build size threshold so very small cases stick to the streaming path. ### Changelog category - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry Improved the performance of `parallel_hash` `JOIN`s on cold builds: when no cached hash-table size statistics are available (the first execution of a query shape, or when statistics collection is off), `parallel_hash` now allocates hash tables up front to the number of distinct keys estimated while building—eliminating the repeated rehashing that previously occurred as tables grew. Best-case performance results showed a 2× speedup (first run of a large `INNER` join on mostly-unique `UInt64` keys), without increased peak memory on duplicate-heavy keys. ### Documentation entry - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
